Platform What is supported Linux every feature, including the examples that run services with odctl Windows through WSL2 the same as Linux, and the recommended way to run desflow on Windows macOS the core library and the command Windows the core library and the command; the service stacks of the examples are not supported

docs.title: Older Docs
docs.text: The docs of each published release stay on the site under its version. A version other than the latest shows a banner that links to the latest. The docs of 0.20.0 to 0.28.0 show no banner, because each was built with the templates of its release, before the banner existed. Those releases came before this policy, so their pages promise no compatibility.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: Releases come in the order shown, without dates: a release ships when it is ready. Each item links to its GitHub issue.

docs.title: What 1.0 means
docs.text: From 1.0, the YAML blueprint format, the desflow command, the public Python API and the published record format stay compatible across every 1.x release. The public Python API is the set of promised import paths, which the Compatibility Policy lists. The package status moves from Beta to Production/Stable. The names kept for compatibility, dynamic_des, ddes and the old registry settings, are removed in 1.0, and Upgrading to 1.0 lists each.

docs.title: From history to simulation
docs.text:
• Model discovery: a model discovered from an event log.
  • Comparison with the log: a run compared with the log.
  • A model kept current: the model updated from new logs.

docs.title: Simulation model
docs.text:
• Maintenance, schedules and incidents: planned maintenance, schedules that repeat by time of day, and incidents that change several parameters at once. 0.22.0 ships random breakdowns with repair and finite schedules, and 1.0 ships a failure clock that runs only while a resource works (clock: busy).
  • More flow and resource features: matching and splitting, setup times, and resources chosen by skill. 1.0 ships batching.
  • Costs and continuous flow: costs and energy per resource state, and levels that rise and fall continuously.
  • Transport on maps: vehicles that move between locations on real roads and publish their positions.
  • Data-driven inputs: arrivals replayed from a database, or taken live from a Kafka topic.
  • Models read from a store: a value that a model reads from a store during a run, such as the trained model of a recommender, with a key of its own. In 1.0 this is a !python function, as Call Python from YAML shows.
  • Decisions from outside: a dispatcher or an agent answers for one order or session, and a run can repeat exactly from a log of those answers.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
• Experiments: experiment designs, optimisation, and calibration against observed data.
  • Fitting and comparison: distribution fitting from more data sources, automatic fault-impact experiments, and fuller run comparison and fidelity scoring.

docs.title: Simulation server
docs.text:
The server ships after 1.0, as 1.x releases installed with the server extra.

  • Server API and MCP tools: desflow serve runs simulations through a REST API: upload, start, stop, change parameters during a run and follow its events. MCP tools, which let an AI agent do the same, are experimental. (#48)
  • Browser UI: the same from a browser, including each simulation's graph from desflow explain. (#49)
  • Schedules: run simulations on cron schedules. (#50)
  • Server image and odctl profile: a published image and an odctl profile run the server locally with nothing installed on the host. (#52)
  • Visualisation: a graph image from desflow explain, animation of a running or recorded simulation, and a map view.
  • Distributed runs: workers on several machines.

docs.title: Writing simulations
docs.text:
• Payloads from your data: record fields generated from a schema or a few sample records, so the records have the real field names, types and value ranges.
  • Visual builder.
  • Conversion: turn a YAML blueprint into builder code, and builder code into YAML with no Python, with an error that names each part that cannot be converted and how to rewrite it.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text:
• More sinks: a webhook sink, a generic SQL sink and more.
  • Error sink: records a sink could not write go to another sink instead of being lost, and a run can fail when too many do.
  • Delivery faults: records delivered late, twice, damaged or not at all, to test how a pipeline handles them.
  • Lineage: each run reported to OpenLineage and OpenMetadata.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
• Orchestrators: Airflow, Dagster and similar tools.
  • AI assistants: the Claude Code plugin and its marketplace.
  • Testing tools: a pytest plugin and a GitHub Action.
  • Query engines and streaming databases.
  • Data quality and evaluation tools.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text: • More speed: cheaper record publishing, which takes about 40 percent of a run's time, with the same published records (#69), and a faster runtime for YAML-only blueprints if measurements show the need.

docs.title: Released
docs.text:
1.0.0: Stable
  • Stable: the YAML blueprint format, the desflow command, the public Python API and the record format stay compatible across 1.x, as the Compatibility Policy sets out. The package status is Production/Stable. #54
  • SimPy's rules: a run ends when no event is left, as in SimPy, and strict and on_unhandled_failure default to SimPy's values. The SimPy Compatibility page shows each SimPy feature in YAML, Builder and Low-level with its status.
  • SimPy's step order at a tie: a task with one wait branch, the task after next, the actions of on: and a resumed job go on in the same simulation step as SimPy's process, so records at one instant can change order. #105
  • YAML with no Python: every known case runs in YAML alone, with --var, --watch, generated values, desflow check and desflow test.
  • SimPy's examples: the seven examples of SimPy's docs in YAML, Builder and Low-level. #95
  • Record contract frozen: the records 1.x keeps. #51
  • Old names removed: dynamic_des, ddes and the other names kept for compatibility. #84
  • Pydantic 2.7.0 or later. #104
  • Rewritten docs. The Gallery, the Generate Data group and the Agent Skill section are new, and every page is rewritten for 1.0.
  • Fixes from reviews of the whole code: the release candidates 1.0.0rc1 to 1.0.0rc4 and two full reads of the code fixed models that ran wrong, hung or failed in the middle of a run. Upgrading to 1.0 lists each change that alters records or refuses input.
0.28.0: Library hooks for the server
  • Parameter changes that report back: change returns a ParamChange or raises ParamRejected, on_change callbacks receive every accepted change with its source, and registry_paths() lists the paths a simulation will have without running it. #70
  • File ingress: FileIngress changes parameters during a run when you edit a local file, with no broker. #86
  • Scenario values checked: a scenario step whose value the registry refuses stops the load or the start, instead of being logged and ignored. #93
  • Drafting from a description: the AI skill teaches an assistant to draft a model from a description of a process. #94
0.27.0: Schema registry formats
  • JSON Schema and Protobuf: serializers and deserializers for both formats, through the Confluent and Glue schema registries, next to Avro. #82
  • Glue wire format: desflow writes and reads it itself, so the glue extra no longer installs aws-glue-schema-registry.
  • Kafka: the kafka extra no longer installs kafka-python, and topics are created through aiokafka.
0.26.0: Storage, schema registry code and Python 3.15
  • Storage: Parquet and JSON Lines files on Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage, and Iceberg tables through SQL catalogs on SQLite or PostgreSQL and the Glue catalog. #32
  • Schema registry code: the Confluent schema registry client moves into desflow, so the confluent extra no longer installs confluent-kafka. #83
  • Python 3.15 is supported. #40
  • Fix: GlueAvroSerializer serializes a record. #85
  • Docs: page addresses follow the sidebar, and each page kind has one shape.
0.25.0: desflow explain
  • desflow explain: desflow explain shows a simulation as a graph, marks each resource OK, congested or unstable (its queue grows without limit), names the bottleneck and suggests changes. #47
  • Commands: desflow dist converts between a distribution's parameters and its mean and standard deviation. desflow run --sample prints a few records from a blueprint, and --stdout sends every record except the system.simulation.lag_seconds readings to the standard output as JSON lines in place of the real sinks.
  • Library: load_context loads a simulation folder from Python. Builder arrivals can name the task they start.
  • Docs: a generated reference page for the desflow command, and in Learn, Complete Model, the explain section of Checking a Model and Check Against Theory. #60
0.24.0: Blueprint schema and AI skill
  • Blueprint schema and AI skill: a JSON Schema for blueprints, shipped in the package and on the docs site, so editors complete keys and flag mistakes as you type, with a YAML Keys reference page generated from it. A skill that teaches an AI assistant to write and check blueprints. #41
  • Public API test: a test that fails when a public name or signature of the library or the desflow command is removed or changed. #67
  • Removal: resource.queue.items, which warns since 0.23.0, is removed: use list(resource.queue).
  • Learn section: the concept pages, Checking a Model, Live Changes, Streaming Out and the How-To pages that do not need explain. #60
0.23.0: SimPy parity
  • SimPy parity: every SimPy 4.1.2 feature natively in YAML, the builder and the low-level API, each checked against SimPy, such as nested conditions, event callbacks, unlimited stores and custom resource types. The SimPy Compatibility page lists each one, and the three differences kept by design. #71
0.22.0: Native core, experiments and replications
  • Native core parity: the operations on the SimPy Compatibility page work natively in YAML, the builder and the low-level API, and each is checked against SimPy. They include signals, interrupts, tasks needing several resources, filtered store gets, stopping and stepping a run, and customers who give up on a queue or never join it. #64
  • Breakdowns, changing demand and replay: a resource that fails and is repaired, a schedule of times at which an arrival rate or a capacity changes, and arrivals read from a local CSV or Parquet file. #65
  • Replications: run a model with many seeds and get each statistic with a 95% interval, so a result is never read from one run. #59
  • Experiments: compare designs and sweep parameters over replications, fail an experiment when a result breaks a limit, fit a distribution to measured data, and write a Markdown report, all on one machine. #66
  • Speed: faster runs that publish the same records. #24
  • Record contract: every record field documented with its type and format, payload keys such as __table__ reserved for desflow, a timezone setting for timestamps, and no lag_seconds from a run at full speed. #51
  • Learn section: the shop tutorial extends one shop model page by page and answers a question with a number on each page. It has 20 pages, and the new pages cover replications, comparing designs, sweeps, fitting, patience, interruptions, end conditions and more. #60
0.21.0: Distributions, flows and statistics
  • Distributions and seeds: more distributions, including empirical, which draws from values measured in a real system. Each distribution draws from its own random stream, so adding an arrival leaves the other draws unchanged. desflow needs Python 3.11 or later. #42
  • Ingress messages: every ingress connector, Kafka, Redis and PostgreSQL, takes a parameter change as path and value, the names a scenario step already uses. #51
  • Stores, containers and priority: tasks take items from stores and amounts from containers, and a resource serves its queue oldest first, newest first or by task priority. #43
  • Flows: routing between tasks by a condition or by probability, entity state that an order keeps from task to task, and delays without a resource. #44
  • Statistics and ground truth: wait and service times, throughput, utilisation and queue length as telemetry, with a warm-up period; and ground-truth records of what a scenario changed, so a detector or an agent can be scored against them. #45
0.20.0: Rename to desflow
  • Rename to desflow: the package, its import name and its command are all desflow. The old names, dynamic-des, dynamic_des and ddes, were removed in 1.0.

The Changelog lists every release.

docs.title: Upgrading to 1.0
docs.text:
This page is for a model, a script or a pipeline that runs on desflow 0.28.0. Each item says what 0.28.0 did, what 1.0 does and what to change. 1.0 follows SimPy's rules for time, ties and failures, so a seeded model can publish other records than it did on 0.28.0, and some YAML forms now mean something else. From 1.0 the Compatibility Policy applies, and a 1.x release no longer changes a result without listing it.

To move a model to 1.0:

  1. Install desflow 1.0 and uninstall dynamic-des if it is still installed, as Removed Names says.
  2. Run desflow check on every blueprint. It names each key or value that 1.0 refuses, with its line.
  3. Run the model's tests, such as desflow test, and compare its stored results. Where a test fails, find the change below that explains it. desflow test --fix writes the new values once you accept them.

docs.title: Removed Names
docs.text:
• dynamic_des and ddes. 0.28.0 kept the import name dynamic_des and the ddes command, each with a warning. 1.0 removes both: import dynamic_des raises ModuleNotFoundError, and no ddes command is installed. Import desflow and run desflow. Uninstall dynamic-des; its last release installs a desflow below 1.0.
  • **registry_kwargs of ConfluentAvroSerializer and ConfluentAvroDeserializer. 0.26.0 deprecated the confluent-kafka keys. 1.0 removes them, and a call that passes one raises TypeError. Pass the named argument instead: basic.auth.user.info (user:password) becomes auth=("user", "password"), ssl.ca.location becomes verify=, ssl.certificate.location, ssl.key.location and ssl.key.password become cert=, and max.retries becomes max_retries=. The bearer.auth.* keys with the source STATIC_TOKEN become headers={"Authorization": "Bearer <token>", "target-sr-cluster": "<logical cluster>"}, with "Confluent-Identity-Pool-Id": "<pool>" when bearer.auth.identity.pool.id was set. Delete cache.capacity and cache.latest.ttl.sec, which had no effect. Connect to a Secured Schema Registry shows the arguments.
  • desflow.core.distributions. The module is gone. DISTRIBUTIONS is in desflow.models.distributions in 1.0, a module path that 1.x does not promise to keep. desflow dist lists the families from the command line.
  • Modules of desflow.core that declare and run a model. desflow.core.context, desflow.core.signals, desflow.core.task, desflow.core.flow, desflow.core.scenario, desflow.core.breakdowns and desflow.core.internal are gone, and so is desflow.blueprint.cli, and importing one raises ModuleNotFoundError. Their code is in desflow.builder and desflow.cli, module paths that 1.x does not promise to keep. The 0.28.0 API Reference showed SimulationContext, Signal, SignalFailed, TaskFailed, Router, Transfer, run_scenario and run_breakdowns at these paths. Import each from desflow: an import of SignalFailed from desflow.core.signals becomes from desflow import SignalFailed. Their loggers moved too, as Logger names under Builder and Low-level API says.

docs.title: Run and Time
docs.text:
• strict defaults to SimPy's rule. In 0.28.0, strict was false in YAML and the Builder unless it was set, and it was never checked at factor: 0. In 1.0 it is true when it is not set and factor is above 0 or go_live_at is set, so a paced run that falls behind the wall clock raises RuntimeError. An explicit strict: true at factor: 0 raises once the wall clock has moved, as SimPy does. --sample, replications, desflow experiment and desflow explain --verify run at factor: 0 and ignore strict. Set simulation.strict: false (SimulationContext(strict=False)) to keep the old behaviour. See Strict Pacing.
  • on_unhandled_failure defaults to stop. In 0.28.0, YAML and the Builder defaulted to continue, so a failure that nobody handled ended one entity's flow and the run went on. In 1.0 the default is stop, as in SimPy and the Low-level API, and the run ends with the error. A model that relies on the old rule adds run: {on_unhandled_failure: continue} (run(on_unhandled_failure="continue")). See Handle a Failure Nobody Handles.
  • Signals fire once. In 0.28.0 a signal re-armed after it fired. In 1.0 a signal fires once by default, as SimPy's Event does: a wait after the firing resumes at once, and a second firing is refused. Give a signal that fires more than once once: false (add_signal(name, once=False), Signal(env, name, once=False)). A once: true signal that fired again dropped the second firing with a warning; it now raises under on_unhandled_failure: stop. See One-Shot Signals.
  • A run with no until ends. In 0.28.0 such a run never ended while statistics were on, or with a sink at a factor above 0, or with an ingress connector. In 1.0 it ends when only desflow's own events are left, and a stop that can no longer happen raises SimPy's RuntimeError. Give such a run an until. A live model meant to run on gives the run an until or is stopped with Ctrl+C. See Stop Early.
  • A Low-level run to an event ends. In 0.28.0, DynamicRealtimeEnvironment.run(until=<event>) ran for ever on desflow's own timers when the event never came. In 1.0, with no ingress set up, it ends with SimPy's RuntimeError when no model event is left; with an ingress it goes on. Name a time as well: env.run(until=event | env.timeout(t)).
  • A scenario step at or after until no longer applies while a drain runs. In 0.28.0 a step due after until still changed its value during the drain, so the records of the drain differed from a run that ends at until. A step that must apply goes before until.
  • No smallest delay. In 0.28.0 a service time or a drawn delay was at least 0.00001 seconds. In 1.0 the floor is 0: a constant 0 takes no time, and a normal draw below 0 is raised to 0. A constant gap of 0 starts entities at one instant without end, so the run never ends and until does not stop it, as in SimPy. Give such an arrival a gap above 0. A breakdown whose time_to_failure and repair both always give 0 is refused at load for the same reason, and one whose draws turn out to be 0 stops the run with an error after 10,000 failures at one instant.
  • sim_ts is not rounded. 0.28.0 rounded sim_ts to three decimals. 1.0 writes the clock as it is, so 1.357 may read 1.3565.... Round sim_ts before you compare it. See Field Values.
  • A number keeps the type it is written in. 0.28.0 converted times, amounts, container capacities and priorities to floats. In 1.0 a number keeps its written type: env.now, peek() and the readings of a step or segment print 5 for a time written 5, where they printed 5.0. A live update keeps the number as written, so 3 written over 2.5 is 3. The record fields capacity, level, wait_max and usage_since are integers when their inputs are, such as 38 where 0.28.0 wrote 38.0. sim_ts stays a float. Iceberg and Parquet sinks still write a statistic's value and usage_since as doubles. Text written over a parameter is still read as a float.
  • A start time is a datetime. 0.28.0 read a number as logical_start_time or go_live_at as Unix seconds, so 20260101 meant a day in 1970. 1.0 refuses a number at load with the line, and the Builder and DynamicRealtimeEnvironment refuse a number, a date or text, naming the setting. Write a datetime such as 2026-01-01T00:00:00.

docs.title: Order at One Instant
docs.text:
These changes make a task go on in the same step as the SimPy process it stands for, so records at one instant can change order, and a unit or an item can go to another entity at a tie. A model with no events at the same time publishes the same records.

  • A task with one wait branch now goes on in the step its event is processed, as yield event does in SimPy. To keep the old order, write the branch under any, as wait: {any: {only: {timeout: 2}}}. A wait: {timeout: 5} with patience: 5 s now starts and finishes at 5, where it reneged; the any form gives the old result.
  • next, on_fail and on_interrupt_next now run the following task in the same process and the same step, so it asks for a unit before a child spawned at that instant, and a process you wait for ends when its whole flow ends. To let the child go first, give the following task wait: {timeout: 0}, which matches SimPy. A subscribe interrupt or a preempted kept unit now reaches the following task, which on_interrupt: abandon cuts short.
  • A task's on: actions now run in the step the task ends, before its next task starts. A flag they set is read by the next task, but not by a next condition on the same task, which is chosen before they run. To run them one step later, fire a signal in the task's on: and put the actions in that signal's on:.
  • Tied replay rows now start in one step, in file order, before any of them takes its first step. 0.28.0 started each row in a separate step.
  • An interrupt reaches an instance made in the same step, from spawn: in on:, context.spawn, context.call or a next chain. In 0.28.0 it found no instance. The task keys spawn: and interrupt: still run interrupt first, so one task's own pair does not reach the new instance; two on: entries in the order spawn, interrupt do.
  • Patience at a tie. When a patience ends at the instant a unit is granted and the patience's event comes first, the task now reneges. 0.28.0 served it. The same holds for a get, a wait branch and a request asked again after a preemption.
  • A grant at the end of a wait. A request, get or put branch counts as won only when it was processed before the wait's condition, as req in result is in SimPy. An item a get was granted after that is lost. A request granted by then keeps its unit until the task ends. Order the events so the grant comes first when the model needs the unit or item.
  • Equal priorities in a priority store now leave in the order SimPy's heap gives, which is not put order from four items on. To keep put order, give each item a priority that rises, such as priority: "1 + process.instance / 1000000"; in the Builder and the Low-level API a pair (priority, number) is a valid priority. See Start With Items and Serve by Priority.

docs.title: Resources, Waits and Interrupts
docs.text:
• A unit is kept through a plain interrupt. With on_interrupt: resume or restart, a plain interrupt no longer gives back a unit the task holds, so the task goes on with it, and other entities wait until the task ends. A task with several resources asks again only for the unit it lost. A unit kept with keep now goes back at once when the next task reneges, fails or has no next task. To give the unit back and queue again, use on_interrupt: abandon with on_interrupt_next naming a task that asks for it. See Interrupts.
  • A granted request branch under restart. In 0.28.0, an interrupt of a task with on_interrupt: restart gave back every granted request branch of its wait and asked again at the back of the line. In 1.0 the task keeps them and starts the other branches again. To queue again as before, write the task with on_interrupt: abandon and on_interrupt_next naming a copy of it, and name both tasks in every interrupt that names the first.
  • Interrupt or preemption at the end of the work. A job interrupted or preempted at the instant its work ends now ends at that instant, publishes no resumed and asks for no unit. In 0.28.0 it waited for a further 0 seconds.
  • keep and a child flow. A child flow started by wait: {task: ...} no longer gives back the unit its parent kept when it starts, balks or is abandoned. The unit stays until the parent's next task starts. A model that counted on the early release ends the parent's task with no keep.
  • Opposite-order acquisition loads. 0.28.0 refused a model whose tasks take shared resources in opposite orders. 1.0 loads it and logs a WARNING from the logger desflow.builder.context, and the run can stop if two tasks wait for each other. A test that expected the ValueError reads the warning instead.
  • Preempting a finished process. A unit held by a process that has ended, such as a Low-level request never released, now fails the flow that preempts it with SimPy's RuntimeError. 0.28.0 took the unit with no error. Release a unit before its process ends, with resource.release(request) or a with block.
  • A priority of NaN is refused. In 0.28.0 a priority of .nan loaded, and a request with a lower priority number could be served after one with a higher number. In 1.0 YAML, the Builder and a Low-level request(priority=...) refuse NaN, also as a starting item of a priority store and as a rank or a store item's priority at run time. .inf and -.inf are accepted and order last and first. A Low-level DynamicResource refuses a queue_limit that is not a whole number, such as NaN, 2.5 or True, where 0.28.0 treated NaN as no limit, and 2.5 and True let 3 and 1 requests wait.
  • A queue or store whose priorities mix numbers and lists is refused when the file loads, in desflow check and at the first request. In 0.28.0 it loaded and ran until two requests of both forms had to be compared, then stopped with a TypeError. Give every priority of one queue the same form, all numbers or all lists.
  • A signal is named once. signals: [go, go] loaded in 0.28.0 as one signal. 1.0 refuses the second name at its line. Keep one.
  • interrupt() with a name that is no task raises ValueError with the closest task name, where 0.28.0 returned 0 and interrupted nothing. Correct the name, or catch the error where the name is optional.
  • utilization at capacity 0. In 0.28.0 the utilization of a resource whose capacity was 0 while units were still held read 0. In 1.0 it reads 100, and utilization_avg averages that. A resource at capacity 0 with nothing held still reads 0. Change a check that expects 0.
  • fail() on a resource that is already down keeps the first start of the outage. In 0.28.0 a second fail() restarted the down time, so downtime counted only the time since the last call and failures counted both. In 1.0 downtime counts the whole outage and failures counts one.
  • Builder preempt as text. task(preempt="f") was kept as text and counted as true. In 1.0, "f", "no", "off" and "0" are false, as in YAML. Write preempt=True or preempt=False.
  • queue_limit is a registry path. A resource now has the path <sim>.resources.<r>.queue_limit, and DynamicResource.queue_limit is a read-only property that follows it, so resource.queue_limit = 5 raises AttributeError. Change it with env.registry.update("<sim>.resources.<r>.queue_limit", 5). compile_parameters() gives a resource as a subclass of CapacityConfig that also holds the limit, so compare its current_cap and max_cap rather than the whole object. See Queue Limit.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
• A task that ends in a run failure runs none of its on: actions, as no statement runs after an uncaught exception in SimPy. That covers a next condition that cannot be evaluated, a wait that fails because its child did, and a function that raises, when no on_fail handles it. A task's own fail condition, and a failure that on_fail handles, keep their actions.
  • A failed evaluation in a task with on_fail. A generator or a step that raises in a task with on_fail now goes to on_fail, where 0.28.0 stopped the run. Remove on_fail from the task when the run must stop.
  • A fail or priority expression that cannot be evaluated, such as payload.a == 2 on a payload without a, and a Builder fail function that raises, now fail the task: it publishes failed with the error as its reason, and the run stops with TaskFailed under stop and goes on under continue. In 0.28.0 the error left the run with no failed record, even under continue.
  • A child flow that fails after its waiter was abandoned no longer raises TaskFailed under continue; the run goes on. Under stop it is unchanged.
  • An empty or zero failure reason is kept. A child flow's or a wait's failure with fail_reason: "" or 0 replaced the reason with the error's text, such as signal 's' failed:. In 1.0, upstream.reason reads the reason as given. Give the failing task a reason that is not empty, or read the empty reason in the handler.
  • on_fail without fail is accepted in YAML and the Builder, and catches a task function that raises. Only fail_reason without fail is refused, as "fail_reason needs a fail condition".

docs.title: Values and Expressions
docs.text:
• A mapping with a gen key is a generator. In 0.28.0 such a mapping was data in attributes, store items, an interrupt cause, a fire, on: or timeout value, a payload, set and a scenario value and record. In 1.0 it is a generator, or a load error with the line. A key named gen directly under set, attributes or record is still a field name. To keep such a mapping as data, write {gen: literal, value: {gen: 5}}, which publishes {"gen": 5}. See Generated Values.
  • item.<field> where no get reaches is refused at load, with the task named. In 0.28.0 it read nothing and failed when the run reached it.
  • An on: action whose path is not a registry path is refused when the model loads or starts, with the line and the closest path, such as Shop.resources.packers.current_cap. In 0.28.0 the model loaded, and the run stopped with KeyError when the action first ran, or never noticed a path that no event reached. Correct the path. A Builder on: action whose constant value its path refuses is refused when start() builds the run, as YAML refuses it when it loads, where 0.28.0 logged an error each time the action fired and went on. Give the path a value it accepts.
  • A level.<name> or registry[...] that names nothing in a spawn count, a wait or open amount, priority or filter, or a family's members, capacity or level is refused when the file loads. In 0.28.0 the run failed when it read the name. Correct the name.
  • An !include key that the included file has. !include {file: f.yaml, key: v} is refused when key is already in f.yaml, with the key and both files. In 0.28.0 the written value replaced the included one with no message. Remove the key from one of the two.
  • A ${NAME:-default} whose default holds ${ is refused. In 0.28.0 the text ${... stayed in the value. Write the default without ${.
  • An empty task or arrival name is refused at its line. In 0.28.0 a task was stored under another key, and an arrival failed when the run started. Give the entry a name.
  • A distribution the run cannot draw from is refused when the model loads: a truncated_normal too far into its tail, where 0.28.0 loaded it and the run did not end; a breakdown variance that overflows; a lognormal whose mean and std squared pass the largest float, whose mean squared rounds to 0, or whose std to mean ratio passes the largest float; integer bounds outside the 64-bit range; and weighted weights that add up past the largest float. Change the parameters.
  • Builder times. True or False as a time, in SimulationContext(initial_time=), warmup, lag_interval, a drain limit or a time-valued distribution parameter, was taken as 1 or 0 seconds. In 1.0 it raises ValueError, as a blueprint does. Write the number of seconds.
  • Builder draws in a wait or open. A generator in a Builder wait or open, such as an each count or a timeout's after, now draws from the stream of its place in the blueprint, so the Builder gives the numbers of the same blueprint. At the same seed it gives other draws than 0.28.0. Compare the stored results of such a model again.
  • Seeded runs draw other numbers. 0.28.0 keyed each random sequence by the CRC-32 of its path, so two paths with the same CRC-32 shared a sequence. 1.0 keys it by a SHA-256 hash of the whole path, so every seeded model draws other numbers than it did, in YAML, the Builder and the Low-level API. Run the model again and replace any figure kept from 0.28.0, and write the new values of a blueprint's tests with desflow test --fix.
  • A sim id with a dot, such as Shop.v2, draws the same random times as the same model with a plain sim id, so its results for a seed differ from 0.28.0. Record its results again.
  • An element named like a kind. A live update of an element is stored by its kind alone. A resource named service, containers or variables has its capacity cast to a whole number, a container named stores keeps a fraction, and a whole-number variable named max_cap or current_cap refuses inf. The same holds for a sim id whose second part is a kind, such as Shop.service.

docs.title: Sinks and Connectors
docs.text:
• A status record (queued, started and each other status of a task) carries sim_id and service beside path_id. 0.28.0 wrote path_id alone. A consumer that checks the fields of a status value, or a table whose columns 0.28.0 records made, gets the two new fields. See Records and Telemetry.
  • Routing keys in a payload. A payload key __topic__ (Kafka), __table__ (Iceberg) or __path__ (Parquet, JSON Lines) now chooses the destination, and the sink removes it. 0.28.0 dropped it with a warning. Rename such a key if it was only data. A __table__ that PostgreSQL and Iceberg share on one record needs the form namespace.table for Iceberg, or a table_router. See Reserved Payload Keys.
  • A sink with upsert_keys now writes the other records of a batch and skips only those that have none of the key columns, with one warning per flush that gives the counts. 0.28.0 lost the whole batch. Check the warning count after a run.
  • upsert_keys as text, and a new column on an Iceberg upsert table. One column name as text, such as upsert_keys: order_id, is one key column; 0.28.0 split it into the letters. An Iceberg table with upsert_keys cannot gain a column, because PyIceberg's upsert fails on rows written before the column existed. A batch that brings a column the table lacks is logged at ERROR with the table and the columns, and is not written; 0.28.0 failed with PyIceberg's own error. Name every column in schemas before the table is created.
  • An Iceberg column that is an integer in the first batch is no longer truncated when a later batch holds a fraction: that batch is logged at ERROR and lost. Iceberg cannot change the type of a column that exists. Name the column as a double in schemas before the table is created, such as schemas: {shop.events: {key: string, v: double}}, or create the table again: run once with table_policy: drop_and_create, which deletes its rows, then set table_policy back to create, because the policy drops the table at the first write of every run. See Iceberg.
  • A statistic and a reading need separate destinations. A statistic's value is a number and a reading's is a mapping, so a table_router or path_router that sends telemetry to Iceberg or Parquet gives readings a table or path of their own.
  • KafkaIngress creates its topic at the start of a run when it is missing. Give topic_policy: manual to keep it from creating one.
  • A Kafka record its serializer refuses is skipped with a warning that names its key and the reason, and the rest of the batch is sent. 0.28.0 stopped the batch and retried the connection. A schema registry that does not answer (a 5xx reply, a timeout or a lost connection) or asks the sink to wait (a 408 or 429 reply, or the Glue error ThrottlingException) is not a refusal: the sink keeps the whole batch and tries again after a wait that grows from 1 to 60 seconds. A registry that refuses the sink's credentials or access (a 401 or 403 reply, or the Glue error AccessDeniedException, or a Glue client that finds no credentials) stops the sink with that error, logged at ERROR, where 0.28.0 retried the connection. KafkaIngress stops on such a reply too, where 0.28.0 skipped each message.
  • A Kafka sink after a broker error sends the rest of the batch that the broker has not confirmed again, so a consumer can read a record twice. In 0.28.0 the records after the failing one were dropped. Make the consumer tolerate a repeated record, The key cannot tell a repeat from a new event, because it is the entity's key and every event of that entity carries it. Put an identifier of your own in the event's value and drop a record whose identifier the consumer has seen.
  • A setting that no retry fixes ends the task of RedisEgress and PostgresIngress. A keyword that redis-py does not take in RedisEgress, or a PostgreSQL role that may not update the table of PostgresIngress, ends the connector's task with its error. In 0.28.0 each error was logged and the connector tried again, every second for RedisEgress and at every poll for PostgresIngress, for the rest of the run. Correct the setting.
  • IcebergStorageEgress builds its catalog when the run starts, and a setting PyIceberg refuses ends the sink's task there with that error. In 0.28.0 the catalog was built at the first write, and each batch was logged as not written for the whole run. Correct the catalog_properties.
  • FileIngress(poll=), PostgresIngress(poll_interval=) and RedisIngress(poll_interval=) refuse a value that is not a number above 0, such as 0, a negative number, NaN, infinity or a bool, and so does poll or poll_interval in YAML. In 0.28.0 such a value was accepted, and 0 or below made the connector check its source in a loop with no wait. Give a value above 0.
  • A schema registry client refuses a bad timeout and a URL scheme other than http or https, and accepts the scheme in upper case. In 0.28.0 the client accepted them when it was built. Correct the setting.
  • A Decimal NaN or infinity in a record is written as null, as a float NaN is, where 0.28.0 wrote the text "NaN". Read a null where the text was.
  • An Avro serializer refuses a number its integer field would change. A fraction in an int or long field, such as 1.5, was written as 1 in 0.28.0, and a value outside the range of an int was written as it was. In 1.0 the Confluent and Glue serializers raise SerializationError, and KafkaEgress skips that record with a warning. Send a whole number, or declare the field double.
  • A PostgreSQL sink with envelope on warns when it skips a record whose value is not a mapping. The reason in that warning, for every sink, now reads "which this sink cannot write as a row".
  • RedisEgress removes every reserved key, a key with two underscores at each end, from a stream entry, with one warning, as the other sinks do. 0.28.0 removed __stream__ and wrote the others, such as __table__, into the entry. A consumer that read one of them renames the key.
  • Parquet, JSON Lines and Iceberg sinks load their libraries before the run starts. In a strict paced run without logical_start_time, the records are stamped behind the wall clock by the load time. A run with strict: false keeps its 0.28.0 timestamps.
  • A Parquet, JSON Lines or Iceberg sink without its extra is refused when it is built, with an ImportError that names the extra. 0.28.0 built it, and the run wrote nothing.
  • ConsoleEgress() with no logging at INFO, such as python FILE with no logging.basicConfig, prints one UserWarning. The records are the same.
  • KafkaAdminConnector.get_state() keys a sim id and a service id that hold a dot by their whole names, such as Shop.v2, where it took one part of each.

docs.title: Builder and Low-level API
docs.text:
• run(drain=...) and sim_id are checked. drain is True, False, None or {"limit": seconds}; 0.28.0 drained for any other value that is true, such as drain="false". sim_id is text that is not empty, in YAML too: SimulationContext(None), SimulationContext(3) and sim_id: "" ran in 0.28.0 and now raise ValueError.
  • A second run() of one context starts from the model's starting values, as a new context does, not from the values the first run changed. Pass other starting values to start() as overrides, or read the values a run ended with from context.env.registry before the next run.
  • compile_parameters() gives the config objects as the model declares them, so a capacity or a stream name left out is None. Read the starting values a run registers from registry_paths().
  • A task function that replaces context.sampler, context.values or context.sim_id during a run no longer changes the arrivals, breakdowns and family members of that run. Set them before start().
  • After a start() that fails before it makes the run's holders, get_resource, get_store and get_container raise KeyError, where they gave the previous run's object.
  • Low-level setup_egress refuses a batch_size that is not a whole number of 1 or more, and a flush_interval or drain_stall_seconds that is not above 0, as add_egress and with_batching do, in batch_sizes and flush_intervals too. In 0.28.0 flush_interval=0 held the run at time 0, and a negative value failed in the middle of the run. Give a batch size of 1 or more and an interval above 0.
  • egress_* lists of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment are read-only: assigning one raises AttributeError, and changing a list it returns does not reach the egress. Pass the sinks to setup_egress.
  • fields of add_arrival_replay and read_trace takes "all" or a list of columns, as a blueprint's replay.fields does. Write fields=["id"] for one column. See Replay.
  • A replay or row CSV whose row has more or fewer values than its header, or whose header names a column twice, is refused with the arrival and the file. 0.28.0 read it, keeping the extra values under a None key and filling the missing ones with None. Make each row as long as the header and rename the repeated column. See Replay.
  • A replay time that is true or false is refused, or skipped with on_invalid="skip". In 0.28.0 it was read as 1 or 0 seconds. Write the time as a number.
  • step() after close() raises RuntimeError. In 0.28.0 it ran the closed run, and its records reached no sink. peek() still gives the time of the next event. start() a new run, or stop stepping at close().
  • add_step and add_scenario refuse a record that is not a mapping, a path that is not text and an interrupt task that is not text, when the step is added. In 0.28.0 a text record published a label record of the text. Write a mapping, and the names as text.
  • A Low-level container and environment refuse a starting level that is NaN, infinite, negative or a bool, and a factor or initial_time that the Builder refuses. In 0.28.0 the container accepted the level, and the environment failed at the first step or wrote NaN times. Correct the value.
  • A Builder on= entry, in task(on=), task(listen=) and add_signal(on=), refuses a key other than the actions, value and when, where 0.28.0 ignored it. Remove the key, or move it into the action's own mapping.
  • An index on a number, such as users.machine[0], is refused when the Builder context starts (run() or start()), not at task(). A Low-level Expression("users.machine[0]") now parses.
  • load_context(folder, "file.py", preview) applies the preview to the Builder file, where 0.28.0 raised ValueError.
  • Logger names. The messages that SimulationContext and its signals log came from the loggers desflow.core.context and desflow.core.signals in 0.28.0. In 1.0 they come from desflow.builder.context and desflow.builder.signals. Set a level on the new names, or on desflow, which holds both. A filter applies only to the messages of the logger it is added to, so add it to each new name, or to the handler.

docs.title: Command Line and Installs
docs.text:
• desflow needs pydantic 2.7.0 or later, where it accepted 2.6.0.
  • desflow run refuses --measure, --level and --workers without --replications. 0.28.0 ignored them and ran a single run. Add --replications, or remove the option.
  • An experiment file refuses three things: an experiment name that is not one folder name (empty, ., .., or with / or \), because the name is the folder results/<name>; a seed that is not a whole number of 0 or more; and a check with min above max, which no value passes. In 0.28.0 the name ../x wrote outside results/, seed: true ran as seed 1 and seed: -1 failed with a NumPy error that names no line. Rename the experiment, write the seed as a number and swap the bounds.
  • replicate and an experiment refuse a warm-up at or after until, where 0.28.0 gave every value for the whole run, and the report showed a negative measured horizon. replicate(measures=[]) raises ValueError, where it ran every replication and measured nothing, and None still means every statistic. Lower the warm-up, and name at least one measure.
  • An observed CSV is read strictly. A file with no rows, a row with a missing or extra cell, and a row whose value is empty, text or NaN are refused with the file and row. In 0.28.0 a file with no rows compared nothing, a NaN was accepted, and another bad value failed with an error that names no row. Correct the file.
  • A compare of a variant with itself is refused at its line. In 0.28.0 it reported a difference of 0 with a half-width of 0, which read as a precise finding of no effect. Remove the entry or name another variant.
  • desflow run FILE.py --sample prints the Builder file's first events. 0.28.0 refused every .py file with exit 2 and told you to run it with python FILE. 1.0 still refuses a .py file without --sample, or with --stdout, and exits 2.
  • desflow fit writes its settings file in the blueprint layout: the comment wrapped at 88 characters, a blank line between keys and long lists wrapped. The file loads to the same settings.
  • desflow fit and fit_column skip poisson and geometric named in candidates, as "counts whole numbers".
  • desflow report and run_experiment build the report without reading results.csv, so a missing results.csv no longer stops the report.
  • desflow report exits 2 for an experiment folder whose checks.csv or comparisons.csv is missing or cut off. In 0.28.0 it exited 0 with "No checks were requested". Run the experiment again.
  • desflow explain --json names an add_process node process:<n>.<name>. 0.28.0 wrote opaque:process.<n>.<name>, which a task or arrival named process.<x> could be mistaken for. Match the new id.
  • desflow requires typer below 0.30, because a typer minor release can change the command line. A project that needs typer 0.30 or later waits for the desflow release that allows it.
  • An experiment's counts are the task and flow counts that are 0 when no entity reached them; another whole-number statistic is no longer listed among them.

docs.title: Error Messages
docs.text:
A test that matches the text of an error matches the new text:

  • The priority, patience and balk checks name seize and open: "needs a resource, a seize or a request in its wait or open".
  • on_balk "needs a balk, a resource, a seize or an open", and the messages on cause.<name> and upstream.<field> also name on_interrupt_run, on_renege, on_balk and on_fail.
  • An index on a number reads "'machine' is not a family; add family: true to its entry".
  • stats with no level: "stats needs a level, unless it sets only trace, when the level is none".
  • A telemetry entry with no function: "a telemetry entry takes exactly one of function and readings".
  • An arrival: "an arrival takes exactly one of dist, replay or gap", and "an arrival with replay takes no distribution parameters".
  • A task with a resource "needs a service or a service_time".
  • A wait timeout: "a wait timeout is seconds, a duration such as '5 min' or an expression".
  • The line of an error inside a wait is the line of the key, not of the wait.
  • The warning of a sink that drops a reserved payload key names each routing key and its sink.

docs.title: Why desflow
docs.text:
I like building demo apps, and every demo app needs data. I could not find enough public APIs that suited my projects, and the fake data scripts I wrote did not work well: each app needed its own, and none of them behaved like a real system.

Then I came across discrete-event simulation (DES). A DES models the process itself: what arrives, which resources serve it and how long each step takes. The data follows from that model, so it has cause and effect, as a real system does. For example, a queue grows because orders arrive faster than packers can handle them. A few numbers, such as an arrival rate, a capacity and a service time, are enough for queues, waits and backlogs that change over time. A simulation also runs much faster than real time, and the same seed gives the same data every time.

SimPy is the standard DES library for Python, but it could not do two things I needed: change the parameters of a simulation while it runs, and write the events to external systems. So I started this project, under the name dynamic-des, to add both.

Later I found that a SimPy model needs a lot of code around it: the environment, the resources, the generators and the record of what happened, all written by hand. I had used the builder pattern in PySpark, so I applied it here and added a builder in Python. Not everyone is a Python programmer, though, so I also added a YAML format, an idea I took from Apache Beam YAML.

Next I looked for ways to manage and schedule simulations from a server, an idea inspired by Airflow, and changed the name to desflow.

From here, I want a simulation to be easier to create, whether it is written by hand, by an AI assistant, or built from the history of a real system. I also want desflow to fit into the tools people already use. Creating a simulation is only the first step: its value is in analysing and testing with it. The server is where these come together, as one place to create, analyse, test, monitor and manage simulations, for people and for AI agents. The Roadmap lists the plans.

When I learned DES, what I needed was spread across textbooks, lecture notes and papers. So I added a Learn section that brings it together in one place and teaches DES itself, not only desflow, with code you can run. It is for anyone who is new to DES, whether or not they use desflow. The desflow command supports this learning too: the Learn pages use its explain command to check a model against queueing theory.

If you already model with SimPy, desflow keeps what you know: a desflow model is SimPy underneath, with the additions above, and it covers everything a SimPy model can do. Coming from SimPy shows where each part of a SimPy model goes.

I use desflow in my own projects, such as the demos in benchtop. It is useful in many kinds of project. A few examples:

  • Simulation studies. A question such as how many packers a shop needs takes many runs of a model. In SimPy you write the replications, the statistics and the confidence intervals yourself. desflow collects the statistics, runs the replications and compares designs from one command, and desflow explain names the bottleneck before anything runs. See Queues and Capacity for the full worked example.
  • Data engineering. Batch and streaming pipelines need data that moves like a real system. desflow writes it to Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Parquet and JSONL files, and Iceberg tables, as history at full speed and then live.
  • ML and MLOps. A model that predicts delays or load needs training data in which queues build and clear for a reason. When a parameter changes during a run, the data shifts at a known time, which is what a drift monitor has to catch.
  • AI. An anomaly detector or an AI agent needs a known answer to be scored against. A seeded run can plant a fault and record what it planted as label records.

docs.title: Agent Skill
docs.text:
The desflow skill gives an AI coding assistant the rules of the library, so that it writes, checks, tests and runs desflow models instead of guessing them.

It is one of the ways desflow makes a simulation quicker to build. A YAML blueprint describes a whole model with no Python. The skill lets an assistant write that blueprint for you and check it. From history to simulation, planned after 1.0, starts a model from an event log.

The skill is a folder, skills/desflow/, in the Agent Skills format that Claude Code and other assistants read. An assistant that supports the format loads the skill when a request mentions desflow, a blueprint, a test of a simulation model, or a SimPy model that streams records. The folder is generated from the code, so it lists what the release has.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
Each page gives the request to type, what the skill tells the assistant to do, and the result on one example: the shop of the Learn tutorial, one packer and an order every 2 seconds, drafted from a description in words.

Task What the assistant gives you Draft a Model a blueprint from a description of a process, with each assumed number marked, checked against queueing theory Port a SimPy Program a desflow model that does what a SimPy program does, compared with the program's output Write Another Form the Builder and Low-level forms of a blueprint, which give the same records Write Tests tests of the statistics with desflow test, with expected values taken from the request Run a Study replications with a confidence interval, and a comparison of designs with desflow experiment Fit a Distribution a distribution fitted to measured times with desflow fit, loaded into the model

docs.title: Install the Skill
docs.text:
1. Install desflow, so the assistant can run the desflow commands that Command Line shows, such as desflow explain and desflow run.

  2. Copy skills/desflow/ into the skills folder of the assistant. Take it from the repository at the tag of the release you installed: v followed by what desflow --version prints. For Claude Code, ~/.claude/skills/desflow/ is for every project and .claude/skills/desflow/ in a project is for that project. With git, these lines copy it for every project:

    # The source of the installed release, which holds the skill
git clone --depth 1 --branch "v$(desflow --version)" https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow /tmp/desflow-src
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R /tmp/desflow-src/skills/desflow ~/.claude/skills/desflow

    The block is for a first install. Before you run it again, delete /tmp/desflow-src and ~/.claude/skills/desflow, because git clone stops at an existing folder and cp -R would put the new copy inside the old one. If CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR is set, use that folder in place of ~/.claude, here and in the check below.

  3. Ask the assistant for a model, such as "write a desflow blueprint for a shop with two packers and a lunch rush, and run it". It reads the skill when the request mentions desflow or a blueprint.

With the GitHub CLI, one command does the copy. gh skill install is a preview command of the GitHub CLI, so it needs gh 2.90.0 or later:

gh skill install jaehyeon-kim/desflow desflow --agent claude-code --scope user

--scope user installs for every project, in your home folder. --scope project, the default, installs for the current project, inside its git repository, so run it from that repository. Another assistant takes its own --agent value, listed in gh skill install --help. Without --agent, gh asks which assistant to install for. When it cannot ask, it installs for GitHub Copilot. At project scope, Copilot uses .agents/skills, a folder several other assistants also read. gh installs the latest release. desflow@v<version> in place of desflow pins one, with <version> the release you installed.

docs.title: Check the Install
docs.text:
The folder must hold SKILL.md, and Claude Code lists the skills it has loaded with /skills, where desflow must appear:

ls ~/.claude/skills/desflow/SKILL.md

docs.title: Other Ways to Teach an Assistant
docs.text:
• Schema. Give the assistant https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/schema/blueprint.schema.json, or the output of desflow schema, to validate what it writes.
  • Documentation as text. https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/llms.txt is an index of the pages, and https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/llms-full.txt holds all of them in one file.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: The folder layout and the SKILL.md fields follow the Agent Skills specification. The folders Claude Code reads are in its skills documentation. The gh skill install flags are those of gh skill install --help in GitHub CLI 2.95.0.

docs.title: Draft a Model
docs.text:
Describe a process in your own words, and an assistant with the skill turns it into a blueprint. It marks every number it had to assume, checks the load against queueing theory, and runs a study before it gives you an answer.

The GIF follows one request, the packing shop of the Learn tutorial, through the steps the skill teaches:

The sections below hold each step's text, so you can copy the request and check each answer.

docs.title: Ask
docs.text:
Paste the request into an assistant that has the skill:

A shop packs customer orders.
An order arrives about every 2 seconds.
One packer packs each order in about 1.5 seconds.
How long does an order wait?

docs.title: Draft
docs.text:
The skill tells the assistant to start from the nearest example (desflow examples list), and to build the model in stages, running the file after each one. It asks you for the numbers the description does not give. When it has to assume one, it marks it with a comment and lists the assumed numbers first in its reply, because you must confirm them.

The description does not say whether orders arrive at random or how much the packing time varies. The draft assumes both:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/ai/drafted_shop.yaml:draft
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0  # no pacing: the run ends as soon as it is done
  random_seed: 42
  # a fixed date, so two runs give the same records
  logical_start_time: '2026-01-05T09:00:00Z'

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}  # said: one packer

services:
  # said: 1.5 seconds; assumed: every order takes the same time
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # said: an order every 2 seconds on average; assumed: orders arrive at random
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

The skill drafts a blueprint, so the drafted model is the YAML tab. Write Another Form has its Builder form.

The skill drafts a blueprint, so the drafted model is the YAML tab. Write Another Form has its Low-level form.

docs.title: Check the Load
docs.text:
Before it runs anything, the assistant checks that the packer can keep up. desflow explain gives the queueing formulas' answer:

desflow explain drafted_shop.yaml

Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 0.5/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack_order (task, rate 0.5/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> exit
Resources
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |      μ | c |    ρ |   Wq |     L | status |
|----------+-----+--------+---+------+------+-------+--------|
| packers  | 0.5 | 0.6667 | 1 | 0.75 | 2.25 | 1.875 | OK     |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
Bottleneck: packers
Hints for utilisation 0.85:
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 0.75, at most 0.85
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 0.85 at a request every 1.76 seconds (34 a minute, 0.5667 a second)

The packer is busy 75% of the time (ρ), so the queue does not grow without limit, and the formulas give a mean wait of 2.25 seconds (Wq). When a model routes on a variable or has scenario steps, desflow explain gives no estimate, and the skill tells the assistant to check the load by hand: the work of one case, times the arrival rate, must fit inside the capacity. Command Line shows more of desflow explain, and Run a Study compares designs.

docs.title: Answer From Replications
docs.text:
One run is one sample, so the skill tells the assistant to answer from replications. 20 runs of an hour, each with its own seed spawned from 42:

desflow run drafted_shop.yaml --replications 20 | grep -E "^measure|wait_mean"

measure                                n          mean    half-width (95%)
tasks.pack_order.wait_mean            20         2.175              0.1305

The mean wait is 2.18 ± 0.13 seconds. The interval, 2.05 to 2.31, holds the 2.25 of the formulas, so the model and the theory agree. The run starts with an empty shop and has no warm-up, which Trusting Results explains how to choose.

docs.title: Check the Reply
docs.text: The skill tells the assistant to copy a checklist into its reply and tick each line: every behaviour the request names, the key that makes it, the record that shows it, and a run of the skill's own check on the files. Read the assumed numbers first. Then check that the answer is an interval from replications, not the result of one run.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/ai/drafted_shop.yaml
# Drafted from a description of the packing shop. Each value says where it came from:
# "said" means the description gives it, and "assumed" means the user has not confirmed
# it.
# Run it with: desflow run drafted_shop.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0  # no pacing: the run ends as soon as it is done
  random_seed: 42
  # a fixed date, so two runs give the same records
  logical_start_time: '2026-01-05T09:00:00Z'

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}  # said: one packer

services:
  # said: 1.5 seconds; assumed: every order takes the same time
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # said: an order every 2 seconds on average; assumed: orders arrive at random
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

egress:
  - {type: Console}

run: {until: 1 hour}  # assumed: one hour answers the question

tests:
  # From the request: an order every 2 seconds is 18,000 orders in 10 hours. The
  # count varies by about 134 between seeds (the square root of 18,000), so 540 is
  # four standard deviations, and an arrival rate 10% higher, 19,800, fails
  - name: orders_packed_in_10_hours
    until: 10 hours  # long enough that a 10% change is more than the spread
    expect:
      tasks.pack_order.finished: {value: 18000, within: 540}
  # From the request: 1.5 seconds of packing for every 2 seconds is 75% of the
  # packer's time. Over 10 hours it varies by about 0.5 between seeds, so 2 is four
  # standard deviations, and the same 10% higher rate, 82.5%, fails
  - name: packer_busy_three_quarters
    until: 10 hours
    expect:
      resources.packers.utilization_avg: {value: 75, within: 2}

Write Another Form has the Builder form.

Write Another Form has the Low-level form.

docs.title: Fit a Distribution
docs.text: Ask for a fit when you have measured times, such as packing times taken at the bench, and want the model to draw from a distribution that matches them. An assistant with the skill fits every family with desflow fit and loads the best fit into the model.

docs.title: Ask
docs.text:
packing_times.csv holds 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds, in the
column packing_seconds. Fit a distribution to them, and use it for packing in
drafted_shop.yaml.

docs.title: What the Assistant Does
docs.text:
The skill gives the assistant one command. It fits every family to the column, ranks the fits, and writes the best as YAML:

desflow fit packing_times.csv --column packing_seconds --lower 0 --out fitted/packing.yaml

--lower 0 says a time cannot be below 0. The command needs the fit extra, which adds scipy and matplotlib: uv tool install "desflow[fit]". The assistant then puts the file where the service was, with packing: !include fitted/packing.yaml under services.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Fitting the Inputs fits the shop's 40 packing times with this command, and shows the table of families it ranks, a plot of the fit, and the file it writes.

The best fit is not always the right choice. On that page the triangular has the lowest AIC, and the gamma is 0.11 behind, too close to tell apart. The two give different mean waits, and only the gamma keeps the data's mean.

docs.title: Check the Reply
docs.text: Ask which families came close to the best fit, and whether the choice changes the answer. Look at the plot that --plot draws: the data and the fit should cover the same range. Input Fitting describes every option of desflow fit.

docs.title: Port a SimPy Program
docs.text: Ask for a port when you have a SimPy program and want its records streamed, its parameters changed during a run, or its study run with desflow's tools. An assistant with the skill writes a desflow model that does what the program does, and compares the two outputs.

docs.title: Ask
docs.text:
Port shop.py, a SimPy program, to desflow.
Keep its behaviour, and compare its mean wait with the desflow model's.

docs.title: What the Assistant Does
docs.text:
The skill gives the assistant a table of the places where desflow behaves differently from SimPy, each with what to write in the port. It checks each row against the program before it writes the model. Some of the rows:

  • A program that counts time in minutes has each time converted to its unit, such as mean: 4 min, because a bare number is seconds.
  • A signal fires once by default. One that the program fires more than once gets once: false.
  • A put with no yield in the program becomes a put with wait: false, which goes on at once.
  • A failure no task handles stops the run. A program that goes on after a child process fails gets on_unhandled_failure: continue.

It picks the way to write the model as for any model: YAML when the program is resources, arrivals and tasks, and the Low-level API when it needs SimPy itself. Then it runs both and compares them: the records with desflow run <file> --sample, or the statistics over replications, within their intervals.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: Coming from SimPy ports the shop, written as a plain SimPy program in the four classes most tutorials teach. Both versions run 10 times for an hour, and their mean waits agree within their intervals. SimPy Examples ports the seven examples that ship with SimPy, each in YAML, the Builder and the Low-level API, and compares each with the program's output.

docs.title: Check the Reply
docs.text: Check that the reply names each row of the table that applies to the program, and what the port writes for it. Then check the comparison: the same records at the same times, or statistics whose intervals overlap. SimPy Compatibility lists every SimPy feature with its form in desflow.

docs.title: Run a Study
docs.text: Ask for a study when you need an answer you can act on. One run is one sample, so an assistant with the skill answers from replications, with a confidence interval, and compares designs with the same seeds.

docs.title: Ask
docs.text:
Does a second packer cut the mean wait of drafted_shop.yaml, and by how much?
Run a study, and give the difference with its interval.

docs.title: What the Assistant Does
docs.text:
The skill gives the assistant these steps:

  1. Set a seed, so the study can be repeated.
  2. Set a warm-up when the model needs time to reach its usual state.
  3. Run replications. Each has its own seed, spawned from the study's seed.
  4. Report each mean with its 95% confidence interval.
  5. To compare designs, write an experiment file and run desflow experiment. It runs every design with the same seeds, compares them seed by seed, and writes report.md.

For the drafted shop, the experiment runs one and two packers for an hour, 20 times each:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/ai/drafted_shop_experiment.yaml:study
model: drafted_shop.yaml

until: 1 h

replications: 20

seed: 42

# Every design runs with the same 20 seeds, so they are compared seed by seed
pairing: common

measures: [tasks.pack_order.wait_mean, resources.packers.utilization_avg]

variants:
  one: {}
  two: {Shop.resources.packers.max_cap: 2, Shop.resources.packers.current_cap: 2}

compare:
  - {baseline: one, variant: two}

run_experiment runs the same study in Python, as Comparing Designs shows.

run_experiment runs the same study in Python, as Comparing Designs shows.

desflow experiment drafted_shop_experiment.yaml

The Comparisons table of report.md gives each difference, two packers minus one, seed by seed:

| Baseline | Variant | Measure | Difference | Half-width | Interval | Random streams |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| one | two | `tasks.pack_order.wait_mean` | -2.043 | 0.1261 | -2.169 to -1.917 | 1 shared |
| one | two | `resources.packers.utilization_avg` | -37.26 | 0.4302 | -37.69 to -36.83 | 1 shared |

A second packer cuts the mean wait by 2.04 ± 0.13 seconds, from 2.18 to 0.13. The packers' utilisation halves, from 75% to 37%. The interval of the difference does not hold 0, so the cut is not chance.

docs.title: Check the Reply
docs.text: Check that the answer is an interval, not one number, and that both designs ran with the same seeds. Read the report's Missing Inputs section: it names each input whose source the experiment does not state. Trusting Results explains how many replications and how long a warm-up a study needs, and Experiments lists every file the experiment writes.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/ai/drafted_shop_experiment.yaml
# Does a second packer cut the mean wait of the drafted shop, and by how much?
# Run it with: desflow experiment drafted_shop_experiment.yaml
experiment: second-packer

question: Does a second packer cut the mean wait of an order, and by how much?

model: drafted_shop.yaml

until: 1 h

replications: 20

seed: 42

# Every design runs with the same 20 seeds, so they are compared seed by seed
pairing: common

measures: [tasks.pack_order.wait_mean, resources.packers.utilization_avg]

variants:
  one: {}
  two: {Shop.resources.packers.max_cap: 2, Shop.resources.packers.current_cap: 2}

compare:
  - {baseline: one, variant: two}

assumptions:
  - Orders arrive at random, at a steady one every 2 seconds.
  - Every order takes 1.5 seconds to pack.

limits: [Each run starts with an empty shop and has no warm-up.]

output: results/second-packer

Comparing Designs has a study in Python with run_experiment.

Comparing Designs has a study in Python with run_experiment.

docs.title: Write Another Form
docs.text: Ask for the Builder or Low-level form of a blueprint when the model needs Python, such as a payload function, or SimPy itself. An assistant with the skill writes a form that gives the same records as the blueprint, and checks that it does.

docs.title: Ask
docs.text:
Write the Builder and Low-level forms of drafted_shop.yaml.
They must give the same records as the YAML at the same seed.

docs.title: What the Assistant Does
docs.text:
The skill gives the assistant the rules that keep the forms equal:

  • A time in YAML and in the Builder takes a unit. The Low-level DistributionConfig takes seconds only, so the unit goes in a comment.
  • The Low-level form draws each time through sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config("<sim_id>.<path>")), as the YAML does, so it draws the same numbers at the same seed.
  • Builder and Low-level code use only the names from desflow import ... gives, never a private attribute.
  • A Python file runs with python <file> and prints its records with ConsoleEgress(format="json").

Then it runs the skill's check on the three files. The check runs each form at the model's seed and the two after it, and compares every record with the YAML's:

python <skill folder>/scripts/check_model.py drafted_shop.yaml drafted_shop_builder.py drafted_shop_low_level.py

ok desflow check
ok imports
ok runs of the Python files
ok seed and start time
ok records of the forms
ok desflow test

Each line is a check that passed. A failed check names the file and line, and what to write instead. seed and start time fails on a model without a fixed logical_start_time, because the timestamps of two runs then differ, so the drafted shop sets one.

docs.title: Check the Reply
docs.text: Check that every line of the check reads ok, and that the reply says it compared the forms at the model's seed and the two after it.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
The three forms of the shop from Draft a Model. Writing a Model explains how the three ways relate.

Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/ai/drafted_shop.yaml
# Drafted from a description of the packing shop. Each value says where it came from:
# "said" means the description gives it, and "assumed" means the user has not confirmed
# it.
# Run it with: desflow run drafted_shop.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0  # no pacing: the run ends as soon as it is done
  random_seed: 42
  # a fixed date, so two runs give the same records
  logical_start_time: '2026-01-05T09:00:00Z'

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}  # said: one packer

services:
  # said: 1.5 seconds; assumed: every order takes the same time
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # said: an order every 2 seconds on average; assumed: orders arrive at random
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

egress:
  - {type: Console}

run: {until: 1 hour}  # assumed: one hour answers the question

tests:
  # From the request: an order every 2 seconds is 18,000 orders in 10 hours. The
  # count varies by about 134 between seeds (the square root of 18,000), so 540 is
  # four standard deviations, and an arrival rate 10% higher, 19,800, fails
  - name: orders_packed_in_10_hours
    until: 10 hours  # long enough that a 10% change is more than the spread
    expect:
      tasks.pack_order.finished: {value: 18000, within: 540}
  # From the request: 1.5 seconds of packing for every 2 seconds is 75% of the
  # packer's time. Over 10 hours it varies by about 0.5 between seeds, so 2 is four
  # standard deviations, and the same 10% higher rate, 82.5%, fails
  - name: packer_busy_three_quarters
    until: 10 hours
    expect:
      resources.packers.utilization_avg: {value: 75, within: 2}
