It needs no assumption about the gaps, the packing times or the order of service. It holds for the queue alone, for the packers alone, and for the whole shop.

In the busy hour of Measuring a Run, 6,488 orders finished in 3,600 seconds, so λ = 1.802 orders a second. The mean wait was 2.0065 seconds, so λ × W = 1.802 × 2.0065 = 3.616. The time-weighted average queue length was 3.618 orders. The two figures agree.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
The law holds because both sides count the same total. Add up, over the hour, the seconds each order spent in the queue. Counted second by second, the total is the number waiting at each moment, added over 3,600 seconds: L × 3,600. Counted order by order, it is the number of orders times their mean wait: λ × 3,600 × W. The two totals are equal, so L = λ × W.

desflow measures the queue length, the arrival count and the wait separately. If they do not agree, one of them is wrong. That makes the law the first check on a model's statistics, before any result is trusted.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Read the five statistics at the end of a run, and compare L with λ × W for the queue and for the whole shop. The number in the whole shop is the queue plus the orders being packed, and the orders being packed are the three packers times their utilisation. This function does the arithmetic on the readings of any run of the shop:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:littles-law
def littles_law(readings: dict, seconds: float):
    """The arrival rate, then L and lambda x W for the queue and for the whole shop."""
    rate = readings["Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished"] / seconds
    in_queue = readings["Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg"]
    packers = readings["Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity"]
    in_service = (
        packers * readings["Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg"] / 100
    )
    wait = readings["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]
    service = readings["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean"]
    return (
        rate,
        (in_queue, rate * wait),
        (in_queue + in_service, rate * (wait + service)),
    )

Each tab runs the Measuring a Run hour and reads its statistics:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
# Utilisation, queue length, mean wait and packing time, and orders finished
desflow run measuring_a_run.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'utilization_avg"|queue_length_avg"|(wait|service)_mean"|orders\.finished"' | tail -5


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg","value":89.98409865705875}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg","value":3.617867825881605}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":2.0065204395584315}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean","value":1.4977034525277377}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished","value":6488}

Put these five values into the arithmetic of littles_law, with 3 packers and 3,600 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:builder
from measuring_a_run import app

app.run(until="1 h")
readings = app.env.stats.readings()

Then littles_law(readings, 3600).

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:low-level
from measuring_a_run_low_level import run

env = run()
readings = env.stats.readings()

Then littles_law(readings, 3600).

All three give the same figures:

arrival rate 1.802 orders a second
queue: L 3.618, lambda x W 3.616
shop: L 6.317, lambda x W 6.315

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: The queue gives 3.618 against 3.616, and the whole shop 6.317 against 6.315. Both agree within 0.1%. The 3 orders still in the shop when the hour ended explain part of the difference for the whole shop: the time they have spent in the shop counts in L, but their full time in the shop is not yet in W. All 3 are being packed and none is in the queue, so their waits are already in W and they do not change the queue's figures. In a long run of a settled shop, a difference of more than a few percent means a statistic is wrong, for example a task that keeps its packer after it finishes. Checking and Validating uses the law as one of its checks.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Parameter Sweeps runs the busy hour with three packers and the measured packing times at four arrival rates, 20 replications each. At 1.6 orders a second (utilisation 0.8) the mean wait is 0.90 seconds. At 1.8 (utilisation 0.9) it is 2.15 seconds. At 1.9 (utilisation 0.95) it is 4.52 seconds. A rise of 6% in the rate more than doubles the wait.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
For one server with exponential gaps and service times (M/M/1), the mean wait in the queue has a closed form: utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation) × the mean service time. With constant service times (M/D/1) it is exactly half. The first part, utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation), grows faster and faster as utilisation nears 1: it is 1 at 0.5, 9 at 0.9 and 19 at 0.95. The bars show this for one packer with a mean packing time of 1.5 seconds:

So a design that only keeps utilisation below 1 is not enough. A shop that is stable can still make orders wait a long time, and a small change in demand changes the wait a great deal.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
The formulas are short enough to compute. These functions are the ones the rest of the page uses:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:theory
def mm1_wait(utilisation: float) -> float:
    """Mean wait in the queue of an M/M/1 queue: utilisation / (1 - utilisation) x service."""
    return utilisation / (1 - utilisation) * SERVICE


def erlang_c(units: int, load: float) -> float:
    """The share of arrivals that find all `units` busy, for a load in packers' worth of work."""
    last = load**units / math.factorial(units) / (1 - load / units)
    return last / (sum(load**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(units)) + last)


def mmc_wait(units: int, arrival_rate: float) -> float:
    """Mean wait in the queue of an M/M/c queue: Erlang C divided by (c / service - lambda)."""
    return erlang_c(units, arrival_rate * SERVICE) / (units / SERVICE - arrival_rate)


def kingman_wait(utilisation: float, arrival_cv: float, service_cv: float) -> float:
    """Kingman's formula for the mean wait in a one-server queue."""
    variability = (arrival_cv**2 + service_cv**2) / 2
    return utilisation / (1 - utilisation) * variability * SERVICE

utilisation 0.5: mean wait M/M/1  1.50 s, M/D/1  0.75 s
utilisation 0.75: mean wait M/M/1  4.50 s, M/D/1  2.25 s
utilisation 0.9: mean wait M/M/1 13.50 s, M/D/1  6.75 s
utilisation 0.95: mean wait M/M/1 28.50 s, M/D/1 14.25 s

desflow explain gives the same figure for a one-packer model: for the shop of First Simulation, M/D/1 at utilisation 0.75, its Wq column reads 2.25 seconds.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Near full use, the wait depends strongly on the exact arrival rate. Before trusting a wait at a utilisation of 0.9 or more, check how good the estimate of the rate is, as Parameter Sweeps does. A run near full use also needs to be long before its mean wait settles, as Output Analysis explains.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The busy hour has three packers with constant packing at utilisation 0.9. Ten long runs of it give a mean wait of 2.06 seconds, as Check a Formula Against the Shop shows. One packer with constant packing at the same utilisation would make orders wait 6.75 seconds on average, by the M/D/1 formula above. Three packers sharing one queue wait far less at the same utilisation.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: With several packers sharing one queue, an order waits only when every packer is busy. For exponential gaps and service times (M/M/c), the share of orders that find every packer busy is the Erlang C formula. The mean wait in the queue is that share divided by (c ÷ the mean service time − the arrival rate). The erlang_c and mmc_wait functions above compute it.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Compare three packers with a queue each against three packers sharing one queue, with the formulas. With a mean packing time of 1.5 seconds and utilisation 0.8, each of the three packers with its own queue is one packer at utilisation 0.8, and gives a mean wait of 6 seconds. Three packers sharing one queue give about 1.6 seconds:

one packer at utilisation 0.8: mean wait 6.0 s
three packers at utilisation 0.8: mean wait 1.62 s

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Pooling packers into one queue shortens the wait at the same load. A design question such as "one fast packer or three slower ones" depends on the measure, so utilisation alone cannot answer it. With one packer three times as fast, with a mean of 0.5 seconds at utilisation 0.8, an order waits 2.0 seconds in the queue and spends 2.5 seconds in the system. With three slower packers sharing a queue, it waits about 1.6 seconds and spends about 3.1 seconds in the system. The formula covers exponential times only, so the shop's own runs answer the question for other times.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Choosing Inputs runs the busy hour with four candidate packing times, all with a mean of 1.5 seconds. The mean waits are 1.88 seconds with constant times, 1.95 with triangular, 1.81 with the measured times and 3.46 with exponential. The same mean with the widest spread, the exponential, gives a much longer wait. The three narrower spreads give waits within 8% of each other in one run, and their order is not that of their spreads.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
Kingman's formula gives an approximate mean wait for one server with any distributions. It measures the spread of each input by its coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean, called variation for short. The variation is 1 for an exponential distribution and 0 for a constant one. The mean wait is the product of three parts:

  • utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation), which grows quickly as utilisation nears 1;
  • (arrival variation² + service variation²) ÷ 2, the effect of the spread;
  • the mean service time.

With exponential gaps (variation 1) and constant service (variation 0), the middle part is 0.5. The formula then gives half the M/M/1 wait, which is the M/D/1 result above. Variation in the gaps counts as much as variation in the packing times. When both variations are 0, the formula gives no wait at all.

docs.title: Pollaczek-Khinchine Formula
docs.text: For one server with exponential gaps and any service times (M/G/1), the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula gives the mean wait exactly: utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation) × (1 + service variation²) ÷ 2 × the mean service time. It is Kingman's formula with an arrival variation of 1. With constant service it gives the M/D/1 wait, and with exponential service it gives the M/M/1 wait.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: The kingman_wait function above computes Kingman's formula, and with an arrival variation of 1 it gives the Pollaczek-Khinchine wait. Use it to judge how much the choice of an input distribution matters before you fit one. Choosing Inputs shows how to compare the candidates by running each.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A model whose inputs are replaced by their averages has no variation, so it shows no queue while utilisation is below 1. Its waits are too short. Common Mistakes lists this among the errors that distort a result.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: A Flow of Tasks adds a checker to the shop. Orders arrive at 1.6 a second, every packed order is checked, and a tenth of the checked orders go back to packing. Four packers take 1.5 seconds an order, and one checker takes 0.4 seconds on average.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
In a network of tasks, work reaches a task in two ways: as new work, and as work routed to it from other tasks. The rate into a task is the sum of the two. This is flow balance. For packing, the rate is 1.6 + 0.1 × the rate into packing. Solving for it gives 1.6 ÷ (1 − 0.1) = 1.6 ÷ 0.9 = 1.778 orders a second. Every packed order goes to the checker, so the checker receives the same 1.778.

Each resource's utilisation follows from its rate. The four packers have 1.778 × 1.5 ÷ 4 = 0.667. The checker has 1.778 × 0.4 = 0.711. The resource with the highest utilisation is the bottleneck, here the checker. It is the first to reach full use when demand grows, and adding units anywhere else does not raise the most the shop can handle.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Work out the rate into each task, then each resource's utilisation:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:flow
# Orders arrive at 1.6 a second, and a tenth of the checked orders go back to packing,
# so the rate into packing solves: rate = 1.6 + 0.1 x rate.
flow_rate = 1.6 / (1 - 0.1)
packers = flow_rate * 1.5 / 4  # four packers, 1.5 seconds an order
checker = flow_rate * 0.4  # one checker, 0.4 seconds an order on average
print(f"rate into packing and into checking: {flow_rate:.3f} orders a second")
print(f"utilisation: packers {packers:.3f}, checker {checker:.3f}")

desflow explain does the same from the model and names the bottleneck, as A Flow of Tasks shows. The last line below is what the Builder's analyze() reports for the same shop:

rate into packing and into checking: 1.778 orders a second
utilisation: packers 0.667, checker 0.711
desflow explain names the bottleneck: checkers

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Add capacity at the bottleneck first. Here a second checker lowers the checker's utilisation to 0.356, while a fifth packer lowers the packers' utilisation but leaves the checker at 0.711, so it does not raise the most the shop can handle. Rework raises the load on every task it passes through, so a model without it underestimates every utilisation.

docs.title: Check a Formula Against the Shop
In the Tutorial
docs.text: The busy hour with exponential packing times is M/M/3 at utilisation 0.9. The Erlang C formula gives a mean wait of 4.083 seconds. Ten one-hour runs of the shop measure 4.784 ± 1.301 seconds, so the formula lies within the interval of the runs.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A formula and a run that agree check each other. The formula shows that the model is built as intended, and the runs show that the formula applies. A model that disagrees with a formula on a case the formula covers has a fault in its logic or its statistics.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

desflow explain --verify runs the model and compares each measure with the analysis. Check Against Theory runs it step by step on this shop with exponential packing times, where the Erlang C wait is 4.083 seconds and ten one-hour runs measure 4.784 ± 1.301 seconds.

This shop takes the gaps and the packing times as exponential or constant by choice:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:shop
def shop(arrival: dict, service: dict, packers: int) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop with the given arrival gaps and packing times, and `packers` packers."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
    app.add_arrival("orders", **arrival)
    app.add_service("packing", **service)
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)
    app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


# Exponential gaps and times are the M of Kendall's notation, constant ones the D
def exponential(mean: float) -> dict:
    return {"dist": "exponential", "rate": 1 / mean}


def constant(mean: float) -> dict:
    return {"dist": "constant", "value": mean}

This function runs ten replications, each leaving out its first 2,000 seconds, and returns the mean wait with its 95% half-width:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:measure
def measured_wait(arrival: dict, service: dict, packers: int, until: int):
    """Mean wait over 10 runs, with its 95% half-width; each run leaves out its first 2,000 s."""
    result = replicate(
        lambda: shop(arrival, service, packers),
        10,
        seed=42,
        until=until,
        warmup=2000,
        measures=["tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"],
    )
    row = result.summary[0]
    return row["mean"], row["half_width"]

--verify does not support low-level models. replicate runs a LowLevelModel the same way, as Replications shows, and its mean and half-width compare with a formula as in the Builder tab.

The Builder tab's checks compare each formula with the runs, and pass when the formula lies within the interval:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:checks
for rho, figures in ((0.5, (1.50, 1.50, 0.06)), (0.75, (4.50, 4.39, 0.31))):
    arrival = exponential(SERVICE / rho)
    check(
        f"M/M/1 at utilisation {rho}",
        mm1_wait(rho),
        measured_wait(arrival, exponential(SERVICE), 1, 20_000),
        figures,
    )
check(
    "M/M/3 at utilisation 0.8",
    mmc_wait(3, 1.6),
    measured_wait(exponential(1 / 1.6), exponential(SERVICE), 3, 30_000),
    (1.62, 1.57, 0.09),
)
arrival = exponential(SERVICE / 0.75)
check(
    "M/D/1 at utilisation 0.75, Kingman",
    kingman_wait(0.75, 1, 0),
    measured_wait(arrival, constant(SERVICE), 1, 20_000),
    (2.25, 2.23, 0.13),
)

M/M/1 at utilisation 0.5: formula 1.50 s, mean of 10 runs 1.50 ± 0.06 s
M/M/1 at utilisation 0.75: formula 4.50 s, mean of 10 runs 4.39 ± 0.31 s
M/M/3 at utilisation 0.8: formula 1.62 s, mean of 10 runs 1.57 ± 0.09 s
M/D/1 at utilisation 0.75, Kingman: formula 2.25 s, mean of 10 runs 2.23 ± 0.13 s

The busy hour itself is M/D/3, which has no closed formula. For one packer, constant service halves the M/M/1 wait. This check compares the M/D/3 runs with half the M/M/3 wait, as an approximation:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:kendall
# The busy hour is M/D/3: exponential gaps (M), constant service (D), three packers.
# The runs are compared with half the M/M/3 wait at this load.
check(
    "M/D/3 at utilisation 0.9, half the M/M/3 wait",
    mmc_wait(3, 1.8) / 2,
    measured_wait(exponential(1 / 1.8), constant(SERVICE), 3, 20_000),
    (2.04, 2.06, 0.17),
)

M/D/3 at utilisation 0.9, half the M/M/3 wait: formula 2.04 s, mean of 10 runs 2.06 ± 0.17 s

These are 10 runs of 20,000 seconds, each without its first 2,000 seconds, not one-hour runs.

Kingman's formula is an approximation, and this check shows where it is not exact. Constant gaps of 2 seconds with exponential service (D/M/1) at utilisation 0.75:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:dm1
mean, half_width = measured_wait(
    constant(SERVICE / 0.75), exponential(SERVICE), 1, 20_000
)
kingman = kingman_wait(0.75, 0, 1)
print(
    f"D/M/1 at utilisation 0.75: Kingman {kingman:.2f} s, mean of 10 runs {mean:.2f} ± {half_width:.2f} s"
)

D/M/1 at utilisation 0.75: Kingman 2.25 s, mean of 10 runs 1.76 ± 0.08 s

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Where a formula is exact, as for M/M/1 and M/M/c, it lies within the interval of the runs. Half the M/M/3 wait is close for the M/D/3 busy hour. Kingman's formula lies outside the interval for D/M/1: it is exact with exponential gaps, accurate near full use, and a rough guide elsewhere. A check that fails on a case the formula covers points to a fault in the model. A check that fails outside the formula's cases says only that the formula does not apply.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Write the model in Kendall's notation first, to know which formulas apply.
  • Work out utilisation for every resource before a run. At 1 or above, the answer is more capacity.
  • Check a run's statistics with Little's law before trusting any result.
  • Expect long waits near full use, and longer ones when gaps or packing times vary.
  • Find the bottleneck with flow balance, and add capacity there first.
  • Check the model against a formula on the cases the formula covers. The simulation answers the cases it cannot: several resources, priorities, breakdowns and changing demand.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Wikipedia: Kendall's notation, Little's law, Kingman's formula, the Erlang C formula and the Jackson network.
  • The explanations and the checks are our own.

docs.title: Readiness and Reporting
docs.text: A model is ready when someone who was not part of the study can see what it answers, how far to trust the answer, and how to repeat it. This page explains what that takes, with the shop's study in The Complete Model as the example. It points to three published checklists written for simulation studies, and shows which parts desflow does for you and which parts only you can write.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• why readiness is a statement about a decision, not about a model;
  • what the three levels of the Model Readiness Checklist ask for;
  • what a report needs, by the STRESS-DES checklist;
  • what to share so that others can run the model, by the STARS framework;
  • which items desflow records for you, and which only you can write.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The shop model is ready to say how many packers the busy hour needs: its inputs came from data, its checks passed, its results carry an interval, and a reader can repeat the runs. It is not ready to say anything about a holiday week, whatever its code looks like.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A model is built and checked for one question. The checks of Checking and Validating show it fits that question, with the inputs and the range of conditions it was checked under. Outside them, nothing has been checked.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Write down the question the model is ready for, as A Simulation Study does, and state the limits of its use. An experiment file keeps them with the runs: The Complete Model lists "One busy hour only; the rest of the day is not modelled" among its limits, and report.md prints them.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A reader who wants to use the model for another question can see at once that it was not built for it. That question needs its own checks before the model answers it.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The shop's study meets most of the first level below. Its replications and warm-up come from Trusting Results, its seeds are fixed, its core logic is checked in Checking a Model, and it is compared with values observed in the shop. The review of the process with the people who know it is the walk-through of Check the Assumptions, which no tool does.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
The open book HSMA: the little book of DES has a chapter, Model Readiness Checklist, that sorts what a model needs into three levels, by the size of the decision:

  • Bronze is the level for small to medium decisions within one organisation. It asks for views of the model running, checks of the core logic, enough replications and a warm-up, a fixed seed, a comparison with the real system, a review of the process with the people who know it, and documentation.
  • Silver is the level for larger or costlier decisions, or for models used across several areas. It adds a formal reporting checklist such as STRESS-DES, documented code, a code review, automated tests, an open licence, version control and a sensitivity analysis.
  • Gold is the level for models that will be reused, adapted or published. It adds:
    • a documentation site and a changelog;
    • identifiers for the authors and an archive of the code;
    • an online environment to run the model in, parallel runs, a web app and an animation;
    • formal methods for the warm-up and the number of replications;
    • tests against historical data.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Choose the level from the decision, then go through its items. Some items cost nothing in desflow, and some need you:

Item In desflow A fixed seed and independent streams random_seed fixes a run, and replicate makes one integer seed for each replication from one seed and records them, so the same call gives the same results and any replication can be repeated alone. See Replications Enough replications, with an interval replicate gives the mean and the half-width of the 95% interval. How many is your decision The designs and the inputs on record An experiment records the compiled parameters of each design and writes its summary, its comparisons, its checks and a report.md. See Experiments A comparison with the real system An experiment can read an observed file and compare it with the model. See Experiment Results. Which data to use is your decision A view of the model running Every event and reading is a record, which you can read or send to a sink. See Egress, Batching and Delivery Core logic checked Yours: Checking and Validating shows the cases to work by hand Assumptions, data sources and limits Yours: they go in the experiment file and the report, and no tool decides them

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A level is met when every item of it is done, not most. An item left out goes into the report as a limit, so that the reader knows which check the model has not had.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The Complete Model's report.md gives the question, the model and its versions, the assumptions, each input with its fitted parameters and where it came from, the run settings, the counts, the results, the comparisons, the checks and the observed comparison, then the limits and any input with no source. Its Comparisons section answers the question with each difference and its interval: a fourth packer cuts the packing wait by 1.77 seconds, with a half-width of 0.16 seconds.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A reader acts on the report alone. The reporting checklist STRESS-DES lists what that reader will ask. It has 20 items in six groups: objectives, logic, data, experimentation, implementation and code access. It is by Monks, Currie, Onggo, Robinson, Kunc and Taylor, and the book gives it in its chapter STRESS-DES Reporting.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Answer each group in one short paragraph of the report, in this order, after the answer and its interval:

  • Objectives: the question and the measures, as in Ask One Question.
  • Logic: the conceptual model, with its assumptions and what it leaves out.
  • Data: where each input came from, and how it was fitted or chosen.
  • Experimentation: the run length, the warm-up, the number of replications and the designs compared.
  • Implementation: the software and its version, and the random number streams.
  • Code access: where the code, the data and the seeds are kept.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: report.md answers the objectives, the data and the experimentation from the experiment file, and gives the software versions. The logic beyond the listed assumptions, how the model was checked, and where the code is kept are yours to add. Common Mistakes lists what to look for before you send the report.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Each tutorial page ends with Full Files: every file its runs need, so a reader can repeat them. desflow itself is under the MIT licence and installs from PyPI with a stated version.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: The framework STARS, by Monks, Harper and Mustafee, says what to share so that others can run and reuse a model. The book gives it in The STARS Framework. A model that only its author can run cannot be checked by anyone else.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
STARS separates essential parts from optional ones:

  • Essential: an open licence; a list of the software the model needs, with its versions; free and open software; a minimum of documentation; an identifier for each author; a citation file; a code repository; and an archive that gives the code a permanent identifier.
  • Optional: fuller documentation, a hosted documentation site, an online environment to run the model in, an interface, and a hosted web app.

Keep the blueprint or the Python files, the experiment file and the observed data in one repository, with the desflow version they ran on.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A model shared with its essential parts can be run again by a reader, with the same seeds and the same results. That is the strongest evidence a report can give.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Ready is a statement about one decision: write down the question and the limits of the model's use.
  • Choose the readiness level from the size of the decision, and meet every item of it.
  • desflow records the seeds, the intervals, the designs, the inputs and the comparisons. The assumptions, the checks and the limits are yours to write.
  • Report the answer first, with its interval, then the six groups of STRESS-DES.
  • Share the model with an open licence, its software versions and its files.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• The open book HSMA: the little book of DES, its chapters Model Readiness Checklist, STRESS-DES Reporting and The STARS Framework. The chapters are under the CC BY-NC-SA licence, so none of their text is copied here. We read the three and link them, and the lists above are our own summaries.
  • Monks, Currie, Onggo, Robinson, Kunc and Taylor, "Strengthening the reporting of empirical simulation studies: Introducing the STRESS guidelines" (Journal of Simulation, 2019).
  • Monks, Harper and Mustafee, "Towards sharing tools and artefacts for reusable simulations in healthcare" (Journal of Simulation, 2024).

docs.title: End Conditions
docs.text:
For an hour the shop now gets an order every 1.43 seconds on average (42 a minute, rate: 0.7). Its one packer takes 1.5 seconds per order, so it packs at most 40 a minute, a little fewer than the 42 that arrive. Orders are still waiting when the hour ends. A report that counts only the orders packed in the hour leaves them out. This page asks: does a fixed horizon answer the same question as closing the doors and packing every order already in the shop?

  • Decision: which way of ending the run the shop's report uses.
  • Measures: the orders started, finished and still in the shop, the mean wait, and the time the run ends.
  • Runs: two runs, each with the seed 42: one stops at the end of the hour, and one stops taking orders then and runs until the last order is packed.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random, and every order takes the same time to pack.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • end a run at a fixed time, or close the doors and drain the orders already in the shop;
  • count the orders started, finished and still in the shop;
  • see which orders a mean wait leaves out.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a drain at the end of the run, which packs every order still in the shop, and the counts that show which orders each way of ending leaves out. The shop is the one from First Simulation, busier: one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing.

docs.title: Count Who Is Still There
docs.text:
An end condition decides which entities a run's results describe. These statistics count the orders:

  • flows.orders.started, from the basic level, counts the orders that entered the shop. An order enters when its first task begins, before any queue.
  • flows.orders.finished, from basic, counts the orders that left.
  • flows.orders.in_system, from basic, counts the orders still in the shop.
  • tasks.pack_order.in_progress, from minimal, counts the orders waiting to be packed or being packed.

The model switches on typical, which also keeps the mean wait:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/end_conditions.yaml:watch
# Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 2 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions.py:watch
# Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=7200)
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions_low_level.py:watch
# Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=7200)

A low-level process reports its entities with env.stats.flow_started(arrival) and env.stats.flow_finished(arrival), as the full file below does.

Every order that started is either finished or still in the shop, so started is finished plus in_system. These counts say how many orders a mean wait leaves out.

docs.title: Close the Doors, Then Finish
docs.text:
Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there. A fixed horizon stops the clock at until, whatever is still going on. A drain stops only the arrivals at until and keeps running until every entity in the model has left. In SimPy that is two steps: interrupt the source process, then run until every admitted process has ended. desflow writes both with drain:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/end_conditions.yaml:run
run:
  # No new orders after one hour
  until: 1 h
  # true: pack every order already in the shop before the run ends
  drain: ${DRAIN:-false}

${DRAIN:-false} reads the environment variable DRAIN, so DRAIN=true desflow run end_conditions.yaml runs the drain, as desflow run end_conditions.yaml --drain does.

docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions.py:run
# No new orders after one hour; with drain, pack every order already in the shop
app.run(until="1 h", drain=drain or None)
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions_low_level.py:run
env.run(until=3600)  # no new orders after one hour
if drain:
    # Stop the source, then run until every admitted order has ended
    source.interrupt()
    env.run(until=env.all_of([o for o in orders if o.is_alive]))

env.all_of(...) is SimPy's AllOf: it happens when every order process has ended. SimPy and desflow explains waiting for all events.

source.interrupt() raises an Interrupt inside the source process, which ends its loop. SimPy and desflow explains interrupts.

o.is_alive is true while a process has not ended.

env.now is the clock, which the script reads to report the end time. SimPy and desflow explains the clock.

The stop at until is an event that SimPy schedules with the URGENT priority, so it comes before the other events at that time. A script that stops its own run at an event can do the same with env.schedule(event, URGENT, delay). In a blueprint, the fire action's urgent and after keys do it, as Signals and Waiting shows.

A drain can also take a limit, drain: {limit: 10 min}, so a model that never empties still ends. A limit of 0, below 0 or NaN is refused, and an infinite limit means no limit. A stop ends the run as soon as an event or a condition happens. Run Length describes both.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
Does a fixed horizon answer the same question as a drain? Not for every order. Each figure here comes from a run with the seed 42: one that stops at the hour, and one that drains after it. The fixed horizon ends at 3,600 seconds with 2,561 orders started, 2,386 finished and 175 still in the shop, one being packed and 174 waiting. The drain ends 261.8 seconds later, at 3,861.8, with all 2,561 finished:

desflow explain shows why so many orders are left, without a run:

desflow explain end_conditions.yaml

Resources
+--------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |      μ | c |    ρ | Wq | L | status   |
|----------+-----+--------+---+------+----+---+----------|
| packers  | 0.7 | 0.6667 | 1 | 1.05 |  - | - | UNSTABLE |
+--------------------------------------------------------+
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: unstable: the queue grows for as long as the run lasts

The packer gets 1.05 seconds of work every second, more than it can do, so the queue grows for as long as orders arrive. The longer the horizon, the more orders it leaves in the shop. A drain packs them all. In Python, context.analyze() gives the same analysis for a builder model. A low-level model has no explain, because its SimPy code makes the links between arrivals, tasks and resources as it runs, so there are none to read.

The mean wait moves less than the count of finished orders: 122.81 seconds with the fixed horizon against 131.27 with the drain. An order's wait is measured when its packing starts, so only the 174 of the 2,561 orders that start packing after the hour change the mean, and they raise it because they waited longer than the orders before them.

Each tab prints both runs: the orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait. A record's sim_ts is the time the run ended.

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
# Stop at the end time: orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait
desflow run end_conditions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'orders\.(started|finished|in_system)"|pack_order\.wait_mean"' | tail -4
# Finish the orders in the shop first
DRAIN=true desflow run end_conditions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'orders\.(started|finished|in_system)"|pack_order\.wait_mean"' | tail -4


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":122.8142837353294}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished","value":2386}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.started","value":2561}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.in_system","value":175}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3861.806114353957,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":131.26839079806425}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3861.806114353957,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished","value":2561}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3861.806114353957,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.started","value":2561}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3861.806114353957,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.in_system","value":0}


python end_conditions.py 2>/dev/null

horizon: ends at  3600.0 s, 2561 started, 2386 finished, 175 left, mean wait 122.81 s
drain  : ends at  3861.8 s, 2561 started, 2561 finished, 0 left, mean wait 131.27 s

python end_conditions_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

horizon: ends at  3600.0 s, 2561 started, 2386 finished, 175 left, mean wait 122.81 s
drain  : ends at  3861.8 s, 2561 started, 2561 finished, 0 left, mean wait 131.27 s

A fixed horizon answers a question about a period, such as how many orders the shop packs in an hour. The orders still in the shop at the end are unfinished work, and in_system says how many there are. A drain answers a question about a batch of orders, such as how long the day's orders take to clear. It serves every admitted order, but the run goes on past the hour. Report the counts beside any mean, so a reader knows which orders it covers. Output Analysis explains the two kinds of run, and Statistics describes each count.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A fixed horizon answers a question about a period. A drain answers a question about a batch of orders.
  • started equals finished plus in_system, so these counts show the orders a result leaves out.
  • Report the counts beside any mean, so a reader knows which orders it covers.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/end_conditions.yaml
# The End Conditions tutorial: a fixed horizon against a drain.
# Run it with: desflow run end_conditions.yaml
# With a drain after the hour: DRAIN=true desflow run end_conditions.yaml
simulation: {sim_id: Shop, factor: 0, random_seed: 42}

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.7, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 2 h}

egress:
  - {type: Console}

run:
  # No new orders after one hour
  until: 1 h
  # true: pack every order already in the shop before the run ends
  drain: ${DRAIN:-false}
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions.py
"""The End Conditions tutorial: a fixed horizon against a drain.

One packer, an order every 1.43 seconds on average (rate 0.7) and 1.5 seconds of
packing, for an hour. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the
counts and the mean wait with a fixed horizon and with a drain at the end. To see only
those lines, run:
python end_conditions.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop of First Simulation, busier: more orders than one packer can pack."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.7)
        # Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=7200)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def outcomes(drain: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour, with or without a drain, and returns the counts and the wait."""
    app = shop()
    # No new orders after one hour; with drain, pack every order already in the shop
    app.run(until="1 h", drain=drain or None)
    r = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.{}".format
    return {
        "started": r[name("flows.orders.started")],
        "finished": r[name("flows.orders.finished")],
        "in_system": r[name("flows.orders.in_system")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("tasks.pack_order.wait_mean")],
        "end": app.env.now,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for drain in (False, True):
        r = outcomes(drain)
        label = "drain  " if drain else "horizon"
        print(
            f"{label}: ends at {r['end']:7.1f} s, {r['started']} started, "
            f"{r['finished']} finished, {r['in_system']} left, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s"
        )
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions_low_level.py
"""The End Conditions tutorial: a fixed horizon against a drain.

One packer, an order every 1.43 seconds on average (rate 0.7) and 1.5 seconds of
packing, for an hour. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the
counts and the mean wait with a fixed horizon and with a drain at the end. To see only
those lines, run:
python end_conditions_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import itertools
import logging

import simpy

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.7)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)},
)


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    env.stats.flow_started("orders")  # the order enters the shop
    publish(
        {"path_id": path_id, "sim_id": "Shop", "service": "packing", "status": "queued"}
    )
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish(
            {
                "path_id": path_id,
                "sim_id": "Shop",
                "service": "packing",
                "status": "started",
            }
        )
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers, orders):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    try:
        for task_id in itertools.count():
            yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
            key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
            orders.append(env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id)))
    except simpy.Interrupt:
        pass  # no new orders after the hour


def run(drain=False, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=7200)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    orders = []
    source = env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers, orders))
    try:
        env.run(until=3600)  # no new orders after one hour
        if drain:
            # Stop the source, then run until every admitted order has ended
            source.interrupt()
            env.run(until=env.all_of([o for o in orders if o.is_alive]))
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(drain: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour, with or without a drain, and returns the counts and the wait."""
    env = run(drain)
    r = env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.{}".format
    return {
        "started": r[name("flows.orders.started")],
        "finished": r[name("flows.orders.finished")],
        "in_system": r[name("flows.orders.in_system")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("tasks.pack_order.wait_mean")],
        "end": env.now,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for drain in (False, True):
        r = outcomes(drain)
        label = "drain  " if drain else "horizon"
        print(
            f"{label}: ends at {r['end']:7.1f} s, {r['started']} started, "
            f"{r['finished']} finished, {r['in_system']} left, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s"
        )

docs.title: First Simulation
docs.text:
This tutorial models a shop that receives and packs customer orders: one packer, an order every 2 seconds on average, and 1.5 seconds of packing per order. It answers one question: how long does an order wait with one packer?

  • Decision: how many packers the shop needs, which later pages decide.
  • Measures: the wait of each order, from the moment it joins the queue to the moment packing starts.
  • Runs: one run of the first 20 seconds, with the seed 42.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random, and every order takes exactly the same time to pack.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • describe a model as an arrival, a resource and a service time, in YAML, the builder or the low-level API;
  • run it and read the event records it prints;
  • read an order's wait from its queued and started events.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text:
This page builds the first model of the shop: a simulation called Shop with an orders arrival, a packers resource with one unit, a packing service and a pack_order task, and a sink that prints each record. The following pages extend the same model, one idea per page.

Each step shows the code three ways, in tabs: a YAML blueprint, the Builder (SimulationContext) and the Low-level API (DynamicRealtimeEnvironment and SimPy processes). Choose the tab for your preferred API; all code tabs on the site switch to that API. The three build the same simulation and print the same records. Writing a Model explains how they relate.

Look at the order of the parts: orders arrive, wait in the packer queue and take the packer for 1.5 seconds. The simulation prints a record of each step to the console. The arrival loop and the task read their values from the registry. The steps below explain each of these parts.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install the core package, which includes the desflow command, as Installation shows.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint needs only the desflow command. Install it with one of these forms, then run the file:

# With uv, the command alone
uv tool install desflow

# Or with pip
pip install desflow

# Run the blueprint
desflow run first_shop.yaml

A builder model is a Python file, so the Python that runs it must be able to import desflow. uv tool install desflow installs the command only. Run the file with one of these forms:

# With uv, outside a project
uv run --with desflow python first_shop.py

# In a uv project, after `uv add desflow`
uv run python first_shop.py

# After `pip install desflow`
python first_shop.py

The pages that follow show the plain python <file>.py form. Run it with whichever form above you use.

A low-level model is a Python file, so the Python that runs it must be able to import desflow. uv tool install desflow installs the command only. Run the file with one of these forms:

# With uv, outside a project
uv run --with desflow python first_shop_low_level.py

# In a uv project, after `uv add desflow`
uv run python first_shop_low_level.py

# After `pip install desflow`
python first_shop_low_level.py

The pages that follow show the plain python <file>.py form. Run it with whichever form above you use.

docs.title: Describe the Shop
docs.text:
In discrete-event simulation (DES), an entity is a thing that moves through the model, here an order. A resource is what an entity needs and may have to wait for, here the packer. A service time is how long an entity holds the resource, and an arrival process sets when entities appear.

In desflow, these are parameters of one simulation. Its name, the sim_id, is Shop here. The shop has a resource called packers with one unit, a service called packing, and an arrival stream called orders.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:shop
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
  random_seed: 42  # the same arrival times on every run

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

services:
  # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # One order every 2 seconds on average; each arrival spawns pack_order
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py:shop
app = (
    # 1 simulated second = 1 real second; a seed gives the same arrivals every run
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # One order every 2 seconds on average
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
)
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py:shop
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)
SEED = 42  # the same arrival times on every run

Packing is constant, so every order takes 1.5 seconds and only the arrivals are random. The gaps between orders are drawn from an exponential distribution with a mean of 2 seconds (30 orders a minute on average), rate: 0.5. The seed makes those draws the same on every run, so your trace matches the one below; Randomness and Seeds explains it.

The registry holds the model's live values: the settings that can change while the simulation runs. Each value has a path, such as Shop.arrival.orders.rate or Shop.resources.packers.current_cap. A scenario, or a message from outside the simulation, changes a value through its path, and the run goes on with the new value. Live Changes does it on the shop, and Live Parameters explains how.

docs.title: Say What an Order Does
docs.text:
In DES terms an order queues for the packer, seizes it when it is free, is delayed for the service time, and releases the packer. desflow calls this a task. A task publishes three events: queued when the order joins the queue for the packer, started when the packer starts on it, and a finished event when packing ends. The value of the finished event is the task's payload.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:order
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The value of the finished event
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

spawn: pack_order on the arrival, in the step above, starts the task for every order.

docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py:order
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Requests a packer, waits the packing time, releases the packer.
    # The returned dictionary is the value of the finished event.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Waits for the next arrival and returns the new order, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1

@app.task publishes the three events and handles the packer for you. The arrival loop waits for each arrival and starts one pack_order for the order it returns.

docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py:order
def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order: wait for a packer, pack it, release the packer."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish(
        {"path_id": path_id, "sim_id": "Shop", "service": "packing", "status": "queued"}
    )
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish(
            {
                "path_id": path_id,
                "sim_id": "Shop",
                "service": "packing",
                "status": "started",
            }
        )
        service = env.registry.get_config(path_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one pack_order for every arrival, keyed orders-1, orders-2, ..."""
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1

These are SimPy constructs. pack_order is a process: a generator function that the environment runs, pausing at each yield until the event it yielded happens. env.timeout(...) is an event that happens after a delay. packers.request() is an event that happens when a packer is free, and leaving the with block releases the packer. env.process(...) starts a process. SimPy and desflow describes what desflow adds to them.

docs.title: Print the Records
docs.text:
A sink, called an egress, receives every record the simulation publishes. ConsoleEgress prints them; Egress lists the others.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:records
egress:
  - {type: Console}
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py:records
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py:records
SINKS = [ConsoleEgress()]  # passed to env.setup_egress in run below

Every event record carries the order's key, orders-1 for the first order, so all the events of one order can be found together. task names the task, and instance counts the task's runs from 0. Records and Telemetry describes every field.

docs.title: Run It
Test the Model
docs.text:
A blueprint can hold the answers you expect from it. A tests entry names a seed and an end time (both default to the file's own) and the statistics the run must give. desflow test runs each entry once, unpaced and with no sink, so it contacts no service, and reports each statistic that differs:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:tests
tests:
  # Run with: desflow test first_shop.yaml
  - name: seven_orders_in_20_seconds
    expect: {tasks.pack_order.finished: 7}

A builder file reads its tests from a tests.yaml in the same folder, with the same entries.

A low-level script has no desflow test. Test a Model tests it with pytest.

desflow test first_shop.yaml

ok first_shop.yaml: seven_orders_in_20_seconds

Seven orders are packed in the first 20 seconds with the seed 42. A number is compared exactly. {value: 7, within: 1} allows a difference. The seed and the desflow version are part of the answer: after an upgrade, desflow test --fix writes the new numbers, and you read them before you keep them. Test a Model shows more.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
How long does an order wait with one packer? It depends on how many orders are ahead of it, as the same records on a timeline show: each order waits (yellow) until the packer is free, then holds it for 1.5 seconds of packing (blue).

These records come from one run of the first 20 seconds, with the seed 42. orders-1 and orders-2 find the packer free, so their queued and started events have the same time. orders-3 is the first order that has to wait: it is queued at 5.024 and started at 6.434, when orders-2 finishes. It waits 1.410 seconds. orders-4 arrives while orders-3 is waiting and waits longer, 1.684 seconds, because two orders are ahead of it.

So with one packer, an order that arrives while the packer is busy waits until every order ahead of it has been packed. The wait depends on when orders happen to arrive, which is why the next pages measure it over many orders.

A discrete-event simulation keeps a list of future events, ordered by time. It takes the earliest one, moves the clock to its time, and runs what it triggers, which may add new events to the list: an arrival schedules the next arrival, and a start of packing schedules its end 1.5 seconds later. The trace above is that list, read in order. What Is DES? explains the event list in more detail.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A model has entities that arrive, resources they wait for, and service times that hold them. desflow calls the work an entity does a task.
  • A task publishes queued, started and a finished event, and an order's wait is its started time minus its queued time.
  • The simulation clock jumps from one event to the next, so a run gives the same records at any pace.

docs.text:
Full files

"""The First Simulation tutorial: the shop, with the SimulationContext builder.

One packer, orders arriving about every 2 seconds, and 1.5 seconds of packing per
order. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

app = (
    # 1 simulated second = 1 real second; a seed gives the same arrivals every run
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # One order every 2 seconds on average
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Requests a packer, waits the packing time, releases the packer.
    # The returned dictionary is the value of the finished event.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Waits for the next arrival and returns the new order, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1


app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until=20)

"""The First Simulation tutorial: the shop, on the low-level API.

One packer, orders arriving about every 2 seconds, and 1.5 seconds of packing per
order. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)
SEED = 42  # the same arrival times on every run


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order: wait for a packer, pack it, release the packer."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish(
        {"path_id": path_id, "sim_id": "Shop", "service": "packing", "status": "queued"}
    )
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish(
            {
                "path_id": path_id,
                "sim_id": "Shop",
                "service": "packing",
                "status": "started",
            }
        )
        service = env.registry.get_config(path_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one pack_order for every arrival, keyed orders-1, orders-2, ..."""
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1


SINKS = [ConsoleEgress()]  # passed to env.setup_egress in run below


def run(until=20, factor=1.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor, strict=False)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(SINKS)

    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=SEED)

    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

docs.title: Measuring a Run
docs.text:
Most of the pages so far read one number, the mean wait. A run knows much more. This page asks: what does a run tell me?

  • Decision: which numbers to read from a run before acting on it.
  • Measures: five of the numbers the run publishes: the packers' utilisation, the mean queue, the mean and longest wait, and the orders packed.
  • Runs: one run of the busy hour, with the seed 42, starting with an empty shop.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random at 1.8 a second, and the times measured at the bench stand for every packer.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • switch on the built-in statistics at a level;
  • read utilisation, queue length, waits and counts at the end of a run;
  • check the statistics against each other with Little's Law.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds stats: typical, the built-in statistics at the level that includes waits. The model simulates the busy hour with 3 packers from Queues and Capacity, and draws each packing time from 40 times measured at the bench, each equally likely. The model calls this an empirical distribution. Real packing times vary, so these times describe the shop better than the constant 1.5 seconds of the earlier pages; Choosing Inputs explains the distribution and compares it with others.

docs.title: Switch On Statistics
docs.text:
desflow keeps statistics about a run as it goes. It publishes them as telemetry every 10 simulation seconds and once more at the end, so the last value of each statistic is the state at the end of the run. Statistics are off by default, because most runs only generate data. A level switches them on: none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each publishing what the one before it does and more. typical adds each task's mean and maximum wait and service time. Statistics lists what each level adds. Switch on typical:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/measuring_a_run.yaml:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
stats: typical
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run.py:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
.with_stats("typical")
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run_low_level.py:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=10)

The environment keeps the statistics in env.stats. Resources report their own changes. A low-level process has no task for desflow to watch, so the process reports each step itself. It calls env.stats.task_queued, task_started and task_finished with the task's name and instance id, and flow_started and flow_finished when the order enters and leaves the shop. The full file below shows them.

The statistics are telemetry, so they reach every sink, and they can also be read in Python at the end of the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/measuring_a_run.yaml:read
# The statistics are telemetry, so every sink receives them
egress:
  - {type: Console}

Every name has the same form, <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there: desflow run measuring_a_run.yaml, python measuring_a_run.py or python measuring_a_run_low_level.py. The run prints about 24,000 lines, because the console also prints every event. These 15 are the statistics published at the end of the hour. The command keeps only the telemetry records stamped 3600.0:

The statistics mean:

  • utilization_avg 89.98: the packers were busy 89.98% of the time. The utilisation statistics are percentages, while desflow explain and --verify give utilisation as a fraction, 0.9 for 90%.
  • utilization 100.0: all three packers were busy at the end.
  • tasks.pack_order.finished: the orders the task finished.
  • flows.orders.finished: the orders that left the shop. The flow is named after the arrival that started them, orders. With one task the two counts are equal.
  • flows.orders.started: the orders that entered the shop, 6,491.
  • flows.orders.in_system: the 3 orders still in the shop when the hour ended. tasks.pack_order.in_progress gives the same 3.

The names use the spelling utilization, and the text uses "utilisation" for the same thing. The mean wait is 2.01 seconds, over the orders that started packing in this one run with the seed 42. End Conditions shows what a run leaves out when it ends.

docs.title: Counts and Averages Over Time
docs.text:
The statistics are of two kinds. A count, such as finished, adds one for each order. An average over time, also called a time-weighted average, such as utilization_avg or queue_length_avg, weighs each value by how long it lasted. Look at the area under the number of busy packers:

desflow adds the area every time the value changes, so the average is exact at any moment. A reading taken now and then, such as every 10 seconds, sees only the value at that instant. The queue in the first five minutes of the hour shows the difference:

The queue rises and falls many times between two readings, and a handful of readings can land on high points by chance. Here the readings average 2.33 orders and the average over time for the same five minutes is 2.30 orders. They are close in this run, but the readings only estimate the average, while the average over time is exact.

docs.title: Wait and Service
docs.text:
The time each order spends in the shop has two parts, both measured from the task's own events:

  • wait runs from queued to started: the time spent waiting for a packer;
  • service runs from started to the finished event: the time spent being packed.

service_mean is 1.50 seconds and service_max is 2.7 seconds. The 40 measured times have the same mean and the same longest time, so the model draws what it was given. wait_max is 11.94 seconds: one order waited almost six times as long as the average one.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
What does a run tell me? One run of the busy hour, with the seed 42, the measured packing times and no warm-up, tells you that:

  • the packers were busy 90.0% of the time on average;
  • the queue held 3.62 orders on average;
  • an order waited 2.01 seconds on average and 11.94 seconds at most;
  • 6,488 orders were packed.

The numbers check each other. Little's Law says that the average number waiting equals the rate at which orders arrive times the average time each waits. 6,488 orders in 3,600 seconds is 1.80 a second, and 1.80 × 2.01 = 3.62, which matches queue_length_avg, 3.62. The utilisation checks the same way: 1.80 orders a second × 1.50 seconds ÷ 3 packers = 0.90. A set of statistics that fails a check like this one points to a mistake in the model or in how it is read, as Checking and Validating explains.

Statistics describes how each one is computed, and the Statistics reference lists every name each level publishes.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Statistics are off by default. A level, such as typical, switches them on, and the run publishes them as telemetry.
  • An average over time weighs each value by how long it lasted, so it is exact, unlike readings taken now and then.
  • Statistics that fail a check such as Little's Law point to a mistake in the model or in how it is read.
