# The mean wait of each task and the picker's busy share, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/competing_resources_low_level.py:watch
# The mean wait of each task and the picker's busy share, at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)

docs.title: One Order of Acquisition
docs.text: Two orders that each hold one resource and wait for the other wait for ever: a deadlock. If a picking task held the picker and waited for the bench while a wrapping task held the bench and waited for the picker, both could stop. SimPy runs such a model, and its run ends with no error when the tasks wait. desflow checks the order when the model loads. A model whose tasks acquire two resources in opposite orders still loads, and the run logs one WARNING that names both places. A seize counts as holding a resource until its release. A keep for a task that requests the same resource in a wait is refused, because that wait would queue behind the unit it keeps. Here every order goes picker first, then bench, so there is nothing to warn about.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
What does holding the picker while waiting for the bench cost? Each figure here is a mean from one run of the hour with the seed 42.

  • When the picker puts the order down and goes back, orders wait 0.35 seconds for the picker and 8.43 seconds for the bench, 8.78 seconds in all.
  • When the picker stays with the order, the wait moves to the picker. Orders wait 14.23 seconds for it and only 1.11 seconds for the bench, 15.34 seconds in all. The picker is then busy 85.2% of the time instead of 40.4%, most of it standing by the bench:

Each tab prints both: the picker's busy share and the mean waits, first with the picker freed, then with it kept.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

The first run is the shop without the handoff. competing_resources_free.yaml is competing_resources.yaml without its keep: [picker] line:

docs/snippets/yaml/competing_resources_free.yaml:tasks
tasks:
  pick_order:
    service: picking
    resource: picker
    payload: {event_type: order_picked}
    next: pack_order
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: bench
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# Without the handoff: the mean waits and the pickers' utilisation
desflow run competing_resources_free.yaml --stdout | grep -E '(pick_order|pack_order)\.wait_mean"|picker\.utilization_avg"' | tail -3
# With the handoff
desflow run competing_resources.yaml --stdout | grep -E '(pick_order|pack_order)\.wait_mean"|picker\.utilization_avg"' | tail -3


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.resources.picker.utilization_avg","value":40.38888888888891}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pick_order.wait_mean","value":0.34588107621855696}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":8.430633032800593}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.resources.picker.utilization_avg","value":85.23420399919257}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pick_order.wait_mean","value":14.229028340474315}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":1.1103379257021557}


python competing_resources.py 2>/dev/null

frees the picker: wait to pick   0.35 s, to pack  8.43 s, picker busy 40.4%
keeps the picker: wait to pick  14.23 s, to pack  1.11 s, picker busy 85.2%

python competing_resources_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

frees the picker: wait to pick   0.35 s, to pack  8.43 s, picker busy 40.4%
keeps the picker: wait to pick  14.23 s, to pack  1.11 s, picker busy 85.2%

Each order brings 2 seconds of packing on average and arrives every 2.5 seconds on average, so the bench is busy 2 ÷ 2.5 = 80% of the time and the picker 1 ÷ 2.5 = 40%. The bench is the busier of the two, the bottleneck. When the picker waits at the bench, it spends its own time in the bench's queue. So the picker is busy longer than its work needs, and the next order waits for it. Releasing a resource as soon as it is no longer needed keeps the waits where the work is.

Queueing Basics explains utilisation. Several Resources describes several resources, handoffs and the order rule.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A task that holds a resource while it waits for another keeps that resource busy without work.
  • The wait then moves to the resource that is held, and the next order waits for it.
  • Release a resource as soon as it is no longer needed, unless the work requires it to stay.

"""The Competing Resources tutorial: an order keeps the picker until it is on the bench.

One picker, one packing bench, and an order every 2.5 seconds on average. Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the waits and the picker's busy share
with and without the handoff at the end. To see only those lines, run:
python competing_resources.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(keep: bool = True) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop; with `keep`, an order keeps the picker until it is on the bench."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("picker", current_cap=1, max_cap=2)
        .add_resource("bench", current_cap=1, max_cap=2)
        .add_service("picking", dist="constant", value=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.4)
        # The mean wait of each task and the picker's busy share, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(
        service_id="picking",
        resource_id="picker",
        # The picker carries the order and stays with it until it is on the bench
        keep=["picker"] if keep else None,
        next="pack_order",
    )
    def pick_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_picked"}

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="bench")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pick_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def outcomes(keep: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns each task's mean wait and the picker's busy share."""
    app = shop(keep)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    r = app.env.stats.readings()
    return {
        "pick_wait": r["Shop.stats.tasks.pick_order.wait_mean"],
        "pack_wait": r["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"],
        "picker_busy": r["Shop.stats.resources.picker.utilization_avg"],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for keep in (False, True):
        r = outcomes(keep)
        label = "keeps the picker" if keep else "frees the picker"
        print(
            f"{label}: wait to pick {r['pick_wait']:6.2f} s, to pack "
            f"{r['pack_wait']:5.2f} s, picker busy {r['picker_busy']:4.1f}%"
        )

"""The Competing Resources tutorial: an order keeps the picker until it is on the bench.

One picker, one packing bench, and an order every 2.5 seconds on average. Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the waits and the picker's busy share
with and without the handoff at the end. To see only those lines, run:
python competing_resources_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import itertools
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.4)},
    service={
        "picking": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1),
        "packing": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5),
    },
    resources={
        "picker": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=2),
        "bench": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=2),
    },
)


def step(env, sampler, key, task, task_id, service):
    """The publish and service-time helpers of one task instance."""
    path_id = f"Shop.service.{service}"

    def status(state):
        value = {
            "path_id": path_id,
            "sim_id": "Shop",
            "service": service,
            "status": state,
        }
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    def finished(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    return status, finished, lambda: sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id))


def pick_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, keep):
    status, finished, duration = step(
        env, sampler, key, "pick_order", task_id, "picking"
    )
    status("queued")
    env.stats.task_queued("pick_order", task_id)
    picker = shop["picker"].request()
    yield picker
    status("started")
    env.stats.task_started("pick_order", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(duration())
    finished({"event_type": "order_picked"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pick_order", task_id)
    if not keep:
        shop["picker"].release(picker)
        picker = None
    # With keep, the picker carries the order and stays with it until it is on the bench
    yield from pack_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, picker)


def pack_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, picker):
    status, finished, duration = step(
        env, sampler, key, "pack_order", task_id, "packing"
    )
    status("queued")
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with shop["bench"].request() as bench:
        yield bench
        status("started")
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        if picker is not None:
            shop["picker"].release(picker)  # the order is on the bench
        yield env.timeout(duration())
        finished({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")


def order_generator(env, sampler, shop, keep):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for task_id in itertools.count():
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pick_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, keep))


def run(keep=True, until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # The mean wait of each task and the picker's busy share, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    shop = {
        "picker": DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "picker"),
        "bench": DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "bench"),
    }
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), shop, keep))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(keep: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns each task's mean wait and the picker's busy share."""
    r = run(keep).stats.readings()
    return {
        "pick_wait": r["Shop.stats.tasks.pick_order.wait_mean"],
        "pack_wait": r["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"],
        "picker_busy": r["Shop.stats.resources.picker.utilization_avg"],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for keep in (False, True):
        r = outcomes(keep)
        label = "keeps the picker" if keep else "frees the picker"
        print(
            f"{label}: wait to pick {r['pick_wait']:6.2f} s, to pack "
            f"{r['pack_wait']:5.2f} s, picker busy {r['picker_busy']:4.1f}%"
        )

docs.title: Filtered Inventory
docs.text:
The shop now sells shirts in three sizes: small, medium and large. Shirts of every size go on one shelf. A new shirt arrives every 10 seconds on average, and a new order also arrives every 10 seconds on average. Each order is for one shirt of a given size. A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes. Half the orders are for medium shirts, but only 4 shirts in 10 are medium. This page asks: which waiting order can use the shirt that arrives, and which orders go unfilled?

  • Decision: whether the shop's mix of shirt sizes is right for its orders.
  • Measures: the orders filled and cancelled for each size, and the shirts left on the shelf.
  • Runs: one run of a working day of 8 hours, with the seed 42, covering only taking shirts from the shelf: packing is left out.
  • Assumptions: shirts and orders of each size arrive at random, each at a steady rate.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • hold items of several kinds on one shelf, in a store;
  • take only an item that matches the order, with a filter;
  • see which orders go unfilled when one kind is short.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a shelf store, and a filter on the order's get that picks a shirt of the order's size. The order task has no resource: it waits only for its shirt, with the Patience of 10 minutes covering that wait.

docs.title: One Shelf of Items
docs.text:
A store holds items, and each item is a value of its own. Here each shirt is a mapping such as {size: M}, and a restock task puts it on the shelf. Stores and Containers describes stores. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:shelf
stores:
  # Shirts of every size on one shelf, each item a mapping such as {size: M}
  shelf: {current_cap: 1000, max_cap: 1000}
docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory.py:shelf
# Shirts of every size on one shelf, each item a mapping such as {"size": "M"}
app.add_store("shelf", current_cap=1000, max_cap=1000)
docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory_low_level.py:shelf
# Shirts of every size on one shelf, each item a mapping such as {"size": "M"}
stores={"shelf": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1000, max_cap=1000)},

The shirts and the orders arrive from six arrivals, one per size, each with a size attribute:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:arrivals
# A shirt every 10 seconds on average: 3 in 10 small, 4 medium, 3 large
shirts_s:
  dist: exponential
  rate: 0.03
  spawn: restock
  attributes: {size: S}
shirts_m:
  dist: exponential
  rate: 0.04
  spawn: restock
  attributes: {size: M}
shirts_l:
  dist: exponential
  rate: 0.03
  spawn: restock
  attributes: {size: L}
# An order every 10 seconds on average: a quarter small, half medium, a quarter large
orders_s:
  dist: exponential
  rate: 0.025
  spawn: take_shirt
  attributes: {size: S}
orders_m:
  dist: exponential
  rate: 0.05
  spawn: take_shirt
  attributes: {size: M}
orders_l:
  dist: exponential
  rate: 0.025
  spawn: take_shirt
  attributes: {size: L}
docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory.py:arrivals
for size, rate in SHIRTS.items():
    name = f"shirts_{size.lower()}"
    app.add_arrival(name, dist="exponential", rate=rate, attributes={"size": size})
for size, rate in ORDERS.items():
    name = f"orders_{size.lower()}"
    app.add_arrival(name, dist="exponential", rate=rate, attributes={"size": size})

SHIRTS and ORDERS map each size to its rate, as the full file shows.

docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory_low_level.py:arrivals
arrival={
    **{
        f"shirts_{s.lower()}": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=r)
        for s, r in SHIRTS.items()
    },
    **{
        f"orders_{s.lower()}": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=r)
        for s, r in ORDERS.items()
    },
},

SHIRTS and ORDERS map each size to its rate. Each arrival process passes its size to the task, as the full file shows.

A shirt becomes an item of the shelf when its restock task puts it there. Each API builds the item from the shirt's size in its own way:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:restock
restock:
  # The shirt goes on the shelf, as a mapping with its size
  put: {store: shelf}
  payload: {}
  attributes: [size]

A put adds the task's finished payload as the item. The payload is empty, and attributes: [size] adds the arrival's size to it, so the item is {size: M}.

docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory.py:restock
# The shirt goes on the shelf, as a mapping with its size
@app.task(put={"store": "shelf"})
def restock(task_id: int, entity):
    return {"size": entity.attributes["size"]}

The item put on the shelf is the dict the function returns.

docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory_low_level.py:restock
def restock(env, shelf, key, size, task_id):
    """The shirt goes on the shelf, as a mapping with its size."""
    yield shelf.put({"size": size})
    env.publish_event(key, {"size": size}, task="restock", instance=task_id)

The item is the argument of shelf.put.

docs.title: Take the Right Item
docs.text:
A plain get takes the oldest item, whatever it is. A get with a filter takes the oldest item the filter accepts and waits while none does. In SimPy this is a FilterStore, whose get takes a function of the item. In desflow the filter is a condition. In it, item.<field> reads a field of the shirt on offer. The condition can also read every name that other conditions read, such as attr.size for the size the order is for:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:take
take_shirt:
  # Takes the oldest shirt of the order's own size; waits while there is none
  get: {store: shelf, filter: item.size == attr.size}
  # A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes
  patience: 10 min
  # Adds the shirt the get took to the finished event
  item_field: shirt
  payload: {event_type: order_filled}

item_field: shirt adds the shirt the get took to the finished event's payload under the key shirt, as id_field adds the task id under the key it names (YAML Keys lists both).

docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory.py:take
@app.task(
    # Takes the oldest shirt of the order's own size; waits while there is none
    get={"store": "shelf", "filter": "item.size == attr.size"},
    # A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes
    patience="10 min",
)
def take_shirt(task_id: int, item):
    # `item` is the shirt the get took
    return {"event_type": "order_filled", "shirt": item}

The builder also takes a function of the item, such as "filter": lambda shirt: shirt["size"] == "M".

docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory_low_level.py:take
def take_shirt(env, shelf, key, size, task_id):
    arrival = key.rsplit("-", 1)[0]

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="take_shirt", instance=task_id)

    publish({"status": "queued"})
    env.stats.flow_started(arrival)
    env.stats.task_queued("take_shirt", task_id)
    # Takes the oldest shirt of the order's own size; waits while there is none
    get = shelf.get(filter=lambda shirt: shirt["size"] == size)
    # A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes
    result = yield get | env.timeout(PATIENCE)
    if get not in result:
        get.cancel()  # out of the queue, so it never takes a shirt later
        publish({"status": "reneged"})
        env.stats.task_reneged("take_shirt", task_id)
        env.stats.flow_ended(arrival)
        return
    publish({"status": "started"})
    env.stats.task_started("take_shirt", task_id)
    publish({"event_type": "order_filled", "shirt": get.value})
    env.stats.task_finished("take_shirt", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished(arrival)

shelf.get(filter=...) is SimPy's FilterStore.get. Cancelling a get that has not succeeded takes it out of the queue, so it never takes a shirt later.

When a shirt arrives, it is offered to the waiting orders one at a time, oldest first, and the first order whose filter accepts it takes it. A medium order waiting at the front does not stop a small order behind it from taking a small shirt, as it would if all orders waited in one line for the next shirt.

patience covers the wait for the get, as it covers a wait for a resource. A get that gives up takes nothing later: the shirt that would have filled it stays on the shelf for the next order.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
Which waiting order can use the shirt that arrives? The oldest order of the shirt's size, and no other. In one run of 8 hours with the seed 42, 199 orders are cancelled: 167 medium, 24 large and 8 small. Medium orders are half of all orders, but medium shirts are only 4 in 10:

Each tab prints the counts:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

The blueprint publishes its statistics once, at the end of the 8 hours:

docs/snippets/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:stats
# The counts of each arrival's orders, published once, at the end of the 8 hours
stats: {level: basic, interval: 8 h}

# Orders finished for each size, and the orders that gave up waiting
desflow run filtered_inventory.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'orders_[sml]\.finished"|take_shirt\.reneged"' | tail -4


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.take_shirt.reneged","value":199}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders_s.finished","value":711}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders_m.finished","value":1181}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders_l.finished","value":779}

Each flows.orders_<size>.finished is the number of filled orders of that size. tasks.take_shirt.reneged counts the cancelled orders of every size together. A cancelled order leaves its flow without finishing it, so a size's cancelled orders are its flow's started minus finished minus in_system, the orders still waiting at the end. For medium orders that is 1,383 − 1,181 − 35 = 167, most of the 199 cancelled orders.

The started and waiting counts of the medium orders, and the shirts left on the shelf, come from the same run:

desflow run filtered_inventory.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'orders_m\.(started|in_system)"|shelf\.level"'

{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.stores.shelf.level","value":197}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders_m.started","value":1383}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders_m.in_system","value":35}
docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory.py:stats
# The counts of each arrival's orders, published once, at the end of the 8 hours
app.with_stats("basic", interval=8 * 3600)

The script reads the same statistics with app.env.stats.readings(). A cancelled order is the flow's started minus finished minus in_system:

python filtered_inventory.py 2>/dev/null

size S:  719 started,  711 filled,  0 waiting,   8 cancelled
size M: 1383 started, 1181 filled, 35 waiting, 167 cancelled
size L:  803 started,  779 filled,  0 waiting,  24 cancelled
shirts left on the shelf: 197
docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory_low_level.py:stats
# The counts of each arrival's orders, published once, at the end of the 8 hours
env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=8 * 3600)

A low-level model reports its own events to the statistics, as take_shirt does with env.stats.flow_started, task_reneged, flow_ended and flow_finished. The script then reads run().stats.readings():

python filtered_inventory_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

size S:  719 started,  711 filled,  0 waiting,   8 cancelled
size M: 1383 started, 1181 filled, 35 waiting, 167 cancelled
size L:  803 started,  779 filled,  0 waiting,  24 cancelled
shirts left on the shelf: 197

A filtered store works like one shelf with a separate queue for each kind of item. Orders and shirts of each size arrive at their own rates, on average:

Size An order arrives A shirt arrives Small every 40 seconds (1.5 a minute, rate: 0.025) every 33 seconds (1.8 a minute, rate: 0.03) Medium every 20 seconds (3 a minute, rate: 0.05) every 25 seconds (2.4 a minute, rate: 0.04) Large every 40 seconds (1.5 a minute, rate: 0.025) every 33 seconds (1.8 a minute, rate: 0.03)

Medium orders outnumber medium shirts all day: they ask for 0.05 shirts a second and get 0.04, a utilisation of 1.25. So their queue would grow without end if customers did not cancel after 10 minutes. There are more small and large shirts than orders of those sizes, so nearly every small and large order is filled before its customer cancels. The few that cancel (8 small and 24 large in this run) are orders that waited for a shirt of their size for more than 10 minutes, because shirts arrive at random times. The shirts left over, 197 at the end of the run, wait on the shelf, which has room for 1,000.

The mix of sizes is therefore not right for the orders: the shop should stock more medium shirts, and fewer small and large ones, until medium shirts are as large a share of the deliveries as medium orders are of the orders.

SimPy and desflow compares stores and containers with SimPy's. Stores and Containers describes filters and cancelled gets.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A filtered store works like one shelf with a separate queue for each kind of item.
  • A kind whose orders outnumber its items has a queue that grows, even when the shelf holds other items.
  • Patience on the wait ends that growth, at the cost of cancelled orders.

docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory.py
"""The Filtered Inventory tutorial: each order waits for a shirt of its own size.

Shirts of three sizes arrive on one shelf, and orders of three sizes take them.
Every record is printed to the terminal. The script then prints, for each size, how
many orders started, were filled, were still waiting and were cancelled, and the shirts left
on the shelf. To see only those lines, run:
python filtered_inventory.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

# A shirt every 10 seconds on average: 3 in 10 small, 4 medium, 3 large
SHIRTS = {"S": 0.03, "M": 0.04, "L": 0.03}
# An order every 10 seconds on average: a quarter small, half medium, a quarter large
ORDERS = {"S": 0.025, "M": 0.05, "L": 0.025}


def shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop with one shelf of shirts and orders of three sizes."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42).add_egress(
        ConsoleEgress()
    )
    # The counts of each arrival's orders, published once, at the end of the 8 hours
    app.with_stats("basic", interval=8 * 3600)
    # Shirts of every size on one shelf, each item a mapping such as {"size": "M"}
    app.add_store("shelf", current_cap=1000, max_cap=1000)
    for size, rate in SHIRTS.items():
        name = f"shirts_{size.lower()}"
        app.add_arrival(name, dist="exponential", rate=rate, attributes={"size": size})
    for size, rate in ORDERS.items():
        name = f"orders_{size.lower()}"
        app.add_arrival(name, dist="exponential", rate=rate, attributes={"size": size})

    # The shirt goes on the shelf, as a mapping with its size
    @app.task(put={"store": "shelf"})
    def restock(task_id: int, entity):
        return {"size": entity.attributes["size"]}


    @app.task(
        # Takes the oldest shirt of the order's own size; waits while there is none
        get={"store": "shelf", "filter": "item.size == attr.size"},
        # A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes
        patience="10 min",
    )
    def take_shirt(task_id: int, item):
        # `item` is the shirt the get took
        return {"event_type": "order_filled", "shirt": item}


    def spawn(arrival: str, task, name: str):
        def loop(context: SimulationContext):
            while True:
                entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)
                context.spawn(task(context.next_instance(name), entity=entity))

        app.arrival_loop(arrival)(loop)

    for size in SHIRTS:
        spawn(f"shirts_{size.lower()}", restock, "restock")
    for size in ORDERS:
        spawn(f"orders_{size.lower()}", take_shirt, "take_shirt")
    return app


def outcomes() -> dict:
    """Runs eight hours; returns each size's order counts and the shirts left."""
    app = shop()
    app.run(until="8 h")
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    result: dict = {}
    for size in ORDERS:
        flow = f"Shop.stats.flows.orders_{size.lower()}"
        started = readings[f"{flow}.started"]
        filled = readings[f"{flow}.finished"]
        waiting = readings[f"{flow}.in_system"]
        # A cancelled order leaves its flow without finishing it
        result[size] = (started, filled, waiting, started - filled - waiting)
    result["left"] = readings["Shop.stats.stores.shelf.level"]
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = outcomes()
    for size in ORDERS:
        started, filled, waiting, cancelled = result[size]
        print(
            f"size {size}: {started:4} started, {filled:4} filled, "
            f"{waiting:2} waiting, {cancelled:3} cancelled"
        )
    print(f"shirts left on the shelf: {result['left']}")
docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory_low_level.py
"""The Filtered Inventory tutorial: each order waits for a shirt of its own size.

Shirts of three sizes arrive on one shelf, and orders of three sizes take them.
Every record is printed to the terminal. The script then prints, for each size, how
many orders started, were filled, were still waiting and were cancelled, and the shirts left
on the shelf. To see only those lines, run:
python filtered_inventory_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import itertools
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicStore,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

# A shirt every 10 seconds on average: 3 in 10 small, 4 medium, 3 large
SHIRTS = {"S": 0.03, "M": 0.04, "L": 0.03}
# An order every 10 seconds on average: a quarter small, half medium, a quarter large
ORDERS = {"S": 0.025, "M": 0.05, "L": 0.025}
PATIENCE = 600  # a customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={
        **{
            f"shirts_{s.lower()}": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=r)
            for s, r in SHIRTS.items()
        },
        **{
            f"orders_{s.lower()}": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=r)
            for s, r in ORDERS.items()
        },
    },
    # Shirts of every size on one shelf, each item a mapping such as {"size": "M"}
    stores={"shelf": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1000, max_cap=1000)},
)


def restock(env, shelf, key, size, task_id):
    """The shirt goes on the shelf, as a mapping with its size."""
    yield shelf.put({"size": size})
    env.publish_event(key, {"size": size}, task="restock", instance=task_id)


def take_shirt(env, shelf, key, size, task_id):
    arrival = key.rsplit("-", 1)[0]

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="take_shirt", instance=task_id)

    publish({"status": "queued"})
    env.stats.flow_started(arrival)
    env.stats.task_queued("take_shirt", task_id)
    # Takes the oldest shirt of the order's own size; waits while there is none
    get = shelf.get(filter=lambda shirt: shirt["size"] == size)
    # A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes
    result = yield get | env.timeout(PATIENCE)
    if get not in result:
        get.cancel()  # out of the queue, so it never takes a shirt later
        publish({"status": "reneged"})
        env.stats.task_reneged("take_shirt", task_id)
        env.stats.flow_ended(arrival)
        return
    publish({"status": "started"})
    env.stats.task_started("take_shirt", task_id)
    publish({"event_type": "order_filled", "shirt": get.value})
    env.stats.task_finished("take_shirt", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished(arrival)


def generator(env, sampler, shelf, arrival, size, task, ids):
    gap = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.arrival.{arrival}")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(task(env, shelf, f"{arrival}-{number}", size, next(ids)))


def run(until=8 * 3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # The counts of each arrival's orders, published once, at the end of the 8 hours
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=8 * 3600)
    shelf = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "shelf")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    restocks, takes = itertools.count(), itertools.count()
    for size in SHIRTS:
        arrival = f"shirts_{size.lower()}"
        env.process(generator(env, sampler, shelf, arrival, size, restock, restocks))
    for size in ORDERS:
        arrival = f"orders_{size.lower()}"
        env.process(generator(env, sampler, shelf, arrival, size, take_shirt, takes))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes() -> dict:
    """Runs eight hours; returns each size's order counts and the shirts left."""
    readings = run().stats.readings()
    result: dict = {}
    for size in ORDERS:
        flow = f"Shop.stats.flows.orders_{size.lower()}"
        started = readings[f"{flow}.started"]
        filled = readings[f"{flow}.finished"]
        waiting = readings[f"{flow}.in_system"]
        # A cancelled order leaves its flow without finishing it
        result[size] = (started, filled, waiting, started - filled - waiting)
    result["left"] = readings["Shop.stats.stores.shelf.level"]
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = outcomes()
    for size in ORDERS:
        started, filled, waiting, cancelled = result[size]
        print(
            f"size {size}: {started:4} started, {filled:4} filled, "
            f"{waiting:2} waiting, {cancelled:3} cancelled"
        )
    print(f"shirts left on the shelf: {result['left']}")

docs.title: A Flow of Tasks
docs.text:
Until now an order was one task: it was packed and left. A real order is picked from the shelves, packed and shipped. Sometimes an item is out of stock, and sometimes a parcel fails its check and is packed again. This page asks: how do orders move through pick, pack and ship?

  • Decision: how much work to plan for beyond one pick and one pack per order.
  • Measures: two shares: how many orders go to backorder, and how many parcels are packed again.
  • Runs: one run of an hour with the seed 42, from an order's arrival to its shipment, with the supplier modelled only as a delay.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random, each picking time is equally likely to be anywhere from 1 to 3 seconds, and packing always takes 1.5 seconds.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • chain tasks so an order is picked, packed and shipped;
  • route a share of the orders to backorder or back to packing;
  • carry an attribute, such as express, through the flow.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text:
This page adds three tasks in a row: pick_order, pack_order and ship_order. It also adds a backorder delay for an order picked while the shelf of boxes from Stock is empty, and an express attribute that each order carries. The shop is set up as follows:

  • It has two pickers and two packers.
  • A regular order arrives every 2.5 seconds on average (24 a minute, rate: 0.4), and an express order every 10 seconds (6 a minute, rate: 0.1).
  • A delivery of 53 boxes comes every 100 seconds, a little more than the orders take.
  • Picking time is uniform from 1 to 3 seconds only to keep the example short. Common Mistakes explains why a real study fits a distribution to measured times instead, as Choosing Inputs does.

Look at the flow first:

docs.title: Chain the Tasks
docs.text:
Choosing where an entity goes next is called routing. In desflow a task names what follows it with next. Tasks and Processes describes tasks. next takes one of three forms:

  • a task name, which always leads there;
  • a list of when rules, each a condition and a task: the first rule that holds wins, and default catches the rest;
  • weights, which Rework shows.

A task with no next ends the order's flow. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:chain
pick_order:
  service: picking
  resource: pickers
  payload: {event_type: order_picked}
  # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
  next:
    when:
      - {condition: "level.stock == 0", task: backorder}
    default: pack_order

Here the arrival loop passes the context to each task after its id. A task started by next receives the same arguments as the task before it. So every task function in the flow declares context.

docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:chain
# The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
@app.task(
    service_id="picking",
    resource_id="pickers",
    next={
        "when": [{"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    },
)
def pick_order(task_id: int, context: SimulationContext):
    return {"event_type": "order_picked"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:chain
# The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
"pick_order": Router(
    {
        "when": [{"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
),

A Router takes the same rules as next and returns the name of the task to start. When a task finishes, its process asks the router and runs the next task with yield from, in the same process and the same step, with the same entity:

docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:next
entity.attributes.update(SETS.get(name, {}))
upstream = Upstream(task_id, entity.key, entity.attributes, finished)
following = ROUTES[name].choose(upstream, env, levels={"stock": shop["stock"]})
if following is None:
    env.stats.flow_finished(entity.arrival)  # the order leaves the shop
    return
instance = next(counters[following])
yield from task(env, sampler, shop, following, entity, instance, counters)

In SimPy terms, yield from runs a generator inside the current process, so the next task is the next statement of one process. A process that started the next task with env.process(...) would begin it in a later step, and at a tie it would ask for a unit after the processes already started. SimPy and desflow describes processes.

The rule reads level.stock, the level of the container stock, at the moment picking finishes. Stores and Containers describes containers. Each name in a condition says where its value comes from: level. for a store or container, attr. for the entity's attributes, payload. for the finished task's payload, and registry["..."] for a live parameter. Task Flow lists everything a condition can use.

Every event of every task carries the order's key, orders-1, so one order can be followed through its whole flow. task names the task, and instance numbers its runs. Each task has one counter, shared by its arrivals and by next, so a re-pick after a backorder gets a new id. In the full builder file the arrival loops take the id from context.next_instance("pick_order"), and the low-level file keeps one counters entry per task.

docs.title: Out of Stock
docs.text:
An order picked while the shelf is empty waits for the supplier for a minute, then is picked again. The wait uses no picker or packer, so backorder has a service and no resource: a timed step. It publishes started at once, with no queued event, waits the sampled time, and publishes its finished event:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:backorder
backorder:
  # A timed step: a service and no resource, so it starts at once
  service: supplying
  payload: {event_type: order_backordered}
  # Applied to the order's attributes when the step finishes
  set: {backordered: 1}
  next: pick_order
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:backorder
# A timed step: a service and no resource, so it starts at once. `set` is applied
# to the order's attributes when the step finishes.
@app.task(service_id="supplying", set={"backordered": 1}, next="pick_order")
def backorder(task_id: int, context: SimulationContext):
    return {"event_type": "order_backordered"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:backorder
"backorder": Router("pick_order"),
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:set
# Applied to the order's attributes when the step finishes
SETS = {"backorder": {"backordered": 1}}

next: pick_order sends the order back to an earlier task. A route back is allowed anywhere in a flow.

docs.title: Rework
docs.text:
One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again. Sending work back to a task it has passed is called rework. weights chooses the next task at random, in proportion to the weights. A weight of infinity or true is refused when the blueprint loads. It draws from the routing task's own random number stream, route.pack_order. So a seeded run repeats, and the choice does not change any other draw:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:rework
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  get: {container: stock, amount: 1}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  # One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again
  next:
    weights: {ship_order: 95, pack_order: 5}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:rework
# One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1},
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 95, "pack_order": 5}},
)
def pack_order(task_id: int, context: SimulationContext):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:rework
# One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again; the generator is set
# in run below
"pack_order": Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 95, "pack_order": 5}}),

The low-level router needs a generator to draw from: ROUTES["pack_order"].rng = sampler.generator("route.pack_order") in run, the stream the builder uses.

docs.title: Carry Attributes
docs.text:
An order is an entity with attributes: values it carries from task to task, such as whether it is express. The arrival gives each new entity its starting attributes, and set on a task changes them when the task finishes, as backorder does with backordered: 1:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:attributes
arrivals:
  # Each order starts with the attributes given here, read as attr.<name>
  orders:
    dist: exponential
    rate: 0.4
    spawn: pick_order
    attributes: {express: 0}
  express:
    dist: exponential
    rate: 0.1
    spawn: pick_order
    attributes: {express: 1}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:attributes
# Each order starts with the attributes given here, read as attr.<name>
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.4, attributes={"express": 0})
app.add_arrival("express", dist="exponential", rate=0.1, attributes={"express": 1})
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:attributes
# Each order starts with the attributes given here, read as attr.<name>
ATTRIBUTES = {"orders": {"express": 0}, "express": {"express": 1}}

Entity(key, arrival, attributes) is the order, created by the arrival process; the full file below shows it.

Attributes are not published. A condition reads them as attr.express, and a payload includes them only when it names them. ship_order names express and backordered, so its finished event carries both. This is orders-851, which was picked while the shelf was empty, backordered, picked again and packed twice. Every tab prints its records to the terminal, so grep finds the order's lines:

docs.title: Networks and Bottlenecks
docs.text:
A shop with several tasks is a network: each task's rate comes from the tasks before it. This version of the shop checks every packed order with one checker, and sends one order in ten back to be packed again. A weight in next.weights is a number or an expression read when the task finishes, such as attr.w, registry[...], level.<store> or t, with no bare name. The draw is one number from route.<task>. A result below 0, or text that is not a number, fails the run with the weight's name, and weights that add up to 0 fail the run. desflow explain makes the cumulative shares once, for numbers only, and gives no shares for expression weights:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/queues_network.yaml:network
arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.6, spawn: pack_order}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}
  checking: {dist: exponential, rate: 2.5}  # 0.4 s on average

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}
  checkers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    next: check_order
  check_order:
    service: checking
    resource: checkers
    payload: {event_type: order_checked}
    # Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
    next:
      weights: {ship_order: 9, pack_order: 1}
  ship_order:
    payload: {event_type: order_shipped}
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity.py:network
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.6, spawn="pack_order")
app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
app.add_service("checking", dist="exponential", rate=2.5)  # 0.4 s on average
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=4, max_cap=10)
app.add_resource("checkers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4)

@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", next="check_order")
def pack_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

# Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="checking",
    resource_id="checkers",
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}},
)
def check_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_checked"}

@app.task()
def ship_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_shipped"}

# print(render_terminal(app.analyze())) prints what desflow explain prints
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity_low_level.py:network
NETWORK = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.6)},
    service={
        "packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5),
        # One check takes 0.4 s on average
        "checking": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=2.5),
    },
    resources={
        "packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=4, max_cap=10),
        "checkers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4),
    },
)
# Each task's service and resource, and the task after it
STEPS = {
    "pack_order": ("packing", "packers", Router("check_order")),
    # Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
    "check_order": (
        "checking",
        "checkers",
        Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}}),
    ),
    "ship_order": (None, None, Router(None)),
}


def step(env, sampler, shop, name, entity, counters):
    """One task of an order, then the task its router chooses."""
    service, resource, router = STEPS[name]
    task_id = next(counters[name])
    if resource is None:
        env.stats.task_finished(name, task_id)
    else:
        env.stats.task_queued(name, task_id)
        with shop[resource].request() as request:
            yield request
            env.stats.task_started(name, task_id)
            config = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.service.{service}")
            yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(config))
        env.stats.task_finished(name, task_id)
    following = router.choose(Upstream(task_id, entity, {}, {}), env)
    if following is None:
        env.stats.flow_finished("orders")
    else:
        yield from step(env, sampler, shop, following, entity, counters)

Router is the object that chooses the task after a finished one, from the same next rule a blueprint uses: a name, when rules or weights. Upstream is what the finished task hands it: the instance id, the entity key, the entity's attributes and the payload. Here no condition reads them, so the router gets an empty Upstream with the entity. counters gives each task's instance numbers, counting from 0. flow_finished tells the statistics that the order has left the shop.

desflow explain does not support low-level models. It reads which arrival starts which task and which resource each task uses, and a low-level model does not declare those links: its SimPy code makes them as it runs.

Every packed order is checked. Packing receives the new orders, 1.6 a second, and also the tenth of the checked orders that come back. Call the rate into packing x: then x = 1.6 + 0.1 × x, which gives x = 1.6 ÷ 0.9 = 1.778 orders a second. desflow explain queues_network.yaml solves this flow balance for every task. This is its output without the hints at the end:

Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 1.6/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack_order (task, rate 1.778/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> check_order (task, rate 1.778/s)
            +-- uses checkers (resource)
            +-- next (share 0.9) -> ship_order (task, rate 1.6/s)
            |   `-- next (share 1) -> exit
            `-- next (share 0.1) -> pack_order (again)
Resources
+----------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |     λ |      μ | c |      ρ | Wq | L | status |
|----------+-------+--------+---+--------+----+---+--------|
| packers  | 1.778 | 0.6667 | 4 | 0.6667 |  - | - | OK     |
| checkers | 1.778 |    2.5 | 1 | 0.7111 |  - | - | OK     |
+----------------------------------------------------------+
packers by units
+-------------------------+
|  c |      ρ | status    |
|----+--------+-----------|
|  1 |  2.667 | UNSTABLE  |
|  2 |  1.333 | UNSTABLE  |
|  3 | 0.8889 | CONGESTED |
|  4 | 0.6667 | OK        |

|  7 |  0.381 | OK        |
|  8 | 0.3333 | OK        |
|  9 | 0.2963 | OK        |
| 10 | 0.2667 | OK        |
+-------------------------+
checkers by units
+---------------------+
| c |      ρ | status |
|---+--------+--------|
| 1 | 0.7111 | OK     |
| 2 | 0.3556 | OK     |

+---------------------+
Bottleneck: checkers
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: no closed formula for c > 1 with non-exponential times; run --verify to measure it
  wait at checkers: its input is not one arrival or a Poisson flow, which Kingman's formula needs; run --verify to measure it

The four packers are at utilisation 0.667 and the checker at 0.711, the higher of the two, so the checker is the bottleneck. In the table by units, 3 packers would be at utilisation 0.889, above the checker. So with 3 packers the packers are the bottleneck, and a fourth packer moves the bottleneck to the checker. Relieving a bottleneck makes the next busiest resource the new one. desflow explain estimates neither wait here, and says why: four packers with constant packing have no closed formula, and the checker's input is the packers' output, which is neither one arrival nor a Poisson flow. --verify, in Check Against Theory, measures both.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
How do orders move through pick, pack and ship? Most go straight through, and a few go to backorder or are packed again. The run publishes the finished count of every task at the end, with stats: basic in the YAML file, with_stats("basic", interval=3600) in the Builder file and env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=3600) in the Low-level file. Each tab prints the four counts:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
desflow run flow_of_tasks.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'tasks\.(pick_order|backorder|pack_order|ship_order)\.finished"'

{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pick_order.finished","value":2011}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished","value":1904}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.ship_order.finished","value":1812}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.backorder.finished","value":198}

python flow_of_tasks.py 2>/dev/null

pick_order: 2011 finished
backorder : 198 finished
pack_order: 1904 finished
ship_order: 1812 finished

python flow_of_tasks_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

pick_order: 2011 finished
backorder : 198 finished
pack_order: 1904 finished
ship_order: 1812 finished

The counts are:

Task Finished in the hour pick_order 2,011 backorder 198 pack_order 1,904 ship_order 1,812

9.8% of picks led to backorder (198 of 2,011), and 4.8% of parcels were packed again (92 of 1,904 packs did not lead to a shipment). The weights set 5% for packing again, and this one run of the hour, with the seed 42, drew slightly fewer.

Flow balance is the rule that, in a flow, each task's arrival rate follows from the rates into it and the routing weights. Every pack leads to a shipment with probability 0.95, so each order is packed 1 ÷ 0.95 = 1.05 times on average, and the packers see 5% more work than there are orders. A rework loop therefore raises utilisation, so it belongs in the load you work out before running. Queueing Basics shows why waits grow quickly near full use. Task Flow describes routing in full.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A task names the task that follows it, by a condition or by weights.
  • In a flow, each task's rate follows from the rates into it and the routing weights.
  • A rework loop adds work to the resources it returns to, so include it in the load you work out before running.

docs.title: Full Files
Interruptions
docs.text:
A quarter of the shop's orders are express, as in Priorities, but now an express order does not wait for the regular order being packed: it takes the packer at once. This page asks: what remains of a regular order's packing when an express order takes its packer, and which way of carrying on keeps regular orders waiting least?

  • Decision: which of three policies a regular order follows when it loses the packer.
  • Measures: the number of preemptions, the mean wait of regular orders, and the orders packed and lost.
  • Runs: three runs of the hour, one for each policy, each with the seed 42.
  • Assumptions: both kinds of order arrive at random, and every order takes the same time to pack.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • let express orders take the packer from regular ones;
  • choose what a preempted order does: resume, restart or abandon;
  • interrupt the orders in the shop from outside.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a packer that can be preempted, as Preemption explains, and an on_interrupt policy on regular orders: resume, restart or abandon. It also recalls the regular orders once: every regular order in the shop receives an interrupt and follows its policy, and the packer stays available. Under resume and restart a recalled order queues for the packer again with the same priority, so it waits behind the express orders and behind the regular orders that queued again before it. Under abandon it is lost. Model Breakdowns shows a packer that is out of use for a time. The shop is the one from Priorities: one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. A regular order arrives every 2.22 seconds on average (rate: 0.45), and an express order every 6.67 seconds (rate: 0.15).

docs.title: Preemption
docs.text:
Priority so far decided only who goes next. Preemption also stops the work in progress. In SimPy, a request may find every unit of a PreemptiveResource busy. A lower priority value is more urgent. When the request is more urgent than a process holding a unit, the resource takes the unit from the least urgent holder, the one with the highest priority value, and that process receives an Interrupt. In desflow it is preempt: true on a resource whose queue is priority. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:packers
resources:
  # An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority, preempt: true}
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:packers
# An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
.add_resource(
    "packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority", preempt=True
)
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:packers
# An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
"packers": DynamicResource(
    env, "Shop", "packers", queue="priority", preempt=True
),

preempt=True gives the resource SimPy's preemption, and the process that holds a unit receives an interrupt when it is preempted. The code below uses three more SimPy names:

  • release(request) gives back the unit a request holds;
  • env.active_process is the process that is running now;
  • request.cancel() takes a request that has not been granted out of the queue.

Equal priorities do not preempt, so one express order does not take the packer from another.

docs.title: Resume, Restart or Abandon
docs.text:
A preempted or interrupted task stops waiting for anything. A preemption takes its packer, so it gives that up. A plain interrupt leaves a packer it already holds with it, as a SimPy process that keeps its request does. A packer it was still waiting for depends on how the task asks for it. With resource:, the request goes back to the end of the line. With seize or a request in a wait, the request keeps its place under resume, and asks again at the back of the line under restart. A packer granted at the instant of the interrupt stays held. A breakdown takes the unit too. Its on_interrupt then says what it does:

  • resume, the default: it goes on at once with a packer it still holds, or queues again and, once it has the packer back, packs for the time it had left;
  • restart: it does the same but packs for a new time, drawn from the same seeded stream, as if the work were spoiled;
  • abandon: it gives back every unit and ends, and its flow with it, unless on_interrupt_next names a task to go to. A task that names a task which asks for the packer again queues behind the orders already waiting.

A task can also do work of its own when the interrupt arrives, without giving up its place in the flow. on_interrupt_run names a task that runs as a child flow of the same entity after each interrupt or preemption under resume or restart. The task then goes on with the time it had left, or with a new time under restart. An interrupt that arrives while the child runs reaches the child, and a child that fails fails the task. on_interrupt_run is refused with abandon, with resource and with a request in a wait, because it is for work that holds no unit of its own.

An order that is abandoned when it loses its packer, and goes to be packed by hand:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_endings.yaml:interrupt-next
# An order that loses its packer to a rush order is packed by hand instead
on_interrupt: abandon
on_interrupt_next: pack_by_hand
docs/snippets/pages/interrupt_next.py:builder
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=1,
    # An order that loses its packer to a rush order is packed by hand instead
    on_interrupt="abandon",
    on_interrupt_next="pack_by_hand",
)
def pack(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "packed"}
docs/snippets/pages/interrupt_next.py:low-level
def pack(env, sampler, packers, counts):
    request = packers.request(priority=1)
    try:
        yield request
        yield env.timeout(
            sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config("Shop.service.packing"))
        )
        counts["packed"] += 1
    except simpy.Interrupt:
        # An order that loses its packer to a rush order is packed by hand instead
        yield from pack_by_hand(env, sampler, counts)
    finally:
        packers.release(request)

In the low-level API the process catches the Interrupt and packs by hand with yield from, in the same process.

The task publishes preempted (or interrupted) when it loses the packer, and resumed when it is served again, also when it never gave the packer up. A preempted request is marked as preempted, so the packer is never given back to it by mistake. If the order that lost the packer has already ended, the preemption fails the flow that asked, with SimPy's RuntimeError. A seize unit is asked for again under resume and restart. A preempted record names the express order that took the packer (preempted_by, its entity key) and the time the regular order had held it (usage_since). In a blueprint, a task that on_interrupt_next names reads the same facts as cause.by, cause.usage_since and cause.left (the service time that was left). An expression reads who holds a unit and who waits as held(packers) and waiting(packers), lists with each entity and its rank and time:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:policy
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  priority: 1
  # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
  on_interrupt: ${POLICY:-resume}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}

${POLICY:-resume} reads the environment variable POLICY, so POLICY=restart desflow run interruptions.yaml runs the second policy.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:policy
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=1,
    # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
    on_interrupt=policy,
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:policy
def pack(env, sampler, shop, arrival, key, task_id, policy):
    """Packs one order; when it loses the packer, it follows `policy`."""
    task, priority = TASKS[arrival]
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    publish(
        {"path_id": path_id, "sim_id": "Shop", "service": "packing", "status": "queued"}
    )
    env.stats.task_queued(task, task_id)
    shop["running"].setdefault(task, []).append(env.active_process)
    shop["keys"][env.active_process] = key
    remaining, started = None, False
    request = None
    while True:
        if request is None:
            request = shop["packers"].request(priority=priority)
        since = None
        try:
            if not request.processed:
                yield request
            status = "resumed" if started else "started"
            publish(
                {
                    "path_id": path_id,
                    "sim_id": "Shop",
                    "service": "packing",
                    "status": status,
                }
            )
            if started:
                env.stats.task_resumed(task, task_id)
            else:
                env.stats.task_started(task, task_id)
            started = True
            if remaining is None:
                remaining = sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id))
            since = env.now
            yield env.timeout(remaining)
            publish({"event_type": "order_packed" if priority else "express_packed"})
            env.stats.task_finished(task, task_id)
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            break
        except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
            if policy == "abandon" or request not in shop["packers"].users:
                # Ask again if queued or preempted; abandon gives a held unit back
                request.cancel()
                shop["packers"].release(request)
                request = None
            if since is not None:
                # resume serves what is left; restart draws a new packing time
                remaining = (
                    remaining - (env.now - since) if policy == "resume" else None
                )
            preempted = isinstance(interrupt.cause, Preempted)
            if preempted:
                value = {
                    "status": "preempted",
                    "resource": "packers",
                    "preempted_by": shop["keys"].get(interrupt.cause.by),
                    "usage_since": interrupt.cause.usage_since,
                }
            else:
                value = {"status": "interrupted", "cause": interrupt.cause}
            publish(
                {"path_id": path_id, "sim_id": "Shop", "service": "packing", **value}
            )
            env.stats.task_interrupted(task, task_id, preempted=preempted)
            if policy == "abandon":
                env.stats.task_dropped(task, task_id)
                shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
                del shop["keys"][env.active_process]
                return
    shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
    del shop["keys"][env.active_process]
    env.stats.flow_finished(arrival)

The process catches simpy.Interrupt. For a preemption, its cause is SimPy's Preempted. A preempted process, or one whose request still waits, cancels its request and requests the packer again. An interrupted process that holds the packer keeps its request. on_interrupt writes that loop for you. SimPy delivers an interrupt as an URGENT event, which End Conditions explains.

The statistics count each preempted, interrupted and resumed. A resumed order's wait is the sum of its waits, and its packing time is the total time it was packed:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:watch
# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:watch
# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:watch
# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)

docs.title: Interrupt a Task
docs.text:
Preemption is one source of interrupts, and a model can send others. An interrupt names a task. Every instance of that task that is running, waiting or being served receives an interrupt with the given cause, and follows its on_interrupt. A where condition, such as attr.order == 3, is read in the scope of each instance, and limits the interrupt to the instances for which it holds. It reads what the instance's own expressions read. wait.<branch>.done is false until the instance's wait has ended. Here a recall at 31 minutes interrupts every regular order:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:interrupt
scenario:
  # A recall at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
  # waiting or being packed, is interrupted
  - at: 31 min
    interrupt: {task: pack_order, cause: recalled}

A task can carry the same interrupt, applied when it finishes.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:interrupt
def recall_orders(context: SimulationContext):
    """A recall at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
    waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
    yield context.env.timeout(1860)
    context.interrupt("pack_order", cause="recalled")

app.add_process(recall_orders)

context.interrupt(task, where=None, cause=None) returns how many instances it reached. It never reaches the instance that calls it.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:interrupt
def recall_orders(env, shop):
    """A recall at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
    waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
    yield env.timeout(1860)
    for process in list(shop["running"].get("pack_order", [])):
        process.interrupt("recalled")

process.interrupt(cause) is SimPy's. The model keeps its own list of the processes it may interrupt.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
What remains of a regular order's packing when an express order takes its packer? Each figure here comes from one run of the hour with the seed 42.

  • With resume, the time it had left remains. After 349 preemptions, regular orders wait 8.17 seconds on average.
  • With restart, nothing remains: each preempted order packs again from the start. Preemptions rise to 389, and the mean wait rises more than fivefold to 44.11 seconds.
  • With abandon, the order is lost. 313 orders are lost, 311 to preemption and 2 to the recall at 31 minutes. The 1,328 packed orders wait only 3.64 seconds on average, because every interrupted order leaves the queue.

The recall at 31 minutes reaches every regular order in the shop at that moment: 3 under resume, 24 under restart, whose longer queue holds more orders, and 2 under abandon:

Each tab prints all three policies: the orders packed, preempted and recalled (interrupted), the mean wait and the mean packing time.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

desflow run interruptions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(preempted|interrupted|finished|wait_mean|service_mean)"' | tail -5
# The restart policy
POLICY=restart desflow run interruptions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(preempted|interrupted|finished|wait_mean|service_mean)"' | tail -5
# The abandon policy
POLICY=abandon desflow run interruptions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(preempted|interrupted|finished|wait_mean|service_mean)"' | tail -5

resume : 349 preempted, 3 recalled, 1640 packed, mean wait  8.17 s, mean packing 1.50 s
restart: 389 preempted, 24 recalled, 1640 packed, mean wait 44.11 s, mean packing 1.67 s
abandon: 311 preempted, 2 recalled, 1328 packed, mean wait  3.64 s, mean packing 1.50 s

resume : 349 preempted, 3 recalled, 1640 packed, mean wait  8.17 s, mean packing 1.50 s
restart: 389 preempted, 24 recalled, 1640 packed, mean wait 44.11 s, mean packing 1.67 s
abandon: 311 preempted, 2 recalled, 1328 packed, mean wait  3.64 s, mean packing 1.50 s

Under restart the packer spends part of its time on packing that is thrown away, so it does more work for the same orders. The mean time packed rises from 1.50 to 1.67 seconds, and the load nears what one packer can do. Waits then grow fast, as Queueing Basics explains. resume loses no work, so its waits are close to those of plain priority. abandon looks best only because the mean leaves out the orders it lost. So report the count of lost orders beside its mean wait. The decision is resume: it loses no order and its mean wait, 8.17 seconds, is the lowest of the two policies that keep every order. Priority and Preemption describes preemption, and Tasks and Processes the task's steps.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Preemption gives an urgent task the resource at once, and the task it takes it from must wait.
  • resume loses no work. restart throws work away and adds load, so waits grow fast near full use.
  • abandon looks best only because the mean leaves out the lost orders, so report their count beside it.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py
"""The Interruptions tutorial: express orders take the packer from regular ones.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. A regular order arrives every 2.22 seconds on
average (rate 0.45), and an express order every 6.67 seconds (rate 0.15). Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints what preemption did to regular orders
under each policy at the end. To see only those lines, run:
python interruptions.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(policy: str = "resume") -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop, where a regular order follows `policy` when it loses the packer."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        # An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
        .add_resource(
            "packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority", preempt=True
        )
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        # An order every 1.67 s on average in all (0.6 a second), one in four express
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.45)
        .add_arrival("express", dist="exponential", rate=0.15)
        # Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(
        service_id="packing",
        resource_id="packers",
        priority=1,
        # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
        on_interrupt=policy,
    )
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=0)
    def pack_express(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "express_packed"}

    for arrival, task, name in (
        ("orders", pack_order, "pack_order"),
        ("express", pack_express, "pack_express"),
    ):

        def loop(context: SimulationContext, arrival=arrival, task=task, name=name):
            while True:
                entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)
                context.spawn(task(context.next_instance(name), entity=entity))

        app.arrival_loop(arrival)(loop)

    def recall_orders(context: SimulationContext):
        """A recall at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
        waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
        yield context.env.timeout(1860)
        context.interrupt("pack_order", cause="recalled")

    app.add_process(recall_orders)
    return app


def outcomes(policy: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns what preemption did to regular orders."""
    app = shop(policy)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "preempted": readings[name("preempted")],
        "interrupted": readings.get(name("interrupted"), 0),
        "finished": readings[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": readings[name("wait_mean")],
        "service_mean": readings[name("service_mean")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for policy in ("resume", "restart", "abandon"):
        r = outcomes(policy)
        print(
            f"{policy:<7}: {r['preempted']} preempted, {r['interrupted']} recalled, "
            f"{r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, mean packing {r['service_mean']:4.2f} s"
        )
