priority is a number or an expression such as attr.priority, for a resource whose queue is priority. patience is seconds, a duration such as 30 s, an expression or a generator; balk is a condition checked before the task joins the queue. resource is one resource or a list, acquired in the order listed; keep hands units to the next task. on_interrupt is resume, restart or abandon, and interrupt interrupts the running instances of a task when this one finishes. wait is what the task waits for first: a signal, a child task, a timeout or a condition, or any or all of several. signal names a signal the task fires when it finishes. fail is a condition checked after the service: when it holds the task publishes failed with fail_reason, and goes to on_fail. fail_reason is text, or a {gen: ...} generator read in the step the failure happens, and it is the reason of the record, of the failed signal and of upstream.reason. get and put take from and add to a store or container. next is a task name, when rules or weights, whose values are numbers or expressions read when the task finishes, with one draw for the choice. set gives the entity attribute values when the task finishes. set_args writes this process's own local names, read as arg.<name> by this task and by the tasks that follow in the same flow (not by a child flow, which has its own). It is read after set, so a payload reads the value from before the write. A parent passes names to a child with args on a task branch of its wait, or on a spawn; a read of a name that was neither passed nor written is a run failure. activate and deactivate turn the sources of the named arrivals on and off when the task finishes, after set_args. cause.<name> reads why the task was interrupted, in a task that an on_interrupt_next edge reaches: by, usage_since and resource after a preemption, value after an interrupt, and left, the service time that was left. upstream.<field> is the payload of the task that routed here, item is the whole item a store get took, and it lasts through the next chain.

on_interrupt_run names a task that runs as a child flow of the same entity after each interrupt or preemption the task meets under resume or restart, and the task then goes on with the time left, or a new time under restart, as a SimPy loop try: yield env.timeout(left) except Interrupt: yield from repair() does. The child runs in the task's process. An interrupt that arrives while it runs reaches the child at its next wait and follows the child's own on_interrupt. The child reads cause.<name> as a task reached by on_interrupt_next does. It is refused with abandon, with a resource and with a request in the wait, because it is for work that holds no unit of its own. A child that fails fails the task. on_renege and on_balk name the task an instance goes to after it reneges (its patience ran out) or balks (its balk condition holds, or the line of its resource, seize or open is full), in place of the end of its flow. The instance still publishes reneged or balked, and that task reads the record as upstream.status. on_fail needs no fail: a failed wait, a failed child flow, a step that raises and an expression that cannot be evaluated go to it, and it reads the failure as upstream.status and upstream.reason. An interrupt is not a failure, and on_fail does not see it. suspend and resume are described on their models.

open names branches that start at once and are not waited for, so a later step can wait for, cancel, release or interrupt them by name. A branch of open is a timeout, request, get, put, task or signal, or an any or all group of timeout, task, signal and handle branches. The other kinds a wait takes (condition, running, at_least, when) are refused at load, as is a request, get or put inside a group.

listen adds callbacks to a signal or to an opened name when the task starts, after open and before wait: its on entries run on the next firing of the event, in the order the callbacks were added, as event.callbacks.append(f) does. An on entry of a task, a signal or a listen may carry a when expression that skips the entry when it is false.

The cause of an interrupt, the holders of a resource and the entries of a queue are lists and mappings an expression reads: held(m) and waiting(m) for a resource, putting(s) and getting(s) for a store or container, running(task) and running(task, condition), peek(), process.key and process.flow_name, signal.<name>.processed, and in the when of a wait group done_count.

A value place takes a constant, a list, a mapping or a {gen: ...} generator: a mapping with a gen key is a generator, and {gen: literal, value: ...} keeps a mapping as data. The kinds of gen are uniform, integer, normal, sample, one_of, weighted, pick, switch (key on), when, boolean, uuid, sequence, now, format_time, format, lower, upper, fake, add, subtract, multiply, divide, min, max, expr, var, attr, entity, param, repeat, literal, object, call, row, lookup, previous, upstream and aggregate; null_rate, unique, omit_rate and omit_when go on any of them. payload may be such a mapping, or one generator that gives a mapping or null. A null gives a finished record whose value is null, which a Kafka sink with envelope: false writes as a tombstone. id_field, item_field and attributes need a mapping, so with them a null fails the task, which on_fail handles as any failure. key_field needs a mapping too, and with it a null fails the run, as a payload without the field does. A store put on the task puts the null as its item. set values and the cause of an interrupt are evaluated when the task finishes or interrupts. vars_once names are drawn once for each entity and task, at the first use, and may be read by a wait timeout value. vars are drawn in order, once for each instance of the task: when it starts if on_start is given, otherwise after the service, just before the payload; a service_time that reads a var draws it first. {gen: entity} gives the entity's key, in a task only. A var reads the vars above it with {gen: var, name: ...} or as a bare name in an expr. on_start values are published as one event record when the task starts. finish_vars are drawn after the service and may read the vars. A bare var name also reads in put, fail and next.when, but not in next.weights, which read the entity and the run. A var name is an identifier, not a name an expression already uses, and is in one of the three groups only. Every generator node draws from its own stream of the run's seed, so adding a node does not change the draws of the others.

A task keeps its last history finished payloads (default 1,000,000) when a lookup or aggregate in the file names it, or when history is written. A task that looks up another does not start before the other has a row: an arrival's start is dropped, and one INFO line says how long the task waited in simulation time. A task reached by next that has no row to look up ends its flow in the same way. previous reads the last finished payload of the same task on the same stream: the arrival, or the entity for an arrival with count or keys. upstream reads the payload of the task that routed here, in a task reached by next. aggregate is mean, sum, min, max or count over the last rows of a task that where, an expression over the row's fields, keeps.

An expression uses Python's arithmetic: / gives a float, and // rounds down and gives an integer for two integers. and and or stop at the first operand that decides the result and do not absorb an error: an operand that cannot be evaluated fails the expression. ** raises to a power (an integer power above 10000 is refused), abs, min, max, round, floor, ceil, sqrt, exp, log, log10, sin, cos and tan are calls on numbers, and has(attr.x) is true when the entity has the attribute x.

An expression also reads a process's local names arg.<name>, the interrupt that reached the task as cause.<name>, the payload of the task that routed here as upstream.<field> (at any depth), process.key and process.flow_name, the bare item and item_priority after a store get, and signal.<name>.processed. held(<resource>), waiting(<resource>), putting(<store or container>) and getting(<store or container>) give lists of mappings (with entity, and rank, time, preempt, key and since for a resource, item for a store put and amount for a container); running(<task>[, <condition>]) counts the instances of a task, and peek() is the time of the next event. Lists [1, 2], mappings {'a': 1}, one-clause comprehensions [x * 2 for x in list if x > 1], subscripts and slices, is None, in, and dotted reads at any depth work on them. The functions len, sum, sorted, range, any, all, str, int, float, bool, get_key(mapping, key, default), set_key(mapping, key, value) and drop_key(mapping, key) work on lists and mappings; min and max take a list. set_key and drop_key give a new mapping. A reading makes at most 1,000,000 items, and % on text is refused.

Key Type Default service text none service_time Generator or integer or number or text or Duration or expression none resource text or Ref or list of text or Ref none payload Payload or !python reference required id_field text none key Value none key_field text none item_field text none attributes list of text priority integer or number or text none patience Generator or integer or number or text or Duration or expression none balk text none get TransferStep none put TransferStep none next text or Next none set mapping of names to Value set_args mapping of names to Value activate text or list of text none deactivate text or list of text none vars mapping of names to Value vars_once mapping of names to Value on_start mapping of names to Value finish_vars mapping of names to Value history integer 1000000 wait SignalWait or TaskWait or TimeoutWait or ConditionWait or AnyWait or AllWait or AtLeastWait or WhenWait or RequestWait or GetWait or PutWait or RunningWait or HandleWait or SuspendWait or EachWait none open mapping of names to SignalWait or TaskWait or TimeoutWait or ConditionWait or AnyWait or AllWait or AtLeastWait or WhenWait or RequestWait or GetWait or PutWait or RunningWait or HandleWait or EachWait none listen ListenSpec none cancel text or HandleRef none seize text or SeizeSpec none release text or Ref or ReleaseSpec none signal text or Ref none fail text none fail_reason Value none on_fail text none on_renege text none on_balk text none keep list of text preempt boolean or text true on_interrupt resume or restart or abandon "resume" on_interrupt_next text none on_interrupt_run text none interrupt InterruptAction none resume ResumeSpec none batch BatchSpec none spawn SpawnAction none subscribe mapping none on list of OnEntry

docs.title: TransferStep
docs.text:
A task's get or put: one container with an amount, or one store.

amount is a number or an expression such as payload.quantity, and 1 when it is left out. priority is for a put into a priority store, lowest served first, and 0 when it is left out. Text is an expression such as attr.priority; any other value is used as written: a number, a list (which orders element by element, as a tuple does), a mapping, null, a date or a bool. filter is a condition for a store get, such as item.size == attr.size, where item.<field> reads the item offered: the get takes the oldest item that matches. wait: false makes the get or put and does not wait for it: the task goes on at once. item is for a store put: the value to put, a constant, text, a list, a mapping or a {gen: ...} generator read as the put is made, a generator nested at any depth of a mapping or list included; left out, the put adds the task's payload. The bare name item in {gen: expr, expr: item} is the whole item a get took, so item: {gen: expr, expr: item} puts it back.

Key Type Default container text or Ref none store text or Ref none amount integer or number or text 1.0 priority None 0.0 filter text none wait boolean true item Value none

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
A task's next: when rules with an optional default, or weights.

Key Type Default when list of Rule default text none weights mapping of names to number or text none

docs.title: Rule
docs.text:
A next.when entry: a condition and the task it leads to.

Key Type Default condition text required task text required

docs.title: SignalWait
docs.text:
A wait branch for a signal's next firing, or for a member of a family of signals, {signal: {of: <family>, key: <expression>}}.

Key Type Default signal text or Ref required

docs.title: TaskWait
docs.text:
A wait branch for a child flow: it starts task for the same entity. args are value places read in the parent's scope when the child starts, and the child flow reads them as arg.<name>; each child has its own, as a SimPy process has its own arguments.

Key Type Default task text required args mapping of names to Value none

docs.title: TimeoutWait
docs.text:
A wait branch of a time place: a number of seconds, a duration such as 30 s, an expression, a {gen: ...} generator, or {after, value} with a value the waiter receives. An expression or a generator is read when the wait starts.

Key Type Default timeout Generator or integer or number or text or TimeoutAfter required

docs.title: TimeoutAfter
docs.text:
A wait timeout with a value: {after: 40 s, value: ...}, as SimPy's env.timeout(delay, value) carries a value the waiter receives. The value is a constant or a {gen: ...} generator evaluated when the wait starts, so it may read vars_once names but no vars. after is a time place: seconds, a duration, an expression or a generator, read when the wait starts.

Key Type Default after Generator or integer or number or text required value Value none

docs.title: ConditionWait
docs.text:
A wait branch for a condition, checked again after each change.

Key Type Default condition text required

docs.title: AnyWait
docs.text:
A wait done when the first of its named branches is.

Key Type Default any mapping of names to SignalWait or TaskWait or TimeoutWait or ConditionWait or AnyWait or AllWait or AtLeastWait or WhenWait or RequestWait or GetWait or PutWait or RunningWait or HandleWait or SuspendWait or EachWait required

docs.title: AllWait
docs.text:
A wait done when every one of its named branches is.

Key Type Default all mapping of names to SignalWait or TaskWait or TimeoutWait or ConditionWait or AnyWait or AllWait or AtLeastWait or WhenWait or RequestWait or GetWait or PutWait or RunningWait or HandleWait or SuspendWait or EachWait required

docs.title: AtLeastWait
docs.text:
A wait done when at least at_least of its named branches are.

Key Type Default at_least integer required of mapping of names to SignalWait or TaskWait or TimeoutWait or ConditionWait or AnyWait or AllWait or AtLeastWait or WhenWait or RequestWait or GetWait or PutWait or RunningWait or HandleWait or SuspendWait or EachWait required

docs.title: WhenWait
docs.text:
A wait done when the expression when holds. It is read each time a branch of of is processed, and once at the start for a branch already processed, as SimPy's Condition(env, evaluate, events) does. It reads wait.<branch>.done, .ok and .value of the branches and done_count. A branch that fails fails the wait, and an empty of succeeds at once.

Key Type Default when text required of mapping of names to SignalWait or TaskWait or TimeoutWait or ConditionWait or AnyWait or AllWait or AtLeastWait or WhenWait or RequestWait or GetWait or PutWait or RunningWait or HandleWait or SuspendWait or EachWait required

docs.title: RequestWait
docs.text:
A wait branch for a resource unit: the task holds it if it wins.

Key Type Default request text or Ref or RequestSpec required

docs.title: RequestSpec
docs.text:
A request of a wait or an open with options: the resource, a priority (a number or an expression read as the request is made) and a preempt flag (true or false, or an expression). With a mapping, the task's priority and preempt do not apply to this request: a key it leaves out is SimPy's default, priority 0 and preempt true. With a name they do.

Key Type Default resource text or Ref required priority integer or number or text none preempt boolean or text none

docs.title: GetWait
docs.text:
A wait branch for a store or container get.

Key Type Default get TransferStep required

docs.title: PutWait
docs.text:
A wait branch for a store or container put.

Key Type Default put TransferStep required

docs.title: RunningWait
docs.text:
A wait branch for the running instances of a task: done when they all end.

Key Type Default running RunningTarget required

docs.title: RunningTarget
docs.text:
A running wait branch target: the task whose running instances to wait for, narrowed by an optional where condition read in each instance's scope. The wait is for the end of the instance's task, or, with whole_flow: true, for the end of the whole flow the instance belongs to (its next chain and the tasks it waits for in child flows), as yield process waits for a SimPy process. A flow selected that way is any flow of the model that is running when the wait begins, or that ended while an instance of a task with such a wait was running and still is; a flow with no match ends the wait at once. Its last task's payload is the branch's value.

Key Type Default task text required where text none whole_flow boolean false

docs.title: HandleWait
docs.text:
A wait branch for an event that open made: handle is the name it was opened under. A handle already processed gives its value at once, and a handle waited for through an interrupt under resume or restart is the same event after it, with its first end and its place in the queue. index names one element of an opened each group; it is read when the wait starts.

Key Type Default handle text required index integer or text none

docs.title: SuspendWait
docs.text:
A wait branch that suspends the instance until a resume of another task wakes it (suspend: true). The branch's value is the value of that resume, so wait.suspend.value reads it. An interrupt that reaches a suspended instance follows the task's on_interrupt: under resume the instance stays suspended in its place, under restart it suspends again behind the others, and under abandon it ends. open does not take it.

Key Type Default suspend boolean required

docs.title: EachWait
docs.text:
A wait on a computed number of events: branch is made once for each element of each, in order, when the wait starts. each is a whole number, a list, an expression or a generator, read once. Inside branch, each.index is the place from 0 and each.value is the element, or the index when each is a number. group is all (the default), any, {at_least: n} or {when: expression}. An empty each is done at once. wait.<name>.values and .flags are lists in element order.

Key Type Default each Generator or integer or text or list of any value required group all or any or AtLeastGroup or WhenGroup "all" branch SignalWait or TaskWait or TimeoutWait or ConditionWait or AnyWait or AllWait or AtLeastWait or WhenWait or RequestWait or GetWait or PutWait or RunningWait or HandleWait or SuspendWait or EachWait required

docs.title: AtLeastGroup
docs.text:
The group of an each wait done when at least at_least elements are, a whole number or an expression read when the wait starts.

Key Type Default at_least integer or text required

docs.title: WhenGroup
docs.text:
The group of an each wait done when the expression when holds, read as for a when wait, with done_count and wait.<name>.values and .flags.

Key Type Default when text required

docs.title: ListenSpec
docs.text:
A task's listen: callbacks added to an event, as event.callbacks.append(f) does, when the task starts, after its open and before it waits.

Exactly one of signal and handle names the event: a signal, or a member of a family of signals {of: <family>, key: <expression>}, takes the callbacks on its next firing; a handle is an event the flow opened, and index picks one element of an opened each group. on lists the entries to run, each read in the scope of the entity that listens. They run once, on the next firing of the signal or the event of the handle, in the order the callbacks were added: before the waiters added later and after the ones added earlier. To go on listening, a flow listens again. A signal whose firing was processed already, or an event that was processed, takes no callback, which fails the task as event.callbacks.append raising does.

Key Type Default signal text or Ref none handle text none index integer or text none on list of OnEntry

docs.title: HandleRef
docs.text:
The name of an opened event, as {handle: <name>}, or one element of an opened each group, as {handle: <name>, index: <expression>}.

Key Type Default handle text required index integer or text none

docs.title: SeizeSpec
docs.text:
A seize with options: the resource, a priority (a number or an expression read as the request is made), a preempt flag (true or false, or an expression), and a patience, which is the task's patience for the time it waits for the unit. priority and preempt default to the task's. A task gives its patience on the task or here, not both.

Key Type Default resource text or Ref required priority integer or number or text none preempt boolean or text none patience Generator or integer or number or text or Duration or expression none

docs.title: ReleaseSpec
docs.text:
A release with options: {handle: <name>} frees the unit of that opened request, and {resource, task, where} frees the units of resource that the instances of task hold, however they asked (resource, seize, open or a request in a wait) and whichever flow they are in, oldest grant first; where is read in the instance's scope, and without it every holder of that task is freed. The holder is not told. A resource name alone frees the oldest unit of it that the flow holds.

Key Type Default handle text none index integer or text none resource text or Ref none task text none where text none

docs.title: BatchSpec
docs.text:
A task's batch: its members wait together and one run of the task's resource and service serves them all.

The batch closes when size members have joined, timeout after its first member, or when close_when holds as a member joins, whichever is first. size is a number, or text read as an expression in the scope of the first member when it joins; 1 or below closes the batch at its first member. close_when reads batch.size (how many members it holds) and batch.age (seconds since its first member). name names the batch and defaults to the task's name: tasks with the same name share one open batch, so they must have the same size, timeout, close_when, resource and service (service or service_time), or the file is refused at load. Values are compared by what they mean, so a generator written the same way, an expression with other spacing and a number written as text agree. Each member keeps its own on_interrupt, patience, payload and next, and follows its own next in the order the members joined.

Key Type Default name text none size integer or number or text required timeout Generator or integer or number or text or Duration or expression none close_when text none

docs.title: telemetry
docs.text:
Type: list of Telemetry. Optional.

A telemetry entry: custom readings published every interval seconds.

It takes exactly one of function and readings. function is a !python function called as function(context), which publishes with context.publish. readings maps a reading name to an expression read over the run (level., users., queue., signal., registry[...], t and the functions of the expression language, and no name of an entity or a task). Each interval publishes one telemetry record for each reading, named <sim_id>.<reading>, as context.publish names one, in the order the readings are written. An expression that cannot be evaluated stops the run. Resource, store and container readings come from stats instead.

Key Type Default interval number required function !python reference none readings mapping of names to text none

docs.title: processes
docs.text:
Type: list of Process or !python reference. Optional.

A processes entry: a generator function and extra keyword arguments.

The function is called as function(context, **kwargs) when the run starts. The processes are made after the arrivals, in the order they are written.

Key Type Default function !python reference required kwargs mapping

docs.title: scenario
docs.text:
Type: list of ScenarioStep. Optional.

A scenario entry: at simulation time at, set path to value, publish a ground-truth record of record, or both.

at is seconds from the start of the run, or a duration such as "10 min". A step with a record publishes a ground-truth record, stream_type: label, with the path, the value before and after, and the record mapping, to the sinks with when: labels only. A step with an interrupt interrupts the running instances of a task, as a task's interrupt does. A value and each record value are constants or {gen: ...} generators: value is evaluated just before the change and record just after it.

Key Type Default at integer or number or Duration required path text none value Value none record mapping of names to Value none interrupt InterruptAction none

docs.title: ingress
docs.text:
Type: list of Connector. Optional.

An ingress entry: a connector type and its constructor arguments.

type is a short name such as Kafka, or a !python class for a connector from another package.

Key Type Default type short name or !python reference required config mapping

docs.title: egress
docs.text:
Type: list of EgressConnector. Optional.

An egress entry, with the per-provider options of add_egress.

when is history, live, events, telemetry, labels, trace, a mapping {expr: ...} or a !python function taking one record. history sends the records stamped before simulation.go_live_at, and live sends the records stamped at or after it. events sends the event records and telemetry the telemetry records. labels sends the ground-truth records of scenario steps with a record, and nothing else. trace sends the records of stats.trace, one for each event the environment processes, and nothing else; no other entry receives them.

envelope: false makes the entry plain output: the sink writes each event's value without the record around it (stream_type, sim_ts, timestamp, key, task and instance), and it receives no telemetry record and no queued or started record of a task. A Kafka sink sends a null value as a tombstone, a message with the record's key and a null value, and sends any other value that is not a mapping as JSON. A Redis sink sends a value that is not a mapping as JSON, null included. A storage, Iceberg or PostgreSQL sink skips it, with one warning. The message key of Kafka stays the record's key, and a topic_router still receives the whole record. Ground-truth records of a when: labels entry are not affected.

Key Type Default type short name or !python reference required config mapping when history or live or events or telemetry or labels or trace or WhenExpr or !python reference none envelope boolean true batch_size integer none flush_interval number none

docs.title: WhenExpr
docs.text:
An egress when written as an expression: when: {expr: <expression>}.

The expression reads the record the sink is offered: record.stream_type (event or telemetry), record.key, record.task and record.value.<field>. A name the record lacks reads as None, so record.value.event_type == 'order_packed' is false for a telemetry record and for an event without that field. The sink receives the record when the expression is true. An expression that fails on a record, such as record.value.amount > 100 on a record whose value has no amount, fails the run.

Key Type Default expr text required

docs.title: batching
docs.text:
Type: Batching. Optional.

The batching section: the arguments of with_batching.

Key Type Default batch_size integer required flush_interval number required max_queued_batches integer none drain_stall_seconds number none

docs.title: stats
docs.text:
Type: Stats or level name. Optional.

The stats section: the built-in statistics level and how often to publish.

Written as a level alone (stats: basic) or as a mapping (stats: {level: all, interval: 60}). The interval is in seconds or a duration such as 5 min. A mapping needs a level, unless it sets only trace, when the level is none. on_change: true also publishes a resource's readings at each request and release call on it, so it needs a level above none. trace: true publishes one record for each event the environment processes, of the kind trace, to the egress entries with when: trace.

Key Type Default level none or minimal or basic or typical or all interval integer or number or Duration 10.0 on_change boolean false trace boolean false

docs.title: run
docs.text:
Type: mapping. Optional.

The run section.

before lists !python functions called with no arguments before the run starts, for setup such as creating topics or tables. stop ends the run before until at the next firing of a signal, {signal: name}, or when a condition first holds, {condition: ...}. drain, true or {limit: 1 h}, stops the arrivals at until and runs on until no entity is left in the model.

segments runs the model in parts and publishes a reading after each, as a SimPy program that calls env.run(until=...) in a loop does: a list of RunSegment, or {every: <time>} for equal parts up to until. steps: true publishes system.simulation.step, {step, now, peek}, after each model event, as a loop of env.step() and env.peek() reads them. sync: true calls env.sync() as the run starts. A run with no until ends when no model event is left, except that a list of segments with no until whose last entry has an until or a stop ends there, as a SimPy program that stops calling env.run does; a last entry {} runs to the end.

Key Type Default until integer or number or Duration none before list of !python reference stop mapping none drain boolean or Drain false on_unhandled_failure stop or continue "stop" segments list of RunSegment or SegmentEvery none steps boolean false sync boolean false

docs.title: Drain
docs.text:
A run.drain mapping: the longest a drain may run after until.

Key Type Default limit number or Duration none

docs.title: RunSegment
docs.text:
A run.segments entry: the run goes on to until or to stop, then waits for the next entry.

An entry has at most one of until and stop; {} runs to the end. After the segment stops, look names a task whose new entity reads the model before any event at the stop time runs, and sync re-anchors the wall clock at the start of the segment. A record at system.simulation.segment reports index, now and peek (null when no model event is left) as the segment ends.

Key Type Default until integer or number or text or Duration none stop mapping none look text none sync boolean false

docs.title: SegmentEvery
docs.text:
run.segments: {every: 10 s}: a segment every every seconds up to run.until.

Key Type Default every integer or number or text or Duration required

docs.title: tests
docs.text:
Type: list of BlueprintTest. Optional.

A tests entry: the statistics a model must give at one seed, checked by desflow test.

expect maps a statistic name, as measures in an experiment file names it (tasks.pack_order.finished), to the number it must have, or to {value, within} for a tolerance. A number is compared exactly. seed defaults to the file's simulation.random_seed and until to run.until. The entry runs the model once, unpaced, with no ingress and no egress, so a test contacts no service.

A test states the measures at one seed in one version of desflow. A new release may draw its random numbers differently, so a test does not promise that exact seeded records or values stay the same across versions; run desflow test --fix to write the new values and read them before you keep them.

Key Type Default name text required seed integer none until integer or number or text or Duration none expect mapping of names to ExpectedWithin or integer or number

docs.title: ExpectedWithin
docs.text:
An expect value with a tolerance: the measured statistic passes when it is within within of value, in absolute terms. Use it for a value whose last digits change with the platform's floating point.

Key Type Default value integer or number required within integer or number required

docs.title: Generators
docs.text:
A value place takes a constant or a generator: a mapping with a gen key that names its kind. null_rate, unique, omit_rate and omit_when go on any kind.

The Generators section has a page for each kind, with its keys, an example and its JSON Schema.

docs.title: SimPy and desflow
docs.text:
desflow is built on SimPy, a Python library for discrete-event simulation. SimPy provides the event list, the clock, processes and resources, and desflow keeps all of them. This page teaches the SimPy constructs one at a time, each on the packing shop in plain SimPy with no desflow in it. A low-level desflow model is ordinary SimPy code with a few additions, which Coming from SimPy lists.

The code is plain SimPy 4.1.2, the version desflow is tested against. We confirmed each statement about a construct against SimPy's source in that version (core.py, events.py, rt.py and the resources package). Every function below runs as a script in the docs tests, and its output is the one shown.

docs.title: Environment and the Event List
docs.text:
An Environment holds the clock, env.now, and the event list. The list is ordered by time, then by priority, then by the order in which events were scheduled. Two events at one time therefore run in the order they were scheduled, unless one has the higher priority (URGENT is 0 and NORMAL is 1, and the lower number runs first). What Is DES? explains why the clock jumps from event to event, and Run Length shows how the order matters at the end of a run.

env.timeout(delay) is an event that SimPy schedules delay seconds from now, and a negative delay raises ValueError. env.step() takes the earliest event, moves the clock to its time and runs the event's callbacks. env.peek() gives the time of the next event, or infinity when none is left. env.run(until=...) calls step until the time or the event you give it. The function below schedules two timeouts in the wrong order and steps through them.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:event_list
def event_list():
    """Two events scheduled out of order are processed in time order."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    env.timeout(2.6)  # order 2 arrives
    env.timeout(1.5)  # order 1 is packed
    seen = []
    while env.peek() != math.inf:  # peek is the time of the next event
        seen.append((env.peek(), env.now))
        env.step()  # take the earliest event, move the clock to its time
    return seen, env.now

Each pair is the time of the next event and the clock before the step. The event at 2.6 was scheduled first, but the list is ordered by time, so the event at 1.5 comes first and the clock ends at 2.6.

event list: [(1.5, 0), (2.6, 1.5)], clock at 2.6

In desflow, env is a DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, which is a SimPy environment with pacing added. In the builder, env.run(until=...), env.step() and env.peek() are app.run(until=...), app.step() and app.peek(). In YAML, the end time is run.until.

docs.title: Events and Callbacks
docs.text:
An event is something that happens once. It starts pending. It becomes triggered when succeed(value) or fail(exception) is called, which schedules it. It becomes processed when the environment takes it from the list and runs its callbacks. A callback is a function that takes the event, and callbacks run in the order they were added. A process that yields an event waits on it by adding its own resume function to the callbacks, so one event can wake any number of processes. Calling succeed twice raises RuntimeError, and a failed event that nothing handles stops the run with its exception.

In the shop, several parts of the model wait for an order to be packed. Here a callback and two couriers wait on one event, and the packer triggers it at 1.5 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:events
def events():
    """An event is triggered once, and its callbacks and waiting processes run when it is processed."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    packed = env.event()
    log = []
    packed.callbacks.append(
        lambda event: log.append(f"callback at {env.now}: {event.value}")
    )

    def courier(name):
        value = yield packed  # every process waiting on the event resumes with its value
        log.append(f"{name} at {env.now}: {value}")

    env.process(courier("courier 1"))
    env.process(courier("courier 2"))

    def packer():
        yield env.timeout(1.5)
        packed.succeed("order 1")  # triggers the event, which schedules it for now

    env.process(packer())
    env.run()
    return log, (packed.triggered, packed.processed, packed.ok)

The callback was added first, so it runs first, and both couriers resume at the same instant with the event's value. The last line shows the three states after the run: triggered and processed are both true, and ok is true because the event succeeded.

callback at 1.5: order 1
courier 1 at 1.5: order 1
courier 2 at 1.5: order 1
triggered, processed, ok: (True, True, True)

In desflow, a signal is an event that tasks wait for and fire, such as a restock. Signal is its low-level form, add_signal its builder form and signals: its YAML form. A signal is one-shot by default, as a SimPy event is, and once: false makes it fire again. A task's listen: {signal: s, on: [...]} adds callbacks to the next firing of the signal when the task starts, in the order they were added and before waiters added later, as event.callbacks.append(f) does. A signal whose firing was processed already takes no callback, which fails the task, as event.callbacks.append raises. A flow that wants to keep listening listens again. A failed event that nothing handles stops the run in all three forms, as it does in SimPy. on_unhandled_failure: continue publishes a failed record and goes on instead. Failures explains both.

docs.title: Processes and Waiting for a Process
docs.text:
A process is a Python generator that SimPy runs: each yield hands SimPy an event, and the process resumes when that event is processed. env.process(generator) starts one. The process is itself an event, which triggers when the generator returns, with the return value. So a process can wait for another by yielding it, and it receives the other's return value. If the child raises an exception, the exception is raised in the parent at its yield.

The shop below takes an order every 2 seconds. Each order starts a pack process and waits for it, and pack takes 1.5 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:processes
def processes():
    """A process is a generator; yielding another process waits for it and returns its value."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    log = []

    def pack(order):
        yield env.timeout(1.5)
        return f"order {order} packed"

    def shop():
        for order in (1, 2):
            yield env.timeout(2)  # time to the next arrival
            result = yield env.process(pack(order))  # wait for the child
            log.append((env.now, result))

    env.process(shop())
    env.run()
    return log

The first order arrives at 2 and is packed at 3.5. The second arrives 2 seconds after the first was packed, at 5.5, and is packed at 7.0.

[(3.5, 'order 1 packed'), (7.0, 'order 2 packed')]

In desflow, a task is a process, and @app.task and @app.arrival_loop write the common ones. A task waits for another task with wait: {task: ...} in YAML, wait={"task": ...} or yield context.call(...) in the builder, and reads the child's last payload as its value. A process you write yourself runs through add_process, which is an extension point.

docs.title: Interrupts
docs.text:
process.interrupt(cause) raises simpy.Interrupt inside the process, at the yield where it waits. The cause is any object, and the process reads it as interrupt.cause. The interrupt is scheduled as URGENT, so it takes effect before any other event at that time. A process that catches the exception may wait again, for the same event or a new one. A process that has ended, or the process itself, cannot be interrupted, and interrupt raises RuntimeError.

Here a packer is interrupted for a break at 1.0 seconds, in the middle of a 1.5 second packing. It works out how much is left, takes the break, and finishes.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:interrupts
def interrupts():
    """A packer is interrupted at 1.0 s and finds how much of the 1.5 s packing is left."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    log = []

    def packer():
        left = 1.5
        while left > 0:
            started = env.now
            try:
                yield env.timeout(left)
                left = 0
            except (
                simpy.Interrupt
            ) as interrupt:  # raised inside the process, at its yield
                left -= env.now - started
                log.append((env.now, interrupt.cause, left))
                yield env.timeout(0.5)  # the break
        log.append((env.now, "packed", 0))

    process = env.process(packer())

    def supervisor():
        yield env.timeout(1.0)
        process.interrupt("break")  # the cause is any object

    env.process(supervisor())
    env.run()
    return log

The packer is interrupted at 1.0 with 0.5 seconds left, rests for 0.5, and finishes the rest at 2.0.

[(1.0, 'break', 0.5), (2.0, 'packed', 0)]

In desflow, on_interrupt: resume, restart or abandon on a task chooses what happens to the work in progress. This code does what resume does. interrupt: sends an interrupt. Interruptions uses all three.

docs.title: Waiting for One or All
docs.text:
a | b is an event that triggers when the first of a and b is processed, and a & b is one that triggers when both are. They are the AnyOf and AllOf classes, and env.any_of(events) and env.all_of(events) build them from a list. The value is a ConditionValue. It holds the events that had been processed when the condition is processed, so event in result tells you which ones, and result.todict() gives their values.

A courier below waits for an order to be packed or for 1 second to pass, whichever is first. Then it waits for the packing and for another 3 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:conditions
def conditions():
    """`|` waits for the first of several events, `&` for all of them."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    log = []

    def courier():
        packed = env.timeout(2.0, value="packed")
        limit = env.timeout(1.0, value="limit")
        first = yield packed | limit  # AnyOf: holds every event processed so far
        log.append((env.now, packed in first, limit in first))
        both = yield packed & env.timeout(3.0)  # AllOf: waits for both
        log.append((env.now, len(both.todict())))

    env.process(courier())
    env.run()
    return log

At 1.0 the limit was processed and the packing was not, so the courier stopped waiting. The second wait ends at 4.0, when the timeout created at 1.0 triggers, and both events are in its value.

[(1.0, False, True), (4.0, 2)]

In desflow, wait: {any: ...} and wait: {all: ...} in YAML and wait={"any": ...} in the builder wait on named branches of signals, tasks and timeouts. To wait on a computed list, as env.all_of(events) does, wait takes each, group and branch: group is all, any, {at_least: ...} or {when: ...}, and branch is the one leaf that each element waits on. Wait for One or All shows ties, failures and the forms of each.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
A Resource(env, capacity) has capacity units, one by default. request() returns an event that triggers when a unit is free, and requests are served in the order they arrive. Used in a with block, a request is released when the block ends, and a request still waiting at that point is cancelled. count is the units in use, users the granted requests and queue the waiting ones.

Three orders arrive at 0 and the shop has one packer. Each waits for the one before it.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:resource
def resource():
    """Three orders at 0 s and one packer: each waits in the queue for the one before."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    packers = simpy.Resource(env, capacity=1)
    log = []

    def order(name):
        with packers.request() as request:  # leaving the block releases the packer
            yield request
            log.append((name, env.now))
            yield env.timeout(1.5)

    for name in "ABC":
        env.process(order(name))
    env.run()
    return log

[('A', 0), ('B', 1.5), ('C', 3.0)]

PriorityResource takes a priority with each request: the lowest number is served first, and requests with the same priority are served in arrival order. In the shop below, the packer is busy with an order at 0. A standard order arrives at 0.5 and an express order at 1.0, and the express order is served first.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:priority
def priority():
    """The packer is busy at 0 s; a lower priority number is served first, ties in arrival order."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    packers = simpy.PriorityResource(env, capacity=1)
    log = []

    def order(name, priority, arrives):
        yield env.timeout(arrives)
        with packers.request(priority=priority) as request:
            yield request
            log.append((name, env.now))
            yield env.timeout(1.5)

    env.process(order("first", priority=1, arrives=0))
    env.process(order("standard", priority=1, arrives=0.5))
    env.process(order("express", priority=0, arrives=1.0))
    env.run()
    return log

[('first', 0), ('express', 1.5), ('standard', 3.0)]

PreemptiveResource adds preemption: a request whose priority number is lower than a current user's, made with preempt=True (the default), takes that user's unit. The user is interrupted, and interrupt.cause is a Preempted object with by, usage_since and resource. The preempted process does not get the unit back, so it must request again if it wants to continue. Below, an express order arrives at 1.0 and interrupts a standard order that has used the packer since 0.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:preemptive
def preemptive():
    """An express order takes the packer from a standard one, which is interrupted."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    packers = simpy.PreemptiveResource(env, capacity=1)
    log = []

    def standard():
        with packers.request(priority=1) as request:
            yield request
            try:
                yield env.timeout(1.5)
                log.append(("standard packed", env.now))
            except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
                cause = interrupt.cause  # a Preempted object
                log.append(("standard preempted", env.now, cause.usage_since))

    def express():
        yield env.timeout(1.0)
        with packers.request(priority=0) as request:  # preempt=True is the default
            yield request
            yield env.timeout(1.0)
            log.append(("express packed", env.now))

    env.process(standard())
    env.process(express())
    env.run()
    return log

[('standard preempted', 1.0, 0), ('express packed', 2.0)]

In desflow, DynamicResource is all three: queue: fifo is Resource, queue: lifo serves the latest request first (SimPy has no class for it), queue: priority is PriorityResource, and preempt: true with it is PreemptiveResource. It also follows a capacity in the registry. Resources and Priority and Preemption explain them.

docs.title: Containers and Stores
docs.text:
A Container(env, capacity, init) holds a quantity, such as boxes on a shelf. put(amount) waits while there is no room, and get(amount) waits until enough is held. level is the quantity held now. Waiting requests are served in order, so a large get at the head holds back smaller ones behind it. Here the packer needs 3 boxes while the shelf holds 2, so it waits for a delivery of 5 at 4 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:container
def container():
    """A shelf holds a quantity of boxes: a get for 3 waits until a put makes them available."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    shelf = simpy.Container(env, capacity=10, init=2)
    log = []

    def packer():
        yield shelf.get(3)
        log.append(("took 3 boxes", env.now, shelf.level))

    def delivery():
        yield env.timeout(4)
        yield shelf.put(5)  # the waiting get is served as the boxes arrive

    env.process(packer())
    env.process(delivery())
    env.run()
    return log

The get is served as the delivery arrives, and the shelf then holds 4 of the 7 boxes.

[('took 3 boxes', 4, 4)]

A Store holds distinct items rather than a quantity. put(item) waits while it is full, and get() waits while it is empty and returns the oldest item. A FilterStore lets get take a function that picks the first item it accepts. A PriorityStore returns the smallest item first, and PriorityItem(priority, item) wraps items that cannot be compared. The three below hold the shop's parcels, which differ in size and in urgency.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:stores
def stores():
    """A store holds distinct items; the filtered and priority kinds change which one a get returns."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    parcels = simpy.Store(env)
    by_size = simpy.FilterStore(env)
    by_urgency = simpy.PriorityStore(env)
    got = {}

    def run():
        for name, size in (("p1", "small"), ("p2", "large"), ("p3", "small")):
            yield parcels.put(name)
            yield by_size.put((name, size))
        yield by_urgency.put(simpy.PriorityItem(2, "standard"))
        yield by_urgency.put(simpy.PriorityItem(1, "express"))
        got["store"] = yield parcels.get()  # first in, first out
        got["filter"] = yield by_size.get(
            lambda item: item[1] == "large"
        )  # first match
        got["priority"] = (yield by_urgency.get()).item  # smallest priority first

    env.process(run())
    env.run()
    return got

{'store': 'p1', 'filter': ('p2', 'large'), 'priority': 'express'}

In desflow, a task's put and get use these: put: {container: stock, amount: 2} for a container, and get: {store: parcels, filter: ...} for a filtered store. A store declared with priority: true is a PriorityStore. get_queue and put_queue, each {rank, ties}, order the waiting gets and puts by an expression, as a resource's queue orders its requests, and a store whose type sets its own queues refuses them. The SortedQueue that a custom store type sets its own queue with stays valid. Stores and Containers and Stock explain them.

docs.title: Real-time Environment
docs.text:
RealtimeEnvironment(factor) is an environment whose clock follows the wall clock: a step of one time unit takes factor seconds of real time. With strict=True, the default, step raises RuntimeError when the model falls behind the wall clock by more than factor seconds. Set strict=False to let it catch up instead. sync() restarts the real-time reference from the present. Here one simulated second takes 0.2 seconds of real time, so a run of 2 simulated seconds takes at least 0.4 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:realtime
def realtime():
    """One simulated second takes 0.2 wall-clock seconds; the run lasts at least 2 x 0.2 s."""
    env = simpy.rt.RealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.2)  # strict=True is the default

    def packer():
        yield env.timeout(2)

    env.process(packer())
    started = time.monotonic()
    env.run()
    return env.now, time.monotonic() - started

clock 2, wall clock at least 0.4 s: True

SimPy's factor is fixed when the environment is made. desflow's environment can switch to real time during a run, as the Clock and pacing row of What desflow Changes shows. Time and Pacing explains it.

docs.title: Coming from SimPy
docs.text:
If you have written a SimPy model, you already know most of what desflow needs. This page takes a plain SimPy model in the structure most tutorials teach and shows where each part goes in desflow. Nothing you know is lost: a desflow model is SimPy underneath. SimPy and desflow teaches each SimPy construct, and the last two sections of this page list what desflow changes and the form each construct takes in desflow. SimPy Examples rewrites the seven examples that ship with SimPy, and an assistant with the Agent Skill can port a SimPy program for you.

The structure comes from the open book HSMA: the little book of DES by Dan Chalk, Sammi Rosser and Amy Heather, which teaches SimPy to health-service modellers. Its chapter The Recommended Structure for DES Models splits a model into four classes: a class of global parameters, an entity class, a model class and a trial class. We read that chapter and the chapter on running large numbers of scenarios. The book's text is under CC BY-NC-SA, so none of it is copied here. The code below is our own. It models the packing shop and follows the same four-class shape.

docs.title: Four Classes
docs.text:
Look at the table for where each class goes. The sections after it explain each row on the shop.

In a plain SimPy model In desflow The global parameters class: arrival and packing times, packers, run length, number of runs Arguments of add_arrival, add_service and add_resource, which are registry paths a run can change, and add_variable (variables in YAML) for values of your own The entity class: the thing that moves through the model, with the facts it remembers An entity with attributes, and statistics that record each order's wait and service for you The model class: one run, with its environment, resources, arrival generator and journey generator SimulationContext, with @app.arrival_loop for the arrival generator and @app.task for the journey The trial class: a loop that builds a model for each run number and collects one result per run replicate, which runs a model n times from spawned seeds and gives an interval over the runs

docs.title: Global Parameters
docs.text:
In the usual structure one class holds every number the model reads, and the model reads them as G.packers. This is the shop's.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:globals
class G:
    """Global parameters: read as G.packers, never instantiated."""

    arrival_mean = 2.0  # seconds between orders
    pack_time = 1.5  # seconds to pack an order
    packers = 1
    run_length = 3600  # seconds
    runs = 10

In desflow these numbers are arguments of the parts they describe:

In G In the builder arrival_mean = 2.0 add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5), an order every 2 seconds on average pack_time = 1.5 add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5) packers = 1 add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=10) run_length and runs arguments of run and replicate, because they belong to the run and not to the system a number of your own, such as a conveyor speed add_variable, or variables in YAML

Each value is stored in a registry under a path such as Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, and the model reads the registry whenever it needs the value. So a value can change while the run goes on, from a scenario or a connector, which a value in G cannot. Each change is checked before it is applied. Live Parameters lists the paths.

docs.title: Entity Class
docs.text:
The entity class is what travels through the model. Here an order carries its number and the time it waited.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:entity
class Order:
    """The entity: what travels through the model, and what it remembers."""

    def __init__(self, order_id):
        self.id = order_id
        self.wait = 0.0

In desflow an arrival creates an entity for you, and attributes on the arrival give it starting facts, such as attributes={"express": 0}. A task can read them to decide what comes next, and change them when it finishes. You do not store the wait yourself: the task records when the order queued, started and finished, and the statistics report the mean wait and service time of every task. Task Flow explains attributes.

docs.title: Model Class
docs.text:
The model class is one run. Its constructor makes the environment and the resources, one generator creates the arriving orders, and another is the journey of one order.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:model
class Model:
    """One run of the shop."""

    def __init__(self, run_number):
        self.env = simpy.Environment()
        self.random = random.Random(run_number)
        self.packers = simpy.Resource(self.env, capacity=G.packers)
        self.waits = []

    def generate_orders(self):
        order_id = 0
        while True:
            order_id += 1
            self.env.process(self.pack_order(Order(order_id)))
            yield self.env.timeout(self.random.expovariate(1 / G.arrival_mean))

    def pack_order(self, order):
        arrived = self.env.now
        with self.packers.request() as request:
            yield request
            order.wait = self.env.now - arrived
            self.waits.append(order.wait)
            yield self.env.timeout(G.pack_time)

    def run(self):
        self.env.process(self.generate_orders())
        self.env.run(until=G.run_length)
        return statistics.mean(self.waits)

In desflow, SimulationContext is that class. It makes the environment, which is a SimPy environment, and the resources from the add_ calls, so the constructor of your own class has nothing left to do. The arrival generator is @app.arrival_loop, and the journey is @app.task, which requests the resource, waits, holds it for the service time and releases it. The task replaces the pack_order method above, and it also publishes queued, started and a finished event as records. If the journey is more than one task, a task names the next one, as A Flow of Tasks shows.

docs.title: Trial Class
docs.text:
The trial class runs the model once for each run number and keeps one result per run. Here the run number also seeds the random generator, so each run differs and each can be repeated.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:trial
class Trial:
    """The runs of one design: one result for each."""

    def run_trial(self):
        return [Model(run).run() for run in range(G.runs)]

In desflow this loop is replicate. It runs the model n times, gives each run its own seed spawned from one seed, reads the statistics at the end of each run, and returns the interval for each measure you name. You do not write the loop, the seeding or the interval. Replications explains the options, and Trusting Results uses it on the shop.

docs.title: Shop in desflow
docs.text:
Here is the whole shop in desflow, with the trial loop beside it. The model is one function that builds a context, and the loop is one call.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:desflow
def shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """The same shop: parameters in the registry, the entity and the statistics built in."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0)
    app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1 / 2.0)
    app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=10)
    app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def trial():
    """The trial loop is `replicate`: one seed for each run, and an interval over the runs."""
    result = replicate(
        shop, 10, seed=42, until=3600, measures=["tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]
    )
    return result.summary[0]

Four parts of the desflow version have no line in the SimPy one:

  • context.wait_for_arrival("orders") waits for the gap to the next order, drawn from the orders arrival's distribution, and returns the new order as an entity.
  • entity=order hands that order to the task, so every record of the task carries the order's key, such as orders-1. Without it the task starts an entity of its own.
  • The dictionary the task returns is the payload of its finished event, so {"event_type": "order_packed"} is published as a record.
  • with_stats("typical", interval=3600) switches on the built-in statistics, such as the mean wait that replicate reads, and publishes them every hour of simulated time.

Builder API describes each call, and Statistics lists the levels.

Both versions run 10 times for one hour from an empty shop, so the two answers estimate the same thing. Each line of the output below gives the mean wait over the 10 runs and the half-width of its 95% interval. The two versions use different random numbers, so the values differ, but the check in the script asserts that they agree within their intervals. This shop is not the busy hour of the tutorials: it has one packer and an order every 2 seconds on average, so its mean wait differs from theirs.

plain SimPy: mean wait 2.30 ± 0.20 s over 10 runs
desflow:     mean wait 2.18 ± 0.24 s over 10 runs

What you take with you is the SimPy you wrote. A model can still be a SimPy generator inside desflow, through the Low-level API, and it keeps the SimPy constructs it uses. What you leave behind is the code around it: the parameters class, the result bookkeeping and the trial loop. What you gain is records, pacing, live parameters and the checks on Output Analysis.

docs.title: What desflow Changes
docs.text:
desflow keeps SimPy's event list, clock, processes and resources. It changes the six things in the table:

Part In SimPy In desflow Clock and pacing Environment runs without waiting; RealtimeEnvironment(factor, strict=True) follows the wall clock and raises RuntimeError when the model falls behind one class, DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, does both: factor=0 runs without waiting, go_live_at switches to real time partway through a run (SimPy's factor cannot change once set), logical_start_time gives every record a date and time, and falling behind is reported as telemetry; strict raises RuntimeError as SimPy's does, with the defaults that Strict Pacing gives; sync() is SimPy's, and resume_pacing() also moves the simulation anchor after a pause; advance(until) runs a started run in segments, as repeated env.run(until=...) does Processes generators started with env.process the same, and the builder adds @app.task, @app.arrival_loop, @app.telemetry_loop and add_process, which write the common ones for you Random times none built in: a model calls random or NumPy itself ten named distributions with checked parameters, drawn by a Sampler from the current values each time; each distribution draws from a random sequence of its own, made from the run's seed and its registry path Resources Resource, Container and Store keep the capacity they were created with: it has no setter, so assigning a new one raises AttributeError (SimPy 4.1). Resource serves requests in the order they arrive, and PriorityResource by priority DynamicResource, DynamicContainer and DynamicStore follow a capacity in the registry, and a resource that shrinks lets busy units finish. A resource serves its queue fifo, lifo or by priority, equal priorities first in, first out. run() builds the stores and containers a model declares, and tasks put to and get from them Parameters Python variables, changed only by the model's own code a registry of named paths, changed by connectors, scenarios or processes, with each change checked Output whatever the model prints or logs events and telemetry with a fixed shape, written to Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, files or Iceberg on background threads

docs.title: Each Construct in desflow
docs.text:
Each row names a construct, its form in the three ways of writing a model, and the area of SimPy Compatibility that lists its features with their status, the conformance checks that run them in plain SimPy and in all three forms, and the gaps. A construct with no native form in one of the three is marked there as a gap or a difference, with the reason.

SimPy construct YAML Builder Low-level Checks Environment: run, step, peek, now run.until app.run(until=), app.step(), app.peek() env.run(until=) Environment timeout a task with service and no resource @app.task(service_id=...) yield env.timeout(delay) Events and Timeout Events and callbacks signals:, on:, listen: add_signal, on=, listen= Signal, event.callbacks.append(fn) Events and Timeout Processes and waiting for one wait: {task: ...} wait={"task": ...}, context.call(...) yield env.process(child()) Processes Interrupts interrupt:, on_interrupt context.interrupt(...), on_interrupt= process.interrupt(cause) Interrupts AnyOf, AllOf wait: {any: ...}, wait: {all: ...} wait={"any": ...}, wait={"all": ...} yield a \| b, yield a & b Conditions Resource, PriorityResource resource: packers, queue: priority or queue: lifo @app.task(resource_id=...), add_resource(queue=...) with packers.request() as req: yield req Resources PreemptiveResource preempt: true, queue: priority add_resource(queue="priority", preempt=True) DynamicResource(queue="priority", preempt=True) Resources Container put and get with container and amount put={"container": ...}, get={"container": ...} yield stock.put(2), yield stock.get(1) Containers Store, FilterStore, PriorityStore put and get with store, filter, priority: true put={"store": ...}, get={"store": ..., "filter": ...} parcels.get(filter=...) Stores RealtimeEnvironment simulation.factor, simulation.strict SimulationContext(factor=, strict=) DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=) Real-Time

Every SimPy form in the table has a construct of its own in YAML and the Builder, so a model needs no Python for it. !python stays valid for code you write yourself, and add_process (Builder) or a process of the low-level API runs SimPy code as it is, as Processes shows. Where a SimPy construct has no form in one of the three, SimPy Compatibility says so for that construct. SimPy Compatibility lists, for each construct, the form that gives it. User Guide pages that build on SimPy name the parts they use in their How It Works section, starting with Arrivals and Services.

docs.title: SimPy Compatibility
docs.text:
This page lists every modelling feature of SimPy 4.1.2, 98 in all, and how to write each one in desflow. The features are grouped by the part of SimPy they belong to.

Each feature starts with what it does in SimPy, in bold, and a link to the page that explains it. Below that are its form in SimPy, in YAML, in the Builder API and in the low-level API, how desflow differs in a detail where it does, and the tests that check it.

  • Native: 96. A conformance test runs a plain SimPy 4.1.2 model and the same model in desflow, and compares the event times, outcomes and balances.
  • Gap: 1. desflow gives other times, order or values than SimPy, or has no key for the feature. Each gap has an id and says how to get SimPy's behaviour.
  • Difference kept by design: 1. desflow behaves differently on purpose, for the reason given.

Where desflow Differs, at the end of the page, explains each gap and difference.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Starts the simulation clock at a given time instead of 0. Explained in Initial time.

  • SimPy: Environment(initial_time)
  • YAML: simulation.initial_time
  • Builder: SimulationContext(..., initial_time=100)
  • Low-level: DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(initial_time=100)

Checked by 1 test in c6_run_control.

Gives the current simulation time. Explained in Current time.

  • SimPy: Environment.now
  • YAML: t in a condition, such as t < 110
  • Builder: context.env.now
  • Low-level: env.now

Checked by 1 test in c6_run_control.

Gives the process whose code is running at this moment. Explained in The running process.

  • SimPy: Environment.active_process
  • YAML: process.name, process.instance, process.target in a condition
  • Builder: context.env.active_process; .name and .target on a process
  • Low-level: env.active_process.name, .target

Checked by 7 tests in c1_process_interaction (5), c2_wait_for_one_or_all (1) and yaml_only (1).

Starts a process that runs alongside the one that started it, which carries on without waiting. Explained in Start a flow without waiting for it.

  • SimPy: env.process(...) without yield
  • YAML: spawn: {task: courier}
  • Builder: @app.task(spawn=...), or context.spawn(generator)
  • Low-level: env.process(generator)

Checked by 23 tests in c1_processes (2), builder_additions (6) and yaml_only (15).

Puts an event on the schedule with a priority and a delay. Explained in Schedule an event with a priority.

  • SimPy: Environment.schedule(event, priority, delay)
  • YAML: fire: {signal: s, after: 5 s} on a signal with once: true
  • Builder: {"fire": {"signal": "s", "after": 5}} in on=, or context.env.schedule(event, priority, delay)
  • Low-level: env.schedule(event, priority, delay)

Checked by 5 tests in c6_environment (3), c2_wait_for_one_or_all (1) and c1_events (1).

Orders events due at the same time: an urgent event is processed before a normal one. Explained in Urgent and normal event priorities.

  • SimPy: URGENT and NORMAL event priorities
  • YAML: fire: {signal: s, urgent: true} or fire: {signal: s, priority: 2} on a signal with once: true
  • Builder: {"fire": {"signal": "s", "urgent": True}} in on= ("priority": 2 for another priority), or simpy.events.URGENT in context.env.schedule
  • Low-level: env.schedule(event, URGENT)

Checked by 3 tests in c6_environment (2) and yaml_only (1).

Processes events due at the same time and with the same priority in the order they were scheduled. Explained in Wait for one event.

  • SimPy: Events at one time run in the order they were scheduled
  • YAML: wait: {any: {stock: {signal: restocked}, limit: {timeout: 3}}}
  • Builder: wait={"any": {...}}
  • Low-level: yield a | b
  • Where desflow differs: Losing signal, timeout and condition branches are dropped when the wait ends; losing child flows keep running, as SimPy leaves processes running. A request branch not yet granted when the wait ends is cancelled; a SimPy with block held over the rest of the task leaves it queued.

Checked by 8 tests in c2_wait_for_one_or_all (2) and yaml_only (6).

Gives the time of the next scheduled event, or infinity when none is left. Explained in Inspect next event time.

  • SimPy: Environment.peek()
  • YAML: run: {steps: true} publishes peek after each step, or SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).start(), then .peek()
  • Builder: app.peek()
  • Low-level: env.peek()

Checked by 1 test in c6_end_conditions.

Processes the next event, and raises EmptySchedule when none is left. Explained in Step one event.

  • SimPy: Environment.step()
  • YAML: run: {steps: true}, or SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).start(), then .step()
  • Builder: app.start(), app.step(), app.close()
  • Low-level: env.step()
  • Where desflow differs: run.steps publishes the step count and the clock after each step of a run; stepping a model by hand is for a script, which steps the context from from_yaml as it steps a builder context.

Checked by 4 tests in c6_end_conditions (1), c6_run_control (1) and yaml_only (2).

Steps through the events of the model one at a time from a script. Explained in A step processes only the model's events.

  • SimPy: A step processes only the model's events
  • YAML: SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).start(), then .step() and .peek(); processes: entries are model events
  • Builder: app.start(), app.step(), app.peek(); add_process functions are model events
  • Low-level: env.step() and env.peek()
  • Where desflow differs: With only desflow's own events left, step() raises EmptySchedule and peek() gives infinity, but the queue is not empty: run() and finish() with an until still process those events, and a run with no until ends when only they are left.

Checked by 7 tests in c6_end_conditions.

Runs until no event is left. Explained in A run with no until.

  • SimPy: run() with no until
  • YAML: run: with no until
  • Builder: app.run() with no until
  • Low-level: env.run() with no until

Checked by 5 tests in c6_end_conditions.

Runs until the clock reaches a given time. Explained in Stop at a time.

  • SimPy: run(until=time)
  • YAML: run.until, or run.segments for several stops with a look at each
  • Builder: app.run(until=...)
  • Low-level: env.run(until=...)

Checked by 3 tests in c6_run_control (1) and yaml_only (2).

Runs until a given event is processed. Explained in Stop at an event.

  • SimPy: run(until=event)
  • YAML: run.stop: {signal: closing} beside run.until
  • Builder: app.run(until=..., stop={"signal": "closing"}), a signal's name, or a function returning an event
  • Low-level: env.run(until=event)
  • Where desflow differs: When the stop and until fall at the same time, until ends the run first, as SimPy's own until would.

Checked by 2 tests in c6_end_conditions.

Returns the value of the event a run stops at, or raises its exception when it failed. Explained in Value of a run stopped at an event.

  • SimPy: The value or exception of run(until=event)
  • YAML: SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).run() returns the value; desflow run exits with an error when the stop failed
  • Builder: app.run(until=..., stop=...) and app.finish() return the value
  • Low-level: env.run(until=event)

Checked by 1 test in c6_end_conditions.

Continues a stopped run up to a later time. Explained in Run in segments.

  • SimPy: run(until=t) again with a later t
  • YAML: app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(file), then app.start(), app.advance(until) and app.finish()
  • Builder: app.start(), app.advance(until), app.finish()
  • Low-level: env.run(until=), called again; env.resume_pacing()

Checked by 9 tests in c6_end_conditions (8) and c6_pacing (1).

Runs the callbacks of the event a run stopped at when the run continues. Explained in Run in segments.

  • SimPy: Callbacks of the stopping event run when the run resumes
  • YAML: app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(file), then app.start(), app.advance(until) and app.finish()
  • Builder: app.start(), app.advance(until), app.finish()
  • Low-level: env.run(until=), called again; env.resume_pacing()

Checked by 9 tests in c6_end_conditions (8) and c6_pacing (1).

Changes how the environment schedules or steps events, in a class of your own. Explained in Subclass the environment.

  • SimPy: A subclass of Environment
  • YAML: simulation: {environment: !python module.Env}
  • Builder: SimulationContext(environment=Env)
  • Low-level: class Env(DynamicRealtimeEnvironment)

Checked by 2 tests in c6_environment.

docs.title: Events and Timeout
docs.text:
Marks an event as successful with a value, and wakes every process that waits for it. Explained in Signal event success and value.

  • SimPy: Event.succeed(value) waking every waiter
  • YAML: signals: [restocked], signal: restocked on the firing task and wait: {signal: restocked}; wait: {suspend: true} and resume: {task, where, value, limit} wake instances that no signal names
  • Builder: add_signal, @app.task(signal=...), wait={"signal": ...}, or context.signal(name).fire(value)
  • Low-level: Signal(env, name): yield signal.wait() and signal.fire(value)

Checked by 2 tests in c1_process_interaction (1) and yaml_only (1).

Marks an event as failed with an exception, which is raised in every process that waits for it. Explained in Signal event failure.

  • SimPy: Event.fail(exception)
  • YAML: a failing task with signal; its waiters fail with its reason
  • Builder: the same, or context.signal(name).fail(reason)
  • Low-level: signal.fail(reason); waiters receive SignalFailed

Checked by 1 test in c1_process_interaction.

Lets an event succeed or fail only once. Explained in One-shot event.

  • SimPy: An event that triggers once
  • YAML: signals: {closing: {}}, or once: false to re-arm
  • Builder: add_signal(name), or once=False to re-arm
  • Low-level: Signal(env, name), or once=False to re-arm

Checked by 2 tests in c1_events.

Gives an event the outcome and value of another event, so one event can set off the next. Explained in Actions when an event happens.

  • SimPy: Event.trigger(event)
  • YAML: on: [{fire: {signal, from}}, {spawn: {...}}] on a task or a signal, fire with fail, defused and priority, when on an entry, and listen on a task for a callback added during the run
  • Builder: on=[...] on @app.task and add_signal
  • Low-level: event.callbacks.append(fn), ev.trigger(other), ev.defused = True

Checked by 32 tests in c1_events (26), yaml_only (4) and c3_interrupts (2).

Holds the functions that run when an event is processed. Explained in Actions when an event happens. Gap M2: see Where desflow Differs.

  • SimPy: Event.callbacks
  • YAML: on: [{fire: {signal, from}}, {spawn: {...}}] on a task or a signal, fire with fail, defused and priority, when on an entry, and listen on a task for a callback added during the run
  • Builder: on=[...] on @app.task and add_signal
  • Low-level: event.callbacks.append(fn), ev.trigger(other), ev.defused = True

Checked by 32 tests in c1_events (26), yaml_only (4) and c3_interrupts (2).

Marks a failed event as handled, so its exception does not stop the run. Explained in Actions when an event happens.

  • SimPy: Event.defused
  • YAML: on: [{fire: {signal, from}}, {spawn: {...}}] on a task or a signal, fire with fail, defused and priority, when on an entry, and listen on a task for a callback added during the run
  • Builder: on=[...] on @app.task and add_signal
  • Low-level: event.callbacks.append(fn), ev.trigger(other), ev.defused = True

Checked by 32 tests in c1_events (26), yaml_only (4) and c3_interrupts (2).

Stops the run with the exception of a failed event that no process or callback handles. Explained in Failure nobody handles.

  • SimPy: A failed event nobody handles stops the run
  • YAML: run: {on_unhandled_failure: continue} to go on, stop is the default
  • Builder: run(on_unhandled_failure=...) or start(on_unhandled_failure=...)
  • Low-level: DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(on_unhandled_failure=...)

Checked by 3 tests in c1_events.

Tell whether an event has been triggered, has been processed and succeeded, and give its value. Explained in Event inspection.

  • SimPy: Event.triggered, processed, ok and value
  • YAML: signal.<name>.count, .ok and .value in a condition
  • Builder: context.signal(name).wait() and its SimPy attributes, or the signal's count, ok and value
  • Low-level: the same attributes of SimPy events and Signal

Checked by 1 test in c1_process_interaction.

Combine events into one that waits for all of them (&) or for the first of them (|). Explained in Wait for one event.

  • SimPy: a & b and a | b
  • YAML: wait: {any: {stock: {signal: restocked}, limit: {timeout: 3}}}
  • Builder: wait={"any": {...}}
  • Low-level: yield a | b
  • Where desflow differs: Losing signal, timeout and condition branches are dropped when the wait ends; losing child flows keep running, as SimPy leaves processes running. A request branch not yet granted when the wait ends is cancelled; a SimPy with block held over the rest of the task leaves it queued.

Checked by 8 tests in c2_wait_for_one_or_all (2) and yaml_only (6).

An event that happens after a delay. Explained in Timed wait.

  • SimPy: Timeout(delay)
  • YAML: a task with service or service_time and no resource
  • Builder: @app.task(service_id=...) with no resource
  • Low-level: yield env.timeout(delay)
