docs.text:
Each page here describes one part of desflow: what it does, how to use it, how it works and its limits. Read a page when you need that part. To learn DES and desflow from the start, follow Learn instead. To do one task step by step, see How-To.

Group What it covers How desflow Works how desflow is built: the parts that run a model, why each exists, and how a run moves through them Writing a Model the three ways to write a model: a YAML blueprint, the builder API and the low-level API Model Parts the parts a model is made of: arrivals and services, input fitting, task flow, and stores and containers Tasks and Processes tasks, processes, the signals they wait for, and failures Resources priority and preemption, tasks that hold several resources, and resource types of your own Time and Pacing the simulation clock, pacing against real time, and how long a run lasts Results what a run measures, replications and experiments Live Runs and Connectors parameters that change during a run, and the connectors that bring changes in and write records out

docs.title: How desflow Works
docs.text:
This page shows how desflow is built: the parts that run a model, why each one exists, and how a run moves through them. Each part links to the How It Works section that describes it in full.

One run moves through the parts of desflow like this:

Whichever way a model is written, it builds one environment, and one run goes the same way from there. The registry paths, the records, the batching and the connectors are therefore the same in all three ways. How It Works follows a model from its file or script to the environment.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
desflow is built on SimPy. SimPy gives the event list, the clock, processes and resources, and desflow keeps all of them. SimPy leaves seven things to the modeller, and each part of desflow adds one of them:

Left to the modeller in SimPy What desflow adds Read the code around a model: a class of parameters, an entity class, a model class and a loop over runs three ways to write a model, each built on the one below Writing a Model one pacing factor, fixed when the environment is made one environment that runs history at full speed, then switches to the wall clock Time and Pacing random times, drawn by the model's own code ten checked distributions, each with a random stream of its own Arrivals and Services parameters that only the model's code changes a registry of named paths that connectors, scenarios and processes change during a run Live Parameters resources, stores and containers that keep the capacity they were made with resources, stores and containers whose capacity follows the registry Resources output, which the model prints or logs records of a fixed shape, written to sinks on a thread of their own Egress statistics, replications and confidence intervals statistics collected during the run, replications, experiments and explain Built-in Statistics

Coming from SimPy compares each change with plain SimPy.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Look first at how a model gets from a file or a script to a run, then at the parts the run holds:

Each of the three ways ends in one DynamicRealtimeEnvironment. A YAML file is read by blueprint: loader reads the file, including !python and !include, models define and check each section, and build turns the sections into calls on SimulationContext; the arrow labelled calls the builder shows them. A builder script makes those calls itself, with the builder's methods and decorators. A low-level script makes neither: it builds the environment by hand and writes SimPy processes against it. Writing a Model helps choose between them.

SimulationContext in builder.context collects what a model declares. run() checks the declarations and builds the environment, then starts the model's loops and processes and runs it, in the order What run() Does lists. The environment holds the parts in the row under it:

  • registry: holds every live parameter (Live Parameters).
  • statistics: collects the measures of the run while it goes on (Built-in Statistics).
  • egress queue: the records that tasks and processes publish are buffered for each sink, and full batches wait in a queue. connectors/egress writes from it, on a thread of its own, and the arrow points the way the records go (Egress).
  • connectors/ingress: read parameter changes from outside, on a thread of their own, and update the registry. The arrow points up, because a change reaches the model only through the registry; the environment applies each one from a queue (Ingress). Threads and Queues shows both queues.

The group at the bottom holds the tools. cli is the desflow command and calls loading, the path by which desflow run and desflow explain turn a blueprint or a builder file into a context (Command Line). analysis runs a model many times for replications and experiments. cli and explain read a blueprint or a builder file; analysis also runs a low-level model, as a LowLevelModel, from Python. explain is in the last row of the table below.

Each part is described in full on its own page. In short:

Part How it works Read Writing a model A YAML blueprint, the builder and the low-level API are layers. from_yaml makes the calls a builder script makes, and the builder's run() makes the calls a low-level script writes by hand. YAML Blueprints, What run() Does Environment and pacing DynamicRealtimeEnvironment is SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment with the registry, the connectors and the statistics added. It runs without waiting at factor: 0 and switches to real time at go_live_at. Time and Pacing Random times A distribution reads its parameters at each draw, so a change applies from the next draw. Each one has its own random stream, made from the run's seed and its registry path. Arrivals and Services Registry Every live value sits under a dot path, such as Shop.service.packing.mean. Each update is checked before it is stored. Live Parameters Resources, stores and containers Each waits on its registry path, so its capacity changes during a run. A resource that shrinks lets its busy units finish. Resources, Stores and Containers Threads, ingress and egress The SimPy thread runs the model. Ingress and egress run their connectors on threads of their own, each on an asyncio loop, so a network wait never stalls a simulation step. Threads and Queues, which also compares these queues with the waiting lines of the model; Ingress, Egress, Write a Connector Measurement and explain One statistics object collects readings while the run goes on. Replications run the model again for each seed and give a Student t interval. desflow explain applies queueing formulas to the model before anything runs. Built-in Statistics, Replications, Experiments, Command Line

docs.title: How a YAML File Becomes Builder Calls
docs.text:
Follow the file down the left column, then look at the group on the right, which joins each section of the file to the builder call it becomes:

  • loader reads the file, replaces ${VAR} with an environment variable, and resolves !python and !include (YAML Blueprints). It keeps the line each key came from, so an error names the line.
  • models checks each section and refuses an unknown key, so a misspelt key is reported, not ignored.
  • build makes one builder call for each entry, so a YAML file and a builder script that make the same calls build the same model. From SimulationContext on, a run goes as the next diagram shows.

docs.title: How a Builder Script Becomes a Run
docs.text:
Look at the two halves: the top shows where the builder keeps what a script declares, and the group below shows what run() does with it, in order. run() is start() then finish(). A script that steps through a run itself calls start(), then step() or advance(), and ends the run with finish() or close():

start() checks the model, builds the run and starts it, and finish() runs it to its end and closes it. What run() Does gives the steps in order.

docs.title: What a Low-Level Script Uses
docs.text:
A low-level script uses the engine directly. Look at the top row for what the script calls, and at the row below it for what the environment holds:

  • environment: the script creates it, registers its parameters, calls setup_stats, setup_ingress and setup_egress, starts its processes with env.process, and calls run().
  • sampler: draws every random time, with one random stream for each distribution (Arrivals and Services).
  • DynamicResource: a resource whose capacity follows its registry path (Resources).
  • rules: the checks a blueprint and the builder share; the registry uses one of them to check a capacity before it stores it.
  • expressions, families and replay serve the builder and YAML: conditions and amounts, resources and signals made from a computed key, and arrivals read from a recorded file.

ARCHITECTURE.md draws the same three diagrams as text, with every module.

docs.title: What the Environment Holds
docs.text: A DynamicRealtimeEnvironment is SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment with four additions: the registry at env.registry, the ingress connectors, the egress connectors with their buffers, and the statistics at env.stats. Whichever way a model is written, SimulationContext.run() builds this environment.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
A run uses three threads, with queues between them. Records flow from the processes to the sinks, and parameter changes flow from the sources to the registry:

  • SimPy thread: runs the model. When a process publishes a record, the record goes into a buffer for each sink, and a full buffer is handed to that sink's queue.
  • Egress thread: runs the sinks' asyncio code, which drains the queues and writes to Kafka, files or databases, so network waits never stall a simulation step.
  • Ingress thread: runs the sources, which put (path, value) pairs on a queue.

docs.title: Two Kinds of Queue
docs.text:
The word queue means two different things in desflow:

  • A waiting line in the model holds entities, such as orders waiting for a packer. A resource keeps its line in queue, ordered fifo, lifo or by priority, and a request past its queue_limit raises QueueFull. Stores and containers have lines of puts and gets that wait. These lines are what a study measures: their lengths and waits are in the records and the statistics.
  • A hand-off queue holds data on its way between the threads above. The ingress queue has no limit, and the ingress monitor applies it. Each sink has its own queue of at most max_queued_batches batches. When a sink's queue is full, the simulation waits, so a slow sink slows the run instead of building a backlog. When it stays full for drain_stall_seconds, the run stops rather than lose records. These queues change how fast the records arrive, never what they hold.

docs.title: Processes the Environment Starts
docs.text:
Besides your own processes, the environment starts these, as events of its own that step() and peek() do not count:

  • an ingress monitor, which applies queued changes every 0.1 simulation seconds;
  • a lag monitor, which publishes system.simulation.lag_seconds every lag_interval, at a factor above 0 or after going live;
  • a timed flush per sink, at a factor above 0;
  • the statistics timer;
  • the warm-up reset.

They share SimPy's one event queue with the model's events, so run() processes them in order with the model's events. A script that steps the model never sees them. advance() and finish() run them in the same way. An environment subclass that overrides step() sees every event inside run(), desflow's own included, and only the model's events when a script steps outside run().

docs.title: SimPy and desflow
docs.text: SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment takes one factor for the whole run, and raises an error when the model falls behind the wall clock. desflow runs without waiting at factor: 0, switches to real time at go_live_at, and stamps every record with a logical time. A paced run is strict by default, as SimPy's is, and strict: false reports falling behind as telemetry instead. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: For Contributors
docs.text: A contributor who changes desflow itself can read ARCHITECTURE.md, which holds the code map and the rules for imports.

docs.title: Live Runs and Connectors
docs.text: A live run changes its parameters while it runs and sends its records out as they happen. Three parts do this: the registry of live parameters, the ingress connectors that change them, and the egress connectors that write the records. The diagram on How desflow Works shows how one run moves through them.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
• Live parameters sit in the registry under named paths, such as Shop.service.packing.mean. An arrival rate, a number of packers or a stock level can change while the run goes on.
  • Ingress connectors bring those changes in from outside: from a file you edit, Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL or a local schedule.
  • Egress connectors, or sinks, write the records the run publishes: to the console, Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Parquet or JSON Lines files, or Iceberg tables.

docs.title: Pages in This Section
docs.text:
• Live Parameters: how to name a parameter, the ways to change it, how to record what a change was for, and what happens to a value once it arrives.
  • Ingress: each source connector, the message it reads, how to send one, and when the change lands.
  • Egress: each sink, how to choose which records each one gets, and how records travel from a task to a sink.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
• A value that should change during a run is a registry path, such as a service's mean or a resource's capacity, or a variables entry for any other value.
  • An ingress entry in YAML, or add_ingress in the builder, adds a source of changes.
  • An egress entry, or add_egress, adds a sink.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: A run uses three threads. The ingress thread runs the sources, which put (path, value) pairs on a queue, and the ingress monitor applies them to the registry every 0.1 simulation seconds. The SimPy thread runs the model, which follows each change: a distribution uses the new parameters from its next draw, and a resource changes its capacity. Each record the model publishes goes into a buffer for each sink, and the egress thread writes full batches to the sinks. How desflow Works shows the threads and the queues between them.

docs.title: Egress, Batching and Delivery
docs.text: An egress connector, or sink, writes the records a run publishes: to the console, Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Parquet or JSON Lines files, or Iceberg tables. This page shows each sink, how to choose which records each one gets, and how records travel from a task to a sink.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
A run publishes three kinds of record in the ordinary case: events, such as a task's queued, started and finished; telemetry, single values such as the statistics; and labels, the ground-truth records of what a scenario changed. Every sink receives every event and every telemetry record, unless its when says otherwise. Labels go only to sinks that ask for them. A run can publish a fourth kind, trace, one record for each event the environment processes, only when stats.trace is set, and only to a sink with when: trace. Records and Telemetry shows each record's shape and what each sink writes.

The tutorial page Streaming Out teaches these features step by step.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Each sink is listed under egress in a blueprint with its type and config, attached with add_egress in the builder, or passed to env.setup_egress in the low-level API. In the builder snippets below, app is a SimulationContext.

In a blueprint, type is one of the short names below, or a !python class from another package. A connector's module is imported only when a blueprint names it, so a blueprint that uses Kafka does not need the PostgreSQL driver. Parquet and JSON Lines are the exception: they import PyArrow when they start writing. A missing package stops the load with its line and the pip install command.

type Class Extra Console ConsoleEgress none Kafka KafkaEgress kafka Parquet ParquetStorageEgress parquet Jsonl JsonlStorageEgress parquet Iceberg IcebergStorageEgress iceberg Postgres PostgresEgress postgres Redis RedisEgress redis

config holds the constructor's arguments. Settings that Python takes as objects are plain values there: a Parquet or JSON Lines filesystem is a mapping with type: local, s3, gcs or azure, and an Iceberg catalog is a mapping of PyIceberg properties. A Postgres tables mapping creates its tables when the run starts. Each table maps to columns, a mapping of column name to SQL type, and an optional primary_key. An ISO time string bound for a timestamp or date column of Iceberg or PostgreSQL is converted before the write. YAML Keys lists the keys of an egress entry.

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
ConsoleEgress has two formats. The default, log, logs each batch at INFO level with one call, one line per record:

  • Each line starts with [EVT] for an event, [TEL] for telemetry or [LBL] for a label. A trace record, which only a when: trace sink receives, starts with [EVT] too.
  • desflow run prints these lines as they are. Its other log lines start with the time, level and logger name.
  • In a script, the logging format the script sets, such as the time and level, starts only the first line of each batch.

One call per batch is much faster than one call per record. In the measurements on Tune Performance, a run that logged each record with its own call took about 50 percent longer in total.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:console-egress
- {type: Console}
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:console-egress
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())

The low-level API passes the same ConsoleEgress() to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

With format="json", ConsoleEgress writes each record to stdout as one JSON line instead: the record as published, with its stream_type. Another program can then read the records. It writes at any log level, because the records are output, not a log. Python's logging writes to stderr by default, so the log stays apart from the records, and a pipe such as | jq .key reads only the records. In a blueprint it is type: Console with config: {format: json}. desflow run --sample and --stdout print through it in place of the file's sinks, as YAML Blueprints describes.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:console-json
# One JSON line per record on stdout, stream_type included
- type: Console
  config: {format: json}
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:console-json
# One JSON line per record on stdout, stream_type included
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress(format="json"))

The low-level API passes the same ConsoleEgress(format="json") to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

A consumer can check each line against the record schema: EventPayload, TelemetryPayload and LabelPayload are the Pydantic models of the three stream types, as Records and Telemetry describes:

docs/snippets/pages/record_schemas.py:validate
# The model of each stream type; a record with a missing or mistyped field raises
SCHEMAS = {"event": EventPayload, "telemetry": TelemetryPayload, "label": LabelPayload}
for line in printed.getvalue().splitlines():
    record = json.loads(line)
    SCHEMAS[record["stream_type"]].model_validate(record)

The trace record has no model in SCHEMAS. A consumer reads it as a record whose value is a mapping with the keys priority, event_id and event.

docs.title: Kafka
docs.text:
KafkaEgress sends events to event_topic and telemetry to telemetry_topic, keyed by the record's key or path_id. Kafka sends all records with one key to one partition, so all events of one entity stay in order. KafkaEgress creates both topics when the run starts, with one partition each, if they do not exist. With a topic_router, it creates neither of them, and only the topics named in topics. Route Records to Topics sends records to other topics, and Connect to Secure Kafka connects to a cluster that uses SASL, mTLS, OAuth or AWS IAM.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:kafka-egress
- type: Kafka
  config:
    bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}
    event_topic: sim-events
    telemetry_topic: sim-telemetry
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:kafka-egress
app.add_egress(
    KafkaEgress(
        bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092",
        event_topic="sim-events",
        telemetry_topic="sim-telemetry",
    )
)

The low-level API passes the same KafkaEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

Topics. topic_policy says what the sink does with its topics when the run starts. It is a word, or a mapping of mode, partitions, replication_factor and topic_configs:

  • create, the default, creates a missing topic and leaves an existing one as it is, with one partition, a replication factor of 1 and no settings of its own.
  • drop_and_create deletes the topic and creates it again, so each run starts with an empty topic.
  • manual creates nothing.

The policy covers the event topic and the telemetry topic. topics gives settings to other topics by name, each with the keys of topic_policy on top of the policy. A topic named there is created by the sink, also when a record chooses it with __topic__ or a topic_router. A topics value must be a mapping, and a key that is not a policy key is refused when the blueprint loads.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:kafka-topics
# The policy covers the event and telemetry topics: three partitions each, with a
# retention setting. sim-audit is created too, with one partition of its own
- type: Kafka
  config:
    bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}
    event_topic: sim-events
    telemetry_topic: sim-telemetry
    topic_policy:
      mode: create
      partitions: 3
      topic_configs: {retention.ms: 3600000}
    topics:
      sim-audit: {partitions: 1}

KafkaEgress takes the same topic_policy and topics as arguments.

The low-level API passes the same KafkaEgress(topic_policy=..., topics=...) to env.setup_egress.

An event whose value has a __topic__ key goes to the topic it names, and the key is removed from the message. A topic_router wins over __topic__, and telemetry always goes to telemetry_topic. The sink also takes a serializer (a mapping with a type of confluent_avro, confluent_json_schema, confluent_protobuf, glue_avro, glue_json_schema or glue_protobuf, with the options of that type, such as schema, schema_file, descriptor_file and message), ssl and sasl_oauth_token_provider ({type: aws_msk_iam, region: ...}), and serializer can also be set for one topic under topics. In a blueprint, a schema_file, a descriptor_file, the verify and cert files of a serializer and the files of ssl are read from the blueprint's folder, as an !include is, so desflow run sub/shop.yaml and cd sub && desflow run shop.yaml read the same files. The Builder reads them from the working directory. Use Schema Serializers and Connect to Secure Kafka use these options. The registry options of the Avro serializers (auth, verify, cert, headers, proxy, timeout and max_retries) are in the step Connect to a Secured Schema Registry.

docs.title: Parquet and JSON Lines
docs.text:
ParquetStorageEgress and JsonlStorageEgress write each batch as a file of its own, on a local disk, S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage, through PyArrow. Without a path_router, each event is one flat row in default_path, with its value mapping unpacked into columns, and telemetry is left out.

A Parquet file has a column for every key of any row in its batch, and a mapping value becomes a struct column. A later batch can change the columns:

  • A key that first appears in a later batch adds a column to the later files. A reader that combines the columns of all the files reads it as null in the earlier rows.
  • An integer column that a later batch gives a float becomes a double in the later files.
  • A nested key that first appears later is dropped, because the first batch with a mapping value fixes the keys of its struct column.

The first batch sets the type of each column. A number in the first batch is read as a double for the value of a telemetry record, for the now and peek of a run.steps or run.segments reading, and for usage_since, so a later fraction is kept. A statistic (a number) and an event or a reading (a mapping) cannot share a file, because the value column has one type. Send them to different files with a path_router, because the default route writes no telemetry.

A batch that cannot be written is logged at ERROR, and the sink goes on with the next one.

Routing by __path__. An event whose value has a __path__ key is written to the file path it names, and the key is removed from the row. A path_router wins over __path__, and a record with no __path__ goes to default_path. __path__ is relative to the working directory or to the sink's filesystem, and it is not placed under the folder of default_path. A path built with {gen: format_time, format: "folder/%Y-%m-%d.jsonl"} gives each simulated day its own files, folder/2026-01-01_<id>.jsonl, with one file for each flush. Write to Cloud Storage runs it.

File names. default_path, and any path a path_router returns or __path__ names, is a file name prefix, not a folder. Each batch is written as a file of its own, <stem>_<8 hex digits><extension>, in the path's folder, so output/events.parquet gives files such as output/events_1a2b3c4d.parquet. Give the extension in the path: output/events gives files with none. The folder is created on the first write.

Columns of a finished event. A task's queued and started events carry path_id and status. Its finished event's value is the task's payload only. So in a finished event's row, path_id and status are null unless the payload has them. The Parquet example adds them to its payload for that reason.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:storage-egress
# Parquet files on the local disk, output/events_<8 hex digits>.parquet
- type: Parquet
  config: {default_path: output/events.parquet}
# JSON Lines files on S3-compatible storage, here SeaweedFS from odctl; a mapping
# becomes PyArrow's S3FileSystem
- type: Jsonl
  config:
    default_path: warehouse/events.jsonl
    filesystem:
      type: s3
      access_key: user
      secret_key: password
      endpoint_override: 127.0.0.1:8333
      scheme: http
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:storage-egress
# Parquet files on the local disk, output/events_<8 hex digits>.parquet
app.add_egress(ParquetStorageEgress(default_path="output/events.parquet"))

# JSON Lines files on S3-compatible storage, here SeaweedFS from odctl
seaweedfs = fs.S3FileSystem(
    access_key="user",
    secret_key="password",
    endpoint_override="127.0.0.1:8333",
    scheme="http",
)
app.add_egress(
    JsonlStorageEgress(default_path="warehouse/events.jsonl", filesystem=seaweedfs)
)

The low-level API passes the same sinks to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

Read the files back as one table with pyarrow.dataset, which reads every file in the folder:

docs/snippets/pages/file_sink.py:read
def read_events(folder="output"):
    """Every file the sink wrote under `folder`, as one table."""
    import pyarrow.dataset as ds

    # format="json" reads the files of a JsonlStorageEgress the same way
    return ds.dataset(folder, format="parquet").to_table()

A second run adds its files beside the first run's, so reading the folder then counts both runs. Give each run a folder of its own, or clear the folder before a run.

Filesystems. filesystem is a PyArrow FileSystem object, or a mapping that desflow builds into one when the run starts. The mapping's type picks the class, and its other keys are the arguments of that class:

type PyArrow class Credentials local (the default) LocalFileSystem none s3 S3FileSystem access_key and secret_key; without them, the standard AWS settings gcs GcsFileSystem anonymous: true; or access_token with credential_token_expiration; without them, Google's default credentials azure AzureFileSystem account_name, always; with it account_key, or sas_token (pyarrow 20.0.0 or later), or client_id, client_secret and tenant_id (pyarrow 21.0.0 or later); with account_name alone, Azure's default credentials

An endpoint_override that starts with http:// or https:// also sets scheme, for s3 and gcs, unless scheme is given. azure has no endpoint_override: blob_storage_authority and blob_storage_scheme point it at an emulator such as Azurite. For gcs, credential_token_expiration is an ISO 8601 time, quoted or not, which desflow converts to UTC, and retry_time_limit is a number of seconds, because YAML has no duration type. A key whose value is empty is left out. PyArrow has AzureFileSystem from 16.0.0, the release the parquet extra requires. sas_token and the client credentials need the later releases the table names. PyPI's pyarrow wheels for Windows include it only from 24.0.0.

The same two sinks write to Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage when filesystem is a mapping. Write to Cloud Storage runs a shop against each store, from start to end:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/storage_backends.yaml:cloud
# Parquet files on Google Cloud Storage, with Google's default credentials
- type: Parquet
  config:
    default_path: my-bucket/events.parquet
    # type: gcs makes PyArrow's GcsFileSystem; without credentials it uses Google's
    # default ones
    filesystem: {type: gcs}
# JSON Lines files on Azure Blob Storage, with Azure's default credentials
- type: Jsonl
  config:
    default_path: my-container/events.jsonl
    # type: azure makes PyArrow's AzureFileSystem; without a key it uses Azure's
    # default credentials
    filesystem: {type: azure, account_name: myaccount}
docs/snippets/pages/storage_backends.py:cloud
# Parquet files on Google Cloud Storage, with Google's default credentials
cloud.add_egress(
    ParquetStorageEgress(
        default_path="my-bucket/events.parquet",
        filesystem={"type": "gcs"},
    )
)
# JSON Lines files on Azure Blob Storage, with Azure's default credentials
cloud.add_egress(
    JsonlStorageEgress(
        default_path="my-container/events.jsonl",
        filesystem={"type": "azure", "account_name": "myaccount"},
    )
)

The low-level API passes the same sinks to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
RedisEgress appends each record to a Redis Stream with XADD, as one payload field holding the record as JSON. A __stream__ key in the record's value picks the stream, and is removed before writing.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:redis-egress
# XADD to the events stream, unless a record's value names another in __stream__
- type: Redis
  config: {url: redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0, stream_name: events}
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:redis-egress
# XADD to the events stream, unless a record's value names another in __stream__
app.add_egress(
    RedisEgress("redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0", stream_name="events")
)

The low-level API passes the same RedisEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
PostgresEgress inserts records into a table in batches. It writes only the records whose value is a mapping, and the labels on a labels sink, each label as sim_ts, timestamp, path, old, new and label. A record's row is its value, changed in four ways:

  • The record's sim_ts, timestamp, key (as event_id) and path_id are added, and replace fields of the same name.
  • Its task and instance are added too, but a value field of the same name keeps its own value.
  • Keys with no matching column are dropped.
  • A __table__ key sends the record only to the sink whose table_name matches.

The columns are those of the one table that the name resolves to, as PostgreSQL reads it in the CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements. A name with capitals reads the table with the lower-case name (PostgreSQL folds only the letters A to Z, so Ärger stays Ärger), and a name with no schema reads the first table of that name on the search_path. table_policy says what the sink does about the tables in tables when the run starts: create, the default, creates the schema of a qualified name and the table when they do not exist, drop_and_create also drops the table first, and manual creates nothing.

The connection string names odctl, the database that the odctl postgres profile creates, with the user user and the password password.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:postgres-egress
- type: Postgres
  config:
    connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl
    table_name: orders
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:postgres-egress
dsn = "postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl"
app.add_egress(PostgresEgress(dsn, table_name="orders"))

The low-level API passes the same PostgresEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

By default a record whose key already exists is skipped. upsert_keys updates that row instead, for a model that changes rows it wrote earlier, such as an order moving from packed to shipped. The key columns, a list or one column name, need a unique index. An update sets only the columns the record carries, and within one flush the last record for a key wins. A record that has no value for a key column, or a null there, is skipped, and one warning at the end of each flush says how many were skipped and why.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:postgres-upsert
- type: Postgres
  config:
    connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl
    table_name: orders
    upsert_keys: [order_id]
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:postgres-upsert
app.add_egress(PostgresEgress(dsn, table_name="orders", upsert_keys=["order_id"]))

The low-level API passes the same PostgresEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

docs.title: Iceberg
docs.text:
IcebergStorageEgress appends records to an Apache Iceberg table through a catalog. One flush is one commit, so this sink needs a large batch_size of its own: every commit writes new metadata, and many small commits slow down queries.

A table the sink creates takes its columns from the records:

  • The first batch gives a column for every key that has a value in some row.
  • A key that is null in every row waits for a batch that gives it a value, because Iceberg has no null type. An example is task in a low-level event published without one.
  • A key that first appears in a later batch is added as an optional column, unless the table is named in schemas, which keeps the columns it gives. A table with upsert_keys that is not named in schemas refuses that batch instead, so name every column of an upsert table in schemas.

The first batch sets the type of each column. A whole number in the first batch gives an integer column, except that a telemetry value, the now and peek of a run.steps or run.segments reading and usage_since are read as doubles. A batch with a fraction for an integer column is logged at ERROR and its rows are not written. No value is truncated. Iceberg cannot change a long column to a double later, so a column that takes fractions is named in schemas before the table is created, such as schemas: {shop.events: {key: string, v: double}}: a table named there is created with exactly the columns listed, and every batch is cast to them. A statistic (a number) and an event or a reading (a mapping) need different tables, because the value column has one type. Send them apart with a table_router, because the default route writes no telemetry. Write to Iceberg Tables runs a batch that is lost and the fix.

An event whose value has a __table__ key, a namespace.table name, is written to that table, and the key is removed. A table_router wins over __table__, and a record with no __table__ goes to default_table. An event that Postgres and Iceberg both receive and that has a __table__ without a namespace is skipped by Iceberg with the warning "names no namespace", and the other records of the batch are written. Give Iceberg a table_router, or write namespace.table in the key.

table_policy says what the sink does about a table at its first write, and every run of a context applies it again: create, the default, creates the namespace and the table when they do not exist, drop_and_create drops the table and creates it again once for each run, and manual creates nothing and fails the write if the table is missing. Each run also makes its own connection pool or client, in its own event loop, and makes the sink's folders again.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:table-policy
# Each run starts with an empty table: dropped and created again at the first write
- type: Iceberg
  config:
    default_table: sim.events
    table_policy: drop_and_create
    catalog:
      name: odctl
      type: rest
      uri: http://127.0.0.1:8181
      warehouse: s3://warehouse/
  batch_size: 200000

IcebergStorageEgress takes the same table_policy as an argument.

The low-level API passes the same IcebergStorageEgress(table_policy=...) to env.setup_egress.

Catalogs. catalog is a PyIceberg Catalog object, or a mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties that desflow passes to load_catalog on the first write. The mapping's optional name key names the catalog. Each catalog below has a test that writes through it:

Catalog type Tested against REST rest the odctl catalog profile SQL on SQLite sql the unit tests, with a database file SQL on PostgreSQL sql the odctl postgres profile Glue glue Floci, an AWS emulator, not AWS itself

The properties of each catalog are listed in PyIceberg's configuration. Write to Iceberg Tables runs a shop through each catalog, from start to end.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:iceberg-egress
# A mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties, here the REST catalog of odctl.
# One commit per flush, so this sink gets a large batch of its own
- type: Iceberg
  config:
    default_table: sim.events
    catalog:
      name: odctl
      type: rest
      uri: http://127.0.0.1:8181
      warehouse: s3://warehouse/
      s3.endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8333
      s3.access-key-id: user
      s3.secret-access-key: password
      s3.region: us-east-1
  batch_size: 200000
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:iceberg-egress
catalog = RestCatalog(
    "odctl",
    uri="http://127.0.0.1:8181",
    warehouse="s3://warehouse/",
    **{
        "s3.endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:8333",
        "s3.access-key-id": "user",
        "s3.secret-access-key": "password",
        "s3.region": "us-east-1",
    },
)
# One commit per flush, so this sink gets a large batch of its own
app.add_egress(
    IcebergStorageEgress(catalog=catalog, default_table="sim.events"),
    batch_size=200_000,
)

The low-level API passes the same IcebergStorageEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, and gives its batch size in batch_sizes, as Batch Size and Flush Interval shows.

A SQL catalog on SQLite needs no service, so it suits a first run. Its database file and the table files are under one folder:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/storage_backends.yaml:sqlite
# The catalog's database and the table files are under the folder iceberg/
- type: Iceberg
  config:
    default_table: sim.events
    # The folder iceberg/ must exist before the run
    catalog:
      name: local
      type: sql
      uri: sqlite:///iceberg/catalog.db
      warehouse: file://${PWD}/iceberg/warehouse
docs/snippets/pages/storage_backends.py:sqlite
# The catalog's database and the table files are under the folder iceberg/
folder = Path("iceberg").resolve()
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
catalog = {
    "name": "local",
    "type": "sql",
    "uri": f"sqlite:///{folder}/catalog.db",
    "warehouse": f"file://{folder}/warehouse",
}
app.add_egress(IcebergStorageEgress(catalog=catalog, default_table="sim.events"))

The low-level API passes the same IcebergStorageEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

upsert_keys upserts on key columns instead of appending, and each table takes a list of columns or one column name. A seeded model rerun over the same window writes rows with the same keys, so the upsert replaces those rows instead of duplicating them. An upsert reads the matching rows first, replaces whole rows, never deletes, and needs pyiceberg 0.9.0 or later. A table with upsert_keys cannot gain a column, because the matching rows in the old data files lack it. When a table with upsert_keys is not named in schemas, a batch that brings a column the table lacks is logged as an error that names the table and the columns, and is not written. A table named in schemas writes only the columns listed there and leaves any other field out. Name every column in schemas before the table is created. A record that lacks a key column, or holds null in it, is skipped, and one warning at the end of each flush says how many were skipped and why. An entry that names its tables in schemas, locations or upsert_keys needs no default_table and no router.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:iceberg-upsert
- type: Iceberg
  config:
    default_table: sim.orders
    upsert_keys: {sim.orders: [order_id]}
    catalog:
      name: odctl
      type: rest
      uri: http://127.0.0.1:8181
      warehouse: s3://warehouse/
  batch_size: 200000
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:iceberg-upsert
app.add_egress(
    IcebergStorageEgress(
        catalog=catalog,
        default_table="sim.orders",
        upsert_keys={"sim.orders": ["order_id"]},
    ),
    batch_size=200_000,
)

The low-level API passes the same IcebergStorageEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, and gives its batch size in batch_sizes, as Batch Size and Flush Interval shows.

docs.title: Choose What Each Sink Gets
docs.text:
Every sink receives every event and telemetry record. when narrows that down:

  • A function taking one record and returning True to send it to this sink, in the builder or as !python in a blueprint.
  • events and telemetry, in a blueprint: only the event records, or only the telemetry records.
  • {expr: ...}, in a blueprint: an expression over the record, written with record.stream_type (event or telemetry), record.key, record.task and record.value.<field>. The sink receives the record when the expression is true. A name the record lacks reads as null, so an equality with it is false. An ordering comparison such as record.value.amount > 100 fails the run on the first record that has no amount, so write record.stream_type == 'event' and ... first. t is refused in a when expression.
  • history and live, in a blueprint: the records stamped before simulation.go_live_at, and the rest, as Clocks and Pacing describes.
  • trace: the event trace of stats.trace, and nothing else. Built-in Statistics sets it up. A run with a trace sink and no stats.trace is refused when it loads.
  • labels: the ground-truth labels, and nothing else. No other sink receives a label, so data and labels always reach different sinks. Live Parameters describes them.
YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/batching.yaml:egress
egress:
  # Small and often for this sink; the other uses the defaults
  - {type: Console, batch_size: 50, flush_interval: 0.5}
  # Only the records stamped before go_live_at
  - {type: Console, when: history}
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:every-sink
app.add_egress(stream).add_egress(lake)  # both receive every record
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:when
# A record's timestamp is an ISO string with its zone offset, so read it as a time
hot_from = datetime.now(timezone.utc)


def is_hot(record) -> bool:
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) >= hot_from


app.add_egress(stream, when=is_hot)  # hot tail
app.add_egress(lake, when=lambda r: not is_hot(r))  # cold history
app.add_egress(audit)  # no predicate: everything

setup_egress takes the functions in predicates, one for each sink by position, as Batch Size and Flush Interval shows.

The events, telemetry and {expr} forms are YAML forms:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:when-forms
# Only the event records
- {type: Console, when: events}
# Only the telemetry records
- {type: Console, when: telemetry}
# Only the events that carry an amount over 100
- type: Console
  when: {expr: "record.stream_type == 'event' and record.value.amount > 100"}

add_egress(sink, when=...) takes a function, as above. A function can test record["stream_type"] and record["value"] for the same result.

predicates in setup_egress takes the same functions.

A labels sink gets the ground-truth labels and nothing else:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/ground_truth.yaml:sinks
egress:
  # The data under test: events and telemetry, and no label
  - {type: Console}
  # The labels only, for a scorer that checks what a detector found
  - type: Jsonl
    config: {default_path: labels/labels.jsonl}
    when: labels
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:labels
app.add_egress(stream)  # events and telemetry, never a label
app.add_egress(audit, when="labels")  # ground-truth labels, and nothing else

labels in setup_egress marks each labels sink with True, by position, as Batch Size and Flush Interval shows.

A file sink such as this one writes one file per batch under labels/, such as labels/labels_1a2b3c4d.jsonl. A run's warmup applies to every sink: none receives a record or telemetry stamped before it. Run Length describes it.

docs.title: Write the Value Alone
docs.text:
A sink normally writes each record with its envelope: stream_type, sim_ts, timestamp, key, task and instance around the event's value. With envelope: false on the entry, the sink writes each event's value alone and receives no telemetry record and no queued or started record of a task. A label record of a when: labels entry is not changed. The Console json format writes the value alone too.

  • A Kafka sink sends the value as the message, with the record's key as the message key. A null value is sent as a tombstone, a message with the key and a null value, which a compacted topic reads as a delete of that key. A topic_router still receives the whole record.
  • A Redis sink sends a value that is not a mapping as JSON, a null included.
  • A storage, Iceberg or PostgreSQL sink skips a value that is not a mapping, with one warning.

A task's key_field names the payload field whose value becomes the key of its finished event, and so the Kafka message key. The queued and started records keep the entity's key, and a payload without the field fails the run. Task Flow describes the key.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/egress_envelope.yaml:envelope
egress:
  # Each event's value alone is written: no telemetry, and no queued or started record
  - {type: Console, envelope: false}

A Kafka sink takes the key in the same way. The value alone is the message, and a null value is sent as a tombstone:

docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:envelope-false
# The value of each event alone is the message: no telemetry, no queued or started
# record, and a null value is sent as a tombstone
- type: Kafka
  config:
    bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}
    event_topic: sim-orders
  envelope: false

app.add_egress(sink, envelope=False) does the same.

setup_egress takes envelopes, a list with True or False for each sink, by position.

docs.title: Batch Size and Flush Interval
docs.text:
A sink receives records in batches. A batch is handed over when it holds batch_size records, or when flush_interval simulation seconds have passed, whichever comes first. At factor: 0, the timer does not start until a go_live_at switches the run to real time, because simulation time is not tied to the wall clock before then.

Setting Default Set with batch_size 500 with_batching, or per sink on add_egress flush_interval 1.0 simulation seconds with_batching, or per sink on add_egress max_queued_batches 2000 with_batching drain_stall_seconds 30.0 seconds with_batching

A size is a whole number of 1 or more and an interval is above 0. YAML and the Builder refuse true, 0, a negative number and NaN. with_batching sets the defaults, and each sink can have its own size and interval. A stream sink needs small, frequent batches to keep latency down. A file or lake sink needs large ones, because each batch becomes one file, and for Iceberg one commit.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/batching.yaml
# The delivery settings of the Egress page, as a blueprint.
# Run it with: desflow run batching.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  # A day of history at factor 0, then 1 simulated second per real second from now;
  # when: history and when: live split the records at this instant
  logical_start_time: -1d
  go_live_at: now

# Defaults for every egress, the arguments of with_batching
batching:
  batch_size: 500
  flush_interval: 1.0
  max_queued_batches: 2000
  drain_stall_seconds: 30

egress:
  # Small and often for this sink; the other uses the defaults
  - {type: Console, batch_size: 50, flush_interval: 0.5}
  # Only the records stamped before go_live_at
  - {type: Console, when: history}

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

run: {until: 60}
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:defaults
app.with_batching(
    batch_size=5_000,  # records per batch
    flush_interval=1.0,  # simulation seconds; not used at factor=0
    max_queued_batches=2_000,  # a full queue makes the simulation wait
    drain_stall_seconds=30.0,  # how long teardown waits for a queue that stopped
)
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:per-sink
app.with_batching(batch_size=500, flush_interval=1.0)  # the default for every sink
app.add_egress(stream, batch_size=50, flush_interval=0.5)  # small and often
app.add_egress(lake, batch_size=200_000)  # large files, the default interval

The lists are matched to the sinks by position, and None means the default:

docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:low-level
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.setup_egress(
    [stream, lake],
    batch_size=500,  # defaults for every provider
    flush_interval=1.0,
    predicates=[None, lambda r: r["stream_type"] == "event"],  # by position
    batch_sizes=[50, None],  # None: the default
    flush_intervals=[0.5, None],
    labels=[False, False],  # True makes a provider a labels sink
    warmup=None,  # simulation seconds before which no provider gets a record
)

setup_egress also takes lag_monitor_interval, the simulation seconds between system.simulation.lag_seconds records. Its default, "auto", is off at factor 0 and 1.0 simulation seconds otherwise. A run that goes live starts it at the go-live instant. None or 0 turns it off. The builder and YAML set it with lag_interval, as Clocks and Pacing describes.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A published record goes through the same steps for each sink:

  1. publish_event, publish_telemetry or publish_label builds the record as a plain dictionary.
  2. Each sink tests it once. A labels sink takes only labels, and only a labels sink takes a label. No sink takes a record stamped before the warm-up. Then the sink applies its when.
  3. The record goes into that sink's buffer. When the buffer reaches batch_size, or the sink's timer fires, the buffer is handed to the sink's queue as one batch.
  4. The egress thread takes batches from each queue and writes them with the sink's connector.

A connector is a class with one method, async run(queue), so a sink desflow does not have takes one class to write: Write a Connector shows how.

Each sink has its own buffer and its own queue. All sinks run as tasks on one thread, so a sink that waits with await does not hold up the others. A sink that blocks the thread holds up every sink. Memory holds each sink's buffer and the batches waiting in its queue. A record that several sinks take is stored once. A queue holds at most max_queued_batches batches. When it is full, the simulation waits for room, so a sink that cannot keep up slows the run instead of building a backlog. When a queue stays full for drain_stall_seconds, the sink has stopped consuming, and the run raises RuntimeError rather than losing records.

Teardown flushes every buffer, then waits for the queues to drain. It keeps waiting while they shrink, and gives up only when they have not shrunk for drain_stall_seconds. Records still queued then are lost, and a warning names the sinks that held them.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A slow sink slows the run. The run slows on purpose: otherwise a backlog would build that teardown would have to throw away.
  • Size or interval, whichever comes first. The effective batch is the smaller of batch_size and what arrives in one flush_interval, so a large size with a short interval never fills. A warning says so once, after one sink has flushed on its timer 20 times in a row with less than a quarter of its batch_size.
  • A labels sink receives only labels, and a data sink never receives one. A label sent to a Kafka sink goes to its event_topic with no key.
  • Records matching no sink are not written anywhere, which is how when drops them.
  • At factor: 0, records leave a buffer only when it is full and at teardown.

docs.title: Ingress
docs.text: An ingress connector brings parameter changes into a running simulation from outside: from a file you edit, Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL or a local schedule. This page shows each connector, the message it reads, how to send one, and when the change lands.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
An ingress connector listens to a source while the run goes on. Every message it reads is one change: a registry path and its new value, the same two names a scenario step uses. The change reaches the registry, and the simulation follows it, as Live Parameters describes. Five ingress connectors bring changes in. The seven connectors described on Egress write records out:

The tutorial page Live Changes teaches these features step by step.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Each connector is attached with add_ingress in the builder, passed to env.setup_ingress in the low-level API, or listed under ingress in a blueprint with its type and config. In a blueprint, type is one of the short names below, or a !python class from another package. config holds the constructor's arguments. A connector's module is imported only when a blueprint names it. A missing package stops the load with its line and the pip install command. YAML Keys lists the keys of an ingress entry.

Connector type Source Message Extra LocalIngress Local a schedule in the code (delay in wall-clock seconds, path, value) none FileIngress File a YAML file you edit path: value lines none KafkaIngress Kafka a topic a JSON object {"path": ..., "value": ...} kafka RedisIngress Redis a Pub/Sub channel the same JSON object redis PostgresIngress Postgres a table, polled a row with the columns path and value, the value as JSON text postgres

docs.title: Local Schedule
docs.text:
LocalIngress applies changes after set delays in wall-clock seconds from the start of the run. It suits a local run. For a change at an exact simulation time, use a scenario step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:local-ingress
# 10 wall-clock seconds after the start, set the packers capacity to 3
- type: Local
  config: {schedule: [[10.0, Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, 3]]}
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:local-ingress
# 10 wall-clock seconds after the start, set the packers capacity to 3
app.add_ingress(
    LocalIngress(schedule=[(10.0, "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3)])
)

The low-level API passes the same LocalIngress to env.setup_ingress, in its list of connectors, as Low-level API shows.

docs.title: File
docs.text:
FileIngress watches a local YAML file of path: value lines and applies a line when you edit it. It needs no service and no extra, so it is the quickest way to change a parameter while a local run goes. It checks the file's modification time every poll wall-clock seconds, 1 by default, and reads the file only when the time has changed.

An entry is applied when it first appears or when its value differs from the last valid read. The file as it stands when the run starts counts as a first read, so the entries in it apply at the start. A save that changes no value applies nothing, and an entry whose value is NaN is not applied again when you edit the file, because two NaN values count as the same. An entry you remove changes nothing, and the model keeps the value it has. A file that does not exist yet is waited for.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:file-ingress
# Applies an entry of params.yaml when it first appears or its value changes
- type: File
  config: {path: params.yaml, poll: 1.0}
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:file-ingress
# Applies an entry of params.yaml when it first appears or its value changes
app.add_ingress(FileIngress("params.yaml", poll=1.0))

The low-level API passes the same FileIngress to env.setup_ingress, in its list of connectors, as Low-level API shows.

The file holds one registry path on each line, with its new value:

Shop.resources.packers.current_cap: 3
Shop.arrival.orders.rate: 0.5

A relative path is relative to the folder the run starts in.

docs.title: Kafka
docs.text:
KafkaIngress consumes a topic and reads each message as a JSON object with path and value, or through a deserializer of your own, such as Avro, JSON Schema or Protobuf, as Use Avro and Pydantic and JSON Schema and Protobuf show. Connect to Secure Kafka connects it to a secured cluster.

At the start of a run, KafkaIngress creates its topic when it is missing, as KafkaEgress does. A consumer that starts before any producer therefore does not wait for a topic that is not there. topic_policy sets this: create is the default, drop_and_create deletes the topic and creates it again, and manual creates nothing and keeps the behaviour before 1.0, when the ingress never created its topic. A desflow run --stdout run keeps its ingress, so it applies the ingress's topic_policy too: it creates the control topic, and with drop_and_create it deletes and recreates it. A --sample run leaves the ingress out.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:kafka-ingress
# Reads {"path": ..., "value": ...} messages from the sim-config topic
- type: Kafka
  config:
    topic: sim-config
    bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:kafka-ingress
# Reads {"path": ..., "value": ...} messages from the sim-config topic
app.add_ingress(KafkaIngress(topic="sim-config", bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092"))

The low-level API passes the same KafkaIngress to env.setup_ingress, in its list of connectors, as Low-level API shows.

KafkaAdminConnector.send_config(topic, path, value) sends one such message. The Kafka example listens on sim-config, and this sets its number of packers:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint has no sender of its own. Send the message from Python, as the Builder tab shows, or from any Kafka client, as below.

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters_kafka.py
"""Sets the packers capacity of the running Kafka example.

`KafkaAdminConnector.send_config` publishes `{"path": ..., "value": ...}` to the
topic `KafkaIngress` reads, `sim-config` in the example. Call `set_packer_capacity(3)`
while the example runs.
"""

import asyncio

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector


def set_packer_capacity(value: int) -> None:
    admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092")
    asyncio.run(
        admin.send_config("sim-config", "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", value)
    )

The sender does not depend on how the model is written: use the function the Builder tab shows.

From any Kafka client, the message is the JSON object itself:

docs/snippets/pages/ingress_senders.py:kafka
async def send_with_kafka(rate: float) -> None:
    """A JSON object with path and value, to the topic KafkaIngress reads."""
    from aiokafka import AIOKafkaProducer

    producer = AIOKafkaProducer(bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092")
    await producer.start()
    try:
        message = {"path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": rate}
        await producer.send_and_wait("sim-config", json.dumps(message).encode())
    finally:
        await producer.stop()

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
RedisIngress subscribes to a Pub/Sub channel and reads each message as the same JSON object.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:redis-ingress
# Reads {"path": ..., "value": ...} messages from a Pub/Sub channel
- type: Redis
  config:
    url: redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0
    channel_name: simulation_params
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:redis-ingress
# Reads {"path": ..., "value": ...} messages from a Pub/Sub channel
app.add_ingress(
    RedisIngress(
        "redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0", channel_name="simulation_params"
    )
)

The low-level API passes the same RedisIngress to env.setup_ingress, in its list of connectors, as Low-level API shows.

docs/snippets/pages/ingress_senders.py:redis
async def send_with_redis(rate: float) -> None:
    """The same JSON object, published to the channel RedisIngress subscribes to."""
    import redis.asyncio as redis

    client = redis.from_url("redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0")
    message = {"path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": rate}
    await client.publish("simulation_params", json.dumps(message))
    await client.aclose()

With the Redis example running, valkey-cli sends one from a shell:

# Change the order arrival rate of the running simulation
docker exec -it valkey valkey-cli --user user --pass password PUBLISH simulation_params '{"path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 10.0}'

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
PostgresIngress polls a table, simulation_params by default, every poll_interval seconds, 2 by default. It creates the table when it is missing, with the columns id, path, value, is_applied and created_at, and first its schema when the name has one that the database does not have, such as dashboard in dashboard.params. It applies the rows in two steps:

  1. At the start, it applies the latest applied value of each path, in the order the changes were made, so a restarted run resumes from the last settings. A current_cap that was made after a max_cap is applied after it, so the new maximum clamps it as it did the first time.
  2. At each poll, it applies every row whose is_applied is false and marks it true, so the table keeps the history of every change.

value is read as JSON, and as plain text when it is not JSON.

The connection string names odctl, the database that the odctl postgres profile creates, with the user user and the password password.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:postgres-ingress
# Applies new rows (path, value) of simulation_params, checking every 2 seconds
- type: Postgres
  config:
    connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl
    table_name: simulation_params
    poll_interval: 2.0
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:postgres-ingress
# Applies new rows (path, value) of simulation_params, checking every 2 seconds
app.add_ingress(
    PostgresIngress(
        "postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl",
        table_name="simulation_params",
        poll_interval=2.0,
    )
)

The low-level API passes the same PostgresIngress to env.setup_ingress, in its list of connectors, as Low-level API shows.

docs/snippets/pages/ingress_senders.py:postgres
async def send_with_postgres(rate: float) -> None:
    """A row in the table PostgresIngress polls; value is JSON text."""
    import asyncpg

    conn = await asyncpg.connect("postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl")
    try:
        await conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO simulation_params (path, value) VALUES ($1, $2)",
            "Shop.arrival.orders.rate",
            json.dumps(rate),
        )
    finally:
        await conn.close()

With the PostgreSQL example running, psql adds one from a shell:

# Change the order arrival rate of the running simulation
docker exec -it postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "INSERT INTO simulation_params (path, value) VALUES ('Shop.arrival.orders.rate', '5.0');"

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The connectors run on the ingress thread, apart from the simulation. Each reads its source, turns every message into a (path, value) pair with one shared check, and puts it on a queue. A SimPy process, the ingress monitor, applies everything queued every 0.1 simulation seconds:

At factor: 1.0, 0.1 simulation seconds take 0.1 real seconds, so a change lands within 0.1 seconds of arriving. The simulation time it lands at depends on when it arrives, so two runs with the same seed and the same messages can differ. A change that must land at an exact simulation time needs a scenario step.

A connector is a class with one method, async run(queue), so a source desflow does not have takes one class to write: Write a Connector shows how.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A bad message is skipped. A message that cannot be decoded, that is not an object, or that lacks a non-empty path or a non-null value is logged as one WARNING line and skipped, and the run goes on. A PostgreSQL row like that is marked applied, so it is read once. A path the model does not have is a warning from the registry. A schema registry that refuses a Kafka deserializer's credentials or access stops KafkaIngress instead, as Connect to Secure Kafka describes.

  • Old keys get a hint. Before 0.21.0, Kafka read path_id, and Redis and PostgreSQL read param_path and param_value. A message with the old keys is skipped with a line that says so, such as this one, which parse_change gives for a Kafka message written for 0.20.0:

    Skipped a Kafka ingress message: expected a non-empty path and a non-null value, got {'path_id': 'Shop.arrival.orders.rate', 'value': 1.0}; path_id, param_path and param_value were renamed to path and value in desflow 0.21.0

  • Old PostgreSQL columns. A table created before 0.21.0 has the columns param_path and param_value. Reading it fails with an error line that gives the two statements to rename them:

    ALTER TABLE simulation_params RENAME COLUMN param_path TO path;
ALTER TABLE simulation_params RENAME COLUMN param_value TO value;

  • An invalid file is skipped. An empty file, which an editor can leave for a moment while it saves, is skipped with no log line. A file that is not valid YAML, or is not a mapping, is logged as one WARNING line that names the file and the parser's error, and nothing from that read is applied. The next valid read is compared with the last valid one. An entry with an empty path or a null value is logged as one WARNING line and skipped, as for the other connectors.

  • LocalIngress follows the wall clock, so at factor: 0 an unpaced run can end before its first change. FileIngress does too.
  • Ingress needs an until. A run that only waits for ingress has no model event of its own, so without until it ends at once. Set until, and Ctrl+C then stops the run before it reaches that time, as Run Length explains.

docs.title: Example: File Steering
docs.text:
The file example has a shop with one packer and more orders than one packer can pack. A File connector reads params.yaml, whose one line sets the packers' capacity. Change the 1 to 5 while the run goes and save the file. The statistics, published every 2 seconds, show the capacity change and the queue shrink. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own after 60 seconds of real time. Each tab shows how the example attaches the connector, then how to download and run it.

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/file.yaml:file-ingress
ingress:

  - type: File
