docs.title: Live Parameters: SimulationRegistry
docs.text: Every parameter of a run can change while the run goes on: an arrival rate, a number of packers, a stock level. This page shows how to name a parameter, the ways to change it, how to record what a change was for, and what happens to a value once it arrives.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Every run has one SimulationRegistry, at env.registry. It maps dot-notation paths, such as Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, to the values the simulation reads. A scenario, an ingress connector or a process changes a parameter by updating its path, and the simulation follows the change without restarting. Changing a parameter takes three steps:

The tutorial page Live Changes teaches these features step by step.

docs.title: Find the Path
docs.text:
A path is the sim_id, the kind of parameter, its name and the field:

Declared with Paths an arrival or a service <sim_id>.arrival.<name>.<parameter> and <sim_id>.service.<name>.<parameter>, one per scalar parameter of its family: .rate for an exponential, .mean and .std for a normal, .low, .mode and .high for a triangular, and so on; an empirical has none a resource <sim_id>.resources.<name>.current_cap, .max_cap and .queue_limit (None while the resource has no limit) a container <sim_id>.containers.<name>.current_cap, .max_cap and .level a store <sim_id>.stores.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap a breakdown of a resource <sim_id>.breakdown.<resource>.time_to_failure.<parameter> and <sim_id>.breakdown.<resource>.repair.<parameter>, one per scalar parameter of each distribution's family, as for a service a variable <sim_id>.variables.<name>

Arrivals and Services lists each family's parameters. An update to a path that does not exist, including a parameter the family does not take, is logged as a warning and ignored, so a misspelt path changes nothing.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint's paths follow from the names it declares, as the table above shows. To list them with their starting values, load it with SimulationContext.from_yaml and call registry_paths() on the context it returns, as the Builder tab does.

compile_parameters() returns the SimParameter a SimulationContext will register, which shows the names to use. A resource appears in it as a ResourceConfig with current_cap, max_cap and queue_limit:

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters.py:compile
print(app.compile_parameters())

registry_paths() returns the paths a run will register with their starting values, in the order a run registers them. It runs no model code and starts no connector. A capacity with no limit has the value math.inf, which JSON cannot hold, so convert it before you write JSON:

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters.py:paths
print(app.registry_paths())

You register the parameters yourself, and read a value with registry.get(path).value:

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:paths
params = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=3.0, std=0.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, max_cap=5)},
    containers={"stock": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=40)},
    variables={"conveyor_speed": 1.5},
)
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(params)
# Registered paths include:
#   Shop.arrival.orders.rate
#   Shop.service.packing.mean, Shop.service.packing.std
#   Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, .max_cap and .queue_limit (None: no limit)
#   Shop.containers.stock.current_cap, .max_cap and .level
#   Shop.variables.conveyor_speed
print(env.registry.get("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap").value)  # 2

docs.title: Send a Value
docs.text:
Each source of a change suits a different job and lands at a different moment:

Source Use it for Lands at a scenario: YAML scenario, builder add_scenario, low-level run_scenario an experiment that must repeat exactly the exact simulation time given LocalIngress a local run with changes after set wall-clock delays a wall-clock delay from the start FileIngress a local run steered by editing a file within one poll of the save KafkaIngress, RedisIngress, PostgresIngress an operator or another program steering a running model when the message arrives a process calling env.registry.update or env.registry.change a change that depends on the state of the simulation when the process makes it

Ingress gives the message each connector reads. A process changes a value directly:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint's process function, listed under processes, calls the same registry.update on context.env.registry, as Processes shows.

A builder process calls the same registry.update on context.env.registry, as Processes shows.

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:update
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3)  # applied
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 9)  # stored as 5, the max_cap
env.registry.update("Shop.service.packing.std", -1.0)  # refused, the old 0.5 stays
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.lath.current_cap", 3)  # no such path: ignored
env.registry.update("Shop.service.packing.rate", 2.0)  # normal has no rate: ignored
env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 150)  # stored as 100, the capacity

docs.title: Know What a Path Accepts
docs.text:
Each path checks a value by its own rule before it stores it:

  • A resource's or a store's max_cap, and a resource's queue_limit, are whole numbers of 0 or more, and a current_cap is a whole number, stored clamped to 0 to max_cap with a warning. Text is accepted only if the whole text is such a number, so "6" is 6 and "abc" is refused. A store capacity with a fraction, such as 2.5, is refused and not rounded down. A queue_limit of None means no limit.
  • A container's level is a finite number. A level above the capacity is stored as the capacity.
  • A path that holds true or false takes true, false or that text. Any other text is refused. true written over a path that holds a number is stored as 1.

A resource's limit changes through its path. DynamicResource.queue_limit is a read-only property that shows the value now, so assigning to it raises AttributeError.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

An on: entry with a path needs a value, and so does a scenario step with a path. A value that the path's rule refuses, such as many for a capacity, is refused when the blueprint loads, with the line of the entry. A path that is not in the registry is logged as a warning with the entry's line.

registry.change, which a process calls, raises ParamRejected for a value that breaks these rules. The next section shows it.

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:rules
# Each path checks a value by its own rule; `change` raises where `update` logs
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.max_cap", "6")  # text of a whole number: 6
env.registry.update(
    "Shop.resources.packers.queue_limit", 4
)  # a limit: whole, 0 or more
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.queue_limit", None)  # no limit again
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2.5)  # refused: not whole
env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", float("nan"))  # refused: not finite

docs.title: Know Whether a Change Was Refused
docs.text:
update logs a refused value and goes on, so its caller cannot tell whether the value landed. registry.change(path, value) runs the same checks and returns a ParamChange for an accepted value. For a refused value it raises ParamRejected, a ValueError whose path, value and reason say what the registry refused. A value that the registry converts or clamps is accepted, and new shows the value it stored.

A ParamChange has these fields:

  • path: the path that changed.
  • old: the value before the change.
  • new: the value stored.
  • requested: the value asked for.
  • at: the simulation time of the change.
  • source, actor and reason: who made the change and why, which change takes as keywords.

Its changed property is True when new differs from old.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint's process function, listed under processes, calls the same registry.change on context.env.registry, as Processes shows for update.

A builder process calls the same registry.change on context.env.registry, as Processes shows for update.

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:change
change = env.registry.change(
    "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
    4,
    source="user",
    actor="alice",
    reason="two packers are on leave",
)
print(change.old, change.new, change.changed)  # 5 4 True
try:
    env.registry.change("Shop.service.packing.std", -1.0)
except ParamRejected as exc:
    # invalid value for 'Shop.service.packing.std': normal std must be 0 or more ...
    print(exc.reason)

docs.title: Follow Every Change
docs.text:
on_change is a list of callbacks. The registry calls each one with the ParamChange of every accepted change, in the order they were added, after it has stored the value. A change that leaves the value as it was is reported too, with changed False. A lower max_cap that lowers the current_cap beside it gives two changes, the current_cap first. A callback that raises is logged, and the other callbacks still run.

The source and actor of a change say where it came from:

  • An ingress connector's change has the source "ingress" and the connector's class name as actor, such as LocalIngress.
  • A scenario step has the source "scenario".
  • The overrides of start() have the source, actor and reason that start() takes.
  • A change that a process or an on: action makes has no source unless the process passes one.
YAMLBuilderLow-level

The context that SimulationContext.from_yaml returns takes the callbacks on context.on_change.

app.on_change takes the same callbacks for every run start() builds, as Builder API says.

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:on_change
changes: list = []
env.registry.on_change.append(changes.append)  # called with every accepted change
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3, source="user")
# Shop.resources.packers.current_cap 4 3
print(changes[0].path, changes[0].old, changes[0].new)

docs.title: Script an Experiment
docs.text:
A blueprint's scenario lists changes, each with the simulation time it applies at. Here a second packer starts at 30 seconds. From one minute, orders arrive twice as fast: the average gap between orders falls from 5 seconds to 2.5 seconds (rate from 0.2 to 0.4). The extra packer leaves at two minutes:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/scenario.yaml
# The first blueprint with a scripted experiment: a second packer starts at 30 s.
# From 1 min, orders arrive twice as fast: the average gap falls from 5 s to 2.5 s
# (rate 0.2 to 0.4). The extra packer leaves at 2 min. Every change lands at
# exactly that simulation time, on every run.
simulation: {sim_id: Shop, factor: 0, random_seed: 1}

egress:
  - {type: Console}

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 3}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 4 s, std: 1 s}

arrivals:
  # An order every 5 s on average (rate 0.2), 2.5 s from 1 min
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# The packers' capacity and queue every 10 seconds, to see each change land
stats: minimal

scenario:
  - {at: 30, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 2}
  - {at: 1 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}
  - {at: 2 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}

run: {until: 3 min}

add_scenario takes the same steps as a list of mappings, as Vary Arrivals by Time shows.

run_scenario takes the same steps as a list of mappings, and runs as a SimPy process, as Vary Arrivals by Time shows.

The builder and the low-level API take the same steps, as a list of mappings. Vary Arrivals by Time shows one schedule in each API.

A scenario is not a connector. It is a SimPy process that waits on the simulation clock, so each step lands at exactly its at, on every run and at any factor, including 0. Its steps follow these rules, and Vary Arrivals by Time shows each case:

  • A step applies before every other event at its time, so an arrival gap drawn at that moment uses the new value.
  • Steps at the same time apply in the order written.
  • A step at or after until never applies.
  • A scenario's paths and values are checked before the run, as Stability and Limits says.

LocalIngress waits on the wall clock instead, and an unknown path is only logged when it is due. A scenario and an ingress connector can run together, so a scripted baseline can run while an operator changes values over Kafka. When both change the same path, the later write wins.

docs.title: Record What a Change Was For
docs.text:
A detector or an agent that watches the data is scored against what really happened. A scenario step with a record publishes a ground-truth record of it: stream_type: "label", with the step's path, the value before (old) and after (new), and the step's record mapping as label. A step can have a record and no path, for something that happened outside the model, and then path, old and new are null.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/ground_truth.yaml:record
scenario:
  # Changes the rate and publishes a ground-truth record of the change
  - at: 30
    path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate
    value: 1.5
    record: {fault: order_surge, cause: flash sale}
  # A record with no change, such as a fault planted outside the model
  - at: 45
    record: {fault: label_printer_offline}

add_scenario takes the same steps, record included. A process publishes a label itself with context.env.publish_label(label, path=..., old=..., new=...).

run_scenario takes the same steps, record included. A process publishes a label itself with env.publish_label(label, path=..., old=..., new=...).

Labels go only to sinks with when: labels, and those sinks receive nothing else. The labels therefore never reach the pipeline under test, and a scorer reads them apart from the data. Choose What Each Sink Gets shows the sinks of this blueprint.

The labels sink writes one file per batch under labels/, such as labels/labels_1a2b3c4d.jsonl, with one line per label:

{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":30.0,"timestamp":"...","path":"Shop.arrival.orders.rate","old":0.5,"new":1.5,"label":{"fault":"order_surge","cause":"flash sale"}}
{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":45.0,"timestamp":"...","path":null,"old":null,"new":null,"label":{"fault":"label_printer_offline"}}

In Python, env.publish_label(label, path=..., old=..., new=...) publishes one, and add_egress(sink, when="labels") or setup_egress(..., labels=[...]) makes a labels sink, as the measuring example shows.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Registration. run(), or register_sim_parameter in the low-level API, flattens the SimParameter into the registry. The registry holds one DynamicValue per path, with the value and a change signal. Beside them, it keeps the configuration objects that the paths belong to, such as each DistributionConfig.

An update. registry.update(path, value) and registry.change(path, value) apply one change by the same checks. update logs a refused value, and change raises ParamRejected. The checks run in order, and an accepted value reaches the parts that read it:

  • A path that does not exist is logged as a warning, and the update is ignored.
  • A value of another type is converted to the type the path holds, so the string "5" sent to an integer path becomes 5. Python's conversion is used, so 2.5 sent to an integer path becomes 2. A value that cannot be converted is logged as an error and ignored.
  • A distribution parameter is checked on a copy of its configuration, by the rules used at build. One out of range is logged as an error, and the old value stays.
  • A current_cap outside 0 to max_cap, or a container level outside 0 to current_cap, is stored clamped to that range, with a warning. A lower max_cap clamps the stored current_cap the same way.
  • A value equal to the current one gives no change signal.
  • Otherwise the value is stored, and the attribute of the configuration object is set too, found by splitting the path at its last dot: Shop.service.packing.mean sets mean on the object at Shop.service.packing. The Sampler reads that object at every draw, so it sees the new value.
  • Then each on_change callback receives the change, in the order they were added; a callback that raises is logged and the others still run.

Change Signal. Each value has a SimPy Store with one slot as its signal. An update puts a token in it if it is empty, and wait_for_change() waits for that token. The slot holds one token, so several changes before a waiter wakes give one signal, and only one waiting process takes it. Resources, stores and containers already wait on their own paths, and a token that your process takes does not reach them. Wait only on paths that nothing else waits on, such as variables:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Waiting on a change needs process code: a process function listed under processes waits on context.env.registry in the same way, as Processes shows for a process.

A builder process waits on context.env.registry in the same way, as Processes shows for a process.

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:wait
def watch_speed(env):
    """Logs the conveyor speed every time it changes."""
    speed = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.conveyor_speed")
    while True:
        yield speed.wait_for_change()
        print(f"t={env.now}: conveyor speed is now {speed.value}")


env.process(watch_speed(env))

A container's level also changes with every put and get. The registry keeps that level, so a reader sees it, but does not signal the container again.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
What follows a change:

  • Distributions. The next draw uses the new value. The arrival already being waited for keeps its gap, and a task that has drawn its service time keeps it.
  • Resources, stores and containers. The capacity follows at once, and a container's level follows its path, as Resources and Stores and Containers describe.
  • Variables. The new value is stored, and a process reads it with env.registry.get(path).value.

A change is easiest to see in the telemetry. With stats: minimal, the scenario above shows the second packer land:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 20.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 2}

The reading at 30 seconds still shows 1. The resource applies a change within the same simulation instant, but after the step that made it. The reading was taken before that. The builder publishes the same readings with with_stats:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

stats: minimal in the blueprint above publishes these readings every 10 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters.py:telemetry
# The packers' capacity, in use, queue and utilization every 2 seconds
app.with_stats("minimal", interval=2.0)

env.setup_stats("Shop", "minimal", interval=2.0) publishes the same readings, as Statistics shows.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• An unknown path is a warning, not an error, for an ingress message or a process that calls update; change raises ParamRejected. The paths of a scenario and of every on: action, and a scenario's values, are checked when the model loads.
  • A scenario's values are checked before the run. Every path and value of a blueprint's scenario is checked against the model's registry when the file loads, so a misspelt path, a path on a family member the family can never have (desk[7] of a family with members: 2 that no task picks by key), or a refused value stops the load with its line. A member that a task can make at its first use is accepted, and a step on it before it is made ends the run with KeyError. start() checks them again with its overrides, and that is where a builder model's scenario is checked. A run still stops with ParamRejected at a step's time when an ingress message, an on: action or a process has changed a related value before the step, because the check cannot know those values. A low-level run_scenario checks nothing in advance, so it raises ParamRejected whenever it reaches a refused value.
  • A family is fixed. There is no path that turns a normal into an exponential. That is a new model.
  • Several changes, one signal. A process waiting on a path wakes once for several changes made before it runs, and reads the latest value.
  • Ingress lands on the wall clock. A message's change lands at whatever simulation time the run has reached when it arrives. A change that must happen at an exact simulation time needs a scenario step.

docs.title: Model Parts
docs.text: A model is made of a few kinds of parts. This page is the map: which block models what, and what it is called in each way of writing. Each block has a page of its own.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
An entity is the thing that flows through a model: an order, a visitor, a support call. It enters through an arrival and does the work its task describes. While it works, it holds a resource, and it may take from or add to a store or container. Then it goes on to the next task. What Is DES? explains discrete-event simulation, the kind of simulation these blocks build. Look at how the blocks connect:

Block What it models YAML Builder Low-level Page Arrival how often an entity enters, and what it starts with arrivals add_arrival, @app.arrival_loop a process that waits for a drawn gap Arrivals and Services Service how long a piece of work takes services add_service a DistributionConfig drawn with a Sampler Arrivals and Services Task what one entity does, with its events tasks @app.task a SimPy process Tasks Resource packers, benches, lanes: whole units held by a task resources add_resource DynamicResource Units and Queues Container an amount, such as a stock of boxes, that tasks take and add containers add_container DynamicContainer Stores and Containers Store items, such as parcels on a shelf, that tasks put and get stores add_store DynamicStore Stores and Containers Task flow the task that follows a finished one, and what the entity carries next, attributes, set next=, attributes=, set= Router, Entity Task Flow Process anything else that runs over time: a break, a drift, a schedule processes add_process env.process Processes Statistics what the run measures about itself stats with_stats env.setup_stats, env.stats Statistics Variable any other live value, such as a speed variables add_variable SimParameter(variables=...) Live Parameters

The shop tutorial, in the Learn section, puts them together one at a time, in a small shop.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: A model declares its blocks, and its tasks use them by name. A task names its service and its resource, and an arrival names the task it starts. The table above gives each block's YAML key, builder call and low-level class. Writing a Model shows a whole model in each form. Input Fitting fits a service or an arrival to measured times, and writes the settings in a form a model loads.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: When the run starts, run() builds the environment, registers every block's parameters in the registry, builds the resources, stores and containers, and starts the arrivals and processes. What run() Does lists the steps in order. From then on, each block reads its live values from the registry: a distribution reads its parameters at each draw, and a resource follows its capacity path.

docs.title: Arrivals and Services
docs.text: Two building blocks set the timing of every simulation. An arrival decides how often a new entity enters the model: an order, a visitor, a support call. A service decides how long a piece of work takes: packing an order, answering a call. Both are distributions of time, and each time one is needed, a value is drawn from the distribution with its current parameters.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Block Answers Used by Example Arrival How long until the next entity? the arrival loop, which starts a task for each one an order every 2 s on average Service How long does this piece of work take? a task, while it holds its resource 3 s of packing, give or take 0.5 s

An arrival draws each gap afresh from its distribution, so the gaps differ and entities arrive at uneven times. Look at the first five orders of the shop in First Simulation:

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Every distribution is a family, dist, and the parameters that family takes. There are twelve families: ten of times, and poisson and geometric for counts. A parameter outside its range, a missing one, or one the family does not take is refused when the model is built, with the YAML line when it comes from a blueprint. Reference, Distributions lists every family with its parameters, rules, mean and variance. On this page, the table below names each family, the list under it gives each family's rules, and one example shows the form.

Family Use it for Parameters exponential Gaps between arrivals that happen independently of each other: orders, calls, visits. Many short gaps and a few long ones, with mean 1 / rate. rate normal Work with a typical time and a small, symmetric spread. mean, std truncated_normal Work with a typical time and a hard minimum. mean, std, low lognormal Times that are never negative and now and then much longer: repairs, support calls. mean, std constant Fixed times: a conveyor, a setup, a step that takes no time. value uniform Any time in a range, all equally likely, when only the range is known. low, high triangular An expert's estimate: the shortest, the most likely and the longest time. low, mode, high gamma Times less variable than exponential. A whole-number shape is the Erlang distribution: that many exponential steps in a row. shape, scale weibull Time to failure: a shape below 1 fails early, a shape above 1 wears out. shape, scale empirical Times taken from real data, when no family fits. values with weights, or edges with counts poisson A count of events in a period, such as the orders in a minute: whole numbers from 0. mean geometric The number of tries up to and including the first success: whole numbers from 1. p

The rules for each family's parameters:

  • exponential: rate above 0, in events per second: 0.5 is one every 2 seconds on average, 2.0 is two a second. It is the one parameter that is not a time, so it takes no duration.
  • normal: mean, and std 0 or more (0 when left out). A std of 0 gives the mean every time. A draw can be negative, and a draw below 0 is raised to 0. In a wide normal, these raised draws raise the mean, so use truncated_normal instead.
  • truncated_normal: mean, std 0 or more, and low, 0 when left out. With std 0, mean must be at least low. A draw below low is thrown away and drawn again, so no draws pile up at the limit. The mean is therefore the truncated distribution's own: 1.29 seconds for mean: 1, std: 1, low: 0. The higher low is above the mean, the fewer plain draws are kept. So when low is more than half a standard deviation above the mean, truncated_normal draws from an exponential proposal instead (Robert, 1995), which stays exact and fast for any low.
  • lognormal: mean above 0 and std 0 or more (0 when left out). Both describe the times you get, not the underlying normal. desflow converts them.
  • constant: value 0 or more. It uses no random number at all. A constant of 0 takes no time.
  • uniform: low and high, with low < high. The mean is halfway between them.
  • triangular: low, mode and high, all required, with low <= mode <= high and low < high. The mean is (low + mode + high) ÷ 3.
  • gamma: shape and scale, both above 0. The mean is shape × scale and the variance shape × scale². From a mean and a standard deviation: shape = (mean ÷ std)² and scale = std² ÷ mean, so a mean of 1.5 seconds with a std of 0.5 is shape 9 and scale 0.1667.
  • weibull: shape and scale, both above 0. The mean is scale × gamma(1 + 1 ÷ shape), where gamma is the gamma function.
  • empirical: either values, each equally likely unless the optional weights give one weight per value; or a histogram of edges and counts, with one count per bin. A histogram draw picks a bin in proportion to its count, then any time inside the bin, all equally likely. Weights and counts are 0 or more and add up to more than 0, and edges increase. The lists are taken when the model is loaded, so an empirical distribution has no registry path and does not change while the run goes on.
  • poisson: mean 0 or more. Every draw is a whole number from 0, and the mean and the variance are both mean.
  • geometric: p above 0 and at most 1. Every draw is a whole number from 1, with mean 1 ÷ p.

poisson and geometric give counts, not times. Use them where a count is read, such as the group and max_events of an arrival in Start Entities. A service or a gap that draws from them takes the count as seconds.

desflow dist lists the families, and desflow dist <family> prints one family's parameters and rules. With --mean and --std it converts them to the family's parameters, so the gamma above needs no arithmetic. --p sets the p of a geometric:

desflow dist gamma --mean 1.5 --std 0.5

parameters: shape 9, scale 0.166667
YAML: {dist: gamma, shape: 9, scale: 0.166667}
Python: dist="gamma", shape=9, scale=0.166667

The last two lines are the service in a blueprint and in the builder. Command Line shows the other conversions.

Three of these families in a blueprint: a labelling time of at least 0.2 seconds, a station that fails more often as it wears, a histogram of measured packing times with three bins, and a scanning time of 0.5 seconds four times in five and 2 seconds otherwise:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:families
# under services: a hard minimum, a time to failure, a histogram of data, and
# weighted values
labelling: {dist: truncated_normal, mean: 1 s, std: 1 s, low: 0.2 s}
station_failure: {dist: weibull, shape: 1.5, scale: 10 min}
measured_packing: {dist: empirical, edges: [1 s, 2 s, 3 s, 4 s], counts: [5, 3, 2]}
scanning: {dist: empirical, values: [0.5 s, 2 s], weights: [4, 1]}
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:builder-families
# A hard minimum, a time to failure, a histogram of data, and weighted values
app.add_service("labelling", dist="truncated_normal", mean=1.0, std=1.0, low=0.2)
app.add_service("station_failure", dist="weibull", shape=1.5, scale=600)
app.add_service(
    "measured_packing", dist="empirical", edges=[1, 2, 3, 4], counts=[5, 3, 2]
)
app.add_service("scanning", dist="empirical", values=[0.5, 2], weights=[4, 1])

Each is a DistributionConfig with the same parameters in seconds, such as DistributionConfig(dist="weibull", shape=1.5, scale=600).

An arrival or a service takes the same form for every family: dist, and the parameters in that family's row of the table. An exponential arrival, in the three ways to write it:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:exponential
# under arrivals: an order every 2 seconds on average
orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack}
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:builder-exponential
# An order every 2 s on average, each starting the task pack
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, spawn="pack")
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:low-level-exponential
gap = DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)  # an order every 2 s on average

An arrival draws its gap from data in the same way. Here a batch arrives 1 second after the last one three times in four, and 5 seconds after it otherwise:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:weighted-arrival
# under arrivals: a gap of 1 second three times in four, and 5 seconds otherwise
batches: {dist: empirical, values: [1 s, 5 s], weights: [3, 1], spawn: pack}
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:builder-weighted-arrival
# A gap of 1 s three times in four, and 5 s otherwise
app.add_arrival(
    "batches", dist="empirical", values=[1, 5], weights=[3, 1], spawn="pack"
)

DistributionConfig(dist="empirical", values=[1, 5], weights=[3, 1]) is the gap.

docs.title: Durations
docs.text:
In a blueprint, every time-valued parameter takes a duration as well as a number of seconds: mean, std, low, mode, high, scale and value, and the values and edges of an empirical. A plain number is seconds, and so is text that is only a number, such as '1e-3' or '5'. rate stays a number per second.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:durations
# under services: every time-valued parameter takes a duration
support_call: {dist: lognormal, mean: 5 min, std: 3 min}

The builder takes seconds: app.add_service("support_call", dist="lognormal", mean=300, std=180).

The low-level API takes seconds: DistributionConfig(dist="lognormal", mean=300, std=180).

docs.title: Seeding
docs.text:
A seed makes every draw the same on every run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:seed
# The same draws on every run; leave it out to draw a seed and log it
random_seed: 42

desflow run arrivals_services.yaml --seed 7 overrides it without editing the file.

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:builder-seed
# The same draws on every run; leave it out to draw a seed and log it
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, random_seed=42)
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:low-level-seed
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # the same draws on every run

In the low-level API you draw yourself, from the current values:

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:low-level-draw
seconds = sampler.sample(packing)  # one draw, in seconds, from the current values

A run without a seed draws one and logs it, so it can be repeated: desflow run logs the command with --seed, and a builder run logs the value to pass as random_seed:

No random_seed was given, so this run uses 3166812249. Pass random_seed=3166812249 to repeat it.

A low-level Sampler() with no seed draws nothing at random, as How It Works explains. Randomness and Seeds shows seeds in use.

docs.title: Replay
docs.text:
An arrival can take its times from recorded rows instead of a distribution. Each row of a CSV or Parquet file, or of a list of dicts, becomes one entity at the row's time. The fields named in fields become the entity's attributes. Here each row of local_replay_orders.csv is an order, at its time in seconds from the start of the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/local_replay.yaml:replay
arrivals:
  orders:
    replay:
      # A CSV or Parquet file, relative to this blueprint
      path: ../local_replay_orders.csv
      time: time
      unit: s
      fields: [order_id, items]
    spawn: pack
examples/builder/local_replay_example.py:replay
# A CSV or Parquet file, or a list of dicts
.add_arrival_replay(
    "orders", TRACE, time="time", unit="s", fields=["order_id", "items"]
)

add_arrival_replay takes spawn= as add_arrival does, which starts the named task for each row. This example writes an @app.arrival_loop of its own instead, where wait_for_arrival("orders") waits for the next row.

examples/low-level/local_replay_example.py:replay
def replay(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one order at each row's time, carrying the row's fields."""
    rows = read_trace(TRACE, time="time", unit="s", fields=["order_id", "items"])
    number = 0
    # Rows with one time start in one step, as the blueprint starts them
    for time, same_time in itertools.groupby(rows, key=lambda row: row.time):
        yield env.timeout(time - env.now)
        for row in same_time:
            number += 1
            key = f"orders-{number}"
            env.process(pack(env, sampler, packers, key, number - 1, row.fields))

read_trace reads and checks the rows, and returns each with its simulation time, row number and fields.

unit is ms, s, min or h from the start of the run, or timestamp for a date and time, placed on the run's clock from logical_start_time. The rows must be in time order, and the arrival follows these rules:

  • Rows at equal times arrive at that time, in the order of the file.
  • A row before the start stops the run, and rows at or after until never arrive.
  • A row without a valid time stops the run, unless on_invalid is skip, which leaves it out with a warning.
  • After the last row, the arrival stops and logs one INFO line.

A CSV field is a number only when it is a CSV number: 1_0, nan and 0x1 stay text, and as a time they are refused. A CSV file may start with a byte order mark. A row with more or fewer values than the header, and a header that names a column twice, are refused with the row or the column named. A Parquet file needs the parquet extra. A replayed arrival has no registry path. Local Replay compares a recorded morning with a model of it.

docs.title: Start Entities
docs.text:
An arrival starts a new entity after each gap. These keys change when it starts, how many it starts and what each carries. Each is a blueprint key, and the builder's add_arrival takes the same names, apart from count, keys and stagger:

  • gap replaces dist when the gap is not a distribution: a number of seconds, a duration, an expression or a generator, read at the start of each gap, so it can read registry[...], level.<name> and t. An arrival takes exactly one of dist, replay and gap, and a boolean is refused in gap and stagger.
  • first_at is the simulation time of the first arrival, in place of a first gap. A time already past arrives at once.
  • max_events is how many times the arrival starts its task in all, read when the source starts. The last start draws no further gap.
  • group is how many entities one arrival starts, read once at each arrival, after the gap. A group of 0 or below starts nobody, draws no attributes and takes no key number, and the next gap still runs. It is not used with count, keys or replay.
  • count makes that many entities, each with a loop of its own that starts the task after each gap, and stagger is the time between the starts of two of them. keys lists the keys instead and gives the number, so it needs no count.
  • key is read once for each entity, for its key, and vars are named values read once for each entity before its attributes and key, which read them as bare names. The order at a start is vars, attributes, key. A start whose key belongs to a running entity of the arrival is skipped with a warning and counts as one. A constant key with a count above 1 is refused when the blueprint loads, because every entity would take the same key.
  • initial creates that many entities when the run is built, with the arrival's keys, before any gap passes. An arrival with initial alone needs no dist, replay or gap.
  • active: false starts a source off. A task's or an on: entry's activate and deactivate turn a source on and off, and each must name an arrival that has a spawn. Under off_mode: drop, the default, an arrival that falls while the source is off is lost and takes no key number. Under restart, the pending arrival is dropped when the source goes off, and activate starts a whole new gap.

A second add_arrival of one name replaces the first entirely. count, keys, max_events and stagger need spawn, and stagger needs count or keys. count, keys, first_at and stagger do not apply to a replay. Every place here reads the run only: attr, payload, item, wait, process and a bare name are refused, and a level, a signal, a resource, a store and a registry name must exist.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrival_options.yaml:options
arrivals:
  # A fixed gap, a first order at 5 s, and a number of orders drawn once: 4 on average
  orders:
    gap: 10 s
    first_at: 5
    max_events: {gen: sample, dist: geometric, p: 0.25}
    # A var is drawn once for each order, and the attributes and the key read it
    vars:
      lane: {gen: integer, bounds: [1, 3]}
    attributes:
      lane: {gen: expr, expr: lane}
    spawn: pack
  # A party of orders at a time: its size is drawn at each arrival, and 0 starts nobody
  parties:
    dist: exponential
    rate: 0.05
    group: {gen: sample, dist: poisson, mean: 2}
    spawn: pack
  # Three scanners, each a loop of its own, starting 2 s apart, with their own keys
  scanners:
    dist: constant
    value: 20 s
    count: 3
    stagger: 2 s
    key: {gen: sequence, format: "scanner-{}"}
    spawn: scan
  # A source that starts off, and starts a whole new gap when it is turned on
  rush: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, active: false, off_mode: restart, spawn: pack}
  # One start at 60 s
  bell: {gap: 1 s, first_at: 60, max_events: 1, spawn: open_rush}
  # One start at 80 s
  lull: {gap: 1 s, first_at: 80, max_events: 1, spawn: close_rush}
  # Two orders that exist when the run starts
  regulars: {initial: 2, spawn: pack}
  # A gap of whole seconds, 4 on average
  walkins: {dist: geometric, p: 0.25, spawn: pack}

A service takes the same families. The count a geometric service draws is read as seconds:

docs/snippets/yaml/arrival_options.yaml:services
services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}
  # Whole seconds with a fixed chance of 0.5 of ending at each: 2 s on average
  checking: {dist: geometric, p: 0.5}
docs/snippets/yaml/arrival_options.yaml:switch
open_rush:
  payload: {event_type: rush_opened}
  # Turns the source of rush on as the task finishes
  activate: rush
close_rush:
  payload: {event_type: rush_closed}
  # Turns the source of rush off again
  deactivate: rush
docs/snippets/pages/arrival_options.py:options
# A fixed gap, a first order at 5 s, and a number of orders drawn once: 4 on average
app.add_arrival(
    "orders",
    gap="10 s",
    first_at=5,
    max_events=generator({"gen": "sample", "dist": "geometric", "p": 0.25}),
    # A var is drawn once for each order, and the attributes and the key read it
    vars={"lane": generator({"gen": "integer", "bounds": [1, 3]})},
    attributes={"lane": generator({"gen": "expr", "expr": "lane"})},
    spawn="pack",
)
# A party of orders at a time: its size is drawn at each arrival, and 0 starts nobody
app.add_arrival(
    "parties",
    dist="exponential",
    rate=0.05,
    group=generator({"gen": "sample", "dist": "poisson", "mean": 2}),
    spawn="pack",
)
# A source that starts off, and starts a whole new gap when it is turned on
app.add_arrival(
    "rush",
    dist="exponential",
    rate=0.5,
    active=False,
    off_mode="restart",
    spawn="pack",
)
# One start at 60 s
app.add_arrival("bell", gap="1 s", first_at=60, max_events=1, spawn="open_rush")
# One start at 80 s
app.add_arrival("lull", gap="1 s", first_at=80, max_events=1, spawn="close_rush")
# Two orders that exist when the run starts, then one every 50 s: the builder always
# takes a dist or a gap
app.add_arrival("regulars", dist="constant", value=50, initial=2, spawn="pack")
# A gap of whole seconds, 4 on average
app.add_arrival("walkins", dist="geometric", p=0.25, spawn="pack")
docs/snippets/pages/arrival_options.py:switch
# Turns the source of rush on as the task finishes
@app.task(activate="rush")
def open_rush(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "rush_opened"}


# Turns the source of rush off again
@app.task(deactivate="rush")
def close_rush(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "rush_closed"}

The builder's add_arrival has no count, keys or stagger. It always takes a dist or a gap, so the regulars above also arrive every 50 seconds.

An @app.arrival_loop starts entities itself: it waits with context.wait_for_arrival("orders"), which reads gap, first_at, key and vars as the page above describes, and starts a task for each entity.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
One registry of distributions. Every family is declared once, in desflow.models.distributions.DISTRIBUTIONS, with its parameters, its range rules, how to draw from it, its mean and variance, and what it gives with no random generator. The YAML models, the builder, DistributionConfig, the Sampler and the registry's live paths all read it, so they accept the same families and parameters. These are 200,000 draws from each of the ten families of times:

A draw reads the live configuration. A DistributionConfig holds the family and its parameters. Sampler.sample(config) reads the parameters at the moment it is called, so a change made while the run goes on applies from the next draw. A task draws its service time once it has its resource and has published started. The arrival loop draws the next gap when it starts waiting. A draw below 0 is raised to 0, so a time is never negative.

One random stream per distribution. A seeded Sampler makes one generator for each name: NumPy's SeedSequence(seed, spawn_key=(the SHA-256 hash of the name, as eight 32-bit numbers)). When the registry registers a distribution, it names it by its path without the sim id, such as arrival.orders or service.packing, and every draw from that distribution comes from that stream. Probability routing draws from route.<task> in the same way, as Task Flow describes. Each stream depends only on the seed and the distribution's name. Adding a distribution therefore leaves every other one's draws unchanged. The name leaves out the sim id, so renaming the simulation does not change them either:

In the low-level API, a DistributionConfig that was never registered draws from the Sampler's main generator instead. Your own code can take a stream of its own with sampler.generator("<name>"):

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint and a builder model register every distribution, so each draws from its own stream. Code of your own takes a stream from context.sampler.generator("<name>") once the run is built.

A blueprint and a builder model register every distribution, so each draws from its own stream. Code of your own takes a stream from context.sampler.generator("<name>") once the run is built.

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:streams
# Each registered distribution draws from the stream named by its path without
# the sim id; register the parameters, and sample() picks the stream
registry = SimulationRegistry(simpy.Environment())
registry.register_sim_parameter(SimParameter(sim_id="Shop", arrival={"orders": gap}))
assert gap.stream == "arrival.orders"
stream = Sampler(seed=42).generator("arrival.orders")  # the same seed, the same name
assert stream is not None and sampler.sample(gap) == stream.exponential(2.0)

Sampler(rng=np.random.default_rng(42)) draws the same numbers as Sampler(seed=42), because the streams come from the generator's seed.

No random generator. A Sampler() with neither a seed nor a generator draws nothing at random: every sample is the distribution's mean, or a constant's value. A run then uses the mean of every input and gives the same output each time, which suits a test. That output is not the model's average result: variation lengthens waits, so a run on mean inputs gives shorter waits than random runs give on average. A truncated_normal gives its mean or its low, whichever is higher.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint and a builder model always have a random generator: the random_seed, or a seed drawn and logged at the start. Draws at the mean are for a low-level test.

A blueprint and a builder model always have a random generator: the random_seed, or a seed drawn and logged at the start. Draws at the mean are for a low-level test.

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:no-generator
fixed = Sampler()  # no random generator: every draw is the mean, or the value
assert fixed.sample(packing) == 3.0 and fixed.sample(gap) == 2.0
assert fixed.sample(checking) == 1.5  # shape × scale

SimPy and desflow. SimPy has no distributions: a SimPy model draws its own times, usually with random.expovariate(0.5) for a gap of 2 seconds on average, and writes yield env.timeout(...) with the result. Nothing checks the parameters, a negative draw makes timeout raise, and the parameters are ordinary variables. desflow names each distribution and its parameters once, checks them, keeps them in the registry, and gives each a stream of its own. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
Each scalar parameter a family takes has a path in the registry: <sim_id>.arrival.<name>.rate for an exponential arrival, <sim_id>.service.<name>.mean and .std for a normal service, .low, .mode and .high for a triangular, .shape and .scale for a gamma or weibull, .value for a constant. A scenario, an ingress message or a process changes it while the run goes on, as Live Parameters explains:

  • The next draw uses the new value. An order already being packed keeps the time it drew, and the arrival already being waited for keeps its gap.
  • An update is checked on a copy of the configuration, by the same rules as at build. A value outside the range is refused with an error log line, and the old value stays:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

A scenario step or an ingress message with an out-of-range value is refused in the same way, with the same error log line.

A scenario step or an ingress message with an out-of-range value is refused in the same way, with the same error log line.

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:refused
packing_path = "Shop.service.packing.std"
registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(sim_id="Shop", service={"packing": packing})
)
registry.update(packing_path, -1.0)  # refused with an error log line
assert registry.get(packing_path).value == 0.5  # the old value stays

Invalid value for 'Shop.service.packing.std': normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0. Update ignored.
  • The family is fixed when the model is built. There is no path that turns a normal into an exponential. An update to a parameter the family does not have, such as .rate on a normal, is refused as an unknown path, with a warning.
  • An empirical distribution has no paths: its lists are taken at load.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Refused at build. The same checks refuse a bad distribution when the model is built. A parameter that is NaN or infinity is refused with its name, at load and on a live update. true is refused at load, and a live update stores it as 1, as Live Parameters says. A negative low or value in a distribution of times (uniform, triangular, truncated_normal and empirical) is refused. So is a parameter whose draw would overflow: a weibull shape, a lognormal mean or a poisson mean. These three are an out-of-range std, a parameter normal does not take, and a mode above high:

    YAMLBuilderLow-level

    desflow run and SimulationContext.from_yaml refuse the same parameters, with the file, the line and the same message: shop.yaml:3: services.packing: Value error, normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0.

    app.add_service and app.add_arrival raise the same ValueError, such as normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0.

    docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:invalid
    refused: List[Dict[str, Any]] = [
    {"dist": "normal", "mean": 3.0, "std": -1.0},  # out of range
    {"dist": "normal", "mean": 3.0, "rate": 2.0},  # a parameter normal does not take
    {"dist": "triangular", "low": 1.0, "mode": 3.0, "high": 2.0},  # mode above high
]
for parameters in refused:
    try:
        DistributionConfig(**parameters)
    except ValueError as error:
        print(error)


    normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0
normal does not take rate; it takes mean, std
triangular needs low <= mode <= high, got low 1.0, mode 3.0, high 2.0

  • A wide normal. When std is half of mean, 2.3% of draws fall below 0 and are raised to the floor. When std equals mean, 15.9% are. The raised draws push the average time up: the 200,000 draws of the normal panel in the chart above, with mean 1 and std 1, average 1.08, not 1. Use truncated_normal.

  • A gap of 0. A constant gap of 0 starts entities at one instant without end, so the run never ends and until does not stop it, as in SimPy. A service of 0 takes no time and does not stop the run.
  • Rate against mean. exponential takes a rate per second, not a mean gap: an order every 30 seconds is rate: 0.0333, not 30.
  • A seed and the timestamps. A seed fixes the draws and so the simulation times, but each record's timestamp also depends on when the run started, unless logical_start_time is set, as Time and Pacing explains.
  • Spread lengthens queues. Two models with the same mean times but a different spread have different queues: more spread means longer waits, as Queues and Capacity and Choosing Inputs measure.

docs.title: Example: Local Replay
docs.text:
The local-replay example has one packer and the 40 orders of a recorded morning, which it replays from a CSV file at their times. The last order arrives at 73 seconds. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own after 120 simulation seconds.

The tutorial page Local Replay teaches these features step by step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local-replay --api yaml
cd local-replay/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run local_replay.yaml

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local-replay --api yaml
cd local-replay/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run local_replay.yaml

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local-replay --api builder
cd local-replay/builder

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow local_replay_example.py

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local-replay --api builder
cd local-replay/builder

# 3. Run it
python local_replay_example.py

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local-replay --api low-level
cd local-replay/low-level

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow local_replay_example.py

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local-replay --api low-level
cd local-replay/low-level

# 3. Run it
python local_replay_example.py

docs.title: Input Fitting
docs.text: A model's distributions should come from data where data exists. Input fitting takes a column of measured times and fits every distribution family of times that desflow has. It checks each result, and also offers the data itself as an empirical distribution. It writes the chosen settings in a form a model loads. This page describes the command and the Python call, every option, each outcome and how to deal with it, and how the fitting is done.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
desflow fit and fit_column fit the families of times of Arrivals and Services to service durations or to the gaps between arrivals, by maximum likelihood with scipy. Maximum likelihood chooses the parameters under which the measured values are most probable. Each family's fit becomes one row of a table, with its parameters in seconds and its diagnostics, and the best is marked. Fitting the Inputs fits the shop's 40 packing times and shows why the best by the numbers still needs checking against the model's answer. Fit a Distribution fits the gaps of an order log.

Fitting needs the fit extra, which installs scipy and matplotlib: pip install "desflow[fit]". A base install runs without the extra: desflow imports scipy and matplotlib only when a fit runs.

docs.title: Fit a Column
docs.text:
The command fits a CSV column, prints the table, writes the best candidate's settings to --out and the plot to --plot. It exits with status 1 when no candidate is usable, and with status 2 when the input is invalid:

# Fit the packing times, write the best fit and plot every candidate
desflow fit packing_times.csv --column packing_seconds --unit s --lower 0 --out packing_fit.yaml --plot fit.png

In Python, fit_column does the same on a list of numbers:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint holds the fit as a file: the YAML that --out wrote, which Load the Settings includes in the blueprint.

examples/builder/fitting_example.py:fit
times = read_column(DATA, "packing_seconds")
result = fit_column(times, unit="s", lower=0)
print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics
examples/low-level/fitting_example.py:fit
result = fit_column(read_column(DATA, "packing_seconds"), unit="s", lower=0)
print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    # An order every 1.25 s on average (rate 0.8)
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.8)},
    # The best candidate's settings, such as dist="triangular", low=0.546332
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(**result.settings())},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, max_cap=4)},
)

read_column(path, column), imported with from desflow.analysis import read_column, reads one CSV column as text. fit_column takes any list of numbers or text, where an empty cell or None is a missing value.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Command option fit_column argument What it sets Default --column the CSV column to fit required --unit unit the data's unit: ms, s, min or h; the settings are always in seconds s --candidates candidates the families to try, such as gamma,lognormal; spaces around a name are ignored, and an unknown name is refused, quoted; poisson and geometric are skipped, as they count whole numbers every family of times --lower, --upper lower, upper the plausible range, in the data's unit: a value outside it is invalid, and a family that can draw outside it is flagged; a NaN bound is refused none --bins bins offer the empirical distribution as a histogram with this many bins the values themselves --min-count min_count the fewest values a family is fitted to 20 --tolerance tolerance how far a fitted mean and standard deviation may be from the data's, as a share of the data's; NaN and a negative number are refused 0.25 --drop-invalid drop_invalid leave invalid values out, counted, rather than stopping off --out result.yaml() write the best candidate's settings as YAML --plot result.plot(path) draw the data against the best candidate

A value is invalid when it is not a number, is not finite, or lies outside --lower and --upper. The table's first line counts the rows, and the values used, missing and invalid.

docs.title: Read the Result
docs.text:
fit_column returns a FitResult:

  • table: one row per candidate, with family, status, reason, parameters, log_likelihood, aic, ks_statistic, ks_p_value, bounds and best. aic is the AIC, where lower is better.
  • best: the best candidate's family.
  • settings(kind=None): the settings of the best, or of the family kind, for add_service(name, **settings). A family that is not usable is refused, and the error names those that are.
  • text(): the table as the command prints it.
  • yaml(kind=None): the settings as the YAML file --out writes.
  • plot(path, kind=None): the PNG --plot draws: the data's histogram over values generated from the candidate, and a Q-Q plot, which puts each sorted data value against the generated value at the same quantile. Points on the diagonal mean that the two agree.

The settings are the same numbers the YAML file holds, so a script and a blueprint that load one fit draw the same values. A number has six significant digits, unless rounding would make the settings fail to load or move the mean or std by more than a thousandth of the std; then it keeps every digit. The lists of an empirical fit (values, edges and counts) keep every digit, because rounding would make close values equal.

docs.title: How the Best Is Chosen
docs.text:
The best is the fitted family with the lowest AIC among those that cannot draw outside --lower and --upper. When every value is the same, it is constant. When no family within the bounds fitted, it is empirical, which never draws outside the data's range. Only when there is no empirical candidate is a fitted family that can draw outside the bounds chosen. A family that is rejected, did not fit or was skipped is never chosen.

When two families' AIC are too close to tell them apart, as AIC and the KS Test explains, check what the choice changes in the model's answer, as Fitting the Inputs does.

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
Each candidate ends with one status. Every one but fitted has a reason, and none stops the fit:

Status Cause What to do skipped fewer values than --min-count collect more data, or use the empirical candidate, which is still offered; lower --min-count only if the values are known to be typical skipped a value of 0 or below, for gamma, weibull or lognormal, which are defined above 0 only find out what the zeros are: rounding (record finer times), a different kind of event (remove it from the data), or real zero durations (use a family with no positive-only support, such as exponential or truncated_normal) skipped poisson or geometric named in --candidates, with the reason " counts whole numbers, and fit tries families of times only" fit the times with a family of times; the two families are for counts, not times skipped every value is the same, so only constant and empirical are fitted use constant, or check that the column is the one meant skipped a value below low, for truncated_normal, whose low is --lower, or 0 set --lower to the true lower bound did not fit scipy's fit raised an error or its search did not settle; the reason is scipy's message the data is far from that family's shape: choose another family; more data can help rejected a fitted parameter is not finite or is out of the family's range as for did not fit rejected the fitted mean or standard deviation is more than --tolerance from the data's look for outliers: correct or remove a value that is a recording error, and keep one that is real. --upper leaves out values above it only with --drop-invalid; without it, such a value stops the fit with status 2. With --upper, only the families bounded above, uniform and triangular, can be chosen as best, then empirical. Or use --bins for an empirical histogram rejected a value lies where the family cannot draw as for the zeros above fitted with a bounds note the family can draw below --lower or above --upper, such as normal below 0 it is chosen only when nothing within the bounds fits; prefer a family with the right support

The command fails only when no candidate is usable, empirical included. empirical is unusable only when there are no values, or when --candidates leaves it out.

docs.title: Load the Settings
docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

!include reads a mapping from another file, relative to the blueprint, so the file --out wrote is loaded and checked as if it were written in place:

examples/yaml/fitting.yaml:include
services:
  # The fitted distribution, read from the file desflow fit wrote
  packing: !include packing_fit.yaml

An arrival also needs its spawn, so the include names the file and adds keys to it: orders: !include {file: fitted/orders.yaml, spawn: pack}. A key the fitted file already has is refused at the !include line, and the error names the key and both files. A YAML syntax error in the included file, or a file that is not a mapping, names that file and its line. A wrong key or value in it is reported at the blueprint's !include line, and so is a missing file. A file that includes itself, directly or through another, is refused at the !include that closes the loop.

examples/builder/fitting_example.py:service
# The best candidate's settings, such as dist="triangular", low=0.546332
.add_service("packing", **result.settings())

DistributionConfig(**result.settings()), as the fit section above shows.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Data first. The values are read, and missing ones are counted and left out. Invalid ones are refused or, with --drop-invalid, counted and left out. They are converted to seconds. Then each family is checked against the data before it is fitted: enough values, positive values where the family needs them, and not a constant column.

Maximum likelihood, location at 0. desflow's families have no location parameter: a gamma or a Weibull starts at 0. scipy can also fit a location, which moves the start of the distribution to wherever the data suggests. For the tutorials' 40 packing times plus one outlier of 120 seconds, a free location puts a gamma's start at 0.70 seconds, the smallest value, with a shape of 0.21 and a scale of 81. desflow has no parameter for that start. So the location of exponential, gamma, weibull and lognormal is fixed at 0, and each fit is converted to desflow's parameters:

Family Fitted with desflow's parameters exponential scipy.stats.expon.fit(x, floc=0) rate = 1 ÷ scale normal scipy.stats.norm.fit(x) mean, std lognormal scipy.stats.lognorm.fit(x, floc=0) the variable's mean = scale × e^(s²/2) and std = mean × √(e^(s²) − 1) truncated_normal the likelihood of scipy.stats.truncnorm with low fixed, maximised by scipy.optimize.minimize mean, std, low uniform scipy.stats.uniform.fit(x) low, high triangular scipy.stats.triang.fit(x) low, mode, high gamma scipy.stats.gamma.fit(x, floc=0) shape, scale weibull scipy.stats.weibull_min.fit(x, floc=0) shape, scale constant every value is the same value empirical the values, or numpy.histogram with --bins values, or edges and counts

Each fit runs on its own, so one that fails is a row, not a crash.

Checks. Every fitted result is checked before it can be chosen. Each parameter must be finite and within the family's rules, the same rules a blueprint's distribution is checked against. The family's mean and standard deviation, from desflow's own formulas, must be within --tolerance of the data's. A result that fails is rejected with the reason. Some bad fits still pass these checks. Fitted to a gamma, the three values 1.0, 1.0000001 and 1.0000002 give a shape of 1.4 × 10¹⁴ and a scale of 7.1 × 10⁻¹⁵, with the right mean and spread. --min-count guards against such fits: no family is fitted to fewer values than --min-count.

Diagnostics. For each fitted family, the table gives the log-likelihood of the data and the AIC. The k in the AIC counts only the fitted parameters: a fixed location does not count. The table also gives the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and p-value from scipy.stats.kstest. The p-value assumes the parameters were known in advance. They were estimated from the same data, so the p-value is approximate and tends to be too high. empirical has no AIC.

Plot. The generated values are drawn through desflow's Sampler, seeded, with the same smallest delay a run applies, so the plot shows what a run draws and repeats exactly.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Size of the extra. These sizes were measured in new Python 3.12 environments on macOS. scipy 1.18.1 takes about 70 MB installed with uv, and about 100 MB with pip, which also compiles bytecode. Its download is 20 to 37 MB, depending on the platform. matplotlib and its dependencies, beyond the NumPy desflow already needs, add about 55 MB with uv and about 70 MB with pip. Fitting is not in the base install because of these sizes.
  • Local files only. The command reads a CSV file. Reading from a database or an object store, and automated selection beyond the lowest AIC, come later.
  • A fit is not a validation. A family that fits the data well can still change the model's answer, and a model whose inputs fit can still answer the question badly. Compare the model's output with the real system's, as Experiment Results does.
  • One column at a time. Each column is fitted on its own, so a dependence between two inputs, such as larger orders taking longer to pack, is not captured.

docs.title: Example: Fitted Inputs
docs.text:
The fitting example fits the 40 packing times of the tutorials and runs one hour of a two-packer shop with the fitted packing time. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page Fitting the Inputs teaches these features step by step.
