docs.title: Stores and Containers: DynamicStore and DynamicContainer
docs.text: A resource is held and given back. Stores and containers hold things that tasks take away and add: items, or an amount. This page shows how to declare them, how tasks put and get, and what a live change does.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
• A store holds items, each one a value of its own: parcels on a shelf waiting for a courier, orders in a buffer. A task puts an item in, and another takes the oldest out.
  • A container holds an amount: boxes in a bin, fuel in a tank, a stock level. A task takes some, and another adds some.

Both have a capacity, or no limit. A task that takes waits while there is not enough, and a task that adds waits while there is no room. Stock uses a container in the shop.

docs.title: Declare Them
docs.text:
A container has three settings. current_cap is its capacity, the largest amount it holds. max_cap is the largest capacity a live change can set. level is the amount it holds when the run starts, 0 when left out. A store has a current_cap and a max_cap, in whole items, and starts empty unless it lists items (Start With Items and Serve by Priority). run() builds a DynamicContainer and a DynamicStore for each one the context declares. A store and a container cannot share a name, and no name is shared with a resource or a signal. A name with a dot or a space is refused, because an expression cannot name it, and so is a name with a character that an expression reads as another, such as µ. A capacity or max_cap below 0, true, or a fraction for a store's whole number is refused, naming the store or container, and so is a container level outside 0 to its capacity. A store's priority is true or false.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:container
containers:
  # An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
  stock: {current_cap: 100, max_cap: 100, level: 20}
docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:store
stores:
  # Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
  parcels: {current_cap: 5, max_cap: 10}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-container
# An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
app.add_container("stock", current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=20)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-store
# Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
app.add_store("parcels", current_cap=5, max_cap=10)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-container
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
        containers={"stock": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=20)},
        # Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
        stores={"parcels": CapacityConfig(current_cap=5, max_cap=10)},
    )
)
stock = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "stock")  # starts at the level above, 20
parcels = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "parcels")

A DynamicContainer built with no init starts at the level its ContainerConfig gives. init= sets another.

A store or container with no current_cap has no capacity limit, as simpy.Store(env) and simpy.Container(env) have: a put never waits for room. current_cap: .inf in YAML, or float("inf") in code, says the same. A max_cap alone gives the current_cap, and a current_cap alone gives the max_cap. A live update can give a store with no limit a capacity. A store's capacity is a whole number of items, so a live update with a fraction is refused and the old capacity stays. .inf or the text "inf" sets no limit again. A store or container with no limit publishes capacity as null.

docs.title: Take and Add
docs.text:
A task takes with get and adds with put. For a container, each names the container and an amount. The amount can be a number, or an expression such as payload.boxes for a field of the previous task's payload. In the builder, it can also be a function of the task id and the previous task's payload. The amount is 1 when left out. For a store, each names the store. A put adds the task's finished payload as the item, or the value of its item, and a get takes the oldest item and passes it to the task's function as item.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:take
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # Takes the boxes the previous task's payload names, once it has a packer
  get: {container: stock, amount: payload.boxes}
docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:put
# Adds its finished payload to the store as an item
put: {store: parcels}
payload: {event_type: order_packed}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-take
# Takes the boxes the previous task's payload names, once it has a packer.
# The amount is a number, an expression, or a function of the task id and the
# previous task's payload, such as lambda task_id, payload: payload["boxes"].
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": "payload.boxes"},
    put={"store": "parcels"},  # adds the finished payload as an item
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


# Takes the oldest parcel, waiting while the store is empty; `item` is that parcel
@app.task(service_id="collecting", get={"store": "parcels"})
def collect(task_id: int, item):
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": item["event_type"]}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-take
def pack(env, order_id):
    yield stock.get(2)  # takes 2 boxes, waiting while fewer are left
    yield parcels.put({"order_id": order_id})  # waits while the store is full


def collect_parcel(env):
    parcel = yield parcels.get()  # waits while the store is empty
    print(f"collected order {parcel['order_id']}; {stock.level:g} boxes left")

get(amount), put(amount), put(item) and get() are SimPy events: yielding one waits until it succeeds, and a store's get() succeeds with the item.

An amount that is not a finite number above 0 is refused, naming the container. A put with item adds that value in place of the payload: a constant, a mapping or a list, or a generator read as the put is made, including one nested in a mapping or a list. After a store get, the bare name item in an expression is the whole item the get took, and it lasts through the task's next chain. So item: {gen: expr, expr: item} puts the item that was taken into another store, and item_priority is the priority of the item a priority store gave. Rank the Waiting Gets and Puts shows both.

A task with a resource gets its unit first and then takes its get, so it waits for stock while holding the unit. A task adds its put after its service time, then publishes the finished event. Tasks and Processes lists every step.

A put or get makes the task wait until it is granted. With wait: false ("wait": False in the builder), the task makes the request and goes on at once, as a SimPy put that is not yielded does. It publishes finished without waiting, and the request stays in the queue until it can be granted. Such a request follows these rules:

  • It is granted first in, first out, together with the requests that are waited for.
  • An interrupt, on_interrupt: abandon and patience never cancel it.
  • A run can end while it still waits, and a drain does not wait for it.
  • A get takes its item later and drops it. So it cannot use item_field or a function that declares item, and its item.<field> can be read only in its own filter.
  • It is refused in a branch of a wait.

The pump task of Example: Fuel Dock puts fuel into a tank this way. The third pump finds room for only 20 units of fuel, so its put stays queued.

docs.title: Start With Items and Serve by Priority
docs.text:
A store can hold items when the run starts, such as parcels left from yesterday. items lists them in the order a get returns them. A store cannot start with more items than its current_cap: the blueprint or add_store is refused with the reason.

A store with priority returns the item with the lowest priority value first, as SimPy's PriorityStore does. Its items are [priority, item] pairs, and a task's put gives each new item its priority. Items of equal priority come out in SimPy's heap order, which is not always the order they went in. A priority can be:

  • a number, or an expression such as attr.priority that gives one;
  • a list such as [1, 2], ordered element by element, as a tuple is;
  • any other value that can be ordered against the others, such as a text.

In the Low-level API a priority keeps the value it is given, so a text priority such as "10" sorts as text, before "9". In the Builder and in YAML a string priority in a task put is an expression, so "10" gives the number 10, and a text priority such as 'P1' comes from attr.grade or payload.grade. A starting item without a generator keeps its string priority as text. A number and a list, or a list and a tuple, in one store raise ValueError at the put that mixes them. A number and a text raise TypeError when the store compares the two, as in SimPy.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/parcel_store.yaml:store
stores:
  parcels:
    current_cap: 10
    max_cap: 10
    # A courier takes the lowest priority value first; equal priorities leave in
    # SimPy's heap order
    priority: true
    # Left from yesterday: [priority, item] pairs, held before the first put
    items:
      - [2, {order: standard-0}]
      - [1, {order: express-0}]
docs/snippets/yaml/parcel_store.yaml:put
pack:
  # Each parcel's priority, read when it is put in the store
  put: {store: parcels, priority: attr.priority}
  payload: {order: standard}
  id_field: number
docs/snippets/pages/parcel_store.py:builder-store
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0)
# A courier takes the lowest priority value first; equal priorities leave in
# SimPy's heap order.
# Left from yesterday: (priority, item) pairs, held before the first put.
app.add_store(
    "parcels",
    current_cap=10,
    max_cap=10,
    priority=True,
    items=[(2, {"order": "standard-0"}), (1, {"order": "express-0"})],
)

A task's put takes the priority the same way: put={"store": "parcels", "priority": "attr.priority"}.

docs/snippets/pages/parcel_store.py:low-level-store
parcels = DynamicStore(
    env,
    "Shop",
    "parcels",
    priority=True,
    # Each pair is held as a PriorityItem
    items=[(2, {"order": "standard-0"}), (1, {"order": "express-0"})],
)


def courier_process(env):
    first = yield parcels.get()  # a PriorityItem; .item is the parcel
    print(f"collected {first.item['order']}")
    # A put of your own wraps the item the same way
    yield parcels.put(parcels.wrap({"order": "express-1"}, 1))

A low-level priority store holds simpy.PriorityItems. wrap(item, priority) returns a plain PriorityItem(priority, item), the same as writing it by hand, and the builder and YAML use it. Equal priorities leave in SimPy's heap order either way. Assigning a list to a store's items replaces them, and a waiting get is served at the next put or get, not at the assignment.

A get on a priority store takes no priority of its own and is refused with one: the item's priority decides the order. Priorities compares priority storage with a resource's priority queue.

docs.title: Pick an Item, or Give Up Waiting
docs.text:
A store get can take a filter, a condition that picks which item it takes, as SimPy's FilterStore does. The filter reads the item on offer as item.<field>, and every name that other conditions read, such as attr.area for the entity's own attribute. The get takes the oldest item that matches, and waits while none does. A waiting get that matches nothing does not stop a later get from taking an item that matches it.

A priority store takes no filter, because SimPy has no store that both ranks and filters. The blueprint or run() refuses a filter on one, and names the task.

A task's patience covers its whole wait: for its wait, then its resource, then its get. When it runs out, the task publishes reneged and its get is cancelled, so it takes nothing later. In the low-level API, cancel() on a put or get event that has not succeeded takes it out of its queue, as in SimPy: a cancelled get takes nothing, and a cancelled put adds nothing. In YAML, item_field adds the item that the task's get took to its payload. A builder function receives the item as item:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:collect
tasks:
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The parcel goes on the shelf as the payload, with its area.
    put: {store: parcels}
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    attributes: [area]
  collect:
    # The oldest parcel for the courier's own area.
    get: {store: parcels, filter: item.area == attr.area}
    # A courier leaves without a parcel after 20 seconds.
    patience: 20 s
    # The parcel the courier took, in the finished event.
    item_field: parcel
    payload: {event_type: parcel_collected}
examples/builder/filtered_inventory_example.py:collect
@app.task(
    # The oldest parcel for the courier's own area
    get={"store": "parcels", "filter": "item.area == attr.area"},
    # A courier leaves without a parcel after 20 seconds
    patience=20,
)
def collect(task_id, context, item):
    """`item` is the parcel the courier took."""
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": item}

A filter can also be a function of the item: "filter": lambda parcel: parcel["area"] == "north".

examples/low-level/filtered_inventory_example.py:collect
def collect(env, sampler, shop, key, area, task_id):
    """Takes the oldest parcel for its own area, or leaves after 20 seconds."""

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="collect", instance=task_id)

    flow = key.rsplit("-", 1)[0]
    env.stats.flow_started(flow)  # the courier enters the shop
    publish({"status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("collect", task_id)
    get = shop["parcels"].get(filter=lambda parcel: parcel["area"] == area)
    yield get | env.timeout(20)
    if not get.triggered:
        get.cancel()  # out of the queue, so it takes no parcel later
        publish({"status": "reneged"})
        env.stats.task_reneged("collect", task_id)
        env.stats.flow_ended(flow)
        return
    publish({"status": "started"})
    env.stats.task_started("collect", task_id)
    publish({"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": get.value})
    env.stats.task_finished("collect", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished(flow)

A store or container get can be a branch of a wait, and a group wait: {when: <expression>, of: {...}} ends when the expression holds. It reads done_count, the number of branches done, and cancels the requests that did not win, as any does. Wait, Signals and Child Flows describes the groups.

item.<field> can also be read in the task's put and next, after its get. Filtered Inventory uses a filter and patience on a shelf of shirts.

docs.title: Rank the Waiting Gets and Puts
docs.text:
Gets and puts that wait are served first in, first out. get_queue and put_queue rank them instead, on a store or a container, as a resource's queue ranks its requests: each is {rank: <expression>, ties: fifo or lifo}. The expression is read once as each get or put is made, in the scope of the task that makes it. A rank that is NaN or text fails the task, with a message that names the task and the value. The lowest rank is served first, and ties serves equal ranks oldest first (fifo, the default) or latest first (lifo). They rank the waiters, not the items: a store's priority still ranks the items. A type that sets its own order refuses both, as Custom Store and Container Types says.

A container serves its waiting gets in queue order and stops at the first one its level cannot meet, as SimPy's Container does. A get that waits for more than the container holds therefore blocks the gets behind it, even a small one that the level could serve.

docs.title: Custom Store and Container Types
docs.text:
A store or container of your own class changes how items or amounts go in and out. Subclass desflow.StoreBase (a simpy.Store) or desflow.ContainerBase (a simpy.Container) and override _do_put or _do_get, set PutQueue or GetQueue, or bind put and get to event classes of your own, as in SimPy. The constructor is SimPy's, (env, capacity=inf) for a store and (env, capacity=inf, init=0) for a container. Name the class with type: !python module.Class in a blueprint, type= in add_store and add_container, or type= in DynamicStore and DynamicContainer.

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/advanced/fuel_dock.yaml:dock
stores:
  # A lane of your own type; it holds two trucks
  lane: {current_cap: 2, max_cap: 2, type: !python fuel_dock_types.Lane}

containers:
  # A tank of 100: two pumps fill 80 of it, so the third put waits for room
  tank: {current_cap: 100, max_cap: 100}

arrivals:
  diesel_trucks:
    dist: constant
    value: 3
    spawn: park
    attributes: {fuel: diesel}
  petrol_trucks:
    dist: constant
    value: 5
    spawn: park
    attributes: {fuel: petrol}
  crew: {dist: constant, value: 7, spawn: unload}
  tankers: {dist: constant, value: 4, spawn: pump}
  marshals: {dist: constant, value: 15, spawn: marshal}

tasks:
  park:
    # The truck waits outside while the lane is full
    put: {store: lane}
    payload: {event_type: truck_parked}
    attributes: [fuel]
  unload:
    # The newest truck in the lane, because of the lane's type
    get: {store: lane}
    item_field: truck
    payload: {event_type: truck_unloaded}
  pump:
    # The tank truck starts the pump and leaves; it does not wait for the put
    put: {container: tank, amount: 40, wait: false}
    payload: {event_type: pump_started}
  marshal:
    # Waits until a truck is held outside the full lane
    wait: {condition: putters.lane >= 1}
    payload: {event_type: overflow_bay_called}

The class is in examples/yaml/advanced/fuel_dock_types.py, next to the blueprint, which !python finds first.

class CountedBin(ContainerBase):
    """A container that counts the puts it grants."""

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.restocks = 0

    def _do_put(self, event):
        granted = super()._do_put(event)
        if event.triggered:
            self.restocks += 1
        return granted


app.add_container("labels", current_cap=10, level=10, type=CountedBin)

# A task's get or put can also be a Transfer, built once and given to several tasks
one_label = Transfer(container="labels", amount=1)


@app.task(get=one_label)
def print_label(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "label_printed"}

A low-level model builds an instance of the class itself, as the Low-level tab above builds the lane and the tank.

The statistics and the conditions follow every change to a store's items or a container's level made by _do_put or _do_get, whether the override calls super() or not, and each change is reported to them once. ContainerBase compares the level before and after, so an override that returns True without changing the level reports nothing. A change to the length of put_queue or get_queue is reported to the conditions that read putters. or getters.. A queue class must support len() and remove(). A cancel() is reported from the event classes, so it works with a queue class of your own.

A task's put stores its payload as the item, and its get passes the item on, unwrapped, whatever the type. A type cannot be given with priority: a type sets its own order, so subclass StoreBase and simpy.PriorityStore for a ranked store. A get with a filter needs a type that subclasses simpy.FilterStore, and a blueprint or run() without such a type is refused, naming the task. A live capacity update reaches a type of your own as it does the default.

docs.title: Registry Paths, Readings and Conditions
docs.text:
A container has three registry paths, <sim_id>.containers.<name>.current_cap, .max_cap and .level. A store has <sim_id>.stores.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap. With statistics at the minimal level or above, each publishes four readings, such as Shop.stats.containers.stock.level:

Reading Store Container capacity items it can hold largest amount level items held amount held getters_waiting tasks waiting to get an item tasks waiting to take an amount putters_waiting tasks waiting to put an item tasks waiting to add an amount

basic adds level_avg, the level averaged over time. Statistics describes it. Below are the readings of stores_containers.yaml, the blueprint whose parts this page shows. They are taken at 30 and 40 simulation seconds, before and after the stock count that Under Live Changes shows:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.level', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.putters_waiting', 'value': 0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.level', 'value': 5}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.putters_waiting', 'value': 0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 40}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 0}

At 30 seconds the bin is empty and two orders wait for boxes. At 40 seconds the stock count has put 50 boxes in, those two have taken theirs, and the shelf of parcels is full, with no packed order waiting for room.

A condition in a task's next reads a level as level.<name>, so an order can go to backorder when level.stock == 0, as Task Flow shows.

A condition can also read how many tasks wait at a store or container, and what a store holds:

Name Reads putters.<name>, getters.<name> the number of puts or gets waiting, not counting one that is granted at once, as the putters_waiting and getters_waiting readings; len(put_queue) and len(get_queue) in the low-level API count(<store>) the number of items the store holds, as level.<store> count(<store>, <condition>) how many items meet the condition, which reads item.<field> of each items(<store>), items(<store>, item.<field>) the list of items, or that field of each; a priority store gives its items unwrapped putting(<store>), getting(<store>) the puts and gets that wait, as a list of mappings with entity and, for a put, item or amount; len() counts them, as putters. does item, item_priority the whole item the task's store get took, and the priority a priority store gave it peek() the simulation time of the next scheduled event, infinity when there is none

in and not in read an items(...) list, as in payload.sku in items(shelf, item.sku), which is true while the shelf holds that sku. The store is a bare name, and count and items cannot be nested inside each other. The names are checked at load: each must name a store, and putters. and getters. may also name a container.

A condition that reads one of these names is checked again when a put or get joins or leaves a queue. A condition that reads none of them, such as level.stock == 0, is not checked again for a queue change. A queue change is not a change of level, so level_avg does not move. The marshal task of Example: Fuel Dock waits on putters.lane >= 1.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A container keeps a level between 0 and its capacity, with a queue of getters and a queue of putters. A get succeeds as soon as the level covers its amount, and a put as soon as there is room for all of it. Until then, each waits in its queue, in the order it arrived:

A store keeps a list of items, up to its capacity. A put adds an item at the end, and a get takes the first, so items leave in the order they came. A get with a filter takes the first item its filter accepts:

SimPy and desflow. desflow builds on three SimPy classes. A container is SimPy's Container. A store is a FilterStore, which serves its gets as Store does while no waiting get has a filter. A priority store is a PriorityStore, which hands out the lowest item first. A full put that waits for room and an empty get that waits for an item or an amount are checked against plain SimPy in all three APIs. SimPy Compatibility lists the checks. SimPy's capacities are fixed when they are created, and desflow's follow the registry. desflow also keeps the registry's level in step with every put and get, and reports each change to the statistics. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
• Capacity follows current_cap, clamped to between 0 and max_cap. A higher capacity wakes waiting putters. A capacity below what is held destroys nothing: puts wait until enough has been taken.
  • A container's level is set by an update to its level path, as a stock count or a restock from outside would. The new level is clamped to between 0 and current_cap, with a warning, and it wakes both queues: a higher level serves waiting getters, and a lower one can make room for putters.
  • A store or container with no limit can be given a number as current_cap during a run, and .inf or the text "inf" sets no limit again. Lowering it destroys nothing, as the Capacity item above says.
  • current_cap is the capacity, not a level. A model that used a container's current_cap as a level, such as the wear of a roll, moves it to level.

The stock count in stores_containers.yaml, in each way of writing:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:level
scenario:

  - {at: 30, path: Shop.containers.stock.level, value: 50}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-level

    """A stock count at 30 seconds: the level path sets what the container holds."""
    yield context.env.timeout(30)
    context.env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 50)


app.add_process(stock_count)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-level
def stock_count_process(env):
    """A stock count: sets the level; waiting gets and puts are woken."""
    yield env.timeout(30)
    env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 50)

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A container that never refills blocks its getters for good, and a task that waits for stock while holding a resource blocks the resource too. Supply has to keep up with demand, as Stock shows.
  • Whole items. A store's capacity is a whole number or no limit, and it holds items, not amounts.
  • A put or get with wait: false is never cancelled, so a supply that outpaces its consumers grows the queue without end. A run drops what is still waiting when it ends.
  • A filter checks every waiting get on each put. For a store with many waiting gets and a filter that rarely matches, the work grows in proportion to both, as SimPy's FilterStore does.
  • One store or container per get or put. A task has at most one get and one put.

docs.title: Example: Stock, Parcels and Express Orders
docs.text:
The stock example combines a container and a store. Packing takes a box from a container and puts the parcel in a store, which starts with two parcels from yesterday. A courier collects the parcels. Express orders go first at the packers, and also at the courier, because the parcels store is a priority store. The stock runs out, so packing waits until a restock at 40 seconds sets the level to 30 boxes. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page Stock teaches these features step by step.

examples/low-level/stock_example.py:pack
def pack(env, sampler, shop, key, priority, task_id):
    """Queued, a packer by priority, a box from stock, packing, then a parcel."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack", instance=task_id)

    publish(
        {"path_id": path_id, "sim_id": "Shop", "service": "packing", "status": "queued"}
    )
    env.stats.task_queued("pack", task_id)  # counted as in progress
    with shop["packers"].request(priority=priority) as req:
        yield req
        # Waits while the stock is empty
        yield shop["stock"].get(1)
        publish(
            {
                "path_id": path_id,
                "sim_id": "Shop",
                "service": "packing",
                "status": "started",
            }
        )
        env.stats.task_started("pack", task_id)
        payload = {"event_type": "order_packed", "priority": priority}
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        # Waits while the store is full; wrap ranks the parcel by its priority
        yield shop["parcels"].put(shop["parcels"].wrap(payload, priority))
        publish(payload)
        env.stats.task_finished("pack", task_id)

docs.title: Example: Fuel Dock
docs.text:
The fuel-dock example combines the parts of this page:

  • Fuel trucks wait in a lane of your own type, which gives back the newest truck first.
  • A crew unloads one truck every 7 seconds.
  • A tank truck puts fuel into a tank that holds 100 units, without waiting for the put. Once the tank is nearly full, the put waits in the tank's queue.
  • A marshal calls the overflow bay once a truck waits outside the full lane.

It needs no Docker service and ends on its own after 40 simulation seconds.

docs.title: Task Flow
docs.text: An entity rarely leaves after completing just one task. An order is checked, perhaps wrapped as a gift, packed, sometimes packed again, and shipped. This page shows how a finished task chooses the next one, what the entity carries from task to task, and which values a task draws and reads on the way.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
A flow is the sequence of tasks one entity passes through. Each task names what follows it: always the same task, the first of several rules whose condition holds, or a task drawn at random by weight. A rule can send the entity back to a task it has passed, for rework. A task that names nothing ends the flow. The entity keeps its key and its attributes through the whole flow, and every task can read them.

Each task also has a key for its records, can draw values for its own use, and can read the records that earlier tasks published.

A Flow of Tasks builds a pick, pack and ship flow step by step.

docs.title: Choose the Next Task
docs.text:
next takes one of these forms:

  • A task name, next: pack_order: always that task.
  • Rules, when with an optional default: each rule is a condition and a task. Rules are tried in order. The first matching rule wins, and default applies if none matches. With no default and no matching rule, the flow ends.
  • Weights, below.
  • In the builder, a function that takes the Upstream and returns a task name or None.
YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:condition
check_order:
  payload: {total: 80}
  # Rules are tried in order; the first match wins. Otherwise, use the default.
  next:
    when:
      - {condition: "level.stock == 0", task: backorder}
      - {condition: "payload.total >= 100 or attr.gift == 1", task: wrap_gift}
    default: pack_order
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-condition
# Rules are tried in order; the first match wins. Otherwise, use the default.
@app.task(
    next={
        "when": [
            {"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"},
            {
                "condition": "payload.total >= 100 or attr.gift == 1",
                "task": "wrap_gift",
            },
        ],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
)
def check_order(task_id: int):
    return {"total": 80}
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:low-level-condition
# The same rules as next, as a Router; choose() returns the next task's name
route = Router(
    {
        "when": [{"condition": "attr.gift == 1", "task": "wrap_gift"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
)
order = Entity("orders-1", "orders", {"gift": 0})  # key, arrival, attributes
finished = Upstream(0, order.key, order.attributes, {"total": 80})
assert route.choose(finished, env=None) == "pack_order"

A Router takes the same rules as next. When a task finishes, its process builds the Upstream, asks route.choose(upstream, env, levels=...) for the next task's name, and starts that task with the same entity. env lets a condition read registry[...] and t. levels, a mapping from store and container names to the objects, lets it read level.<name>.

The condition is evaluated when the task finishes, after its set. payload. reads the payload of the task that just finished, attr. the entity's attributes, level. a store's or container's level, and registry["..."] a live parameter. How It Works lists everything a condition can use.

docs.title: Weights
docs.text:
weights maps task names to numbers or expressions, and the next task is drawn in proportion to them. The draw comes from a random stream of the routing task's own, route.<task>, so a seeded run repeats it and it changes no other draw:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:weights
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  get: {container: stock, amount: 1}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  # A task drawn in proportion to its weight: one in ten is packed again
  next:
    weights: {ship_order: 9, pack_order: 1}
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-weights
# A task drawn in proportion to its weight: one in ten is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1},
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}},
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:low-level-weights
# Weights draw from a generator: the routing task's own stream, as the builder's do
rework = Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}})
rework.rng = Sampler(seed=42).generator("route.pack_order")
choices = [rework.choose(finished) for _ in range(1000)]

A weight written as an expression is read when the task finishes. It may use attr.<name>, registry["..."], level.<name>, t and the task's vars, as weights: {ship_order: 9, pack_order: "attr.rework"} does. A weight of infinity or true is refused when the blueprint loads. A weight below 0, or text that is not a number, fails the run with the weight's name. Weights that add up to 0 fail the run.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
An arrival gives each new entity its starting attributes, and a task's set changes them when the task finishes. Each entity gets its own copy. Attributes are not published: a condition reads them as attr.<name>, and a payload includes them only when it asks.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:attributes
arrivals:
  # Each order starts with these attributes, read as attr.gift
  # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
  orders:
    dist: exponential
    rate: 0.5
    spawn: check_order
    attributes: {gift: 0}
  # A gift order every 10 s on average (rate 0.1)
  gifts:
    dist: exponential
    rate: 0.1
    spawn: check_order
    attributes: {gift: 1}
docs/snippets/yaml/task_flow.yaml:set
# Applied to the order's attributes when the task finishes
set: {backordered: 1}

A task's attributes list adds the named attributes to a mapping payload, as ship_order does in the full blueprint, task_flow.yaml.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-attributes
# Each order starts with these attributes, read as attr.gift
# An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, attributes={"gift": 0})
# A gift order every 10 s on average (rate 0.1)
app.add_arrival("gifts", dist="exponential", rate=0.1, attributes={"gift": 1})
docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-set
# `set` is applied to the order's attributes when the task finishes
@app.task(service_id="supplying", set={"backordered": 1}, next="check_order")
def backorder(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_backordered"}

An Entity(key, arrival, attributes) carries them. The process updates entity.attributes itself after a task, as the low-level tab of A Flow of Tasks shows.

docs.title: Record Key and Fields
docs.text:
Each arrival starts a new entity, keyed by the arrival's name and a counter from 1: orders-1, orders-2. Every event of every task in its flow carries that key as its record key, so a sink can follow one order through the whole flow. Kafka sends records with the same key to one partition, so it keeps one order's events in order. The builder can replace the key with a function of the counter:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint arrival uses the default key.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-key
# Keys ret-00001, ret-00002 instead of returns-1, from the counter, which starts at 1
# A return every 20 s on average (rate 0.05)
app.add_arrival("returns", dist="exponential", rate=0.05, key=lambda n: f"ret-{n:05d}")

The process that creates each Entity gives it its key.

Below are the finished events of gifts-5 in task_flow.yaml, the blueprint whose parts this page shows. The gift order is checked while the shelf has stock, so it is not backordered and its shipping record shows backordered: None. It is wrapped, packed and shipped, all under one key:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 33.55388955498106, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'check_order', 'instance': 17, 'value': {'total': 80}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 36.55388955498106, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'wrap_gift', 'instance': 3, 'value': {'event_type': 'gift_wrapped'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 38.05388955498106, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 12, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 39.55388955498106, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 13, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 39.55388955498106, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'gifts-5', 'task': 'ship_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_shipped', 'gift': 1, 'backordered': None}}

A task can also set the key of its own records. A blueprint task has these keys, and the builder's @app.task takes the same names:

  • key_field names a payload field. Its value becomes the key of the task's finished record, and so the Kafka message key. The queued and started records keep the entity's key. A payload without the field fails the run.
  • key is a value place for the key of all the task's records: text, a whole number or a generator. It is drawn once for each instance, at its first record, and written as text. Write key or key_field, not both.
  • id_field adds the task's instance id to a mapping payload under that name, item_field adds the item the task's store get took, and attributes adds the named entity attributes. They need a mapping payload, and a null payload fails the task.
  • payload: null publishes no finished record, and the task runs its other steps. It is refused together with a store put, key_field, id_field, item_field, attributes and a payload. read.
YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_values.yaml:key
sign_up:
  payload:
    customer_id: {gen: sequence, format: "c-{}"}
  # The finished record carries the customer id as its key
  key_field: customer_id
docs/snippets/pages/task_values.py:key
customer = Template(
    {"customer_id": {"gen": "sequence", "format": "c-{}"}}, name="tasks.sign_up"
)


# The finished record carries the customer id as its key. A builder task keeps the
# rows that a lookup reads only when it asks, with history
@app.task(key_field="customer_id", history=1000)
def sign_up(task_id):
    return customer

A process gives the key to env.publish_event(key, value, ...) itself, as the low-level tab of Tasks shows, so it can publish any record under any key.

docs.title: Upstream
docs.text:
A task started by next receives what the task before it handed on, the Upstream: the finished task's instance id, the entity's key and attributes, and the finished task's payload. A builder function gets it by declaring a parameter called upstream, and gets the entity by declaring entity. A function that declares neither is called without them. The first task of a flow gets upstream=None.

A task that on_fail, on_renege or on_balk reaches reads the record that sent it there as upstream.status and, after a failure, upstream.reason.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint task has no function to declare upstream. Its payload names the attributes it carries, its generators read the finished task's payload as {gen: upstream, path: <field>}, and an expression reads it as upstream.<field>. Its next conditions read the finished task's payload as payload.<field> and the entity's attributes as attr.<name>.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:builder-upstream
# A function declaring `upstream` receives what the previous task handed on,
# and `entity` the order itself; a payload includes attributes only when it asks
@app.task()
def ship_order(task_id: int, upstream, entity):
    return {
        "event_type": "order_shipped",
        "packed_by": upstream.task_id,  # the instance of pack_order before it
        "gift": entity.attributes.get("gift"),
        "backordered": entity.attributes.get("backordered"),
    }


# A rule can also be a function of the Upstream, returning a task name or None
@app.task(next=lambda upstream: "check_order" if upstream.payload["ok"] else None)
def inspect_return(task_id: int):
    return {"ok": False}

A low-level process holds the order and its attributes itself. It can build an Upstream and call Router.choose, as in Choose the Next Task, or decide the next step in plain Python.

docs.title: Values a Task Draws
docs.text:
A task can draw values for its own use. They come in three groups:

  • vars are drawn in order, once for each instance of the task, and each can read the vars above it.
  • vars_once are drawn once for each entity and task, at the first use. A task that an entity runs again, as a rework does, keeps its vars_once.
  • finish_vars are drawn after the service and can read the vars.

on_start values are published as one record when the task starts. A task that has on_start draws its vars when it starts. Without on_start, the task draws them after the service, just before it builds its payload, and a service_time that reads a var draws it first.

A payload reads a var as {gen: var, name: <name>}. The expr and format generators and the put, fail, next.when and next.weights expressions of the same task read it by its bare name. A wait timeout value may read vars_once names but no vars. A var name is an identifier that is not a name of the expression language (all, any, len, sum, cause, waiting and the others) and not the name of a var that is visible there. It is in one group only. A task that can end early (patience, balk, wait, on_interrupt: abandon or queue_limit) refuses an on: value that reads a var.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_values.yaml:draws
pack:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # Drawn once for each order, so a second packing keeps the box
  vars_once:
    box: {gen: one_of, choices: [small, large]}
  # Drawn for each packing, when it starts because on_start is written
  vars:
    weight: {gen: uniform, low: 0.5, high: 5, decimals: 1}
  # Published as one record when the packing starts
  on_start:
    weight: {gen: var, name: weight}
  # Drawn after the service, and able to read the values above
  finish_vars:
    fee: {gen: expr, expr: "round(weight * 0.4, 2)"}
  payload:
    box: {gen: var, name: box}
    weight: {gen: var, name: weight}
    fee: {gen: var, name: fee}
    # The total of the order that came here
    total: {gen: upstream, path: total}
  # One packing in ten is done again
  next:
    weights: {pack: 1, finish: 9}
docs/snippets/pages/task_values.py:draws
packed = Template(
    {
        "box": {"gen": "var", "name": "box"},
        "weight": {"gen": "var", "name": "weight"},
        "fee": {"gen": "var", "name": "fee"},
        # The total of the order that came here
        "total": {"gen": "upstream", "path": "total"},
    },
    name="tasks.pack",
)


@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    # Drawn once for each order, so a second packing keeps the box
    vars_once={"box": {"gen": "one_of", "choices": ["small", "large"]}},
    # Drawn for each packing, when it starts because on_start is written
    vars={"weight": {"gen": "uniform", "low": 0.5, "high": 5, "decimals": 1}},
    # Published as one record when the packing starts
    on_start={"weight": {"gen": "var", "name": "weight"}},
    # Drawn after the service, and able to read the values above
    finish_vars={"fee": {"gen": "expr", "expr": "round(weight * 0.4, 2)"}},
    # One packing in ten is done again
    next={"weights": {"pack": 1, "finish": 9}},
)
def pack(task_id):
    return packed

A process draws its values with its own Sampler generators and keeps them in Python variables, so it has no groups to order. A generator it names, such as sampler.generator("pack.weight"), draws from its own stream of the run's seed.

Every generator node draws from its own stream of the run's seed, so adding a value does not change the draws of the others.

docs.title: Read Earlier Records
docs.text:
A task can read the records that tasks finished before it. A generator reads them, in place of a function that keeps its own list:

  • lookup takes a field of a row of another task's finished payloads, chosen at random unless strategy is first or last. histogram splits the rows, in the order they were written, into bins with a share each, latest_by keeps the newest row of each value of a field, and distinct draws without replacement inside one repeat.
  • previous takes a field of the last finished payload of the same task on the same stream. The stream is the arrival, or the entity for an arrival with count or keys. It gives null when there is none and no default is written.
  • upstream takes a field of the payload of the task that routed here.
  • aggregate gives the mean, sum, min, max or count of a field over the last rows of a task. where, an expression over the row's fields, keeps some of them. It does not wait for a row.

A task keeps its last history finished payloads, one million by default, when a lookup or aggregate in the file names it or when history is written. Look Up Other Records and Build on the Last Value work through them.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_values.yaml:earlier
place_order:
  # A value drawn here is read by name below
  vars:
    total: {gen: uniform, low: 5, high: 200, decimals: 2}
  payload:
    # A customer who signed up earlier
    customer_id: {gen: lookup, task: sign_up, path: customer_id}
    total: {gen: var, name: total}
    # This stream's last running_total plus this order's total
    running_total:
      gen: add
      args:
        - {gen: previous, path: running_total, default: 0}
        - {gen: var, name: total}
  next: pack

A generator that reads records can also set how long a task takes. These tasks run one after another. deliver takes the mean weight of the last 5 packings over 1 kg, restock the newest weight of one customer, and inspect two past weights drawn without replacement, mostly from the older part of the rows. settle takes as long as the last settling, and 2 seconds for the first, and finish as long as the settling before it:

docs/snippets/yaml/task_reads.yaml:reads
deliver:
  # The mean weight of the last 5 packings over 1 kg, as seconds
  service_time:
    gen: aggregate
    task: pack
    path: weight
    last: 5
    where: weight > 1
    function: mean
  payload: {event_type: delivered}
  next: restock
restock:
  # The newest weight of one customer, chosen from the newest row of each customer
  service_time:
    gen: lookup
    task: pack
    path: weight
    strategy: last
    latest_by: customer_id
  payload: {event_type: restocked}
  next: inspect
inspect:
  # Two past weights, drawn without replacement, mostly from the older part of the
  # rows
  service_time:
    gen: expr
    expr: sum(weights)
    names:
      weights:
        gen: repeat
        times: 2
        value:
          gen: lookup
          task: pack
          path: weight
          distinct: true
          histogram:
            - {bin: 2, frequency: 8}
            - {bin: 8, frequency: 2}
  payload: {event_type: inspected}
  next: settle
settle:
  # As long as the last settling took, and 2 s for the first
  service_time: {gen: previous, path: took, default: 2}
  payload:
    took: {gen: uniform, low: 1, high: 3, decimals: 1}
  next: finish
finish:
  # As long as the settling that came before took
  service_time: {gen: upstream, path: took}
  payload: {event_type: finished}
docs/snippets/pages/task_values.py:earlier
order = Template(
    {
        # A customer who signed up earlier
        "customer_id": {"gen": "lookup", "task": "sign_up", "path": "customer_id"},
        "total": {"gen": "var", "name": "total"},
        # This stream's last running_total plus this order's total
        "running_total": {
            "gen": "add",
            "args": [
                {"gen": "previous", "path": "running_total", "default": 0},
                {"gen": "var", "name": "total"},
            ],
        },
    },
    name="tasks.place_order",
)


# A value drawn here is read by name below
@app.task(
    history=10,
    vars={"total": {"gen": "uniform", "low": 5, "high": 200, "decimals": 2}},
    next="pack",
)
def place_order(task_id):
    return order

A process keeps the earlier values itself, in a list or a variable, and reads them where it needs them.

A task whose generators look up another task does not start before that task has a row. An arrival, a spawn or a next that would start it is dropped, with one INFO line that gives the wait in simulation time, and a task that never started gets one more line at the end of the run. A dropped start runs none of the task's on: actions. A lookup in an arrival place fails when there is no row. In where, a field of the row wins over t.

The blueprint is refused when it loads if no task starts the target of a lookup, if the path is not in the target's payload, if lookups form a cycle, if previous is outside a task, if upstream is in a task that no next reaches or that on_fail or on_interrupt_next also reaches, or if distinct is outside the value of a repeat.

docs.title: Carry Values and Switch Arrivals
docs.text:
A task can write names of its own process with set_args. This task and the tasks that follow in the same flow read them as arg.<name>. A child flow has its own, and a parent passes names to it with args on a task branch of its wait or on a spawn. A spawn evaluates args once for each child. A read of a name that was neither passed nor written is a run failure. set_args is read after set, so a payload reads the value from before the write.

activate and deactivate turn the sources of the named arrivals on and off when the task finishes, after set_args. Each must name an arrival that has a spawn, and the blueprint and the builder refuse a name that is not an arrival. A source with count or keys obeys them too. Under off_mode: drop an arrival that falls while its source is off is lost and takes no key number. Under restart the source starts a whole new gap when it goes on. Arrivals and Services describes the arrival keys.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_values.yaml:carry
close_shop:
  payload: {event_type: shop_closed}
  # Written now, and read as arg.closed_at by this task and the tasks after it
  set_args:
    closed_at: {gen: expr, expr: t}
  # Turn on the source of the night sign-ups, as the task finishes
  activate: night
  next: day_report
day_report:
  payload:
    closed_at: {gen: expr, expr: arg.closed_at}
    mean_total:
      gen: aggregate
      task: place_order
      path: total
      last: 10
      function: mean
docs/snippets/pages/task_values.py:carry
report = Template(
    {
        "closed_at": {"gen": "expr", "expr": "arg.closed_at"},
        "mean_total": {
            "gen": "aggregate",
            "task": "place_order",
            "path": "total",
            "last": 10,
            "function": "mean",
        },
    },
    name="tasks.day_report",
)


@app.task(
    # Written now, and read as arg.closed_at by this task and the tasks after it
    set_args={"closed_at": {"gen": "expr", "expr": "t"}},
    # Turn on the source of the night sign-ups, as the task finishes
    activate="night",
    next="day_report",
)
def close_shop(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "shop_closed"}


@app.task()
def day_report(task_id):
    return report

A process passes values to the next one as plain arguments, and decides in its own code which arrival processes keep running.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Conditions. A condition is a Python expression, parsed with Python's ast module and checked against a list of what is allowed before it is ever evaluated. Nothing goes through eval. Each name carries its source as a prefix, so adding a payload field cannot change what an attribute of the same name means. Names an Expression Reads lists every name by the place an expression sits in:

Name Value payload.<field>, attr.<name>, attr["<name>"] a field of the payload of the task that just finished, an attribute of the entity, and an attribute whose name Python reads as a word level.<name> the level of a store or container users.<name>, queue.<name> how many units of a resource are held, and how many requests wait for it (Units and Queues) putters.<name>, getters.<name> how many puts and gets wait at a store or container count(<store>), items(<store>) how many items a store holds, and the list of them (Stores and Containers) item, item.<field>, item_priority the item the task's store get took, a field of it at any depth, and the priority a priority store gave it (Stores and Containers) arg.<name>, cause.<name>, upstream.<field> a name set_args wrote or a parent passed, why the task was interrupted, and a field of the payload of the task that routed here held(<resource>), waiting(<resource>) the holders in grant order and the waiting requests in queue order, as mappings with entity, rank, time, preempt and key, and since for a holder putting(<store>), getting(<store>) the puts and gets waiting at a store or container, with entity and, for a put, item or amount running(<task>), running(<task>, <condition>) how many instances of a task run, or meet the condition wait.<branch>.done, .ok, .value, signal.<name>.count, .ok, .value, .processed, handle.<name>.triggered, .processed, .ok, .value, .alive, done_count the task's wait, the signals, the names the task opened, and in the when of a wait group how many branches are done (Signals and Waiting) process.name, .instance, .target, .key, .flow_name the running process (Processes) registry["<path>"] a live parameter, written whole because its path contains dots t, peek() the simulation time in seconds, and the time of the next scheduled event a var name a var of the task, read bare in put, fail, next.when, next.weights, expr and format

It may also use numbers, text, True, False and None; the arithmetic +, -, *, /, //, % and ** (a power above 10,000, or one with a result of more than 1,000,000 bits, is refused); the comparisons <, <=, >, >=, ==, !=, is None, in and not in; and, or, not and a if c else b; list and mapping literals, subscripts, slices and one-clause list comprehensions; and the functions abs, min, max, round, floor, ceil, sqrt, exp, log, log10, sin, cos, tan, len, sum, sorted, range, any, all, str, int, float, bool, has(attr.<name>), get_key, set_key and drop_key. Text may be compared, indexed, added with + and passed to the key functions, and % on text is refused. One reading of an expression that makes more than 1,000,000 items in all is a named run failure. Anything else is refused with a message that names it:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint condition that uses anything else is refused when the blueprint is built, with the same message.

docs/snippets/pages/task_flow.py:refused
for text in ("payload.total @ 2", "x > 1", "open('orders.csv')"):
    try:
        Expression(text)
    except ValueError as error:
        print(error)

A low-level Router takes these conditions, as in Choose the Next Task, and a process can also decide in plain Python.

'payload.total @ 2' uses the operator MatMult, which an expression cannot
'x > 1' uses the name 'x' (write payload.<field>, attr.<name>, level.<name>, users.<name>, queue.<name>, putters.<name>, getters.<name>, item.<field>, item, item_priority, arg.<name>, cause.<name>, upstream.<field>, count(<store>), items(<store>), held(<resource>), waiting(<resource>), putting(<store>), getting(<store>), running(<task>), peek(), wait.<branch>.<part>, signal.<name>.<part>, process.<name>, registry["<path>"] or t), which an expression cannot
'open('orders.csv')' uses a Call other than count(<store>), items(<store>), has(attr.<name>), held, waiting, putting, getting, peek, running, members or abs, min, max, len, sum, sorted, range, any, all, str, int, float, bool, get_key, set_key, drop_key, round, floor, ceil, sqrt, exp, log, log10, sin, cos, tan, which an expression cannot

A blueprint is checked when it loads, and each error names its YAML line. Every condition must parse, and every task a rule names must exist. Every level.<name> must name a store or container, every users.<name> and queue.<name> a resource, every putters.<name> and getters.<name> a store or container, and every count(...) and items(...) a store. Every registry["..."] must be a path of the model. An item.<field> in a place that no get reaches is refused. The builder makes the same checks when run() starts. A name that is missing when a condition is evaluated, such as a payload field, raises an error naming the expression.

Weights. Weights that are numbers are turned into cumulative shares once. Weights that are expressions are read each time the task finishes. Each choice draws one uniform number from the routing task's stream and picks the task whose share it falls in.

Starting the Next Task. When a task finishes, it applies set, builds the Upstream and asks its rules for the next task. It runs that task next, in the same SimPy process and the same step, with the same entity and the next instance id from the task's counter. An arrival that spawns the task uses the same counter, so no two runs of a task share an id. In SimPy terms, the next task is the next statement of one process. SimPy and desflow describes processes.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Flow balance. The rate into each task follows from the rates into the tasks before it and the routing shares. With weights of 9 to ship and 1 back to packing, one packing in ten sends the order back to be packed again. Every order is packed once, one in ten a second time, one in a hundred a third time, and so on. An order is therefore packed 1 + 0.1 + 0.01 + ... = 1 ÷ 0.9 = 1.11 times on average, so the packers see 11% more work than there are orders. Weights that are expressions give desflow explain no shares, so it reports no flow balance for them.
  • Rework raises utilisation. Work the load out with the rework included, as Queues and Capacity does, or a rework loop can push a resource past full use. Queueing Basics explains utilisation.
  • Refused expressions. A call other than the listed functions, a name without a source, payload["total"] (write payload.total), a comprehension with more than one clause or over a mapping, lambda, ~ and the shift operators are refused. ** with a negative base and a fractional exponent, and round(x, -n) with a very large n, fail the run when the expression is evaluated, naming the expression. An expression nested more than 200 levels is refused when it is read.
  • A loop needs time. A loop of tasks that take no service time, resource, wait or get never lets the clock move. The run stops with an error that names the tasks after the flow has run 10,000 instances at one instant, as a resource breakdown does. Give one task of the loop a service_time above 0, or a way out in its next rules.
  • One entity, one flow. A task leads to at most one next task. Splitting one order into several, or joining several into one, comes after 1.0.
  • decide is kept free. The task key decide is kept for decisions sent from outside for one entity, planned after 1.0. Today it is refused like any unknown key.

docs.title: Example: A Flow of Tasks
docs.text:
In the flow example, orders are picked, gift orders are wrapped, one parcel in ten is packed again, and every order is shipped. Wrapping and shipping are timed steps. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page A Flow of Tasks teaches these features step by step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api yaml
cd flow/yaml

# 3. Find the bottleneck, with no run
desflow explain flow.yaml

# 4. Run it
desflow run flow.yaml

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api yaml
cd flow/yaml

# 3. Find the bottleneck, with no run
desflow explain flow.yaml

# 4. Run it
desflow run flow.yaml
examples/yaml/flow.yaml:routes
tasks:
  pick:
    service: picking
    resource: pickers
    payload: {event_type: order_picked}
    # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest.
    next:
      when:
        - {condition: "attr.gift == 1", task: wrap}
      default: pack
  wrap:
    # A timed step: a service and no resource, so no queued event and no wait.
    service: wrapping
    payload: {event_type: gift_wrapped}
    # Applied to the entity's attributes when the task finishes.
    set: {wrapped: 1}
    next: pack
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    # Drawn from this task's own random sequence: one parcel in ten is packed again.
    next:
      weights: {ship: 9, pack: 1}

The whole file is examples/yaml/flow.yaml.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get flow --api builder
cd flow/builder

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow flow_example.py

# 1. Install

# 2. Download the example

cd flow/builder

# 3. Run it
python flow_example.py
examples/builder/flow_example.py:routes
@app.task(
    service_id="picking",
    resource_id="pickers",
    # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
    next={"when": [{"condition": "attr.gift == 1", "task": "wrap"}], "default": "pack"},
)
def pick(task_id, context):
    """Picks the order's items."""
    return {"event_type": "order_picked"}


# A timed step: a service and no resource, so no queued event and no wait.
# `set` is applied to the entity's attributes when the task finishes.
@app.task(service_id="wrapping", set={"wrapped": 1}, next="pack")
def wrap(task_id, context):
    """Wraps a gift."""
    return {"event_type": "gift_wrapped"}


# Drawn from this task's own random sequence: one parcel in ten is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    next={"weights": {"ship": 9, "pack": 1}},
)
def pack(task_id, context):
    """Packs the order."""
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
