docs.title: Resources
docs.text: This page is the map of the section: what a resource is, and which page shows what.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A resource is a number of identical units: packers, packing benches, checkout lanes, loading bays. A task asks for one unit, waits in the resource's queue while every unit is busy, holds the unit while it works, and gives it back. How many units there are is the resource's capacity, and it can change while the run goes on, as when packers go on a break.

docs.title: Pages in This Section
docs.text:
• Units and Queues: declare a resource, order its queue, limit the line, read who holds a unit, and see what a change of capacity does.
  • Priority and Preemption: rank waiting requests by task priority or an expression, let a more urgent request take a unit from a less urgent task, and fail a resource at random. A lower priority value is more urgent.
  • Several Resources: hold several resources in one task, and the order in which tasks acquire them.
  • Custom Resource Types: change how a resource grants units with your own class.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Pick the page by the job:

To do this Read Give a task a resource and set how many units there are Units and Queues Let an order give up waiting, or turn it away from a long line Tasks and Queue Limit Serve urgent work first, or let it take a unit Priority and Preemption Hold a picker and a bench together Several Resources Take packers off the floor for a time Units and Queues Grant units by a rule of your own Custom Resource Types

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: A resource keeps a line of waiting requests and a list of the requests that hold a unit, as SimPy's Resource does, and follows its capacity in the registry. How It Works on Units and Queues describes the grant. Amounts and items that tasks take and add, rather than hold, are Stores and Containers.

docs.title: Custom Resource Types
docs.text: A resource can grant its units by a rule of your own. This page shows how to write one.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: Some shops grant their units by a rule of their own, such as sharing a packer between customer classes by weight. A custom resource type replaces the rule by which a resource grants its units, and keeps the capacity that follows the registry.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
To change how a resource grants units, subclass ResourceBase and name the class in type. ResourceBase is built on the hooks of SimPy's BaseResource, as a subclass of SimPy's Resource is. A subclass can change these:

  • Override _do_put(request) to decide when a request is granted, and _do_get(release) to decide what a release gives back. An override calls the base method, which wakes when_busy() and when_idle(), so a breakdown that counts busy time still works.
  • Set PutQueue to the class of the waiting line. It can be SimPy's SortedQueue, written staticmethod(functools.partial(SortedQueue, maxlen=2)). On a store or container, a type that sets its own queues refuses get_queue and put_queue.
  • Set request to BoundClass(MyRequest), for a request class that subclasses DynamicResourceRequest, or set release the same way, for a release class that subclasses DynamicRelease. Both base classes are in desflow.resources. A request or release class calls the base constructor, which publishes the on_change reading.

This resource keeps how long each request waited:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/resources_custom.yaml:declare
resources:
  # A subclass of ResourceBase that keeps how long each request waited
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, type: !python shop_logic.LoggedPackers}

The class is in shop_logic.py, beside the blueprint:

docs/snippets/yaml/shop_logic.py:logged-packers
class LoggedPackers(ResourceBase):
    """A resource that keeps how long each request waited before it was granted."""

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.waits = []

    def _do_put(self, request):
        super()._do_put(request)
        if request.triggered:  # the request was granted just now
            self.waits.append(self.env.now - request.time)
docs/snippets/pages/custom_resources.py:builder
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0)
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, type=LoggedPackers)

The class is the one the Low-level tab shows.

docs/snippets/pages/custom_resources.py:class
class LoggedPackers(ResourceBase):
    """A resource that keeps how long each request waited before it was granted."""

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.waits = []

    def _do_put(self, request):
        super()._do_put(request)
        if request.triggered:  # the request was granted just now
            self.waits.append(self.env.now - request.time)
docs/snippets/pages/custom_resources.py:low-level
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop", resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)}
    )
)
packers = LoggedPackers(env, "Shop", "packers")


def order(env):
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        yield env.timeout(2.0)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: DynamicResource is ResourceBase with nothing changed. The constructor is DynamicResource's, because the resource reads its capacity from the registry. A subclass that defines __init__ therefore takes *args, **kwargs and passes them on. A PutQueue of your own sets its own order and length, so it takes no queue_limit. The tests run each of these beside the same SimPy subclass in all three APIs.

docs.title: Priority and Preemption
docs.text: This page covers three features of a resource. Task priority ranks the waiting requests: a lower priority value is served first. Preemption lets a request take a unit from a task whose priority value is higher than its own. A breakdown takes every unit away until a repair.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: In a shop, some work cannot wait its turn. An express order goes before regular ones, an urgent job takes a packer from a routine one, and a machine breaks down and must be repaired. Priority orders the waiting line, preemption lets an urgent task take a unit that is in use, and a breakdown takes a resource out of service for a time.

docs.title: Task Priority
docs.text:
Under queue: priority, waiting requests are served by priority, not in the order they arrived. A lower priority value is served first, and a task with no priority ranks 0, as a SimPy PriorityRequest does. Requests with equal priorities are served first in, first out, as in SimPy's PriorityResource. A task's priority can be:

  • a number, the same for every run of the task;
  • an expression, read when the task joins the queue, such as attr.tier for the entity's attribute tier, or payload.<field> for the previous task's payload;
  • in the builder, a function of the task id and the entity's attributes.

A priority cannot read the task's own payload, because the payload does not exist yet when the request joins the queue. For a rule that ranks by an expression of the run, see Rank the Line by an Expression.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/resources.yaml:priority
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # A number, or an expression read when the order joins the queue
    priority: attr.tier
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:priority
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority")
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, attributes={"tier": 2})
)


# Each order's own priority, from its attributes, when it joins the queue;
# a number or an expression such as "attr.tier" works too
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=lambda task_id, attributes: attributes["tier"],
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

A low-level process passes the priority to the request: packers.request(priority=entity.attributes["tier"]), as the queue-order example above does. A request with no priority has priority 0. A resource whose queue is fifo or lifo ignores it.

A priority on a task whose resource does not have queue: priority is refused when the blueprint loads, or when run() starts. A priority that is NaN or text fails the task, with a message that names the task and the value. Priorities shows what priority does to waits.

docs.title: Preemption
docs.text:
On a resource with preempt: true, which needs queue: priority, a request does not always wait for a unit to come free. When every unit is busy, it takes a unit from a task with a higher priority value, as SimPy's PreemptiveResource does. That task is preempted: it loses the unit before its service ends. The task with the highest priority value loses it, and only when that value is higher than the new request's. Among tasks with equal values, the one that asked last loses it. A task with the same priority as the new request keeps its unit. A task with preempt: false never takes a unit this way. Look at an express request that arrives while both packers serve regular orders:

The request of a preempted task is marked as preempted. If the unit belonged to a flow that has ended, the preemption fails the flow that asked, as SimPy's RuntimeError does. A seize unit is asked for again under resume and restart. The preempted task publishes preempted with the resource's name, the key of the entity that took the unit (preempted_by) and the time the task was granted the unit (usage_since). It then follows its on_interrupt: resume, restart or abandon, and on_interrupt_run or on_interrupt_next where the task names one (Interrupts, and the tutorial Interruptions). The interruptions example lets express orders preempt regular ones:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/interruptions.yaml:packers
# A lower priority value takes the packer from a higher one.
packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority, preempt: true}
examples/yaml/interruptions.yaml:pack
tasks:
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: attr.priority
    # A preempted order queues again and serves what it had left; an interrupted one
    # goes on with its packer.
    on_interrupt: resume
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    attributes: [priority]
examples/builder/interruptions_example.py:packers
# A lower priority value takes the packer from a higher one
.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority", preempt=True)
examples/builder/interruptions_example.py:pack
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority="attr.priority",
    # A preempted order queues again and serves what it had left; an interrupted one
    # goes on with its packer
    on_interrupt="resume",
)
def pack(task_id, context, entity):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed", "priority": entity.attributes["priority"]}
examples/low-level/interruptions_example.py:pack
def pack(env, sampler, shop, key, priority, task_id):
    """Packs one order; a preemption sends it back to the queue with the packing
    time it had left, and an interrupt keeps its packer, as `on_interrupt` does."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack", instance=task_id)

    env.stats.flow_started(key.rsplit("-", 1)[0])  # the order enters the shop
    publish(
        {"path_id": path_id, "sim_id": "Shop", "service": "packing", "status": "queued"}
    )
    env.stats.task_queued("pack", task_id)
    remaining, started = None, False
    shop["packing"].append(env.active_process)
    shop["keys"][env.active_process] = key
    request = None
    while True:
        if request is None:
            request = shop["packers"].request(priority=priority)
        since = None
        try:
            if not request.processed:
                yield request
            if not started:
                started = True
                publish(
                    {
                        "path_id": path_id,
                        "sim_id": "Shop",
                        "service": "packing",
                        "status": "started",
                    }
                )
                env.stats.task_started("pack", task_id)
            else:
                publish(
                    {
                        "path_id": path_id,
                        "sim_id": "Shop",
                        "service": "packing",
                        "status": "resumed",
                    }
                )
                env.stats.task_resumed("pack", task_id)
            if remaining is None:
                remaining = sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id))
            since = env.now
            yield env.timeout(remaining)
            payload = {"event_type": "order_packed", "priority": priority}
            publish(payload)
            env.stats.task_finished("pack", task_id)
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            break
        except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
            if since is not None:
                remaining -= env.now - since
            if request not in shop["packers"].users:
                # Queued, or preempted: ask again. A unit still held is kept.
                request.cancel()
                request = None
            if isinstance(interrupt.cause, Preempted):
                value = {
                    "path_id": path_id,
                    "sim_id": "Shop",
                    "service": "packing",
                    "status": "preempted",
                    "resource": "packers",
                    "preempted_by": shop["keys"].get(interrupt.cause.by),
                    "usage_since": interrupt.cause.usage_since,
                }
                publish(value)
                env.stats.task_interrupted("pack", task_id, preempted=True)
            else:
                value = {
                    "path_id": path_id,
                    "sim_id": "Shop",
                    "service": "packing",
                    "status": "interrupted",
                }
                publish({**value, "cause": interrupt.cause})
                env.stats.task_interrupted("pack", task_id)
    shop["packing"].remove(env.active_process)
    del shop["keys"][env.active_process]
    env.stats.flow_finished(key.rsplit("-", 1)[0])

DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers", queue="priority", preempt=True) builds the resource, and request(priority, preempt=True) asks for a unit. The process that loses its unit receives simpy.Interrupt with a SimPy Preempted cause, whose resource, by (the process that took the unit) and usage_since say what happened.

A gift order with preempt: false is served before any regular order that waits. But it waits for the packer to be free, rather than take it from a regular order being packed:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/preemption.yaml:no-preempt
pack_gift:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # Served before any regular order that waits, but waits for the packer to be free
  priority: 0
  preempt: false
  payload: {event_type: gift_packed}

@app.task(..., priority=0, preempt=False) sets the same on a builder task.

request(priority=0, preempt=False) asks for a unit without taking one from a lower-priority order.

docs.title: Rank the Line by an Expression
docs.text:
queue: {rank, ties} ranks the line by an expression instead of a task priority. rank is read as each request is made, in the scope of the task that makes it, and the lowest rank is served first. ties orders equal ranks: fifo, the default, serves the oldest first, and lifo the latest first. It changes the order of the line only, not who preempts. A task priority for a resource that has a rank is refused when the blueprint loads.

preempt on a resource can be a rule, preempt: {when, victim}. when is tested when a request finds no free unit, and the request takes a unit if it holds. victim gives each holder a value, and the holder with the highest value is the one when is tested on, the first granted among equals. Both read request.rank, request.time, request.preempt and request.key, and holder.rank, holder.time, holder.preempt, holder.key, holder.since and holder.attr.<name>. A preempt on a task, a seize or a request mapping is a boolean, a word such as "t" or an expression. A request: {resource, priority, preempt} branch of a wait gives each branch its own rank. A mapping that leaves out priority or preempt is SimPy's request(), with priority 0 and preempt true, and does not take the task's values. A rank or priority that is NaN or text is refused naming the holder and the task.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/priority_rules.yaml:rank
resources:
  packers:
    current_cap: 1
    max_cap: 3
    # The line is ranked by an expression read as each request joins; the lowest rank
    # is served first, and equal ranks are served the latest first
    queue: {rank: attr.tier, ties: lifo}
    # A request takes a unit only from a holder whose rank is 2 or more above its own
    preempt: {when: "holder.rank - request.rank >= 2", victim: holder.rank}

app.add_resource("packers", queue={"rank": "attr.tier", "ties": "lifo"}, preempt={"when": "...", "victim": "..."}) takes the same mappings.

A request carries its priority, and a subclass of ResourceBase decides the order and who is taken (Custom Resource Types).

docs.title: Read Who Holds a Unit
docs.text:
An expression reads the holders and the line of a resource: held(r) lists the requests that hold a unit and waiting(r) the requests in line, each a mapping with entity, rank, time, preempt, key and since. A task that an on_interrupt_next edge reaches reads why it was interrupted as cause.by, cause.usage_since and cause.left; cause.<name> is refused where no on_interrupt_next edge reaches the task.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/priority_rules.yaml:read
payload:
  event_type: packed
  # held(r) lists the units in use and waiting(r) the requests in line, each with
  # its entity, rank and time
  in_use: {gen: expr, expr: "len(held(packers))"}
  waiting: {gen: expr, expr: "len(waiting(packers))"}

A task function reads the resource directly, as Units and Queues shows; a Template takes the same expressions as the YAML tab.

packers.users and packers.queue are the lists, and a request has usage_since.

docs.title: Breakdowns
docs.text:
A breakdown makes a resource fail at random and be repaired. time_to_failure is the time from the start, or from a repair, to the next failure. With clock: calendar, the default, it counts all simulation time from the start or the last repair, busy or idle. With clock: busy it counts only the time a unit is in use, and a seize, a resource:, a wait request and an open unit all count as in use. A custom resource type calls the base _do_put and _do_get, which wake when_busy() and when_idle(), so its busy time counts too. repair is how long a repair takes. While the resource is down its effective capacity is 0 and no request is granted:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/breakdowns.yaml:station
resources:
  station:
    current_cap: 2
    max_cap: 3
    breakdown:
      # Calendar time from a repair, or the start, to the next failure.
      # A failure every 60 s on average (rate 0.0167)
      time_to_failure: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.0167}
      repair: {dist: uniform, low: 5 s, high: 15 s}
      # The orders being packed are interrupted, and follow their on_interrupt.
      work: interrupt
examples/builder/breakdowns_example.py:station
.add_resource("station", current_cap=2, max_cap=3)
.add_breakdown(
    "station",
    # Calendar time from a repair, or the start, to the next failure
    # A failure every 60 s on average (rate 0.0167)
    time_to_failure={"dist": "exponential", "rate": 0.0167},
    repair={"dist": "uniform", "low": 5, "high": 15},
    # The orders being packed are interrupted, and follow their on_interrupt
    work="interrupt",
)
examples/low-level/breakdowns_example.py:station
breakdowns={
    "station": BreakdownConfig(
        # Calendar time from a repair, or the start, to the next failure
        # A failure every 60 s on average (rate 0.0167)
        time_to_failure=DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.0167),
        repair=DistributionConfig(dist="uniform", low=5, high=15),
        # The orders being packed are interrupted
        work="interrupt",
    )
},

Start run_breakdowns(env, station, sampler, work="interrupt") as a SimPy process beside the arrivals. station.fail() and station.repair() put a resource down and back by hand.

A resource can set the clock in the three forms: clock: busy under breakdown in YAML, add_breakdown(clock="busy") in the Builder, and run_breakdowns(clock="busy") or BreakdownConfig(clock="busy") in the Low-level API. Model Breakdowns shows each.

work says what happens to the tasks being served. Under interrupt, the default, each task is interrupted with the cause breakdown and follows its on_interrupt. Under finish, the tasks finish their work. Each failure and repair publishes an event keyed by the resource's name, with status down or repaired and reason: failure. Model Breakdowns checks the downtime of the example, and Interruptions explains on_interrupt.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
SimPy ranks a request by (priority, time, not preempt). So among requests with equal priorities made at the same time, a request that may preempt goes before one with preempt: false. The tests check it, ties included, in all three APIs (SimPy Compatibility).

SimPy's exact rule

SimPy sorts the tasks holding a unit by (priority, request time, may not preempt). The task that sorts last loses its unit, but only when it also sorts after the new request. A task with the same priority asked earlier than the new request, so it sorts before it and keeps its unit. The one exception is a task with the same priority that asked at the same moment, with preempt: false: it sorts after a request that may preempt, and loses its unit.

docs.title: Example: Interruptions
docs.text:

docs.title: Several Resources
docs.text: A task can hold more than one resource at once. This page shows how.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: Some work needs more than one resource at a time: an order needs a picker and a bench, and a patient needs a doctor and a room. A task can hold several resources at once, or keep a unit and hand it to the next task of its flow.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
A task can hold several resources at once: resource: [picker, bench] asks for a picker, then, while it holds the picker, for the bench. The task is served once it holds all of them, and it releases all of them when it finishes. While it waits for the bench, it holds the picker. The units are granted one at a time, never together, so a task can hold some of its resources while it waits for the rest. patience covers the whole acquisition. A plain interrupt keeps the units already held and asks again only for the one it waits for, and on_interrupt: abandon gives every unit back.

A task can also hand a unit to the next task of its flow with keep: the next task holds it from the start and gives it back once it publishes started. An order can therefore keep the picker until it is on the packing bench, as Hand Off to a Resource shows step by step. A task that reneges, whose wait fails with no on_fail, or that has no next task gives it back when it ends. If the unit is preempted while the next task holds it, that task is interrupted and follows its on_interrupt. The unit a task keeps stays with the entity until that next task starts. A child flow started by wait: {task: ...} gives back only the units its own tasks asked for. The competing-resources example does both:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/competing_resources.yaml:tasks
tasks:
  pick:
    service: picking
    resource: picker
    # The picker stays with the order until pack has started.
    keep: [picker]
    payload: {event_type: order_picked}
    next: pack
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: bench
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  wrap:
    service: wrapping
    # Holds the picker, then the bench too: acquired in this order.
    resource: [picker, bench]
    payload: {event_type: gift_wrapped}
examples/builder/competing_resources_example.py:tasks
# The picker stays with the order until pack has started
@app.task(service_id="picking", resource_id="picker", keep=["picker"], next="pack")
def pick(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "order_picked"}


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="bench")
def pack(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


# Holds the picker, then the bench too: acquired in this order
@app.task(service_id="wrapping", resource_id=["picker", "bench"])
def wrap(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "gift_wrapped"}
examples/low-level/competing_resources_example.py:tasks
def pick(shop, key):
    """Picks an order and keeps the picker for pack, which gives it back."""
    env, stats = shop.env, shop.env.stats
    task_id, publish, status, duration = shop.step(key, "pick", "picking")
    stats.flow_started("orders")  # the order enters the shop
    status("queued")
    stats.task_queued("pick", task_id)
    picker = shop.picker.request()
    yield picker
    status("started")
    stats.task_started("pick", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(duration())
    publish({"event_type": "order_picked"})
    stats.task_finished("pick", task_id)
    yield from pack(shop, key, picker)


def pack(shop, key, picker):
    env, stats = shop.env, shop.env.stats
    task_id, publish, status, duration = shop.step(key, "pack", "packing")
    status("queued")
    stats.task_queued("pack", task_id)
    with shop.bench.request() as bench:
        yield bench
        status("started")
        stats.task_started("pack", task_id)
        shop.picker.release(picker)  # the order is on the bench
        yield env.timeout(duration())
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        stats.task_finished("pack", task_id)
    stats.flow_finished("orders")


def wrap(shop, key):
    """Holds the picker, then the bench too: acquired in this order."""
    env, stats = shop.env, shop.env.stats
    task_id, publish, status, duration = shop.step(key, "wrap", "wrapping")
    stats.flow_started("gifts")
    status("queued")
    stats.task_queued("wrap", task_id)
    with shop.picker.request() as picker:
        yield picker
        with shop.bench.request() as bench:
            yield bench
            status("started")
            stats.task_started("wrap", task_id)
            yield env.timeout(duration())
            publish({"event_type": "gift_wrapped"})
            stats.task_finished("wrap", task_id)
    stats.flow_finished("gifts")

In the low-level API several resources are nested requests, and a handoff is a request released by the next process.

docs.title: Hold a Unit Between Steps
docs.text:
seize asks for a unit at the start of a task and keeps it until a release, in this task or a later one of the flow, so the unit is held across steps that name no resource. seize is a resource name, or {resource, priority, preempt, patience}. release frees the oldest unit of a resource that the flow holds from a seize or an open, and does nothing when it holds none. A unit still held when the flow ends stays held, as in SimPy, so a flow writes release before it ends. A unit lost to a preemption is asked for again under resume and restart, and is gone under abandon. release also takes {handle: name} for one opened request and {resource, task, where} for the units that other flows of a task hold. A priority on a seize needs the resource to set queue: priority, as picker does here. The clear task below frees the picker from every rush order that holds it.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/seize_release.yaml:seize
tasks:
  pick:
    service: picking
    # Asks for the picker now, with priority 1 and without taking the unit from
    # another order, and keeps it across the next task
    seize: {resource: picker, priority: 1, preempt: false}
    payload: {event_type: order_picked}
    next: pack
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: bench
    # Gives the picker back once the order is on the bench
    release: picker
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  # Frees the picker from every rush order that still holds it
  clear:
    release: {resource: picker, task: pick, where: attr.rush}
    payload: {event_type: picker_cleared}

@app.task(seize="picker") and @app.task(release="picker") take the same values.

The process holds the request itself: picker = shop.picker.request() and yield picker, then shop.picker.release(picker) when the order is on the bench.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: One order of acquisition. Two tasks that acquire the same two resources in opposite orders can each hold one and wait for ever for the other. desflow loads such a model and logs one WARNING, from the logger desflow.builder.context, that names both tasks. A unit held with seize counts as held. Every task should acquire shared resources in one order. The rule also covers keep handoffs and the request branches of a wait, and a keep for a request branch of a wait is still refused when the model is built (Wait for a Unit, an Item or Room). Competing Resources shows what a partial holding costs.

docs.title: Units and Queues
docs.text: A resource is what an entity must hold while it works, and may have to wait for. This page shows how to declare one, how its queue is ordered, how it hands out units, and what happens when its capacity changes during a run. The class behind it is DynamicResource.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A resource is a number of identical units: packers, packing benches, checkout lanes, loading bays. A task asks for one unit, waits in the resource's queue while every unit is busy, holds the unit while it works, and gives it back. How many units there are is the resource's capacity, and it can change while the run goes on, as when packers go on a break.

docs.title: Declare a Resource
docs.text:
Two whole numbers set the size of a resource, and both may be left out:

  • current_cap is the number of units now. Left out, it is 1, so packers: {} is a resource of one unit, as simpy.Resource(env) is.
  • max_cap is the most units a live change can set. Left out, it equals current_cap.

current_cap: .inf (float("inf") in Python) is a resource with no limit. Every request is granted at once, capacity is published as null and utilization as 0. A capacity or queue_limit below 0, true or a fraction for a whole number is refused, naming the resource. A name used by two of the resources, stores, containers and signals is refused too, because they are one set of names, and so is a name with a dot or a space, which an expression cannot name, or with a character that an expression reads as another, such as µ.

queue_limit sets the most requests that may wait, as Queue Limit describes. run() builds a DynamicResource for each resource the context declares. In the low-level API you build it yourself, after registering the parameters. A resource of one unit needs no registration at all:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/resources.yaml:queue-order
resources:
  # fifo (the default), lifo or priority; priority serves the lowest number first,
  # and equal priorities first in, first out
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority}
docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:declare
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0)
# fifo (the default), lifo or priority
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority")
docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:resource
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # capacity from the registry: 2


def order(env, order_id):
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request  # waits until a unit is free
        yield env.timeout(10.0)  # holds the unit for 10 s
    # leaving the with block releases the unit

packers.request() is an event that happens when a unit is granted, and leaving the with block gives the unit back. A request whose with block is left before it is granted, for example after a timeout, is cancelled and never takes a unit.

docs.title: Queue Order
docs.text:
queue sets the order in which a resource serves the requests waiting for it:

  • fifo, the default: the oldest first;
  • lifo: the newest first;
  • priority: the lowest priority number first, and the oldest first among equal priorities.

Four requests that join while the only unit is busy are served in these orders:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

queue sits beside the capacity: packers: {current_cap: 1, queue: lifo}.

app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, queue="lifo").

docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:queue-order
def served_order(queue):
    """Four requests join while the only bench is busy; returns who is served when."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
        SimParameter(
            sim_id="Shop",
            resources={"benches": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
        )
    )
    bench = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "benches", queue=queue)
    served = []

    def use(name, priority, after=0.0):
        yield env.timeout(after)
        # The priority counts only under the priority order
        with bench.request(priority=priority) as request:
            yield request
            served.append(name)
            yield env.timeout(1.0)

    env.process(use("first", 1))  # takes the bench at once
    for name, priority in [
        ("orders-1", 1),
        ("express-1", 0),
        ("orders-2", 1),
        ("express-2", 0),
    ]:
        env.process(use(name, priority, after=0.1))  # all join while it is busy
    env.run(until=10)
    return served[1:]


for queue in ("fifo", "lifo", "priority"):
    print(f"{queue:<8} {', '.join(served_order(queue))}")

fifo     orders-1, express-1, orders-2, express-2
lifo     express-2, orders-2, express-1, orders-1
priority express-1, express-2, orders-1, orders-2
capacity 2, in use 4

The last line is a capacity drop, which Under Live Changes describes below. The same four requests, drawn:

docs.title: Queue Limit
docs.text:
queue_limit sets the most requests that may wait for a resource. With a limit of 5, a request made while five requests wait already is refused, as SimPy's SortedQueue(maxlen=5) does. Set it with queue_limit: 5 in a blueprint, add_resource(..., queue_limit=5) in the builder, or the same argument of DynamicResource. The refusal comes before a grant or a preemption, so a limit of 0 refuses every request.

A task that is refused balks: it leaves without being served. It gives back the units it holds, publishes balked with the name of the resource, counts as balked and ends its flow. When it balks depends on how it asked:

  • A task whose first resource is the limited one, with no wait before it, balks before it publishes queued.
  • A request branch of a wait, in an any or an all, fails the wait at once, with SimPy's message "Cannot append event. Queue is full.".
  • A request branch that has won its wait and then loses the unit to preemption asks for a unit again. The task balks if the line is full then. It reneges, that is, leaves the line, if its patience runs out while it waits, as for a resource: unit.
  • In the low-level API, request() raises QueueFull (in desflow.resources), a RuntimeError with that message. Your process catches it as it would catch a balk condition.

A request that reneges or is cancelled leaves the line and makes room for the next. A limit can change during a run through the registry path <sim_id>.resources.<name>.queue_limit, set by a scenario step, an on: action or a low-level registry.update. It applies from the next request, a smaller limit removes nobody who waits, and null is no limit. A resource with a PutQueue of its own has no such path. A limit is changed through the path and not by assigning queue_limit, which is read-only. Refuse to Join shows the other way an order balks, by a condition of its own.

In a blueprint, queue_limit sits beside the capacity. packers has the default of one unit, and refuses a fourth waiting request:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/resources_read.yaml:declare
resources:
  # No capacity: one unit. At most 3 requests wait; a fourth is refused.
  packers: {queue_limit: 3}
  # No limit: every request is granted at once
  benches: {current_cap: .inf}

app.add_resource("packers", queue_limit=3) and app.add_resource("benches", current_cap=float("inf")).

DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers", queue_limit=3).

docs.title: Cancel and Release
docs.text:
A task leaves a queue when its patience runs out, when it is interrupted, or under on_interrupt: abandon. It then cancels its request, so the request is never granted later. Once a unit is granted, the task gives it back when it finishes, under on_interrupt: abandon, and when it is preempted (the preempting task has it then). A plain interrupt under resume or restart leaves the unit with the task. In the low-level API these are SimPy's calls:

docs/snippets/pages/resource_cancel.py:cancel
held = packers.request()  # granted at once: the packer was free
waiting = packers.request()  # waits behind it

waiting.cancel()  # leaves the queue at once; it is never granted
held.cancel()  # granted already, so this releases nothing, as in SimPy
assert packers.in_use == 1 and packers.queue == []

released = packers.release(held)  # gives the packer back
assert released.request is held  # the release is an event that holds its request
packers.release(held)  # a second release does nothing

request.cancel() takes a waiting request out of the queue, and does nothing to a granted one. packers.release(request) gives a granted unit back once. Releasing it again, or releasing a request that was never granted, gives nothing back. A release is an event, a DynamicRelease, as SimPy's Release is. Its request is the request it releases (with no request, the oldest unit held). It is triggered as soon as it is made, and the next waiting request is granted one event later, when the release is processed. A with block does both on its way out, as in SimPy.

docs.title: Read the Queue and Users
docs.text:
A resource counts the units held and the requests waiting. In a condition, users.<resource> is how many units are held, and queue.<resource> is how many requests wait. A task can therefore turn an order away when the line is long, or wait until nobody holds a unit. The names are checked when the blueprint loads, as level.<name> is:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/resources_read.yaml:conditions
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # Turn an order away when two are waiting already
    balk: queue.packers >= 2
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  close_up:
    # Wait until nobody holds a packer
    wait: {condition: users.packers < 1}
    payload: {event_type: packers_idle}

context.get_resource("packers") returns the running DynamicResource. Its count is the number of units held. users lists the requests that hold them, in the order of their grants. queue lists the waiting requests in the order they will be served, so queue[0] is served next. A request has usage_since, the time it was granted its unit, and proc, the process that made it. A task's process has the task's name.

docs/snippets/pages/resource_read.py:builder
def look(context):
    """A process of the model: reads the packers every 30 seconds."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(30)
        held = [
            request.proc.name for request in packers.users
        ]  # the tasks holding a unit
        seen.append((packers.count, len(packers.queue), held))


app.add_process(look)
docs/snippets/pages/resource_read.py:low-level
requests = [packers.request() for _ in range(4)]  # two are granted, two wait

assert packers.count == len(packers.users) == 2  # the units held now
assert packers.users == requests[:2]  # the granted requests, in the order of the grants
assert len(packers.queue) == 2  # the requests waiting
assert packers.queue[0] is requests[2]  # the next to be served
assert packers.users[0].usage_since == 0.0  # when this request was granted its unit

count is the same as in_use, SimPy's name for it. queue is a list of the waiting requests, in service order.

docs.title: Make a Family of Resources
docs.text:
A resource with family: true is a family. Each member is an ordinary resource named after the family and its key in brackets, such as desk[3] or desk['a.b']. members makes that many when the run starts, and a member not made yet is made at its first use. A capacity written as text is read once, when the member is made, in the scope of the entity that makes it; a family with members reads the run, so attr. is refused there. A family's name alone in a place that wants a name is refused when the blueprint loads, and so is a declared name that starts with the family's name and a bracket. A registry path takes a bracketed part as one part, such as S.resources.desk['a.b'].current_cap. A scenario step or an on: action on a member's path is refused when the member has no such attribute, or when the family can never have the member: a family with members: 2 makes only desk[0] and desk[1], unless a task names the family with a key. It ends the run with KeyError when a task makes the member at its first use and it is not made yet at the step's time. A task picks a member with {of: desk, key: ...} or {of: desk, lowest: ...} (Pick a Member of a Family).

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/families.yaml:desks
resources:
  # Three desks, desk[0] to desk[2], each an ordinary resource of one unit
  desk: {family: true, members: 3, current_cap: 1}

app.add_resource("desk", family=True, members=3, current_cap=1) declares the same family.

A family is a dictionary of resources that your code keeps, one DynamicResource for each key.

docs.title: Registry Paths and Readings
docs.text:
Each resource has three registry paths, <sim_id>.resources.<name>.current_cap, .max_cap and .queue_limit (None when unset), which a scenario, an ingress message or a process can change. A live write is checked by the path's rule. compile_parameters() returns a ResourceConfig for a resource, which holds all three. Live Parameters explains how. A resource that breaks down adds <sim_id>.breakdown.<name>.time_to_failure and .repair, its two distributions.

With statistics at the minimal level or above, each resource publishes four readings, such as Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization:

  • capacity: the number of units, or null for a resource with no limit.
  • in_use: the units held by tasks.
  • queue_length: the requests waiting.
  • utilization: the units in use as a percentage of the capacity, or 0 for a resource with no limit.

A resource that breaks down adds down, which is 1 while it is down. Statistics lists what the other levels add, among them downtime and failures.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A DynamicResource grants units the way SimPy's Resource does, with two lists. queue holds the waiting requests, ranked by the queue order and then by a sequence number, so requests that rank the same are served in the order they arrived. users holds the granted requests. A request is granted when it is made if a unit is free and nothing waits ahead of it. Otherwise it waits, and each release grants the head of the queue when its release event is processed, one event later, as SimPy's Release does:

Because each step is the one SimPy takes, two events at the same simulation time are granted in SimPy's order. A patience whose event comes before the grant at the same instant reneges, and this holds on a request branch of a wait too. This is SimPy's reneging pattern, result = yield request | env.timeout(patience) with request not in result when the patience wins. in_use counts users: it goes up when a request is granted and down when a unit is released.

A waiting request leaves the queue at once when it is cancelled. A with block cancels it when the block is left before the grant, and request.cancel() does the same by hand. packers.release(request) gives a granted unit back. Cancelling a granted request releases nothing, and releasing a request twice, or one never granted, gives nothing back, as in SimPy. Every release still tries the head of the queue when its release event is processed, as SimPy's does: when a request that reneged was the head, the request behind it may then be granted or preempt a user.

SimPy and desflow. SimPy's Resource serves requests in the order they arrive, and PriorityResource by priority. Both take their capacity when they are created and keep it: capacity has no setter, so assigning a new one raises AttributeError (SimPy 4.1). desflow builds its own resource, so that the capacity can follow the registry and the queue order can be chosen. The request() call and the with block are SimPy's, so code written for SimPy works unchanged. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
A change to current_cap takes effect at once, without stopping any work:

  • Growing grants waiting requests at once, up to the new capacity.
  • Shrinking stops nothing. The units still busy above the new capacity are owed: each one given back brings the busy count down, and no waiting task starts until the busy count is within the new capacity.
  • Growing again before the owed units are given back cancels them first, so only the rest of the rise grants waiting requests.
  • A current_cap outside 0 to max_cap is clamped to that range, with a warning.
  • Lowering max_cap lowers the capacity with it. A current_cap above the new max_cap is stored as max_cap, with a warning.
  • During a repair the capacity is 0 and current_cap keeps the planned value. A change to it sets the capacity the resource returns to and does not end the repair.

The example below takes three of five packers off the floor while four orders are being packed: the capacity is 2 at once, and in_use stays 4 until two orders finish. The animation steps through it:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A scenario step makes the same change at a set time: scenario: [{at: 5, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 2}]. Live Parameters explains the steps.

app.add_scenario([{"at": 5, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2}]) makes the same change at a set time.

docs/snippets/pages/resources.py:shrink
def capacity_drop(env):
    """Takes 3 of 5 packers off the floor at t=5 s. Orders being packed are not stopped."""
    env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 5)
    yield env.timeout(5.0)
    env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)
    yield env.timeout(0.1)  # the resource applies the change in its own process
    print(f"capacity {packers.capacity}, in use {packers.in_use}")

Until the owed units finish, in_use is above capacity, and the utilization reading is above 100%.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Utilisation decides waits. A resource whose load is at or above its capacity has a queue that grows for as long as the run lasts. Queues and Capacity shows how to work it out, and Queueing Basics explains utilisation.
  • Priority needs queue: priority. A task priority on a resource of another order, or on one with a rank, is a load error, while a low-level request's priority is ignored under fifo and lifo.
  • Priority can starve. Under priority, a request with a high number is served only when no lower number is waiting. If the low numbers alone keep the resource busy, it is never served.
  • One order of acquisition. A model whose tasks acquire two resources in opposite orders loads and logs one WARNING. Several Resources explains why.
  • A shrink never stops work. Lowering current_cap lets busy units finish. Work in progress stops only for an interrupt, a preemption or a breakdown: Interruptions, and Model Breakdowns for a machine that fails.
  • A preempted task queues again. With resume or restart it joins the back of its priority among the waiting requests, as a new SimPy request does. The time it waited before counts in its wait.

Amounts and items that tasks take and add, rather than hold, are Stores and Containers.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: A run publishes records, and it can also measure itself. One run gives one sample, many runs give an interval, and several designs give a comparison. The pages of this section go from one run to a whole study.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
• Statistics are collected during one run: how busy each resource was, how long tasks waited, how many entities finished. A warm-up period can be left out.
  • Replications run the same model with many seeds and give each statistic a mean and a 95% interval.
  • Experiments run replications of several designs, compare the designs seed by seed, check them against bounds and observed values, and write the results and a report to files.

docs.title: Pages in This Section
docs.text:
• Built-in Statistics: how to switch the statistics on, what each level publishes and costs, how each value is computed, and how to add readings of your own.
  • Replications: how to run replications from the command line and from Python, what they return and send to the sinks, and how the seeds and intervals are made.
  • Experiments: the experiment file, the Python call and every setting.
  • Experiment Results: what an experiment compares, checks and writes, and its report.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
• For one run, switch the statistics on with stats in YAML or with_stats in the builder.
  • For an interval, run replications with desflow run --replications.
  • To compare designs, run an experiment with desflow experiment.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Each layer uses the one below it. The statistics measure one run while it goes on. Replications build the model again for each seed, run it unpaced with no ingress and no egress, read the statistics at the end of each run, and give a Student t interval over the runs. An experiment runs replications for each design and compares the designs seed by seed.

docs.title: Experiment Results
docs.text:
This page shows what an experiment compares, checks and writes: the comparison of designs, the checks, the observed values, the files and the report.

The tutorial page Parameter Sweeps teaches these features step by step.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: An experiment gives the numbers that answer a question about the shop: which design keeps the wait under a target, how much one design differs from another, and whether the model agrees with values measured in the real shop. It writes them to files and a report.

docs.title: Compare Designs
docs.text: For each measure and each sweep point, a compare pair gives three things: the variant's value minus the baseline's in each replication, the mean of those differences, and the mean's Student t half-width. An interval that does not contain 0 says the designs differ at that confidence level.

docs.title: Check Results
docs.text:
A check bounds one measure of one variant, or of every variant when variant is left out:

  • max and min: the bound, or both for a range.
  • on: interval, the default, compares the far end of the interval with the bound: the upper end with max and the lower end with min. A mean below the bound only by chance does not pass.
  • on: mean compares the mean, for a quick look, not a decision.

A check whose measure is not in measures is refused. The experiment writes every file before it reports a failed check, so the report shows what failed.

docs.title: Compare With Observed Values
docs.text:
observed names a CSV of values measured in the real system, with the columns measure, value, unit, population and horizon. Each row is placed beside the simulated interval of variant (the first variant when it is not given), and the report says whether the value lies inside it. That interval is for a mean, so one observed period can lie outside it while the model is right, as Checking and Validating explains. A value means something only beside a simulated value of the same kind, so the experiment refuses a row whose unit, population or horizon differs from the measure's:

Statistic Unit Population wait_* of a task, recorded when an instance starts work s started instances service_* of a task, recorded when an instance finishes s finished instances utilization and utilization_avg percent end of run and time average downtime of a resource s sum over the horizon other *_avg, such as queue_length_avg count, or amount for a container time average task and flow counts, such as finished and started count count over the horizon in_system of a flow and in_progress of a task count end of run other readings, such as queue_length count, or amount for a container end of run

The horizon is until minus the warm-up, in seconds or a duration such as 57 min. The horizon describes a run that ends at until, so with a stop or a drain, the observed values must cover the same entities as the simulated ones. The observed comparison checks the model's output against the real system's. It does not fit an input distribution, which Input Fitting covers.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
An experiment writes six files to its output folder:

File Holds experiment.json the settings, the question, assumptions, inputs and limits; the model's source and its SHA-256, its sim id and its compiled parameters; desflow, SimPy, NumPy and Python versions; each design's registry values, seeds and the streams each run drew from; the counts' names; the observed comparison results.csv one row per design, replication and statistic: design, variant, a column per swept path, replication, seed, statistic, kind (measure or count), unit, population and value summary.csv one row per design and statistic: unit, population, n, mean, half_width, low, high and level comparisons.csv one row per compared pair, sweep point and measure: both means, difference, half_width, low, high, and the streams in streams_both, streams_baseline_only and streams_variant_only checks.csv one row per check, design and bound: on, bound, limit, the checked value and passed report.md the report, built from the five files above

docs.title: Read the Report
docs.text:
report.md has the sections below, and a section with nothing to report says so:

  • Question, Model and Assumptions.
  • Inputs and Provenance: every distribution of the model with its parameters, and its provenance from inputs or "not stated".
  • Run Settings.
  • Counts: the mean of each count the statistics publish, such as finished orders, for each design.
  • Results, with the population each measure is taken over.
  • Comparisons, Checks, Observed Comparison and Limits.
  • Missing Inputs: what the experiment does not state, such as an input without a provenance. The report names it rather than filling it in.

The middle of the example's report follows. It is for the example's own shop, not the busy hour of the tutorials:

## Results

Each measure's mean over the replications, with its 95% confidence interval.

| Design | Measure | Population | Mean | Half-width | Interval | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| two | `tasks.pack.wait_mean` | started instances | 4.524 | 0.5731 | 3.951 to 5.097 | 20 |
| two | `resources.packers.utilization_avg` | time average | 80.14 | 1.104 | 79.04 to 81.25 | 20 |
| three | `tasks.pack.wait_mean` | started instances | 0.534 | 0.0476 | 0.4864 to 0.5816 | 20 |
| three | `resources.packers.utilization_avg` | time average | 53.46 | 0.7236 | 52.73 to 54.18 | 20 |

## Comparisons

Each difference is the variant's value minus the baseline's, seed by seed, with the confidence interval of the mean difference.

| Baseline | Variant | Measure | Difference | Half-width | Interval | Random streams |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| two | three | `tasks.pack.wait_mean` | -3.99 | 0.5316 | -4.521 to -3.458 | 2 shared |
| two | three | `resources.packers.utilization_avg` | -26.69 | 0.39 | -27.08 to -26.3 | 2 shared |

## Checks

Checks passed: 1 of 1.

| Design | Measure | Checked | Bound | Value | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| three | `tasks.pack.wait_mean` | the upper end | max 2 | 0.5816 | passed |

## Observed Comparison

| Design | Measure | Observed | Unit | Simulated interval | Inside |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| two | `tasks.pack.wait_mean` | 4.6 | s | 3.951 to 5.097 | yes |

desflow report results/packers builds the report again from the other five files, such as after editing experiment.json by hand.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Each replication of each design gives one row per statistic in results.csv, and summary.csv holds each design's mean and interval over its replications. A comparison pairs the replications of two designs that ran with the same seed, so the two runs of a pair draw the same times wherever they share a random stream. comparisons.csv holds the mean difference and its interval, and lists the streams both designs drew from and those only one did. The checks and the observed comparison read these intervals. report.md is built from the other five files. The experiment writes every file before it reports a failed check, so the report shows what failed.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text: An experiment answers a question with many runs rather than one. It runs several designs of a model, each with replications. It compares the designs seed by seed, checks them against bounds, and places them beside values observed in the real system. It writes its results and a report to files. This page describes the experiment file, the Python call and every setting. Experiment Results describes the files an experiment writes and its report. It runs on one machine and needs no server.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A design is the model with some registry values changed before the clock starts: a variant, or a variant at one point of a sweep. An experiment runs every design with the same number of replications, reads the built-in statistics at the end of each run, and summarises each with a mean and a 95% interval. Comparing Designs and Parameter Sweeps use one on the shop.

docs.title: Reading the Results
docs.text: The next page, Experiment Results, shows how to compare designs, check results against bounds, place observed values beside them, and read the files and the report.

docs.title: Write an Experiment
docs.text:
An experiment names its model, how long and how often to run it, what to measure, the designs and what to compare and check. In a file:

examples/yaml/experiment.yaml
# An experiment in YAML: does a third packer keep the mean wait under 2 seconds?
#
# The YAML version of experiment_example.py, which --api builder downloads. The model is
# experiment_shop.yaml. The experiment runs one hour of it 20 times with two packers
# and 20 times with three, with the same seeds, after a 3-minute warm-up. It
# compares the two designs seed by seed, checks the three-packer design against a
# 2-second bound, and compares the two-packer design with the mean wait observed in
# the real shop. It writes its artifacts and report to results/packers, and exits 1
# if the check fails.
#
# Needs no containers.
# Run it with: desflow experiment experiment.yaml

experiment: packers

question: Does a third packer keep the mean wait under 2 seconds?

model: experiment_shop.yaml

assumptions:
  - Orders arrive at random, at a steady rate, through the hour.
  - Every packer works at the same speed.

inputs: {Shop.service.packing: 40 packing times measured at the bench}

until: 1 h

warmup: 3 min

replications: 20

seed: 42

# Both designs run with the same 20 seeds, so they are compared seed by seed
pairing: common

measures: [tasks.pack.wait_mean, resources.packers.utilization_avg]

variants:
  two: {}
  three: {Shop.resources.packers.current_cap: 3}

compare:
  - {baseline: two, variant: three}

checks:
  # The upper end of the interval must be under 2 seconds
  - {measure: tasks.pack.wait_mean, variant: three, max: 2}

observed:
  # The mean wait measured in the real shop, which has two packers
  file: ../observed_waits.csv
  variant: two

limits: [One hour of steady demand; the rest of the day is not modelled.]

output: results/packers

In Python the same settings are a mapping, and the model is a blueprint path, a builder factory or a LowLevelModel. The table lists every setting:

Setting What it sets Default experiment the experiment's name, one folder name with no / or \, because the files go to results/<experiment> required question the question the experiment answers, the report's first section not stated model a blueprint path, such as experiment_shop.yaml; to build the model in code instead, !python module.function, a function returning a new SimulationContext, or {function: !python module.function, sim_id: Shop}, a low-level function required assumptions sentences the report lists none inputs each distribution's registry path, such as Shop.service.packing, and where its values came from none until where each run's arrivals stop, in seconds or a duration such as 8 h; the run ends there unless stop ends it earlier or drain runs on required stop ends each run when it happens: {signal: name} or {condition: "..."}; for a low-level model, given in Python, a function of the environment that returns the event a blueprint's run.stop drain at until, stop the arrivals and run on until the model is empty: true, or {limit: 1 h}; a low-level model is drained when its function returns its arrival processes a blueprint's run.drain warmup each run's warm-up the model's own replications runs of each design, 2 or more required seed the seed every run's seed is spawned from: a whole number of 0 or more, not true required level the confidence level of every interval 0.95 pairing common or independent common measures the statistics to summarise, such as tasks.pack.wait_mean; a name given twice counts once required variants each variant's name and the registry values it sets {base: {}} sweep registry paths and the values each takes none compare pairs of variants, {baseline: ..., variant: ...} none checks bounds on measures, {measure, variant, max, min, on}, with min not above max none observed {file: ..., variant: ...}, values measured in the real system none limits sentences the report lists none output the folder the files are written to results/<experiment> workers how many runs go at once, each in its own process 1

A key the experiment does not know is refused with its line, as in a blueprint. In a file, the paths of the model, the observed file and output are read from the experiment file's folder. In a Python mapping, they are read from the working directory.

docs.title: Run It
docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level 
desflow experiment experiment.yaml

--output writes the files to another folder. The command exits with status 1 when a check fails, after writing every file, and with status 2 when the experiment is invalid.

docs/snippets/pages/experiments.py:run
EXPERIMENT = {
    "experiment": "packers",
    "model": shop,  # a blueprint path, a builder factory or a LowLevelModel
    "until": "1 h",
    "warmup": "3 min",
    "replications": 10,
    "seed": 42,
    "measures": ["tasks.pack.wait_mean"],
    "variants": {"two": {}, "three": {"Shop.resources.packers.current_cap": 3}},
    # A sweep would run every variant at each rate, an order every 2.86, 2.5 or
    # 2.22 seconds on average: 6 designs
    # "sweep": {"Shop.arrival.orders.rate": [0.35, 0.4, 0.45]},
    "compare": [{"baseline": "two", "variant": "three"}],
    "checks": [{"measure": "tasks.pack.wait_mean", "variant": "two", "max": 2}],
}
try:
    result = run_experiment(EXPERIMENT)  # writes results/packers, then checks
except CheckFailed as failed:
    result = failed.result  # every file is written before it is raised
    print(failed)

run_experiment takes an experiment file, a mapping or an ExperimentSpec, and returns an ExperimentResult. With raise_on_failure=False a failed check raises nothing, and result.failed lists it. output= writes the files to another folder.

The same call takes LowLevelModel(model, sim_id="Shop") as the model. Here model is a function that builds the shop from an environment and a sampler, as the example shows.

The result holds every row the files hold:

docs/snippets/pages/experiments.py:read
for row in result.summary:  # one row per design and statistic, counts included
    print(row["design"], row["statistic"], row["mean"], row["half_width"])
for row in result.comparisons:  # the variant minus the baseline, seed by seed
    print(row["measure"], row["difference"], row["half_width"])
print([row["design"] for row in result.failed])  # the failed checks
print(result.output / "report.md")

docs.title: Variants and Sweeps
docs.text:
Each variant sets registry paths before the clock starts, as a live update would. Paths are set in the order the variant lists them, so a variant that lowers max_cap below the model's current_cap sets current_cap first. The experiment stops before anything runs, with an error that names the variant's line, when a variant sets:

  • a path the model does not have;
  • a value the registry refuses, or lowers to its limit, such as a capacity above max_cap.

A sweep runs every variant at every combination of its paths' values. So one variant and one swept path with three values give three designs: a one-factor sensitivity experiment, which changes one input to see how much the answer changes. A path is set by a variant or by the sweep, not both. A design's name is its variant followed by its swept values, such as three Shop.arrival.orders.rate=0.5 (an order every 2 seconds on average).

docs.title: Pairing and Random Streams
docs.text:
With pairing: common, every design runs with the same seeds. A design's replication 3 and another design's replication 3 then meet the same arrivals and service times, so most of the random variation cancels in their difference (Comparing Designs). With pairing: independent, each design's seeds are spawned from a seed of its own, and compare is refused.

The same seeds pair two runs only where both draw from the same random streams. Each distribution has a stream of its own, named by its registry path without the sim id, such as service.packing. The experiment records the streams each run drew from, and each comparison lists the streams both designs used and any that only one used. A stream only one design uses, such as a gift-wrap step only one design has, is not paired.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Before running. The experiment builds the model once without running it, records its compiled parameters, and refuses an inputs path that is not a distribution. It then builds each design the same way, so a bad registry path or value fails before any run. It reads the observed file and refuses a row that does not match its measure.

Runs. Each design runs its replications as Replications describes: each run builds the model again, unpaced, with no ingress and no egress, and reads the statistics at its end. The statistics level is the lowest that publishes every measure, and at least basic, so the counts are there. A low-level model's parameters are put back after each replication, so the next replication never starts from a variant's value or a live change left by the one before.

Intervals. Every interval, of a design's mean and of a difference, is the Student t interval of Replications, at the experiment's level.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Finite designs only. Variants and sweeps list their values. Latin hypercube designs, sampling uncertain inputs and searching for the best design are not part of an experiment.
  • No event records. An experiment writes its files and sends nothing to the model's sinks. Run one design with one seed to see its records.
  • End of a run. A run ends at until, unless stop ends it earlier or drain runs it on until the model is empty. A blueprint's own run.stop and run.drain apply when the experiment does not set them. Entities still in the model at the end are not finished, so a count of finished entities leaves them out. The Counts section of the report (Read the Report) shows what each design started, finished and left.
  • Observed values are outputs. The observed comparison is a check of the model's output against the real system's for the question asked. It does not fit inputs, and one value inside an interval does not make a model valid for every question.
  • One machine. workers runs replications in parallel processes on one machine. There is no distributed or server executor.

docs.title: Example: An Experiment
docs.text:
The experiment example is the experiment above. It runs one hour of the shop with two packers and with three, 20 replications of each with the same seeds. It makes one comparison and one check, and places the mean wait observed in the real shop beside the result. Its shop is not the busy hour of the tutorials: an order arrives every 2.5 seconds on average and packing takes 4 seconds on average, so its waits differ from theirs. The example needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page Comparing Designs teaches these features step by step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get experiment --api yaml
cd experiment/yaml

# 3. Find the bottleneck, with no run
desflow explain experiment_shop.yaml

# 4. Run it
desflow experiment experiment.yaml

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get experiment --api yaml
cd experiment/yaml

# 3. Find the bottleneck, with no run
desflow explain experiment_shop.yaml

# 4. Run it
desflow experiment experiment.yaml

The model is experiment_shop.yaml, beside the experiment file:

examples/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml
# The model of the experiment in experiment.yaml: one hour of the shop.
#
# The YAML version of the shop function in experiment_example.py, which --api builder
# downloads. Two packers, orders every 2.5 seconds on average and a packing time of 4
# seconds on average. It has no sinks and no statistics level: the experiment runs it
# without sinks and keeps the statistics its measures need.
#
# Needs no containers.
# Run the experiment with: desflow experiment experiment.yaml

simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  # The experiment gives each run its own seed; 42 is for a run on its own.
  random_seed: 42

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 2, max_cap: 4}

services:
  # A mean of 4 seconds (shape times scale).
  packing: {dist: gamma, shape: 4, scale: 1}

arrivals:
  # An order every 2.5 s on average (rate 0.4)
