docs.title: Replications
docs.text: One run of a model is one sample: another seed draws other times and gives other values. Replications run the same model with many seeds and summarise each built-in statistic with a mean and a 95% interval. This page shows how to run them from the command line and from Python, in each of the three ways to write a model, what they return and send to the sinks, and how the seeds and intervals are made.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A replication is one run of the model with a seed of its own. N replications give N independent values of each built-in statistic, such as the mean wait of a task. Their mean is the estimate, and the half-width of its 95% interval says how precise it is: with 95% confidence, the true value lies within the mean plus or minus the half-width. Trusting Results shows on the shop why one run is not an answer and how to choose the number of replications.

docs.title: Run Replications
docs.text:
Give the model, the number of replications, the seed they are spawned from and the time the arrivals stop:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
desflow run replications.yaml --replications 20 --measure tasks.pack.wait_mean

--seed overrides simulation.random_seed, and --until overrides run.until, as for one run. --level sets the confidence level (0.95 when it is not given), --workers sets how many replications run at once, each in its own process, and --drain drains every replication, as run.drain: true does. The command prints the summary, the seed of each replication and the command that repeats one. The blueprint's own warmup applies to every replication:

examples/yaml/replications.yaml:seed
# The replications' seeds are spawned from this one; --seed overrides it
random_seed: 42
warmup: 3 min
docs/snippets/pages/replications.py:builder
# shop is a function returning a new SimulationContext, called once per run
result = replicate(shop, 3, seed=42, until="1 h", warmup="3 min", measures=MEASURES)

shop is a function with no arguments that returns a new SimulationContext, such as the example's, because each replication starts from a new context. A blueprint path works here too.

docs/snippets/pages/replications.py:low-level
def model(env, sampler):
    """Builds the shop in the environment it is given, drawing from sampler."""
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.process(orders(env, sampler, DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")))


def low_level():
    shop = LowLevelModel(model, sim_id="Shop")
    return replicate(shop, 3, seed=42, until=3600, warmup=180, measures=MEASURES)

LowLevelModel takes a function that builds the model, given an environment and a sampler, and the sim_id that the model's statistics are published under. The function registers the parameters, builds the resources and starts the processes. It sets up no statistics, because replicate does, and it sets up no sinks. Its tasks report their steps to env.stats, as Statistics shows.

replicate takes these options:

Option What it sets Default n how many replications, 2 or more seed the seed the replications' seeds are spawned from, a whole number of 0 or more and not true; None draws one and logs it until where each replication's arrivals stop, in seconds or a duration such as "1 h"; the replication ends there unless stop ends it earlier or drain runs on a blueprint's run.until stop ends each replication when it happens, as for run(): {"signal": name}, a signal's name, or {"condition": "..."}; for a LowLevelModel, a function of the environment that returns the event a blueprint's run.stop drain at until, stop the arrivals and run each replication on until no entity is left: True, or {"limit": "1 h"}; a LowLevelModel is drained when its function returns its arrival processes and reports its entities with env.stats.flow_started and flow_finished a blueprint's run.drain warmup the end of each replication's warm-up the model's own measures the statistics to summarise every statistic the run publishes, at least up to typical level the confidence level of the half-widths 0.95 workers how many replications run at once, each in its own process 1 overrides registry paths and the values every replication starts with, such as {"Shop.resources.packers.current_cap": 3}, set in the order given; a value the registry would refuse or clamp is refused, so a max_cap below the current current_cap needs current_cap set first none

docs.title: Choose the Measures
docs.text:
A measure is a statistic's published name without the sim id and stats, such as tasks.pack.wait_mean for Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean. Reference, Statistics lists them. Each replication keeps the statistics level its measures need, whatever level the model sets: basic for counts and time averages, typical for means and maxima of waits and services, and all for percentiles. A higher level the model sets stays.

A name that no replication publishes is refused, with the names the model does publish. The exception is a count that the statistics leave out while it is 0: a task's in_progress, finished, balked, reneged, failed, interrupted, preempted and resumed, and a flow's finished, started, in_system and failed. Such a count is 0 in a replication that did not publish it, also when no replication published it, once a replication published another statistic of the same task or flow. A name of a task or flow that no replication published anything of is still refused. desflow test, an experiment's counts and desflow explain --verify read these counts the same way. A mean with no observation in a replication, such as the wait of a task that never started, is refused with the replication's number rather than left out.

docs.title: Read the Result
docs.text:
replicate, imported with from desflow import replicate, returns a Replications. Its summary has one row per measure: a mapping with measure, n, mean, half_width and level. The interval runs from mean - half_width to mean + half_width. Its table has one row per replication and measure, with the replication's number and seed, and seeds lists the seeds in order:

docs/snippets/pages/replications.py:read
print(result.summary_text())  # each measure's n, mean and half-width
for row in result.summary:  # measure, n, mean, half_width and level
    low, high = row["mean"] - row["half_width"], row["mean"] + row["half_width"]
    print(f"{row['measure']}: {low:.2f} to {high:.2f} ({row['level']:.0%})")
print(result.seeds)  # replication i ran with seeds[i - 1]
for row in result.table:  # one row per replication and measure
    print(row["replication"], row["seed"], row["measure"], row["value"])

The summary of the three replications above:

measure                               n          mean    half-width (95%)
tasks.pack.wait_mean                  3         4.327               1.776
resources.packers.utilization_avg     3         80.55               4.613

Three replications give a wide interval. Trusting Results shows how to choose enough.

docs.title: Repeat One Replication
docs.text: Each replication's seed is a plain integer, recorded in seeds and in every row of the table. Any replication can therefore be repeated on its own, with the same end time, drain and warm-up: desflow run shop.yaml --seed <its seed>, random_seed in a builder context, or Sampler(seed=...) in the low-level API. That run publishes its event records, which replications do not.

docs.title: What the Sinks Receive
docs.text:
When the model has sinks, a blueprint's egress or a builder's add_egress, they receive the result once, as telemetry stamped at the end time: each replication's value, then each measure's mean, half-width and count. A low-level model has no sinks of its own. Below are the records a Console sink receives from the three replications above, with each value rounded to 10 significant digits because the last digits differ between platforms:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean.replication.1', 'value': 4.074824798}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean.replication.2', 'value': 3.77331804}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean.replication.3', 'value': 5.134222175}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg.replication.1', 'value': 78.48408509}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg.replication.2', 'value': 81.07923191}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg.replication.3', 'value': 82.08253291}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean.mean', 'value': 4.327455004}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean.half_width', 'value': 1.775561705}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean.n', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg.mean', 'value': 80.54861664}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg.half_width', 'value': 4.61299164}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg.n', 'value': 3}

Records and Telemetry lists the names.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Seeds. The replications' seeds are numpy.random.SeedSequence(seed).spawn(n), each turned into one plain integer. The same seed gives the same list, and a longer list starts with the shorter one, so 40 replications begin with the 10 that n=10 runs. Within a replication each distribution draws from a random sequence of its own, as in any run (Randomness and Seeds).

One replication. Each replication builds the model again: it reads the blueprint, calls the factory, or calls the low-level function with a new environment and sampler. It runs unpaced, at factor 0, with no ingress, no egress and no statistics timer. It applies the warm-up and the overrides before the clock starts, and reads env.stats.readings() at its end. A blueprint's run.before functions run once per replication, and once more when the model has sinks, for the build that sends them the result.

Intervals. The half-width is t × s ÷ √n. Here s is the sample standard deviation of the n values, and t is the Student t quantile at (1 + level) ÷ 2 with n − 1 degrees of freedom. desflow computes the quantile itself, by bisection on the t distribution's cumulative probability, so replications need nothing beyond a base install. The tests check it against a published table.

Workers. With workers above 1, replications run in a pool of that many processes. Each process imports the model. The model must therefore be a blueprint path or a function defined at the top of a module. A lambda, or a function defined inside another function, is refused with that reason. The values are the same as with one worker.

Sinks. When the model has sinks, it is built once more after the last replication, with its sinks, without its ingress, and with the clock at the end time. This build is not run. Its own statistics are switched off, so the sinks receive only the result. A model without sinks is not built again.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• No event records. Replications send no event records: the orders of twenty replications, each with its own seed, would mix in one sink and could not be told apart. Repeat one replication with its seed to get its records.
  • Independent seeds only. Every replication of one call has its own seed. Comparing two designs with the same seeds, and checking that their random streams line up, is an experiment's job (Experiments).
  • Same model each time. A builder factory must return a new context on every call. A context that has run keeps its entity counters and is not a new replication.
  • Built-in statistics only. A replication summarises the built-in statistics at its end. Readings of your own, published with context.publish, are not summarised.
  • Steady state and terminating runs. The warm-up applies to each replication. A run with a natural start and end, such as a shop day, keeps its empty start and needs no warm-up. Output Analysis explains the two kinds of run.

docs.title: Example: Replications
docs.text:

docs.title: Built-in Statistics
docs.text: A run can measure itself: how busy each resource was, how long tasks waited, how many entities finished. This page shows how to switch the statistics on, what each level publishes and costs, how each value is computed, and how to add readings of your own.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: The built-in statistics are measures that desflow keeps while the run goes on and publishes as telemetry, under fixed names such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean. They need no code of yours in the builder or YAML, and they reach every sink like any other telemetry. They are off by default, because most runs only generate data. Measuring a Run reads them on the shop.

docs.title: Choose a Level
docs.text:
A level switches them on. Each level publishes what the levels before it publish, and answers one more question:

Level Question Adds none nothing; the default minimal What is happening now? resources: capacity, in_use, queue_length, utilization, and down for one that breaks down; stores and containers: capacity, level, getters_waiting, putters_waiting; tasks: in_progress basic How much got done, and how busy was it? tasks and flows: finished; flows: started and in_system; tasks: balked, reneged, failed, interrupted, preempted and resumed, and flows: failed, once one happens; resources: utilization_avg, queue_length_avg, and downtime and failures for one that breaks down; stores and containers: level_avg typical How long did tasks take? tasks: wait_mean, wait_max, service_mean, service_max all How long did the slowest take? tasks: wait_p50, wait_p95, wait_p99, service_p50, service_p95, service_p99

They are published every interval of simulation time, 10 seconds when it is not given. The first publication comes one interval after the start, and one more comes at the end of the run. When the timer has already published at the end's time, the end publishes only the values that changed since:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics.yaml:levels
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation time and once at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 min}

stats: typical is the short form, with the 10-second interval. The interval takes seconds or a duration.

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:builder-levels
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation seconds and once at the end
app.with_stats("typical", interval=60)
docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-levels
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=60)  # before or after the resources

Resources, stores and containers add themselves to env.stats when they are built. Tasks are your own processes, so each reports its steps:

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-report
# A low-level task reports its own steps to the statistics
env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
with packers.request() as request:
    yield request
    env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
env.stats.flow_finished("orders")  # the order leaves the shop

docs.title: Publish at Each Change
docs.text:
The readings of a resource are published every interval. With on_change, a resource also publishes them right after each request and each release on it, so a change between two intervals is on record. It needs a level above none, because it publishes the readings that level selects. A grant that a release makes later, and a cancel, publish none of their own.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics_readings.yaml:on-change
# The readings of level minimal, and one more set after each request and release
stats: {level: minimal, on_change: true}
docs/snippets/pages/statistics_options.py:on-change
# The readings of level minimal, and one more set after each request and release
on_change.with_stats("minimal", on_change=True)
docs/snippets/pages/statistics_options.py:low-level-on-change
env.stats.on_change = True  # a reading after each request and release

docs.title: Trace the Events
docs.text:
trace publishes one record of the kind trace for each event the environment is about to process, with the value {priority, event_id, event}. Only a sink with when: trace receives it, and that sink receives nothing else. A stats mapping with only trace may leave out level, which is then none. A blueprint with a when: trace sink and no stats.trace is refused when it loads. Records and Telemetry shows the record.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics_trace.yaml:trace
egress:
  # Only a sink with when: trace receives the trace records
  - {type: Console, when: trace}

# With only trace set, the level is none
stats: {trace: true}
docs/snippets/pages/statistics_options.py:trace
# Only a sink with when="trace" receives the trace records
trace.add_egress(ConsoleEgress(), when="trace")
trace.with_stats("none", trace=True)
docs/snippets/pages/statistics_options.py:low-level-trace
env.setup_egress([sink], traces=[True])  # a trace sink gets only the trace
env.trace_events()

docs.title: Read the Names
docs.text:
Every statistic is published as telemetry named <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, where the kind is resources, stores, containers, tasks or flows. A flow is named by the arrival that started its entities: Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished counts the orders that left the model. Reference, Statistics lists every name with what it measures. Below are the statistics that statistics.yaml, the blueprint whose levels part is shown above, publishes at the end of its two-minute run:

The same values can be read by name, during or after the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

app.env.stats.readings() gives the same values, by name, during or after the run.

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-read
# Every statistic the level publishes, by its published name
readings = env.stats.readings()
print(f"mean wait {readings['Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean']:.2f} s")

docs.title: Which Entities a Count Covers
docs.text:
When the statistics are read, every entity that has arrived belongs to one population. Each population has its own counts, published from basic unless the table says otherwise. A mean wait or service time covers only the instances that reached that step, so report the counts beside it:

Population Which entities Counts completed left the model after their last task flows.<arrival>.finished; tasks.<task>.finished per task still present started and not yet ended when the statistics are read flows.<arrival>.in_system; tasks.<task>.in_progress, the instances queued or started, from minimal rejected refused to join a queue, as their balk held tasks.<task>.balked abandoned left a queue when their patience ran out, or ended by an interrupt under on_interrupt: abandon tasks.<task>.reneged; an abandoned flow leaves in_system without adding to finished or failed, and tasks.<task>.interrupted counts the interrupts failed ended in a failure that no on_fail handled flows.<arrival>.failed; tasks.<task>.failed counts failed instances warm-up-crossing started before the warm-up ended and ended after it in finished but not in started; an instance still queued at the end of the warm-up adds its whole wait, and one in service adds its whole service time and no wait; an instance that started before the warm-up ended, was preempted and resumes after it adds no wait for the time since the preemption, because its first wait belongs to the statistics that the reset replaced

An entity a task spawns (Start a Flow Without Waiting) counts as a flow of its own under the spawned task's name. So flows.<task>.* and tasks.<task>.* cover it as they cover any arrival's flow. The spawning entity's key is in attr.parent.

Without a warm-up, started is finished plus in_system plus the entities that balked, reneged, failed or were abandoned. A warm-up starts started, finished, failed and the outcome counts again from zero, and leaves in_system and in_progress as they are. After a warm-up, finished also counts the warm-up-crossing entities, which started leaves out, so finished can be larger than started. End Conditions counts each population of a run.

docs.title: Add Readings of Your Own
docs.text:
Anything else is a custom reading: a value that is published at an interval of simulation time as <sim_id>.<name>. In YAML, a telemetry entry gives each reading as an expression. An expression can read a resource's queue, a registry value and the time t. It cannot read an entity or a task.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics_readings.yaml:readings
telemetry:
  # Readings of your own: two expressions, evaluated every 30 seconds
  - interval: 30
    readings:
      waiting_per_packer: "queue.packers /
        max(registry['Shop.resources.packers.current_cap'], 1)"
      arrival_rate: "registry['Shop.arrival.orders.rate']"
docs/snippets/pages/statistics_options.py:readings
# Readings of your own: two expressions, evaluated every 30 seconds
readings.add_readings(
    30,
    {
        "waiting_per_packer": "queue.packers / max(registry['Shop.resources.packers.current_cap'], 1)",
        "arrival_rate": "registry['Shop.arrival.orders.rate']",
    },
)

A process that loops, publishes with env.publish_telemetry(name, value) and waits with env.timeout(interval) does the same.

Each reading is published at the start and then every interval, in the order given. The readings divide by the planned capacity, registry['Shop.resources.packers.current_cap'], because the expression language has no name for the live capacity. For a resource that breaks down, the planned and the live capacity differ while it is down.

Keep a function for a reading that an expression cannot make. The function runs at an interval and publishes with context.publish(name, value):

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics.yaml:custom
telemetry:
  # Readings of your own: called as packers_report(context) every 30 seconds
  - {interval: 30, function: !python shop_logic.packers_report}

The function is in shop_logic.py, beside the blueprint:

docs/snippets/yaml/shop_logic.py:packers-report
def packers_report(context):
    """A custom reading: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get(f"{context.sim_id}.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate
docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:builder-custom
@app.telemetry_loop(interval=30.0)
def packers_report(context: SimulationContext):
    """Readings of your own: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate

A process that loops, publishes with env.publish_telemetry(name, value) and waits with env.timeout(interval) does the same.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The environment keeps one Statistics object, env.stats, which collects nothing until a level above none is set. Its timer publishes every value at each interval, and the teardown publishes them once more. When the timer has already published at the teardown's time, the teardown publishes only the values that changed since.

Readings now. capacity, in_use, queue_length and level are read from the object at the moment of publishing. in_use counts the units held by tasks, and a capacity drop does not take busy units away. After a drop, in_use can therefore be above capacity, and utilization (in_use ÷ capacity × 100) can be above 100%. At a capacity of 0 with units still held, utilization is 100. A resource with no limit (current_cap: .inf) publishes capacity as null and a utilization of 0. A store or container with no limit publishes its capacity as null too.

Breakdowns. A resource with a breakdown reads down now: 1 while it is down, 0 otherwise. downtime adds the length of each down period, and of one still going on. failures adds one at each failure. Model Breakdowns checks both against the events.

Averages over time. utilization_avg, queue_length_avg and level_avg weigh each value by how long it lasted. Each resource, store and container reports every change, and the statistics add the area under the value since the last change, so the average is exact at any moment rather than sampled:

Counts. finished adds one when a task instance finishes, and a flow's finished adds one when an entity's last task has no next task. A flow's started adds one when an entity's first task instance begins, before its balk check and its queue, whether or not it is then served. An entity that the spawn key or an on: spawn action starts is counted at the spawn when the spawn has no after. With an after, it is counted when the spawned task starts, after the delay. in_system is the number of the flow's entities in the model now: started, and not yet finished, failed or gone. Which Entities a Count Covers shows how started adds up. A task's in_progress is the number of its instances queued or started and not yet ended, now. A low-level process reports an entity's start with env.stats.flow_started(arrival). It reports an entity that leaves without finishing or failing with env.stats.flow_ended(arrival). A task's balked adds one when an instance refuses to join its queue, reneged when one leaves the queue after its patience, and failed when one fails (Failures). A flow's failed adds one when an entity's flow ends in a failure no on_fail handles. interrupted and preempted add one for each interrupt or preemption an instance receives, and resumed when it is served again. Each is published once it is above 0. A balked, reneged or failed instance adds no wait or service time. An interrupted instance that resumes adds one wait, the sum of all its waits, and one service time, the time it was served. A low-level process counts them with env.stats.task_balked(task, instance), env.stats.task_reneged(task, instance), env.stats.task_failed(task, instance), env.stats.flow_failed(arrival), env.stats.task_interrupted(task, instance, preempted=...) and env.stats.task_resumed(task, instance).

Wait and service. The wait of a task instance runs from its queued step to its started step, and its service from started to finished. A task that never queues, such as a timed step, waits 0. typical keeps only a count, a total and a maximum of each, so the memory they use does not grow with the run. all keeps every observation and computes the percentiles exactly with NumPy's percentile at each publication, so its memory grows with the number of tasks.

Warm-up. A run's warmup resets every statistic once, at that time: the averages start again from zero area, and the counts and observations from zero. An instance that was queued before the reset and starts after it counts with its whole wait. Time and Pacing describes the warm-up.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Cost. minimal reads a few values at each publication. basic adds a little work at every change of a resource, store or container. typical adds a little at every task step. all keeps every wait and service time in memory for the whole run. Use it for runs of thousands of tasks, not for a generator that runs for days.
  • One way to get resource readings. Before 0.21.0, a telemetry entry could publish <resource>.<reading> by name. That shortcut is gone: stats: minimal publishes the same readings, under Shop.stats.resources.<name>.<reading>. telemetry now takes only readings and functions, for values of your own.
  • One run is one sample. The statistics describe one run with one seed. Values from the same run are not independent of each other, and another seed gives other values. Replications give independent values. Trusting Results shows what that means for a result, and Replications run a model with many seeds.
  • A task appears once it has run. At typical and all, a task's statistics are published from the first time it starts. At basic, they are published from the first time it finishes.

docs.title: Example: Measuring a Run
docs.text:
The measuring example publishes every statistic of the packers and the pack task every 5 minutes of simulation time, and leaves out a 3-minute warm-up. When packing slows down, it sends a ground-truth record to a sink of its own. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page Measuring a Run teaches these features step by step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api yaml
cd measuring/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run measuring.yaml

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api yaml
cd measuring/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run measuring.yaml
examples/yaml/measuring.yaml:measure
# Every level: readings, counts and time averages, mean and maximum wait and service,
# and their 50th, 95th and 99th percentiles, such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_p95.
stats: {level: all, interval: 5 min}

scenario:
  # Packing slows from 4 to 4.8 seconds on average. The record is the ground truth.
  - at: 12 min
    path: Shop.service.packing.scale
    value: 1.2
    record: {fault: slow_packing, cause: new packing material}

The whole file is examples/yaml/measuring.yaml.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api builder
cd measuring/builder

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow measuring_example.py

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api builder
cd measuring/builder

# 3. Run it
python measuring_example.py
examples/builder/measuring_example.py:fault
def slow_packing(context):
    """Packing slows from 4 to 4.8 seconds on average at 12 minutes, with its label."""
    yield context.env.timeout(720)
    path = "Shop.service.packing.scale"
    registry = context.env.registry
    old = registry.get(path).value
    registry.update(path, 1.2)
    context.env.publish_label(
        {"fault": "slow_packing", "cause": "new packing material"},
        path=path,
        old=old,
        new=registry.get(path).value,
    )


app.add_process(slow_packing)

The whole file is examples/builder/measuring_example.py.

docs.title: Tasks and Processes
docs.text: This page is the map of the section: what a task and a process are, and which page shows what.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A task is what one entity does: an order being packed, a return being logged. A process is anything else that runs over time: packers going on a break every hour, a speed that drifts, a shift plan. Both are SimPy generators, functions that yield to wait. The builder and YAML write the common ones for you, and the low-level API writes them by hand.

docs.title: Pages in This Section
docs.text:
• Tasks: write a task, its keys, how an order leaves the line, what a task does when it is interrupted, what run() does and what a task does step by step.
  • Processes: run work alongside the tasks that belongs to no entity.
  • Signals and Waiting: wait for signals, conditions and child flows, start flows, and run actions when an event happens.
  • Failures: when a task fails, what a failure does, and what happens to one nobody handles.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Pick the page by the job:

To do this Read Write the work one order does, and the records it publishes Tasks Let an order give up waiting, or turn it away Tasks Choose what an order does after a task Task Flow Run a break, a drift or a schedule Processes Make a task wait for another task, a signal or a time Signals and Waiting Handle a task that cannot finish Failures

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
run() builds the environment, registers the parameters, builds the resources, stores and containers, and starts the arrivals and processes. What run() Does lists the steps in order, and What @app.task Does lists the steps of one task.

The diagram follows one task instance through its eight steps. Watch the box with the thick outline move along the steps, and the records it has published grow underneath.

Each box names the keys that act at that step. A step whose keys the task does not set passes at once: a task with no wait does not wait, and a task with no batch joins no batch. The instance publishes queued when it has something to wait for: a resource, a get, a wait, a seize or a batch. It publishes started before its work, and finished or failed when it ends. A balk ends it at the first step with balked, and a renege ends it while it waits with reneged. The last step starts the next task as a new instance for the same entity, in the same SimPy process.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text: This page shows when a task fails and what happens next.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
A failure is a task that does not finish its work: an order that fails its check, a wait that fails, code that raises an error. desflow records it, then sends the entity to a task that handles it, or ends the entity's flow.

A task fails in these cases:

  • Its fail condition holds after its service. fail reads the task's own payload as payload.<field>, as next does.
  • The wait it needs fails, or the child flow it waits for fails.
  • A step raises an error, or an expression cannot be evaluated: a service_time, a payload field, a gen: expr. A builder task's function that raises an exception fails it too.

docs.title: Declare a Failure
docs.text:
A task declares when it fails with fail, why with fail_reason, and where the entity goes with on_fail. fail_reason is text, a number or a generator read when the task fails. A reason of None, such as a generator that returns nothing, falls back to the text of the fail condition, and an empty text or 0 stays as the reason. An error in the generator fails the task, with the error's type and place as the reason. The task that on_fail names reads the failure as upstream.status (failed) and upstream.reason. on_fail needs no fail: a failed wait, a failed child flow, a step that raises and an expression that cannot be evaluated go to it too.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/failures.yaml:fail
pack:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # The task fails when this condition holds after its service
  fail: t > 12
  # The reason is text, a number or a generator
  fail_reason: after the cut-off
  # Where the order goes after a failure; it reads upstream.status and upstream.reason
  on_fail: refund
  payload: {event_type: packed}
refund:
  payload:
    event_type: refunded
    why: {gen: expr, expr: upstream.reason}
docs/snippets/yaml/failures.yaml:on-fail-alone
check:
  # The wait fails when the child flow fails; on_fail needs no fail condition
  wait: {task: inspect}
  on_fail: hold
  payload: {event_type: checked}
inspect:
  service: packing
  fail: t > 12
  fail_reason: failed inspection
  payload: {event_type: inspected}
hold:
  payload:
    event_type: held
    why: {gen: expr, expr: upstream.reason}

@app.task(fail="t > 12", fail_reason="after the cut-off", on_fail="refund") takes the same keys, and keeps an empty or 0 reason as YAML does. The Builder tab of Handle a Failure Nobody Handles runs a task that fails with no on_fail.

A process catches the exception of the child it yields, as SimPy code does: try: yield env.process(inspect()) with except Exception as error:. It then starts what on_fail would start.

docs.title: Handle a Failure Nobody Handles
docs.text:
run.on_unhandled_failure sets what happens to a failure of a task, child flow or one-shot signal that nobody handles. It has two values:

  • stop, the default in YAML, the builder and the low-level API: the failure stops the run, as plain SimPy does. A root task that fails with no on_fail raises an exception, and so does a one-shot signal failed with nobody waiting. The exception reaches the caller of run().
  • continue: the failure is marked as handled (SimPy calls this defused), and the run goes on. A data generator should not stop on one failed order.

The builder and YAML switch to continue with run(on_unhandled_failure="continue") or run: {on_unhandled_failure: continue}, and the low-level API with DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(on_unhandled_failure="continue"). In the low-level API, an exception raised in a process always reaches the process that yields it, and one nobody handles stops the run, as in SimPy. One signal failure can be defused alone with defused (Signals and Waiting).

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Under run:

docs/snippets/yaml/task_endings.yaml:unhandled
# stop, the default, raises a failure nobody handles to the caller of run();
# continue defuses it and the run goes on
on_unhandled_failure: continue

Under stop, the failure reaches the caller of run() as an exception. TaskFailed names the task and the reason, and this prints pack failed: after the cut-off:

docs/snippets/pages/failures.py:task-failed
# Under stop, the first failure that no on_fail handles reaches the caller of run()
try:
    shop().run(until=60, on_unhandled_failure="stop")
except TaskFailed as failure:
    print(f"{failure.task} failed: {failure.reason}")

stop is the default. DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(on_unhandled_failure="continue") switches to continue.

A run that stops on a signal raises SignalFailed when the signal fails, as Run Length describes:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

run.stop names the signal. When the signal fails, desflow run reports the reason and exits with an error.

This prints closing failed: the till did not balance:

docs/snippets/pages/failures.py:signal-failed
# A run that stops on a signal raises the reason the signal failed with. The packing
# failures are left to continue, so only the signal ends the run
try:
    shop().run(until=60, on_unhandled_failure="continue", stop={"signal": "closing"})
except SignalFailed as failure:
    print(f"{failure.signal} failed: {failure.reason}")

env.run(until=event) on the signal's event raises the exception the event failed with, as in SimPy.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A failed task then does three things, in order:

  1. It publishes failed instead of its finished payload, with a reason: the condition's text, or its fail_reason.
  2. It fails its signal, so every task waiting for the signal fails too.
  3. It goes to its on_fail task. Without on_fail, the entity's flow ends, and a child flow fails the task waiting for it, with the same reason. A failure nobody handles then follows on_unhandled_failure.

At the basic statistics level and above, each failure is counted as tasks.<task>.failed, and each flow that ends in one as flows.<arrival>.failed. The inspect task of the example in Signals and Waiting fails a gift and sends it to be wrapped.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text: A process runs alongside the tasks. This page shows how to write one.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A process is anything in the shop that runs over time but is not one entity's work: a break for the packers, a drift in a parameter, a delivery schedule. An arrival starts one task per entity, while a process starts once, when the run starts, and runs alongside the tasks. A process can wait, change values in the registry, publish records or start tasks.

docs.title: A Process
docs.text:
This process sends the packers on a 5-second break every 50 seconds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint writes this without Python. One entity exists when the run starts, and two tasks hand it to each other: each waits, writes the capacity with an on: action, and names the other as its next.

docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:break-arrival
# One entity exists when the run starts and drives the breaks
shifts: {initial: 1, spawn: take_break}
docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:break
# The packers go on a 5-second break every 50 seconds: wait, set the capacity with
# on:, and hand over to the other task, which sets it back
take_break:
  wait: {timeout: 50 s}
  on:
    - {path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 0}
  payload: {event_type: break_started}
  next: end_break
end_break:
  wait: {timeout: 5 s}
  on:
    - {path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}
  payload: {event_type: break_ended}
  next: take_break

A processes entry names a Python function of your own, for work the keys cannot say:

docs/snippets/yaml/tasks_process.yaml:process
processes:
  # Called as breaks(context, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5)
  - function: !python shop_logic.breaks
    kwargs: {resource: packers, every: 50, duration: 5}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-process
def breaks(context: SimulationContext, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """Takes every packer off for a break of `duration` seconds every `every` seconds."""
    path = f"{context.sim_id}.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    registry = context.env.registry
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(every)
        normal = registry.get(path).value
        registry.update(path, 0)
        yield context.env.timeout(duration)
        registry.update(path, normal)


app.add_process(breaks, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5)
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-process
def breaks_process(env, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """What add_process starts, by hand: a plain SimPy generator."""
    path = f"Shop.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(every)
        normal = env.registry.get(path).value
        env.registry.update(path, 0)
        yield env.timeout(duration)
        env.registry.update(path, normal)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
add_process(func, **kwargs) starts func(context, **kwargs) when the run starts, and a YAML processes entry does the same with a !python function. Inside it, context.env is the DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, so a process can do anything a low-level script does: context.env.timeout, context.env.registry.update, context.env.publish_event. A process is how low-level code joins a builder or YAML model.

context.env.active_process is the running SimPy process. Its name is the task's name, because a task's process is named after the task. Its target is the event it waits on now, or None once it has ended. A condition reads the same three values as process.name, process.instance (the task's instance id, the instance field of its records) and process.target, a string such as timeout, signal.<name>, task.<name>, condition, resource.<name>, get.<name>, put.<name> or service. In a task's own expressions they name that task. In an interrupt or running where, they name each instance tested.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A process is not an entity. It has no key, no instance and no records of its own unless it publishes them. Work that one entity does is a task.
  • A capacity of 0 stops new work only. Setting current_cap to 0 does not stop the work in progress: Units and Queues explains what happens to busy units when a capacity drops.
