docs.title: Tasks
docs.text: A task is what one entity does: an order being packed, a return being logged. This page shows how to write a task, which keys a task has, how an order leaves the line, what a task does when it is interrupted, what run() does with tasks, and what a task does step by step. Processes shows work that does not belong to one entity.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A task is a SimPy generator: a function that yields to wait. The builder and YAML write the common ones for you, and the low-level API writes them by hand. A task waits for what it needs, does its work for a sampled time, publishes an event at each step, and may lead to the next task.

docs.title: A Task
docs.text:
A task with a service and a resource asks for a unit of the resource, holds it for a time drawn from the service, and releases it. A task with neither takes no time and holds nothing: it publishes its payload at once. Such a task suits a step that only records an event, such as logging a return.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:task
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing  # how long the work takes
    resource: packers  # what it holds while it works
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}  # the finished event's value
    next: print_label  # the task that follows; Task Flow has the other forms
  return_logged:
    # No service and no resource: publishes its payload at once
    payload: {event_type: return_logged}

A payload mapping may hold generated fields. This task adds a delivery to the finished event, standard for nine orders in ten and express for the tenth:

docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:payload-mapping
# A payload with generated fields: nine orders in ten are standard, one is express
pack_with_delivery:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  payload:
    event_type: order_packed
    delivery:
      gen: weighted
      options: {standard: 0.9, express: 0.1}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-task
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", next="print_label")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Runs when the order gets a packer, before the packing time.
    # The returned dict is the finished event's value.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.task()  # no service and no resource: publishes at once
def return_logged(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "return_logged"}

The function is called with the task id and whatever the caller passes. It also receives entity, upstream and item by keyword when it declares a parameter of that name: the entity, what the previous task handed on, and what a store get took. A function that declares none of them is called without them.

A function that returns a Template gives the same generated fields as the YAML tab:

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-payload-mapping
# A payload with generated fields: nine orders in ten are standard, one is express
delivery = Template(
    {
        "event_type": "order_packed",
        "delivery": {"gen": "weighted", "options": {"standard": 0.9, "express": 0.1}},
    },
    name="tasks.pack_with_delivery",
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_with_delivery(task_id: int):
    return delivery
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-task
def pack_order_process(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, label_ids):
    """What @app.task does, by hand."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish(
        {"path_id": path_id, "sim_id": "Shop", "service": "packing", "status": "queued"}
    )
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish(
            {
                "path_id": path_id,
                "sim_id": "Shop",
                "service": "packing",
                "status": "started",
            }
        )
        payload = {"event_type": "order_packed"}
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish(payload)
    # next: print_label, a new instance for the same order
    yield from print_label_process(env, sampler, key, next(label_ids))

This is ordinary SimPy: packers.request() waits for a unit, env.timeout waits the service time, and leaving the with block releases the unit. The env.publish_event call at each step produces the records.

A task can also take from or add to a store or container (get, put), rank its requests (priority), and name the task that follows it (next). Stores and Containers, Units and Queues and Task Flow describe each.

docs.title: A Timed Step
docs.text:
A task with a service and no resource is a timed step: work that takes time but needs nothing that can be busy, such as printing a label or waiting for a supplier. It publishes started at once, with no queued event, waits the sampled time, and publishes its finished event. Its wait is 0. It is SimPy's env.timeout: the tests check that it ends at the same simulation time as a plain SimPy timeout in all three APIs (SimPy Compatibility).

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:timed-step
print_label:
  # A service and no resource: a timed step that starts at once
  service: labelling
  payload: {event_type: label_printed}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-timed-step
@app.task(service_id="labelling")  # a service and no resource: starts at once
def print_label(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "label_printed"}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-timed-step
def print_label_process(env, sampler, key, task_id):
    """A timed step: started at once, with no queued event."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.labelling"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="print_label", instance=task_id)

    publish(
        {
            "path_id": path_id,
            "sim_id": "Shop",
            "service": "labelling",
            "status": "started",
        }
    )
    yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
    publish({"event_type": "label_printed"})

docs.title: Arrivals Start Tasks
docs.text:
An arrival starts one task per arrival. The loop draws a gap from the arrival's distribution, waits for that duration, starts a task for the new entity, and repeats. The task runs on its own while the loop waits for the next arrival.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:arrival
arrivals:
  # Each arrival spawns one pack_order, and one return_logged
  # An order every 5 s on average (rate 0.2)
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}
  # A return every 10 s on average (rate 0.1)
  returns: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1, spawn: return_logged}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-arrival
# Each arrival starts one pack_order
# An order every 5 s on average (rate 0.2)
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.2, spawn="pack_order")

spawn= starts the named task for each arrival's entity, whose key is the arrival name and a counter: orders-1, orders-2. The record's instance comes from the task's one counter, which next and other arrivals share, so no two runs of the task share an id. A spawn that names a task never added is refused when run() checks the model.

@app.arrival_loop runs a generator of your own. The loop below starts one return_logged for each return, which is what spawn="return_logged" does in one argument, as the YAML tab writes it. A loop is needed only when it does more than start one task, such as choosing the task from the entity's attributes. context.wait_for_arrival returns the new Entity. Pass it to the task with entity=. A task called without one starts an entity of its own, keyed by the task's name and a counter, such as return_logged-1. The task_id becomes the record's instance. Take it from context.next_instance, the task's one counter.

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-arrival-loop
# A return every 10 s on average (rate 0.1)
app.add_arrival("returns", dist="exponential", rate=0.1)


@app.arrival_loop("returns")
def returns(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        # Draws the next gap, waits for it, and returns the new entity, keyed returns-1, ...
        parcel = yield context.wait_for_arrival("returns")
        task_id = context.next_instance("return_logged")  # the task's one counter
        context.spawn(return_logged(task_id, entity=parcel))  # the loop goes on at once
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-arrival
def orders_process(env, sampler, packers):
    """What an arrival with spawn does, by hand."""
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    label_ids = itertools.count()
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order_process(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, label_ids))
        task_id += 1

In the low-level API every loop is started once, before the run:

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-start
env.process(orders_process(env, sampler, packers))  # start each loop once
env.process(breaks_process(env, "packers", every=50, duration=5))

docs.title: Task Keys
docs.text:
A task has these keys. Each row names where the keys are described, and YAML Keys lists every key with its type.

Keys What they set Described in service, service_time, resource how long the work takes, and the resource it holds A Task and Units and Queues priority, preempt the task's place in a resource's line, and whether it may take a unit Priority and Preemption keep, seize, release holding a unit across tasks, or from one step to another Several Resources patience, balk, on_renege, on_balk leaving the line Leave the Line on_interrupt, on_interrupt_next, on_interrupt_run what the task does when it is interrupted Interrupts interrupt, subscribe interrupting other tasks, and being told when a flow ends Signals and Waiting payload, id_field, item_field, attributes the value of the finished event A Task and Task Flow key, key_field the key of the task's records Task Flow next, set, set_args, activate, deactivate where the entity goes next and what it carries Task Flow vars, vars_once, on_start, finish_vars, history values drawn for the task, and the rows it keeps Task Flow get, put taking from and adding to a store or container Stores and Containers wait, open, listen, cancel, resume waiting for, naming and watching events Signals and Waiting signal, spawn, on what happens when the task ends Signals and Waiting fail, fail_reason, on_fail when a task fails and where it goes Failures batch serving several entities with one run of the service Serve Entities Together

docs.title: Leave the Line
docs.text:
An order that waits too long may leave, and an order that finds the line long may not join it. Four keys set this:

  • patience is the longest the task waits for its wait, its resource and its get. It is a number of seconds, a duration such as 8 s, an expression or a generator. A task whose patience runs out reneges: it publishes reneged, gives back what it holds and leaves.
  • balk is a condition read before the task joins the line. When it holds, the task publishes balked and leaves. A resource whose queue_limit is full makes the task balk too (Units and Queues).
  • on_renege and on_balk name the task that gets the entity next. Without them the flow ends. That task reads how the entity left as upstream.status, reneged or balked.

This model has orders that give up after 8 seconds or do not join the line from 150 seconds on, and send both kinds to a follow-up task:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_options.yaml:leave
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  priority: 1
  # The order leaves the line when it has waited 8 seconds
  patience: 8 s
  # The order does not join the line from 150 seconds on
  balk: t >= 150
  # Where an order goes after it leaves the line; it reads upstream.status
  on_renege: follow_up
  on_balk: follow_up
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}
follow_up:
  payload:
    event_type: order_left
    how: {gen: expr, expr: upstream.status}
docs/snippets/pages/task_options.py:leave
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=1,
    patience="8 s",  # the order leaves the line when it has waited 8 seconds
    balk="t >= 150",  # the order does not join the line from 150 seconds on
    # Where an order goes after it leaves the line; it reads upstream.status
    on_renege="follow_up",
    on_balk="follow_up",
)
def pack_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


order_left = Template(
    {"event_type": "order_left", "how": {"gen": "expr", "expr": "upstream.status"}},
    name="tasks.follow_up",
)


@app.task()
def follow_up(task_id):
    return order_left

SimPy's reneging pattern races the request against a timeout: result = yield request | env.timeout(patience), and request.cancel() when request not in result. A balk is an if before packers.request(). Add Reneging and Balking shows both in the three forms, and Patience teaches them step by step.

docs.title: Interrupts
docs.text:
A task is interrupted by a preemption, a breakdown, an interrupt action or a scenario step. on_interrupt says what it does next:

Value What the task does resume The default. It goes on at once with a unit it still holds, or queues again, and then serves the time it had left. restart The same, but it serves a new time, drawn from the same stream. abandon It gives back every unit and ends, unless on_interrupt_next names a task for the entity to go to.

on_interrupt_next is for abandon. The task it names reads why the entity was interrupted as cause.<name>: by, usage_since and resource after a preemption, value after an interrupt, and left, the service time that was left.

on_interrupt_run is for resume and restart. It names a task that runs as a child flow of the same entity after each interrupt, and then the task goes on with the time it had left, or a new time under restart. It is the SimPy loop try: yield env.timeout(left) with except Interrupt: yield from repair(). The child reads cause.<name> as a task reached by on_interrupt_next does. It is for work that holds no unit of its own, so it is refused with a resource and with a request in the wait.

A gift order that loses its packer is packed by hand instead (abandon). A label that is interrupted by a jam is retooled and then printed with the time it had left (on_interrupt_run):

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_options.yaml:abandon
pack_gift:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  priority: 1
  # A gift that loses its packer gives it up and is packed by hand instead
  on_interrupt: abandon
  on_interrupt_next: pack_by_hand
  payload: {event_type: gift_packed}
pack_by_hand:
  service: packing
  payload: {event_type: packed_by_hand}
docs/snippets/yaml/task_options.yaml:run
print_label:
  service: labelling
  # After an interrupt, retool runs as a child flow of the same entity, and then
  # the label goes on with the time it had left
  on_interrupt: resume
  on_interrupt_run: retool
  payload: {event_type: label_printed}
retool:
  service: repairing
  payload:
    event_type: retooled
    left: {gen: expr, expr: cause.left}
docs/snippets/pages/task_options.py:abandon
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=1,
    # A gift that loses its packer gives it up and is packed by hand instead
    on_interrupt="abandon",
    on_interrupt_next="pack_by_hand",
)
def pack_gift(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "gift_packed"}


@app.task(service_id="packing")
def pack_by_hand(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "packed_by_hand"}
docs/snippets/pages/task_options.py:run
@app.task(
    service_id="labelling",
    # After an interrupt, retool runs as a child flow of the same entity, and then
    # the label goes on with the time it had left
    on_interrupt="resume",
    on_interrupt_run="retool",
)
def print_label(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "label_printed"}


retooled = Template(
    {"event_type": "retooled", "left": {"gen": "expr", "expr": "cause.left"}},
    name="tasks.retool",
)


@app.task(service_id="repairing")
def retool(task_id):
    return retooled

The process catches simpy.Interrupt. For a preemption, its cause is SimPy's Preempted. A process that is preempted, or whose request still waits, cancels its request and asks again, and a process that holds its unit keeps the request. Interruptions shows the loop, and Priority and Preemption says what takes a unit.

docs.title: Records of a Task
docs.text:
Every event of a task carries three fields beside its value: key, the entity's key; task, the task's name; and instance, the number of this run of the task, counted from 0 for each task. The first order of the blueprint in A Task, packed and then labelled:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 1.6063438520913942, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'sim_id': 'Shop', 'service': 'packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 1.6063438520913942, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'sim_id': 'Shop', 'service': 'packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.58163205023515, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.58163205023515, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'print_label', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.labelling', 'sim_id': 'Shop', 'service': 'labelling', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 7.58163205023515, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'print_label', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'label_printed'}}

All five events share the key orders-1, so an order can be followed through every task it passes. The finished event's value is exactly the payload. Records and Telemetry describes every field.

docs.title: What run() Does
docs.text:
run() builds everything the context describes and runs it, in this order:

Until run() is called nothing exists but the description, and the runtime helpers that Builder API lists raise RuntimeError. Teardown runs in a finally block, so the last statistics are published and every sink is flushed even when the run stops with an error or Ctrl+C.

docs.title: What @app.task Does
docs.text:
@app.task turns your function into a SimPy process that does these steps, publishing a record at three of them:

  1. If its balk condition holds, it publishes balked and stops.
  2. It publishes queued if it has a wait, a resource or a get, and starts its patience timer, which runs only while it waits. It starts its open branches, makes its listen callbacks and runs its cancel. Then it asks for the units named by seize.
  3. It waits until its wait ends.
  4. It asks for the resource, in the resource's queue order, then takes its get from a store or container, waiting while there is not enough.
  5. It publishes started, calls your function, and keeps what it returns as the payload. The payload is computed before the service time, so it can use the state of the simulation at that moment.
  6. It waits the service time, drawn from the live distribution.
  7. It adds its put to a store or container, waiting while there is no room, and checks its fail condition.
  8. It publishes the payload as the finished event, or failed, and releases the resource.
  9. It fires its signal (or fails it) and sends its interrupt action to the tasks it names. It applies set to the entity's attributes and set_args to the process's local names, and runs the on: actions. It frees the units named by release. A unit still held when the flow ends stays held, as in SimPy, so a flow that used seize writes release before it ends.
  10. It starts the next task that its next chooses, or its on_fail, on_renege or on_balk task, as a new instance for the same entity.

A YAML task and its spawn make the same task and arrival loop that the builder code above makes. The code that runs these steps is TaskRun in desflow/builder/task.py. In SimPy terms each flow of tasks is one process started with env.process, and each arrival loop is another. SimPy and desflow describes processes.

A process outside a task runs as Processes describes.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Resources are acquired in one order. A task can hold several resources and hand one to the next task. Tasks that acquire two resources in opposite orders still load, and the model logs one WARNING, because two of them could then wait for each other for ever: Several Resources.
  • abandon gives back everything. An interrupted task cancels its waits. Under resume and restart it keeps a unit it holds through a plain interrupt and asks again only for a unit it lost, at the back of the line. A preemption or a breakdown takes the unit. Under abandon it releases every unit before it follows on_interrupt_next: Interruptions.
  • A finished event is exactly the payload. It has no status or path_id unless the payload includes them.
  • A condition branch checks after every change. In a model with many waits on conditions and many changes, the work grows in proportion to both.
  • Runtime helpers need a running simulation. They raise RuntimeError before run(), as Builder API lists. Call them inside a loop, task or process.

docs.title: Time and Pacing
docs.text: A run has two clocks of its own, simulation time and logical time. A run can follow the wall clock, ignore it, or ignore it at first and follow it later. This page shows how to read the current time and which parts of the environment run on each thread. Clocks and Pacing shows the clock settings, and Run Length shows the warm-up and how long a run lasts.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Simulation time is the number of seconds SimPy has advanced, starting at initial_time, 0 by default. Every record carries it as sim_ts. Logical time is the date and time a record carries as timestamp: logical_start_time plus the simulation time. factor sets how simulation time relates to the wall clock, and go_live_at switches that relation once during a run. One hour of simulation time is one hour of logical time, and takes as long on the wall clock as factor says:

The settings are the same on DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, on SimulationContext and in the simulation section of a blueprint.

docs.title: Pages in This Section
docs.text:
• Clocks and Pacing: the logical start time, the time zone, the factor, going live, the lag and strict pacing.
  • Run Length: the warm-up, the initial time, how long a run lasts, stopping early, draining, stepping and running in segments.

docs.title: Read the Current Time
docs.text: t is the simulation clock in a condition or an expression, the value of context.env.now in the builder and env.now in the low-level API. A route or a balk can depend on it, such as next: {when: [{condition: "t < 110", task: early}], default: late}. A wait: {condition: ...} that reads t is not a timer. A condition is checked again only after a change of state, not as time passes. To wait for a time, use a timeout branch.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Before each event, the environment checks the logical clock. Until go_live_at it paces the run at factor, and from there at one simulation second per real second. Clocks and Pacing describes how the pacing switches during a run, and Run Length how the model and the run end. The threads that run a model, the two kinds of queue and the processes the environment starts are in How desflow Works. SimPy and desflow compares the two environments.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A run with no until ends when no model event is left. A run with an arrival, a sink or an ingress connector never runs out of events, so it needs until, a stop or Ctrl+C, as Run Length explains.
  • At factor: 0 no timed flush runs, so records leave a buffer when it reaches batch_size and at teardown, as Egress explains. LocalIngress follows the wall clock, so its changes can land after an unpaced run has ended. A scenario follows the simulation clock. No system.simulation.lag_seconds is published unless lag_interval is set, and it reads 0.
  • warmup drops, go_live_at routes. Records before a warm-up are gone. Records before go_live_at go to the sinks that take history.
  • A model slower than the wall clock falls behind at factor: 1.0 and does not catch up by skipping events. lag_seconds shows by how much.

docs.title: Clocks and Pacing
docs.text: This page shows the clock settings of a run, described in Time and Pacing: the logical start time, the time zone, the factor, going live, the lag and strict pacing.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A run's records carry dates and times, as the events of a real shop would. The logical start time and the time zone set those dates. The factor sets how fast the run goes against the wall clock: a backfill of last week runs without waiting, and a live demo runs in step with the wall clock. Going live switches from the first to the second within one run.

docs.title: Logical Start Time
docs.text:
logical_start_time is the date and time that simulation time 0 maps to. Without it, the run uses the moment the environment is created. A run with a backdated start writes history:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

logical_start_time under simulation takes now, a signed duration or an ISO datetime. This blueprint starts a day before the file is loaded:

docs/snippets/yaml/environment.yaml:logical-start
# Read against the moment the file is loaded: a day of history up to now
logical_start_time: -1d
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:logical-start
app = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,
    logical_start_time=datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=7),  # a week
)

DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(logical_start_time=...) takes the same datetime.

A datetime without an offset is read in the run's time zone, described next. In a blueprint it takes now, a signed duration such as -7d, or an ISO datetime, as YAML Blueprints describes.

docs.title: Time Zone
docs.text:
timezone names the zone that record timestamps are written in, as an IANA name such as Australia/Melbourne. Every timestamp carries the offset of its moment, such as 2026-10-03T12:00:00.000+10:00, or +00:00 in UTC. By default the zone is that of logical_start_time when it has one, and UTC otherwise. A logical_start_time or go_live_at without an offset, now, and the default start are read in that zone:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/environment.yaml:timezone
# Under simulation: timestamps written in Melbourne time, with its offset; the
# start and now are read in it. UTC by default
timezone: ${SIM_TIMEZONE:-Australia/Melbourne}
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:timezone
# Timestamps in Melbourne time, with their offset: 2026-10-03T12:00:00.000+10:00
melbourne = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,
    timezone="Australia/Melbourne",
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 3, 12, 0),  # read in Melbourne time
)
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:low-level-timezone
zoned = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
    factor=0.0,
    timezone="Australia/Melbourne",
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 3, 12, 0),
)
print(zoned.start_datetime)  # 2026-10-03 12:00:00+10:00

The clock runs in UTC, so a daylight-saving change in the zone never adds or drops simulation time. In Melbourne, the clocks went forward an hour on 4 October 2026. A run of 24 simulation hours from 12:00 on 3 October therefore ends at 13:00 on 4 October, 2026-10-04T13:00:00.000+11:00. A replayed timestamp without an offset is read in the zone too.

docs.title: Factor
docs.text:
The wall-clock duration of a stretch of the run is its simulation duration times factor:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

factor under simulation, here read from an environment variable:

docs/snippets/yaml/environment.yaml:factor
# An unquoted value is read after the replacement, so this is the number 0
factor: ${SIM_FACTOR:-0}

SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0) takes the same number.

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:factor
live = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=1.0)  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
twice_as_fast = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.5)  # takes half a real second
unpaced = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # takes no real time at all
  • factor: 1.0 follows the wall clock: a process that waits 5 simulation seconds waits 5 real seconds. It suits a live twin feeding a dashboard.
  • factor: 0 does not wait at all: the run goes as fast as the machine allows. It suits history, tests and experiments. At factor: 0 each event is processed by SimPy's own Environment.step, without the real-time arithmetic. strict left unset is false here, because there is no wall clock to fall behind. A pending go_live_at is still checked before each event, and pacing starts at it.

docs.title: Go Live
docs.text:
factor applies until the logical clock reaches go_live_at, and from that instant the run is paced at one simulation second per real second. With a backdated logical_start_time and factor: 0, one run writes the history as fast as it can, then keeps going in real time:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/batching.yaml:go-live
# A day of history at factor 0, then 1 simulated second per real second from now;
# when: history and when: live split the records at this instant
logical_start_time: -1d
go_live_at: now

SimulationContext(factor=0.0, logical_start_time=..., go_live_at=...) takes the same two times as datetimes.

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:go-live
go_live_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
    factor=0.0,  # until go_live_at
    logical_start_time=go_live_at - timedelta(days=7),
    go_live_at=go_live_at,  # from here, 1 simulated second per real second
)

A sink with when: history receives the records stamped before go_live_at, and one with when: live the rest, so the two halves can go to different places:

Why one run rather than two. A demo of a data lake beside a live stream usually needs two datasets: a backdated history sitting in a lake, and a live stream arriving now. They have to be the same shop, with the same packers, the same distributions and the same task ids, or the join between them is meaningless.

Producing them needs two values of factor that conflict. History needs factor=0.0, so that a week of events is generated as fast as the machine allows. A live tail needs factor=1.0, so that events arrive at one simulated second per real second.

Without go_live_at, the only way to get both is to start two processes with the same random_seed and the same logical_start_time, one fast-forwarding into Parquet and one pacing into Kafka. That costs:

  • A second full execution of the same simulation, so the history is generated twice.
  • The seed and the start instant are written in two places, which have to be edited together. If one changes and the other does not, the two halves stop being the same shop, with no error.
  • Nothing makes the two halves meet. Each process decides on its own where its half ends, so the two halves can overlap or leave a gap.

go_live_at replaces both processes with one. The run generates history unpaced up to that logical instant, then switches to real-time pacing and keeps going. There is one seed, one start instant and one instant where history ends and the live tail begins.

Three settings. Three separate settings make up the feature, and each answers a different question.

Setting Question it answers logical_start_time Where does the logical clock start? Set it in the past to backdate the history. go_live_at At which logical instant does pacing stop being factor and become real time? when on a sink Which sink receives each record?

They are independent. go_live_at changes pacing only. It never routes a record. when routes records only. It never changes pacing. Used together, they give the history and the live stream from one run. In a blueprint, when: history and when: live compare each record's timestamp with go_live_at themselves. A Python predicate has to compare with the same instant. Otherwise the records switch sinks at a different instant from the one where the pacing switches.

On a DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, env.factor reports the run's factor, such as 0.0, until the logical clock reaches go_live_at, and 1.0 afterwards.

Parquet History, Kafka Live builds such a run.

docs.title: Lag
docs.text:
At a factor above 0 the run follows the wall clock, and system.simulation.lag_seconds says how many seconds it is behind its pace, as telemetry. A run that keeps its pace reads about 0 at any factor, and the reading grows when the run falls behind. lag_interval sets how often it is published, in simulation seconds or a duration. By default, it is published every simulation second at a factor above 0. At factor: 0 it is off by default, because such a run has no pace to fall behind, and a lag_interval that turns it on reads 0. A run at factor: 0 that goes live starts publishing it at the go-live instant. A lag_interval of 0 turns it off:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/environment.yaml:lag
# Under simulation: how far the run is behind the wall clock, every 10 s; by
# default off at factor 0 and every second otherwise, and 0 turns it off
lag_interval: 10 s
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:lag
# system.simulation.lag_seconds every 10 simulation seconds; 0 turns it off
paced = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, lag_interval="10 s")
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:low-level-lag
# The low-level API sets it with the sinks; the default "auto" is off at factor 0
# env.setup_egress(sinks, lag_monitor_interval=10)

docs.title: Strict Pacing
docs.text:
A paced step that starts more than factor real seconds late has fallen behind the wall clock. With strict on, the run raises RuntimeError (Simulation too slow for real time (1.500s).), as SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment does. With strict off, the run goes on and system.simulation.lag_seconds reports the delay. A run that leaves strict unset gets the same default in every API:

  • Paced run: strict is true at a factor above 0, and when the run has a go_live_at.
  • Unpaced run: strict is false at factor: 0 with no go_live_at, because an unpaced run has no wall clock to fall behind.

SimulationContext(strict=None) and DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(strict=None) are the defaults, and simulation.strict left out of a blueprint means the same. Write strict: false for a live run with a sink that can block, so the run goes on when the sink is slow. An explicit strict: true is checked at factor: 0 with no go_live_at too, and raises at the first step after the wall clock has moved, as SimPy's check does.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/environment.yaml:strict
# Under simulation: true by default for a paced run and false at factor 0; false
# lets a live run go on when a slow sink makes it fall behind the wall clock
strict: false
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:strict
# A paced run is strict unless it says otherwise; false lets a live run go on when a
# slow sink makes it fall behind the wall clock
tolerant = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, strict=False)
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:low-level-strict
# Left unset, strict is true at a factor above 0 and false at factor 0, as SimPy's
# RealtimeEnvironment would raise at the first step of an unpaced script
raising = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=1.0)
unpaced_strict = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
low_level_tolerant = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=1.0, strict=False)

Before go_live_at, strict is never checked, whatever its value. After a pause, SimPy's env.sync() moves only the wall-clock anchor to now. The next event would then wait factor seconds for each simulation second since env_start. env_start is the start of the run, the go-live instant once the run has gone live, or the last resume_pacing(). env.resume_pacing() moves both anchors, so the next event waits factor seconds for each simulation second after now:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A context from SimulationContext.from_yaml runs in segments as the builder does, and resumes pacing with app.env.resume_pacing() in the same way.

The builder's environment is app.env. Call app.env.resume_pacing() before the next advance() of a run in segments, as Run in Segments describes.

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:resume-pacing
paused = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.01, strict=False)  # 1.0 follows the clock
paused.run(until=10)
# ... a pause, such as a stop in a debugger: the wall clock is now ahead of the run
paused.resume_pacing()  # from here, factor real seconds per simulation second
paused.run(until=20)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Pacing and the switch. Before each event, the environment checks the logical clock. At the first event at or after go_live_at, it sets the factor to 1.0 and moves its two anchors, env_start and real_start, so that the go-live instant counts as now. Without this move, the first paced event would wait on the wall clock for the whole backfill. The switch happens once, and always sets the factor to 1.0. A go_live_at at or before logical_start_time paces the whole run, with a warning. A run that ends before its go_live_at stays unpaced. A go_live_at or logical_start_time without an offset is read in the run's time zone, so the two can be compared whichever way each is written.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text: The limits of this page are listed with those of the whole section, in Stability and Limits on the Time and Pacing page.

docs.title: Run Length
docs.text: This page shows how a run starts and ends, described in Time and Pacing: the warm-up, the initial time, the run length, stopping early, draining, stepping and running in segments.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A study decides how long to watch the shop: a working day that ends at closing time, or a long run that leaves out its empty start. These settings decide when a run starts measuring, when it stops, and what happens to the orders still in the shop at the end.

docs.title: Warm-up
docs.text:
warmup leaves the start of a run out of what it reports. It is one time per run, in simulation seconds or a duration. No sink receives a record or telemetry stamped before it, and the built-in statistics are reset once at that moment, so they describe the rest of the run. A run without it sends everything, which is what a data generator usually wants.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/trusting_results.yaml:warmup
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; 0 keeps everything
warmup: ${WARMUP:-2 min}
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:warmup
# No sink receives a record stamped before 10 minutes, and the statistics restart then
measured = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, warmup="10 min")
# In the low-level API, the warm-up is set with the sinks:
# env.setup_egress(sinks, warmup=600)

The warm-up is an argument of the sinks, because it is the sinks that leave records out: env.setup_egress(sinks, warmup=600). A run with no sink has no records to leave out. When the warm-up is set through the builder, the statistics are also reset at it.

The warm-up drops early records. go_live_at drops nothing, and only decides which sink gets each record. Trusting Results shows how to choose a warm-up length.

docs.title: Initial Time
docs.text:
initial_time is the reading of the simulation clock when the run starts, 0 when left out, in seconds or as a duration. A model of a shift that starts at 8 in the morning can start its clock at 8 hours. Every event time, every record's sim_ts and until then read that clock. A record's timestamp is still logical_start_time plus sim_ts, to within 1 millisecond, because timestamp is written to the millisecond and the rest is cut off:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/initial_time.yaml:initial-time
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  # The clock starts at 8 h, so the first order at 8 h 10 min is at sim_ts 29400
  initial_time: 8 h
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:initial-time
# The clock starts at 8 hours: event times, sim_ts and until all read it
shift = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, initial_time="8 h")
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:low-level-initial-time
# The clock starts at 8 hours, in seconds, as in SimPy's Environment(initial_time=)
morning = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0, initial_time=8 * 3600)

until is a clock reading too, so a run with initial_time: 8 h and until: 16 h lasts 8 hours. A scenario step's at and the warmup are different: they are lengths of time from the start of the run. Look at where each falls on the clock of that run:

With initial_time: 8 h, a step at 30 min applies at 8.5 hours, and a warm-up of 10 min ends at 8 hours 10 minutes.

The state the run starts with holds from the initial time, before the first arrival: a resource's current_cap, a container's level, a store's items and an arrival's attributes. The tests check each against plain SimPy (SimPy Compatibility).

docs.title: Run Length
docs.text:
until is in simulation seconds. run() and a blueprint's run.until also take a duration such as "10 min", "8 hours" or "1 week". A month counts as 30 days and a year as 365.

desflow run FILE --until TIME overrides run.until for one run, without editing the file: desflow run shop.yaml --until "10 min" runs shop.yaml for 10 simulation minutes, whatever its run.until says.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/environment.yaml:run-length
run:
  # A duration, such as 1 week, or a number of seconds
  until: ${RUN_FOR:-1 hour}
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:run-length
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
app.run(until="1 week")  # 604,800 simulation seconds; a number is seconds too

env.run(until=604800) takes seconds only, as SimPy's run does.

The run stops at until before any event due at exactly that time, as SimPy's run(until=...) does: an order due at the horizon never arrives, and a task due to finish there stays unfinished. Statistics published at teardown read the model at until.

Events due at the same time run by priority, and then in the order they were scheduled (SimPy 4.1.2, core.py: schedule and run; URGENT and NORMAL in events.py). A priority of 0 is urgent and 1 is the default. run(until=...) schedules its stop at urgent priority, so the stop comes before the ordinary events due at that time. A fire action with a priority takes part in the same order, and its after gives the delay. How a scenario step or a change from an ingress connector ranks among them is in Live Parameters. Here two orders are packed at 5 seconds, and one is due at the horizon of 10 seconds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint has no way to schedule a bare event. Its fire action takes priority and after, as Signals and Waiting describes, and the Low-level tab shows the order with three processes.

The builder schedules no bare event either. Signal.fire(priority=...) and the fire action of task(on=...) take the same priority, and the Low-level tab shows the order with three processes.

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:same-time
ties = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
packed = []


def pack(name, seconds):
    yield ties.timeout(seconds)
    packed.append(name)


ties.process(pack("first", 5))
ties.process(pack("second", 5))  # due at the same time: runs after "first"
ties.process(pack("at the horizon", 10))
ties.run(until=10)
print(packed)  # ['first', 'second']: nothing due at 10 runs

Without until, a run ends when no model event is left, as SimPy's does. The events of desflow's own, such as the statistics timer and the flush timers, repeat for as long as the run lasts, so they never keep it going. A run with an arrival never runs out of model events, and a run that waits for changes from an ingress connector has none of its own. Give such a run an until, a stop or a drain, or stop it with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Stop Early
docs.text:
stop ends the run before until when something happens. It takes these forms:

  • {signal: name} ends the run at the next firing of a signal. {signal: {of: family, key: expression}} names one member of a family of signals. desflow reads the key once, as the run starts, outside every task, so a key that reads attr. is refused when the file loads.
  • {condition: ...} ends it at the first moment a condition holds. The condition is checked after every change of a level, a capacity, a registry value or a signal, and after every finished task.
  • In the builder, run(stop=...) also takes a signal's name, or a function of the context that returns any SimPy event, such as lambda context: context.env.timeout(30). The function is called once the run is built.
  • In the low-level API, the same is SimPy's env.run(until=event).

The run ends at whichever comes first, stop or until, and no other event at that moment runs after it. When both fall at the same moment, until ends the run, as SimPy's own until would.

run() and finish() return what SimPy's env.run(until=event) returns: the value of the event that ended the run:

What ended the run Value returned A stop on a signal the signal's value, such as the finished payload of the task that fired it A stop on a condition True A stop on a function's event the event's own value until, a drain, or until and the stop at the same moment None

If the signal fails, the run still closes, and the sinks receive their records. Then run() raises the SignalFailed the signal failed with, as SimPy raises the exception of a failed event. desflow run reports it and exits with an error.

docs.title: Drain
docs.text:
A fixed horizon cuts the run at until with orders still in the shop. A drain stops the arrivals at until and keeps running until every entity in the model has left. Set it with drain: true, or with drain: {limit: 1 h} to stop at the latest 1 hour after until. desflow run --drain sets it from the command line. The environment's own processes, such as the statistics timer, never hold a drain open. The end-conditions example closes the shop at 120 seconds, drains for at most a minute, and stops at once if the boxes run out:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/end_conditions.yaml:run
run:
  # No new orders after closing time.
  until: 120
  # Then pack the orders in the shop, for at most 60 seconds.
  drain: {limit: 60}
  # Stop at once when the last box is taken.
  stop: {condition: level.boxes == 0}
examples/builder/end_conditions_example.py:run
app.run(
    # No new orders after closing time
    until=120,
    # Then pack the orders in the shop, for at most 60 seconds
    drain={"limit": 60},
    # Stop at once when the last box is taken
    stop={"condition": "level.boxes == 0"},
)

context.stop_arrivals() stops the arrival loops by hand, as a drain does at until.

examples/low-level/end_conditions_example.py:run
def run_to_end(env, shop, source):
    """Runs to closing time, then drains for at most 60 s, or until no boxes are left."""
    out_of_boxes = env.event()

    def check():
        if shop["boxes"].level == 0 and not out_of_boxes.triggered:
            out_of_boxes.succeed()

    env.watch_changes(check)
    # Closing time, unless the boxes run out first, which ends the run at once
    env.run(until=env.timeout(120) | out_of_boxes)
    if out_of_boxes.triggered:
        return
    source.interrupt()  # no new orders after closing time
    packed = env.all_of([p for p in shop["orders"] if p.is_alive])
    env.run(until=packed | env.timeout(60) | out_of_boxes)

The low-level API writes a drain as SimPy does: interrupt the source process, then run until all the admitted processes end.

An arrival with max_events stops itself after its last start. An arrival with count or keys has one loop for each entity, and stop_arrivals() and a drain end all of them. The run ends when the loops have stopped and the flows have drained.

With statistics at basic or above, flows.<arrival>.started, finished and in_system say how many entities entered, left and are still in the model. From minimal, tasks.<task>.in_progress says how many instances of each task are queued or being served. End Conditions compares a fixed horizon with a drain, and desflow examples get end-conditions downloads this model in all three forms.

docs.title: Step and Peek
docs.text:
start() builds everything run() builds and starts every process, with the clock still at its start. Two methods then move through the model one event at a time, as SimPy's env.step() and env.peek() do:

  • step() processes the next event of the model.
  • peek() gives the time of the next event, or infinity when none is left.

Both count only the model's events, so a script steps the model as it would in SimPy. The events desflow adds do not count: the statistics timer, the flush timers, the lag and ingress monitors, and a resource's capacity watcher. peek() skips them, and step() runs those due before the model's next event in the same call. When only desflow's events are left, step() raises EmptySchedule and peek() gives infinity. finish() and run() still process them. Once a row generator with on_end: stop, or the last entry of run.segments, has ended the run, step() raises RuntimeError, as advance() does, and peek() gives infinity, so a loop of peek() and step() ends.

The blueprint reads the same clock after each model event: run: {steps: true} publishes system.simulation.step, with the step number, now and peek, and run: {sync: true} calls env.sync() as the run starts. The builder takes run(steps=True, sync=True), and a run with steps takes no segments, stop or drain:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/run_steps.yaml:steps
run:
  until: 1 min
  # system.simulation.step after each model event
  steps: true
  # env.sync() as the run starts
  sync: true
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:run-steps
stepper = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0)
stepper.add_arrival("orders", dist="constant", value=20, spawn="tick")


@stepper.task()
def tick(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


# system.simulation.step after each model event, and env.sync() as the run starts
stepper.run(until="1 min", steps=True, sync=True)

The low-level API reads env.now and env.peek() in a loop of env.step(), as SimPy does.

The first readings of the blueprint, with the order the model made at each step:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 0.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'system.simulation.step', 'value': {'step': 1, 'now': 0, 'peek': 20.0}}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 20.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'system.simulation.step', 'value': {'step': 2, 'now': 20.0, 'peek': 20.0}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 20.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 20.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'system.simulation.step', 'value': {'step': 3, 'now': 20.0, 'peek': 20.0}}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 20.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'system.simulation.step', 'value': {'step': 4, 'now': 20.0, 'peek': 40.0}}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'system.simulation.step', 'value': {'step': 5, 'now': 40.0, 'peek': 40.0}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-2', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}

finish() runs a started run on to the end that run() would reach (until, the stop or the end of the drain), then closes it. run() is start() followed by finish(). After advance() or step(), finish() closes the run as follows:

  • When the clock has reached until or passed it, and there is no stop or drain, finish() closes the run at once, as a run that ended at until does.
  • When step() brought the clock to exactly until, the records hold the run's records, which end with the final statistics. They also hold the records of the events at until that step() processed, as in SimPy. A statistics reading due at until is not published again, and the close adds only the values that changed after it.
  • After steps past until, the run closes where the steps stopped, with the final statistics at that time.

close() ends the run where it is. A context from from_yaml steps the same way:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

SimulationContext.from_yaml("shop.yaml") returns a context with the same start(), peek(), step() and close(), as the Builder tab shows.

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:step
def every_ten(context):
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(10)


stepped = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0).add_process(every_ten)
stepped.start()  # builds everything run() builds; the clock is still at 0
while stepped.peek() < 30:  # the time of the next event
    stepped.step()  # processes the next model event, after desflow's own events due before it
print(f"stopped before {stepped.peek()} at {stepped.env.now}")
stepped.close()  # the teardown run() does at its end

env.peek() and env.step() on a DynamicRealtimeEnvironment skip desflow's own events in the same way, and env.run(until=...) runs on from where the steps stopped.

It prints stopped before 30 at 20. Stepping does not stop at until: compare peek() with the time you want to stop at.

docs.title: Run in Segments
docs.text:
advance(until) runs a started run up to a time and returns with the run still open, so a script can read the model, change it with context.env, or wait, then run the next segment. finish() runs on to the end, as it does after start():

YAMLBuilderLow-level

run.segments lists the parts. A segment ends at an until or when a stop holds, and {} runs to the end. look names a task whose new entity reads the model where the segment stops, before any event due at that time runs. The task must take no time: a look task with a service time, or a wait that does not end at once, stops the run with an error that names it. sync: true on a segment moves the wall-clock anchor to the start of the segment. After each segment the run publishes system.simulation.segment with the segment's index, now and peek, which is null when no model event is left:

docs/snippets/yaml/run_segments.yaml:look
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  # An order of this task reads the model where a segment stops, before any event due
  # at that time runs
  look:
    payload:
      event_type: queue_read
      waiting: {gen: expr, expr: queue.packers}
docs/snippets/yaml/run_segments.yaml:segments
run:
  until: 3 min
  segments:
    - {until: 1 min, look: look}
    # Ends at the first moment 4 orders wait; sync re-anchors the wall clock for the
    # segment, which changes nothing at factor 0
    - stop: {condition: queue.packers >= 4}
      look: look
      sync: true
    # No end of its own: runs to the end of the run
    - {}

The readings of the first two segments:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 60.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'look-1', 'task': 'look', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'queue_read', 'waiting': 1}}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 60.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'system.simulation.segment', 'value': {'index': 0, 'now': 60.0, 'peek': 60.0}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 180.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'look-2', 'task': 'look', 'instance': 1, 'value': {'event_type': 'queue_read', 'waiting': 2}}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 180.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'system.simulation.segment', 'value': {'index': 1, 'now': 180.0, 'peek': 180.0}}

The second segment ends at 180 seconds, the end of the run, because 4 orders never waited at one moment in this run, so its stop condition did not apply.

segments: {every: 30 s} makes equal parts up to until, which must be finite. A list whose last entry has an until or a stop and a run with no until end there, and a last entry {} runs to the end:

docs/snippets/yaml/run_segments_every.yaml:every
run:
  until: 2 min
  # A segment every 30 seconds up to until
  segments: {every: 30 s}

run(segments=[...]) takes the same entries as dictionaries. advance() runs a started run in parts by hand:

docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:run-segments
shop = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, random_seed=42)
shop.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1)
shop.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=40)
shop.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.05, spawn="pack_order")


@shop.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@shop.task()
def look(task_id):
    """An order of this task reads the model where a segment stops."""
    return {
        "event_type": "queue_read",
        "waiting": len(shop.get_resource("packers").queue),
    }


shop.run(
    until="3 min",
    segments=[
        {"until": "1 min", "look": "look"},
        {"stop": {"condition": "queue.packers >= 4"}, "look": "look", "sync": True},
        {},  # no end of its own: runs to the end of the run
    ],
)
docs/snippets/pages/pacing.py:segments
def pulse(context):
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(10)


segmented = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0).add_process(pulse)
segmented.start(until=60)
segmented.advance(25)  # runs the model to 25; the events at 25 wait for the next call
segmented.advance("40 s")  # a duration is seconds from the start, not from now
print(f"paused at {segmented.env.now}")
segmented.finish()  # on to start()'s until, 60, and closes

Call env.run(until=...) again for each segment, as in SimPy. The records are the same as those of one run.

It prints paused at 40.0. A run in segments gives the same records as one run(), the telemetry and statistics included, because nothing is flushed at a segment boundary. The same holds for a script that calls env.run(until=...) again on a low-level environment, as in SimPy. A few rules:

  • until is a reading of the simulation clock after now, in seconds or as a duration such as "10 min". It can also be an event, as the third rule in this list describes. A time that is not after now raises ValueError, as SimPy does. advance() before start() or after close() raises RuntimeError.
  • The run stops at the earlier of until and its own end: start()'s until, the stop or the end of a drain. A later advance() raises RuntimeError, so call finish() or close(). finish() returns the end's value: None for until or a drain, and the stop's value for a stop. For a failed stop, it raises the stop's exception again.
  • until may be an event, such as context.signal("gate").wait(): the run stops where the event fires and returns its value, and the next advance() goes on, as SimPy's env.run(until=event) does.
  • The event that ends a segment stays in the queue: peek() gives the segment's time and step() processes it.
  • advance() does not move the wall-clock anchor. A paced run that waited between segments is behind when it goes on, so call env.resume_pacing() first.

docs.title: Set Up Before the Run
docs.text:
run.before lists functions called with no arguments, once, at the start of run(). Connectors already create what they write to when they can: Kafka its event and telemetry topics, Postgres the tables under tables, and Parquet and JSONL their folders. run.before is for any other setup, such as creating the topics of a router.

Put such setup in a function rather than at the top of the module. The module is imported when the file is loaded, so its top-level code runs even when a blueprint is loaded and never run. This function creates the folder events when the run starts:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/run_before.yaml:before
run: {until: 1 min, before: [!python run_before_logic.make_output_folder]}
docs/snippets/yaml/run_before_logic.py
"""Python for docs/snippets/yaml/run_before.yaml: a setup function."""

import os


def make_output_folder() -> None:
    """Called once by run.before, when the run starts, not when the file is loaded."""
    os.makedirs("events", exist_ok=True)

The Builder API has no run.before: call the function before run(), as the YAML form calls it.

The low-level API has no run.before: call the function before env.run(), as the YAML form calls it.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: The end of the model and the end of the run. The model ends when the clock stops: at until, at a stop, or when a drain empties the model. The run ends after that, at close(), which run() calls in a finally block. close() publishes the last statistics, still stamped at the time the model ended. It then flushes and stops the egress connectors, and then stops the ingress connectors. A sink may take a while to drain its queue, but no record it receives is later than the model's end.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text: The limits of this page are listed with those of the whole section, in Stability and Limits on the Time and Pacing page.

docs.title: Example: End Conditions
docs.text:
The end-conditions example shows a drain after closing time, a stop when the boxes run out, and the counts of orders still in the shop. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page End Conditions teaches these features step by step.
